DMAR 1.0.x planned such a call as if both tails were their average: for two predictors correlated .3, correlated .4 and .3 with Y, and a width of .3, alpha_lower = 0 with alpha_upper = .05 gave 157, the plan for tails of .025, and the noncentral search (noncentral = TRUE, the default of ss_aipe_src()) did not end; alpha_lower = .6 with alpha_upper = .01 gave 14; and two tails of .5 gave 5 (2p + 1), or 3 with assurance = .9, which leaves no residual degrees of freedom.

  • A nonzero tail area below 1e-9 is refused by ci_nc_t() and by the intervals and plans of a regression coefficient, a contrast, and a correlation. ci_reg_coef(), ci_rc(), ci_src(), ci_c(), ci_sc(), ci_sc_ancova(), ci_r(), ci_sm(), ci_cv(), ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), ss_aipe_src(), ss_aipe_c(), ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_r(), ss_aipe_r_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_cv() check the floor once their tails are resolved, and ci_nc_t() checks it for every interval and plan whose limits come from it, among them ci_smd(), ci_smd_c(), smd_trimmed(), ss_aipe_smd(), ss_aipe_sm(), and the sensitivity functions of these planners. Functions that form one of these intervals at their own conf_level refuse the same levels: cles(), proportion_of_superiority(), nnt_from_smd(), and plot_smd() through ci_smd(), ss_aipe_c_sensitivity() through ci_c(), and ss_aipe_equivalence_r_sensitivity() through ci_r(). A tail of 0, a one-sided interval, is accepted wherever it was. Below 1e-9 the noncentral t limits lose accuracy: the tail probability a limit is found from carries an absolute error of up to about 1e-12, a growing share of a smaller tail. The central intervals of a contrast, a correlation, and a regression coefficient and the plans for them keep the same floor, so that an interval and the plan for it accept the same tail areas. DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0 returned what they computed. ci_reg_coef(reg_coef_j = .5, se_reg_coef_j = .1, N = 50, p = 2, conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = .025, alpha_upper = 1e-20, noncentral = TRUE) (b_j and SE_b_j in 1.0.0) gave an upper limit of 1.549 in 1.0.0 and 1.435 in the development versions, where the limit is 1.554. With noncentral = FALSE the upper limit was Inf, as it was for ci_c(means = c(1, 0), s_anova = 1, c_weights = c(1, -1), n_per_group = c(20, 20), conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = .025, alpha_upper = 1e-20) (n in 1.0.0). ci_r(r = .3, N = 50, conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = .025, alpha_upper = 1e-20) (n in 1.0.0) gave an upper limit of 1, and -1 for the lower limit with the tails exchanged. ci_sc() with the means and tails of that ci_c() call gave an upper limit of 4.126 in 1.0.0 and 3.782 in the development versions. ss_aipe_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = .1, true_R2_j_X_without_j = .2, p = 2, true_reg_coef_j = .1, width = .4, conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = 1e-20, alpha_upper = .05) (rho2_Y_X, rho2_j_X_without_j, and b_j in 1.0.0) returned 114 in 1.0.0, the plan for two tails of .025, and stopped in the development versions with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. ss_aipe_sc(true_std_contrast = .5, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .5, conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = 1e-20, alpha_upper = .025), and ss_aipe_sc_ancova() with the same contrast and width and both tails 1e-20 (psi_standardized in 1.0.0 for both), stopped with the same message in 1.0.0 and refused ‘width’ (“needs more than 2^53 per group”) in the development versions. A level is held to the floor through its tails, (1 - conf_level) / 2 each, so conf_level = 1 - 1e-12 is refused by every function above, and .999999998 is the largest level accepted. At conf_level = 1 - 1e-12, ss_aipe_reg_coef() with the planning values above returned 1,459 in 1.0.0 and the development versions, ss_aipe_c(true_var_error = 1, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .5) (error_variance in 1.0.0) returned 1,640, ss_aipe_r(true_cor = .3, width = .2) (rho in 1.0.0) returned 4,189, and ci_smd(smd = .5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50) returned [-0.953, 1.948]. At .999999998 the floor leaves these plans as they were; ss_aipe_reg_coef() gives 1,032, where 1.0.0 gave 1,033, through the change in its plans without assurance (see Changes to Earlier Results). The refusal has class dmar_argument_invalid, reason "tail_below_floor", arg naming the tail or tails below the floor (conf_level when the tails came from it), value, and floor (1e-9). Its message reads, for example, “‘alpha_upper’ is 1e-20, a tail area above 0 and below 1e-9, the smallest nonzero tail area accepted. Below 1e-9 the noncentral t limits lose accuracy (…), so a limit or a sample size could be off without notice. The central intervals of a contrast, a correlation, and a regression coefficient, and their plans, keep the same floor, so that an interval and the plan for it accept the same tail areas. Give a tail area of at least 1e-9, or 0 for a one-sided interval.” In ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_sc(), and ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), which refuse a tail of 0, and ss_aipe_cv(), which refuses one as alpha_upper, it ends “Give a tail area of at least 1e-9.” For a level the message reads “‘conf_level’ of 0.999999999999 leaves a tail area of 5e-13 on each side, below 1e-9, … Give a conf_level of at most 0.999999998.” At the floor, the noncentral limits in six cases (t from -3 to 10, 10 to 1,000 degrees of freedom) at 66 tail areas from 1e-6 down to 1e-9 were within 1.4e-4 of the exact ones (6.0e-6 of the width of the interval). “Small tail areas” in ?ci_nc_t gives the numbers.

  • An assurance above .999999998 is refused by ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_sm(), and ss_aipe_smd(), and by their sensitivity functions when they plan with it. The published assurance step with which DMAR 1.0.x planned them finds noncentral t limits with tail areas of (1 - assurance) / 2 and 1 - assurance (in ss_aipe_smd() through ci_smd()), which then fall below the floor of 1e-9 of the entry above. ss_aipe_sc(true_std_contrast = .5, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .5, assurance = 1 - 1e-10) (psi_standardized in 1.0.0) returned 151 per group in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0, as did ss_aipe_sc_ancova() at the same values and ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = .5, width = .5, assurance = 1 - 1e-10) (delta in 1.0.0), and ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = .5, width = .5, assurance = 1 - 1e-10) (sm in 1.0.0) returned 116. Each came from limits below the floor. The refusal names assurance, not the tails of the step, which the caller did not give (class dmar_argument_invalid, reason "tail_below_floor"): “‘assurance’ of 0.9999999999 is too close to 1: the published assurance step, with which DMAR 1.0.x planned, finds noncentral t limits with tail areas of (1 - assurance) / 2 and 1 - assurance, and (1 - assurance) / 2 is below 1e-9, the smallest nonzero tail area accepted, below which those limits lose accuracy. Give an assurance of at most 0.999999998.” The check is made whatever assurance_method is, so whether a call is refused does not depend on it.

  • ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), and ss_aipe_src() refuse an abbreviation of "Lower" or "Upper", as they refuse those values. They plan only for the full width, but DMAR 1.0.0 checked which_width with char.expand() and then tested the value as given, so "L", "Lo", "U", "Up", and "" were planned for the full width. In DMAR 1.0.0, ss_aipe_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = .3, true_R2_j_X_without_j = .2, p = 5, true_reg_coef_j = .25, width = .15, which_width = "L") (rho2_Y_X, rho2_j_X_without_j, and b_j in 1.0.x) and ss_aipe_rc() with the same arguments returned 607, the plan of "Full", and ss_aipe_src(true_R2_Y_X = .3, true_R2_j_X_without_j = .2, p = 5, true_std_reg_coef_j = .25, width = .15, which_width = "L") (Rho2_j_X_without_j and beta_j in 1.0.x) returned 626, also the plan of "Full". These three calls now stop with a refusal of class dmar_argument_invalid (arg = "which_width") whose message says that "L" stands for "Lower". "F" and "Fu" still give the plan of "Full": 606 from ss_aipe_reg_coef() and ss_aipe_rc(), 625 from ss_aipe_src() (a case below 1.0.0; see Changes to Earlier Results). ss_aipe_R2(true_R2 = .5, width = .15, which_width = "", p = 5, random_predictors = FALSE) is refused the same way; DMAR 1.0.0 returned NULL for it (population_R2 in 1.0.x).

  • mr_cv() and mr_smd() check every argument. Each refusal names the argument and has class dmar_argument_invalid, or dmar_count_invalid for m0 and n_per_group. In DMAR 1.0.x:

    • mr_cv() given scores with a negative mean returned the risk and the decision of the same scores with their signs reversed, beside a negative coefficient of variation; a data frame stopped with “is.atomic(x) is not TRUE”; and three observations returned a risk of NaN and a decision of NA. data must be a numeric vector of at least 4 finite observations with a positive mean.
    • A sampling_cost of -75 gave a negative criterion and a stopping rule that was met, and a sampling_cost of 0, an epsilon of 0, or a gamma of -1 gave a pilot sample size of Inf. sampling_cost, A, structural_cost, and epsilon must each be a single positive finite number, and a call without sampling_cost is refused by name.
    • gamma = .5 was accepted. gamma must be strictly between 0 and 1/2, the interval on which the stopping rule is defined (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016, Equation 23).
    • mr_cv() returned an m0 of 4.5 or of 2 as the pilot sample size. m0 must be a whole number of at least 4 in both functions.
    • pilot = 1 and pilot = 0 were read as TRUE and FALSE, and pilot = "yes" stopped with “object ‘Outcome’ not found”. pilot and verbose must be TRUE or FALSE.
    • mr_smd() given a sample size per group of -5 (n in 1.0.x) returned a negative risk and a decision of NA, accepted 74.5, and stopped with “arguments imply differing number of rows” for a vector there or in d. d must be a single finite number and n_per_group a whole number of at least 2.
    • mr_cv(pilot = TRUE, A = 1e300, sampling_cost = 1e-10) returned a pilot sample size of Inf. A divided by sampling_cost must be a finite number in both functions.

  • ss_aipe_cv() refuses assurance together with alpha_lower = 0, a one-sided upper confidence bound, with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid that names both arguments and advises planning without assurance. The assurance step of Kelley (2007) was written for a two-sided interval and does not give the requested probability for a bound; the numbers are on ?ss_aipe_cv under “Edge cases”. DMAR 1.0.0 returned no plan for a call with alpha_lower = 0 (see the entry above on a plan that cannot exist).

  • ss_aipe_cv() refuses a planning value or a tail area that is not one admissible number, each by name (class dmar_argument_invalid). With conf_level = NULL, a tail area that is left out, NA, or a vector stopped in DMAR 1.0.0 with an error of R’s own (“missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” for a tail left out or NA); the refusal now says that each of alpha_lower and alpha_upper is a single number at least 0 and below 1. A vector true_cv (C_of_V in 1.0.x) stopped with “the condition has length > 1”. true_mean and true_sd (mu and sigma in 1.0.x) must each be positive: DMAR 1.0.0 planned a negative mean with a negative standard deviation as their positive ratio.

  • ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() checks every input that defines its simulation. DMAR 1.0.0 refused a true_cv that was left out or not positive and an estimated_cv (now supposed_cv) that was not positive. It did not check that either was one finite number, and it did not check mean (now true_mean) or, when specified_N was given, specified_N, width, or assurance. true_cv, supposed_cv, and true_mean are now each a single finite positive number; specified_N is a whole number of at least 4, the smallest sample size ss_aipe_cv() plans (class dmar_count_invalid), so that a character string does not turn the value column into text and a fraction is not echoed as a sample size; width, when given, is a single finite positive number, also with specified_N; and assurance is checked on entry (class dmar_assurance_invalid), also with specified_N, where it is only echoed.

  • var_cv() refuses an NA or infinite true_cv or N. In DMAR 1.0.x, where the arguments were cv and n, a numeric NA in either (NA_real_, as a computation returns it) stopped with R’s “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, an infinite coefficient returned Inf in both rows, and an infinite sample size returned 0 and NaN. Each of these calls now stops with a refusal of class dmar_argument_invalid that names the argument and states the value given.

  • ss_aipe_R2() refuses assurance with a half-width. With which_width = "Lower" or "Upper" the function plans for the distance from the expected sample value to one limit, and assurance given with either stops with a refusal of class dmar_argument_invalid (arg = c("assurance", "which_width")). In DMAR 1.0.0 every such call with "Upper" stopped with the R error “unused argument (random_predictors = random_predictors)”, and with "Lower" the function returned a sample size that did not deliver the probability asked for. ss_aipe_R2(true_R2 = .30, width = .10, p = 3, which_width = "Lower", assurance = .99) (population_R2 in 1.0.x) returned 253, the plan without assurance, and at 253 the distance from the sample squared multiple correlation to its lower limit was no larger than .10 in 52 percent of 20,000 simulated samples. With true_R2 = .10 and width = .05 it returned 486 for an assurance of .80, again the plan without assurance (52 percent), and 637 for .99 (95 percent); with true_R2 = .70 and width = .10 it returned 153 for .80 (72 percent).

  • ss_aipe_R2() and ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity() refuse a call without width. ss_aipe_R2(true_R2 = .5, p = 5) (population_R2 in 1.0.x) stopped in DMAR 1.0.0 with R’s “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” and now stops with a refusal of class dmar_argument_invalid that names width (arg = "width"), as a call without p or true_R2 is refused in the name of the argument left out. ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity() (where width was w in 1.0.x) stopped with the same error of R’s when w or true_R2 was left out, and with “invalid ‘times’ argument” when p was left out beside specified_N. Each of true_R2, width, and p left out is now refused in its name, with supposed_R2 and with specified_N.

Conditions That Gained a Class

A condition with a class can be caught or muffled by name, whatever its wording. Every error and every warning DMAR signals on purpose now has a class. Every error is a dmar_refusal and carries a code, so tryCatch(expr, dmar_refusal = function(e) ...) catches whatever DMAR refused, and an error without that class came from R, from another package, or from match.arg(). The check of an argument (its type, length, or range, arguments that cannot be given together, a column that is not in the data, a model the function does not cover) is a dmar_argument_invalid, which carries the names of the arguments at issue as arg (NULL where the refusal is not about a named argument, and in some checks whose message names the argument only in running text). Three more general classes cover the errors that have no class of their own: dmar_package_required (a package the analysis needs is not installed; field package), dmar_computation_failed (the arguments were accepted and a search, a fit, a refit, or a bootstrap made with them gave no result), and dmar_internal_error (a state DMAR’s own code should not reach). Two cover the warnings that have none: dmar_result_qualified (the result is returned with something to know before using it) and dmar_argument_ignored (an argument given has no effect on the call). The more specific classes (dmar_not_converged, dmar_no_maximum, dmar_lavaan_error, dmar_inadmissible, and the others the sections below name) are dmar_refusals as well; dmar_bootstrap_cancelled and dmar_progress_error, which come from the caller’s progress function, are not. In 1.0.0 nearly every error was a plain error and no error was a dmar_refusal. Messages are worded as before, except that some of the oldest checks now name the argument and state the rule (for example “‘c_weights’ must sum to zero.” in place of “The sum of the coefficients must be zero”). The help of dmar_metadata() lists the classes.

ss_aipe_cv() and ss_aipe_sm() refuse an assurance that is not NULL or a single number strictly between 0 and 1 with dmar_assurance_invalid (the condition carries the value given; the message says why neither end is accepted). dmar_argument_invalid, which carries the name or names at issue as arg, is the class of the refusals of ss_power_R2_change() for a p_restricted not below p_full, for squared multiple correlations that cannot belong to nested models, and for an effect stated in more than one way; of the partial and semipartial correlation functions for a p below 2; and of smd() and smd_c() for unbiased = TRUE without the sample sizes. One warning joins a class its siblings already gave: ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() reports replications without an interval with dmar_replications_without_interval (fields n_without_interval and G). The count of noncentral F lower-limit clamps that ss_aipe_R2() reports after its search has the new class dmar_nc_F_clamp_search, with the field n_evaluations. The wording of each message is unchanged, except that the refusals of smd() and smd_c() now also say why the sizes are needed. The warnings about the accurate range of the noncentral t distribution that ci_nc_t() and the searches built on it gave in DMAR 1.0.x are gone, since every limit is now computed exactly (see Exact Noncentral t and Studentized Range Distributions).

  • A which_width that is not a single character string is refused with a class. In DMAR 1.0.0, ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), ss_aipe_src(), and ss_aipe_R2() with which_width = 1 stopped with the error of base R “‘input’ and ‘target’ must be character vectors”, and with which_width = c("Full", "Lower") with “‘input’ must have length 1”. They now stop with dmar_argument_invalid (arg = "which_width").

Where a check’s message opens with the name of the argument and the check did not store it, arg is read from the message, so tryCatch(bayes_one_sample_t(mean = .5, sd = 1, N = 30, prior_location = NULL), dmar_refusal = function(e) e$arg) returns "prior_location" where it returned NULL.

A Two-Level Planner and a Sensitivity Function That Describe One Design

  • ss_aipe_mixed_effects() plans for a predictor at either level and for three ways of centering it, and ss_aipe_mixed_effects_sensitivity() simulates what it plans. In DMAR 1.0.x the planner was for an individual-level (i.e., Level 1) predictor centered at its cluster mean, and the sensitivity function generated a cluster-level (i.e., Level 2) predictor, whose slope has a far larger variance; its intervals were much wider than the plan and the comparison tested nothing. Both functions now take predictor_level (1, the default, or 2), centering ("cluster_mean", the default; "grand_mean"; "none"), and the intraclass correlation of an individual-level predictor (true_icc_X, with supposed_icc_X for the planning value in the sensitivity function), share one set of expressions, and form one interval, the estimate plus and minus a t quantile times its standard error, on K(m - 1) - 1 degrees of freedom for an individual-level predictor and K - 2 for a cluster-level one.
    • The planner’s default call returns the same number of clusters as before or more (19 against 18 for true_total_var = 1, true_var_X = 1, true_icc = .10, width = .20, and clusters of 20; 88 against 70 with clusters of 5), because it uses the t quantile and the expected standard error of the interval computed from data, where 1.0.x used the normal quantile and the total sample size.
    • A cluster-level predictor centered at its cluster mean is refused (it is 0 for every individual), as is true_icc_X given for one.
    • Centering at the grand mean and not centering give the same slope and the same plan; both are accepted so that a call can say what the analysis does.
    • The sensitivity function computes the two cases with a closed form directly (the within-cluster regression, and the regression of cluster means) and fits the pooled case with lme4, which it asks for only then. It evaluates as few as 2 clusters for an individual-level predictor and 3 for a cluster-level one, where it refused fewer than 5, and reports expected_width, predictor_level, true_icc_X, and supposed_icc_X rows.
    • In 4,000 simulated data sets for each of six designs the mean width was within 0.3 percent of the planned width in the four designs with an exact expression, and 0.5 and 1.3 percent narrower in the two with a pooled slope.

Overview

A minor release, and a large one. DMAR 1.0.1 was prepared but never submitted to CRAN; its changes are part of this release, and its section below is kept as the record of them.

Factor analysis gets its own names and new models. fa_confirmatory() is the 1.0.0 cfa_k() and fa_exploratory() its new exploratory partner, with cfa_k() and plot_cfa_k() kept as aliases, efa_k() a new alias of fa_exploratory(), and the 1.0.0 result class kept after the new one; fa_exploratory() fits incomplete items by FIML, gives rotation-aware intervals, and rotates to a target; factor_count() and parallel_analysis() compare numbers of factors; fa_bifactor() and fa_second_order() fit the bifactor and second-order models, with delta method intervals for their indices; factor_scores() gives per-case standard errors and the determinacy of each factor, beside 2 rho^2 - 1, the lowest correlation two equally consistent sets of scores can have; and factor_congruence() gives Tucker’s congruence between two solutions. Structural equation models get measures of fit, precision, and comparison (sem_fit_measures(), sem_residual_fit(), sem_information_criteria(), sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(), equivalence_rmsea(), compare_sem()) and sem_sam(), which estimates the structural relations after the measurement models.

A missing data family states what the missing values cost: the fraction of missing information for every parameter of a FIML fit, the patterns and coverage behind it, the maximum likelihood covariance matrix of incomplete data, and small-sample degrees of freedom with a t reference distribution for Wald intervals, taught in a new vignette. Two-stage maximum likelihood is a missing data option for the CFA family, measurement invariance, and coefficients alpha and omega, and sample size planning for a reliability coefficient can allow for the missing values it will be estimated from. The omega of reliability_omega(), reliability_omega_categorical(), and bifactor_indices() can take either the observed or the model implied variance as its denominator and says which it used; categorical omega no longer needs mvtnorm, no longer drops a correlation the data do not determine, and takes incomplete items; coefficient H is computed from a fitted model; the bifactor indices get bootstrap intervals; and the reliability bootstrap counts the fate of every replication, runs on several processes, refuses a solution that leaves no coefficient, and takes a progress callback that can cancel it.

New intervals, tests, and plans: Dunnett’s T3 (ci_dunnett_t3()); the difference between two proportions measured on the same units, with tests of noninferiority and equivalence (ci_proportion_paired(), equivalence_proportion_paired()); Fieller’s confidence set for the ratio of two means (ci_ratio_of_means(), ci_ratio_of_means_paired()); nonsuperiority in equivalence_c(); the marker variable adjustment for common method variance with its interval and test (common_method_adjusted_r()); planning the interval for a single mean (ss_aipe_mean()) and the assurance of a contrast’s interval when the errors are not normal (true_kurtosis in ss_aipe_c()); a crossed design of units and raters (ci_crossed(), ss_aipe_crossed()); and two-phase sampling, a costly measurement with an inexpensive proxy (ci_two_phase(), ss_aipe_two_phase(), ss_aipe_two_phase_cost(), ss_seq_two_phase()). A new vignette fits classical tests as path models in lavaan, and a knitted result table now carries every line the console prints under it. A result table prints its numbers to three decimal places, where 1.0.x printed three significant figures (see Changes to Earlier Results). eta_squared(), omega_squared(), and their intervals report the total and the partial value of each effect and take sums of squares from a published table; ss_aipe_smd(), ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), and ss_aipe_src() can find the sample size for assurance from the probability that the interval is no wider than asked for, computed exactly or simulated from the exact sampling distribution; ss_power_indirect_effect() takes its power from the joint sampling distribution of the two path tests, with the predictor measured or fixed by design; and the noncentral t distribution and the studentized range are computed exactly wherever R’s pt(), qt(), dt(), qtukey(), and ptukey() are not accurate.

Some defaults change results. DMAR 1.1.0 gives no warning when a result or a default differs from 1.0.x; these notes describe every such change. The changed defaults are described under Changes to Earlier Results, each with the argument that restores the 1.0.x analysis where there is one; ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity() also corrects how it forms its intervals, which no argument restores. fa_confirmatory() (with its alias cfa_k(), and with cfa_1() and cfa_2()) fits raw data by full information maximum likelihood and takes the standard errors that match the estimator (Huber-White under MLR, where 1.0.x took the standard ones), and reliability_omega(), reliability_alpha(), and measurement_invariance() fit incomplete data that way (as does reliability_H(), which takes data for the first time in this release); reliability_omega() forms the default interval of the model implied omega on the logit scale; and ci_rmsea(), ss_aipe_rmsea(), and ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity() form and plan a 90 percent RMSEA interval by default, where 1.0.x used 95 percent. ss_aipe_semipartial_r() without the new true_R2_full plans for the largest variance over every full-model R2, which raises the sample size when true_r_sp squared is above 1/2 (true_R2_full = true_r_sp^2 restores the 1.0.x plan), and ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity() simulate one more variable partialed out than 1.0.x did for the same model, which no argument restores. ss_aipe_partial_r() and ss_aipe_semipartial_r() find the sample size for assurance from the sampling distribution of the estimate, where 1.0.x multiplied by a chi square factor that does not apply to these intervals, and ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity() simulates the raw-scale interval it plans, where 1.0.x simulated Fisher’s Z interval; no argument restores the first, and fisher_z = TRUE gives the Fisher interval, planned and simulated, for the second. Every function names the total sample size N, the number of predictors p, a planner’s planning value true_X, a sensitivity function’s planning value supposed_X, and the desired width width, and names an argument for the quantity it holds (true_cor, true_contrast, true_reg_coef_j, true_cov_matrix) rather than for a symbol; the 1.0.x names are not accepted, eta_squared_partial(), omega_squared_partial(), and ci_eta_squared_partial() are removed, and the count of the partial and semipartial correlation functions is the number of predictors, one more than the 1.0.x count of variables partialed out (see Breaking Changes in 1.1.0). vargha_delaney_A() refers its test statistic to Student’s t with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which gives a larger p-value than the standard normal reference of 1.0.x (test = "z" restores it). With assurance, ss_aipe_smd(), ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_rc(), ss_aipe_reg_coef() with its default noncentral = FALSE, and their sensitivity functions return the smallest sample size, not below the plan without assurance, at which the exact probability that the interval is no wider than width reaches the request (the new argument assurance_method, "analytic" by default), where DMAR 1.0.x returned published approximations that could attain more or less than the request. ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_reg_coef() with noncentral = TRUE, ss_aipe_src(), and their sensitivity functions return the published approximations by default, and assurance_method = "simulation" returns the smallest sample size at which a simulated estimate of that probability reaches the request. The four regression and ANCOVA planners without assurance return the smallest sample size that meets the width, where 1.0.x could return a case or more above it (a few more per group in ss_aipe_sc_ancova()), and the approximations, which start from that plan, move with it. No argument restores the plans of ss_aipe_r(), ss_aipe_smd(), and ss_aipe_sc() with assurance, the central plans of ss_aipe_reg_coef() and ss_aipe_rc() with assurance or with unequal tails, the plans without assurance of ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), ss_aipe_src(), and ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), which can be a case or more smaller, and the approximations that start from them, the plans and true values of ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() when the variances of Y and of the targeted predictor differ, the plans of ss_aipe_equivalence_smd() and its sensitivity function and of the standardized cluster randomized planners, the power and plans of ss_power_indirect_effect(), the rows of var_alpha(), or the simulated contrasts of ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity(), each corrected in this release. fa_confirmatory() on complete data gives the same estimates as 1.0.x, but under ML its standard errors come from the observed information, the item intercepts join the table, and AIC and BIC count them; and its omega, average variance extracted, and H rows get limits formed on the logit scale, as reliability_H()’s already were, as described under Exploratory Models and Structural Relations. Its RMSEA interval stays at the 90 percent of 1.0.0, now with an argument of its own, rmsea_conf_level: every RMSEA interval in the package, and the SRMR interval of sem_residual_fit(), defaults to 90 percent, whose limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05, while the other intervals keep 95 percent (see Every RMSEA Interval at 90 Percent by Default).

Every RMSEA Interval at 90 Percent by Default

  • RMSEA and SRMR intervals default to 90 percent, and every output states the level. A 100(1 - 2 alpha) percent interval for the RMSEA decides the one-sided tests of close and not close fit at level alpha (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996, p. 136), and its lower limit is 0 exactly when the test of exact fit does not reject at alpha, so the limits of a 90 percent interval decide those tests at .05, the level conventionally used with them and the default at which ss_power_sem() plans them; sem_fit_measures() reports the tests’ p-values beside the interval, and the 90 percent limits agree with those p-values compared with .05. A 95 percent interval decides them at .025. Every RMSEA interval in the package therefore defaults to 90 percent, as lavaan’s does, and so does the SRMR interval of sem_residual_fit(), whose test of close fit pairs with its interval in the same way; the package’s other intervals keep 95 percent. Where a function reports both kinds, the RMSEA interval has an argument of its own. The functions and their arguments:

    • ci_rmsea(), ss_aipe_rmsea(), and ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(): conf_level = 0.90, where 1.0.x defaulted to 0.95. conf_level = 0.95 restores the 1.0.x result of ci_rmsea() and ss_aipe_rmsea(), and the 1.0.x level of ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(), whose intervals were also corrected, with no argument to restore them (see Changes to Earlier Results).
    • sem_fit_measures(): conf_level = 0.90, which also sets the gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat intervals, mapped from the same noncentrality limits.
    • sem_residual_fit(): conf_level = 0.90 for the interval of the unbiased SRMR, lavaan’s default too.
    • factor_count(): conf_level = 0.90, the level of its RMSEA intervals and of nothing else; the Monte Carlo limits of the parallel analysis reference in its parallel_analysis attribute keep the 95 percent of parallel_analysis().
    • fa_confirmatory() (and cfa_k()), cfa_1(), cfa_2(), fa_bifactor(), and fa_second_order(): the new rmsea_conf_level = 0.90 sets the RMSEA interval of the fit rows, which the rmsea_ci_level row and the glance() column of that name record, while conf_level = 0.95 sets the intervals of the parameters and indices and no longer reaches the RMSEA interval. cfa_k(), cfa_1(), and cfa_2() thereby report the RMSEA interval of DMAR 1.0.0, which took lavaan’s 90 percent whatever conf_level was; a development version of 1.1.0 made it follow conf_level, and that change is withdrawn. In fa_confirmatory() (and so cfa_k()), cfa_1(), and cfa_2(), whose arguments DMAR 1.0.0 fixed in order, rmsea_conf_level comes after ..., beside wald_df, so a 1.0.0 call that gives its arguments by position works as before and the new argument is given by name.
    • fa_exploratory() (and efa_k()): the new rmsea_conf_level = 0.90 sets the RMSEA interval of the fit line and of the fit_measures attribute, while conf_level sets the intervals of the solution. factor_count() passes its conf_level to it.
    • irt_grm(): the new rmsea_conf_level = 0.90, passed to lavaan, sets the RMSEA interval of the fit_measures attribute, which held lavaan’s 90 percent interval before with no way to choose it, and is recorded as the rmsea_conf_level attribute.
    • equivalence_rmsea() keeps alpha_level, whose 1 - 2 alpha interval is 90 percent at its default of .05.

    For 95 percent intervals pass conf_level = 0.95 to ci_rmsea(), ss_aipe_rmsea(), ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(), sem_fit_measures(), sem_residual_fit(), and factor_count(), and rmsea_conf_level = 0.95 to the factor analysis functions and irt_grm(). The level is stated wherever such an interval is shown: the line beneath a printed table (“Confidence level: 90%”, and for the factor analysis tables, whose parameter intervals are at another level, “Confidence level: 95% (90% for the RMSEA interval)”), the fit line of fa_exploratory() (“RMSEA with 90% interval”), the line beneath factor_count()’s table, results_sentence(), the conf_level column tidy() puts on the RMSEA rows of sem_fit_measures() and beside the RMSEA columns of factor_count(), and a new rmsea_conf_level field of dmar_metadata(), which holds the level of a table’s RMSEA interval beside conf_level.

  • The help of rmsea_conf_level in fa_confirmatory(), fa_bifactor(), and fa_second_order() (and so in cfa_1() and cfa_2(), which inherit it) now says where the argument reaches: the table DMAR returns and its glance(). output = "summary" returns the lavaan summary, which shows lavaan’s 90 percent interval whatever the argument is.

Exploratory Models and Structural Relations

  • fa_exploratory() and fa_confirmatory() name the exploratory and the confirmatory factor analysis. fa_confirmatory() is the function DMAR 1.0.0 released as cfa_k(); cfa_k() remains as an alias, as plot_cfa_k() does for plot_fa_confirmatory(), and its results keep the 1.0.0 class dmar_cfa_k after dmar_fa_confirmatory, so code written for 1.0.0 still runs, though on incomplete items its default analysis has changed (FIML in place of listwise deletion; see Changes to Earlier Results). efa_k() is the alias of fa_exploratory(), whose name is DMAR’s own so that attaching lavaan, whose efa() it calls, masks nothing. fa_exploratory() fits common-factor ML or MLR models directly to incomplete raw observations with FIML, or explicitly requested WLSMV models to ordered items. Rotated loadings, factor correlations, and communalities carry rotation-aware confidence intervals. The estimator, missing-data method, and selected rotation travel with the result. The factor count and rotation are conditioned on, not treated as known without qualification. estimator = "ULS" adds the minimum residual (minres) solution of Harman and Jones (1966): unweighted least squares fitted to the correlation matrix (lavaan’s correlation = TRUE), whose loadings and communalities equal those of psych::fa(fm = "minres") and of a direct minimization of the squared off-diagonal residuals. With raw data the standard errors are lavaan’s normal theory sandwich for a least squares estimator (robust.sem.nt); from a supplied matrix they are NA, since the sandwich needs the raw data. ULS has no likelihood, so incomplete data are refused under the default missing = "fiml" rather than deleted or imputed silently: missing = "listwise" fits the complete cases, and S takes a correlation matrix estimated from every case (for example cov_fiml()’s). The ULS statistic, N - 1 times the ULS discrepancy of the correlations, has no reference distribution, so in the fit_measures attribute the chi_square row holds it without a p-value, the RMSEA rows and the CFI, TLI, RNI, and IFI are NA, and the NFI and the SRMR are reported; sem_fit_measures() says why in the terms of a correlation structure, in a warning of class dmar_uls_standard_statistic that fa_exploratory() reads by class. glance() carries the fitted structure ("correlation" or "covariance").

  • fa_exploratory() prints the solution, not the parameter list. One row per item with its standardized pattern loading on each factor and the loading’s interval, its communality with its interval, and Hofmann’s (1978) complexity; above the table the sample, estimator, missing data method, rotation and its form, and standard error method; beneath it the variance each factor accounts for (the diagonal of Phi Lambda’ Lambda, as a sum of squared loadings and as proportions of the total and of the common variance, in the new variance_accounted attribute), the factor correlations with their intervals, and a fit line read from the fit_measures attribute with its version lines. knit_print() and as_kable() show the same display. The table keeps every parameter in both metrics for tidy(), now with the complexity rows (op "complexity"), and a subset of it prints as an ordinary table. The rotation list opens from three criteria to ten, each applied in the form the help names and refused if lavaan applied it otherwise: oblique oblimin, quartimin, geomin, simplimax, oblimax, infomax, and Bentler; orthogonal varimax and quartimax; and the unrotated solution. The result carries the class dmar_fa_exploratory in front of dmar_factor_analysis, and the help states the covariance-first rule (Cudeck, 1989) with its two correlation-structure exceptions, minres and ordered items.

  • fa_exploratory() reports each factor’s determinacy and coefficient H. The determinacy is the correlation of the regression factor score with its factor, the multiple correlation of the factor with the items (Grice, 2001; the factor determinacy index of Ferrando & Lorenzo-Seva, 2018), whose square is the factor’s maximal reliability under the model; H is Hancock and Mueller’s (2001) closed form on the factor’s standardized loadings alone, as Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) apply it to one factor of a multidimensional solution. Each carries a delta method standard error over lavaan’s covariance matrix of the standardized estimates and Wald limits formed on the logit scale (Browne, 1982), as reliability_H() forms them by default. They are rows of the table (ops "determinacy" and "H"), the new factor_quality attribute, and a block of the display under the factor correlations. With one factor H is the squared determinacy, and its standard error is the one fa_confirmatory()’s H row carries for the same model fitted the same way. Beside each determinacy rho the display and the attribute give 2 rho^2 - 1, the lowest correlation two sets of factor scores equally consistent with the model can have (Guttman, 1955, as Grice, 2001, presents it), with its delta method standard error and the determinacy’s limits mapped through it; it is zero when rho^2 is .5 and negative below, and no line is drawn.

  • fa_confirmatory()’s omega, average variance extracted, and H rows take one interval form. Each keeps lavaan’s delta method standard error, and its limits are formed on the logit scale and transformed back to the scale of the coefficient (Browne, 1982; Kelley, 2007), as reliability_H() and fa_exploratory() form H’s, so they lie within (0, 1) and are asymmetric near one; for H with one factor the three functions give the same interval for the same fit. A finite wald_df puts its t quantile on the logit scale; under wald_df = "missing_information" these rows keep the normal reference, as reliability_omega()’s logistic intervals do, and only the loadings take the t reference. Through this change the limits were the estimate plus or minus the normal quantile times the standard error, which can exceed one.

  • fa_exploratory() rotates to a partially specified target. rotation = "target" (oblique; Browne, 1972b) and rotation = "target_orthogonal" (Browne, 1972a) take the target in the new target argument, either as fa_confirmatory()’s named list of item keys, which targets each item at zero on every factor it is not keyed to, or as a matrix of items by factors with NA for each unspecified loading; with no items, the items the target names are analyzed, from raw data or from S alike, and the number of factors is read from the target. lavaan’s rotation checks neither the target nor whether it identifies the rotation (an unidentified one comes back with finite standard errors and no warning), so DMAR checks the identification counts before fitting and the rank condition on the standardized unrotated loadings (Algina, 1980; Browne, 2001), and refuses a target that fails with an error of class dmar_target_unidentified (a target it cannot read, with dmar_target_invalid; both inherit dmar_refusal). The target’s mask is passed explicitly, so nonzero target values are kept, and no row weights are applied. lavaan reflects all the factors or none, so when any specified value is nonzero no factor is reflected: a factor with a nonzero value takes its sign from the target, and one whose specified values are all zero takes the sign of the random start that reached the minimum, which seed fixes (the help says so). Loadings the rotation attains exactly, which lavaan reports with a standard error of zero and a meaningless test, are shown as fixed by the target, at the target value and without a standard error; when every specified loading is attained the solution is the confirmatory model with those loadings fixed, and the tests check it against lavaan::cfa(). The rotation line of the display counts the specified loadings, the target prints beneath the table with a line mapping lavaan’s factor names to the target’s, and the method attribute carries the target and that count. The help summarizes the simulation of Myers, Jin, Ahn, Celimli, and Zopluoglu (2015) and says that the intervals condition on a target fixed before the data were seen.

  • New factor_count() compares factor counts. It fits the exploratory model with one factor, two, and so on (by default up to the largest count that keeps a degree of freedom) and sets beside each count the chi square test, RMSEA with its interval, CFI, TLI, and SRMR of that model (from fa_exploratory(), under the same version policy), lavaan::lavTestLRT()’s test of the previous count against it, the AIC, BIC, SABIC, and HBIC of sem_information_criteria() with the comparison compare_sem() draws by a chosen criterion (BIC by default: each count’s gap from the lowest, its relative weight, and the log Bayes factor of the best count over it), the reduced eigenvalue at that rank with its parallel analysis reference (parallel_analysis(), Horn, 1965), and Velicer’s (1976) average squared partial correlation after that many components (the MAP). A count whose model does not converge or is improper is a row that says so, with its fit withheld and the counts beyond it still fitted. The lines under the table name the counts with the lowest criteria, how far the eigenvalues exceed their reference, and where the MAP is smallest; no cutoff is applied and no count is chosen. fa_exploratory()’s refusal of a fit without a proper solution now carries the class dmar_efa_no_solution and a reason (not converged, improper, or standard errors unavailable), with a message that says which.

  • fa_exploratory() takes its fit measures from the unrotated solution. lavaan’s FIML-corrected (robust) RMSEA, CFI, and TLI of a rotated efa object depend on the rotation, since the rotated parameterization counts more free parameters than the model has: on six Holzinger and Swineford items the robust 95 percent RMSEA interval of one two-factor model was [0, 0.075] unrotated and [0, 0.154] under oblimin, with the same chi square statistic; the standard indices do not depend on it. The fit line and the fit_measures attribute now come from the unrotated fit of the same model, so every rotation reports the same fit, and factor_count() reports those values.

  • fa_exploratory() can return the point estimates alone. With the new point_estimates_only = TRUE (the default FALSE gives the full analysis, unchanged) the table has the rows and the estimates of the full analysis, the determinacy, H, variance accounted for, and every fit measure included, with its standard errors, tests, and limits NA, because none of them is computed: lavaan is asked for no standard errors (se = "none"), the rotated fit is made without the test statistic DMAR never reads from it, and the delta method intervals of the standardized solution, the determinacy, and H are skipped. The fit measures, the robust statistic and FIML-corrected indices of MLR and the scaled and shifted statistic of WLSMV among them, come from the unrotated fit as before and are identical, and the RMSEA interval keeps its own level, rmsea_conf_level. A loading a target rotation attains exactly is recognized by its value and shown at its target, as in the full analysis. The input, target, convergence, proper-solution, and no maximum refusals are unchanged. The refusal of a solution without rotation-aware standard errors, which guards against a solution that is not identified at its estimates, is kept by inverting the information of the unrotated fit, the cheap expected information first (a failure confined to the rotation’s part of those errors is not detected); a FIML fit whose errors would need unavailable H1 information is not refused, since none are computed, and its fit measures are withheld as before. The display says that standard errors and intervals were not computed, and states no confidence level beside the RMSEA’s on the fit line, and the setting travels as the point_estimates_only attribute and a column of tidy() and glance(). The time saved is largest for a rotated solution: about a third on the nine classic Holzinger and Swineford tests under ML and MLR, more than half under WLSMV, and from 29 s to 17 s for the rotated solution of 18 items with 410 patterns of missing values under MLR with FIML, where what remains is the unrotated fit’s robust statistic and FIML-corrected fit indices; an unrotated analysis saves little or nothing, so a program that fits both the rotated and the unrotated model saves on the rotated fit alone (45 s against 34 s there).

  • New factor_congruence() compares the factors of two solutions. It takes two loading matrices, fa_exploratory() tables, or single-group lavaan fits (such as fa_confirmatory(output = "fit"); the result tables of fa_confirmatory(), cfa_1(), and cfa_2() are refused with a pointer to that route), reads fits in the standardized metric, and aligns the items by name. The factors of y are paired one to one with those of x by the assignment that maximizes the sum of the absolute coefficients (the Hungarian method, with ties kept in the listed order), and a factor whose match is negative is reflected; match = "order" pairs them by position instead, signed. Each row gives the coefficient of a pair and the largest absolute coefficient of the row’s factor with any other factor of the other solution, a surplus factor of the larger solution has a row of its own, and the full matrix, the aligned loadings of y, and its reflected factor correlations are attributes. loadings = "structure" compares the structure loadings of fa_exploratory() tables and lavaan fits, not of a matrix. The help describes Lorenzo-Seva and ten Berge’s (2006) study of how analysts judged similarity as a finding about the analysts, and the table applies no threshold. The coefficients agree with psych::fa.congruence() to 1e-12, and procrustes_phi(), the coefficient of one pair of vectors, links to it.

  • parallel_analysis() uses the same fixed one-factor ML communality reduction for observed and reference correlation matrices. Normal and independently resampled-response references remain distinct, with ordered margins respected when requested. Reference quantile limits describe Monte Carlo error, not observed-eigenvalue sampling uncertainty or confidence in a factor count. The output counts failed and defined boundary reference fits. A complete-case reference size alongside a FIML correlation matrix is explicitly a benchmark, with no effective-sample- size or conservativeness guarantee.

  • fa_exploratory(), factor_count(), and parallel_analysis() read items with a covariance matrix as they read it with raw data: S is reduced to the named rows and columns, in the order given, before its entries are checked. Naming six items of a nine-item S therefore analyzes exactly what S[items, items] would: a missing entry outside the six does not refuse the call, nor does a whole matrix that is indefinite (as one from pairwise deletion can be) while the six-item submatrix is positive definite. A name that is not an item of S is refused, with a message that lists the names not found.

  • factor_count() and parallel_analysis() fit complete ordered items with missing left out, as fa_exploratory() does. Such items were refused with the message meant for incomplete ordered items (factor_count() passed on its own default, "fiml"; a direct call of parallel_analysis() stopped with “Ordered parallel analysis requires explicit pairwise or listwise handling”), while missing = "listwise" ran. The three functions now resolve the default by one rule: with no value missing, leaving missing out analyzes the items as they stand, factor_count() uses that method for every fit, correlation, and parallel analysis, and the method attributes record "listwise". On six four-category items (400 cases) under estimator = "WLSMV", leaving missing out gives the table of missing = "listwise" exactly (chi square 46.972 on 9 df for one factor). Ordered items with a value missing still require "pairwise" or "listwise", and "fiml" or "ml" is refused for ordered items; every call that rule refuses is refused by fa_exploratory() too, with the class dmar_argument_invalid, before anything is computed or any random number drawn.

  • sem_sam() provides local structural-after-measurement estimation for complete continuous data, using ML/twostep or MLR/twostep.robust. Independent measurement fits and derivatives of the corrected latent covariance reproduce the point estimates and normal or robust uncertainty, including lavaan’s optional finite-sample Gamma correction. This is numerical agreement for the documented scope, not a coverage calibration. Incomplete data, derived cross-stage effects, and other unverified models are refused with a pointer to joint latent SEM where appropriate.

Estimation, Eligibility, and Inferential Records

  • dmar_metadata() is new, and refusals carry a class. A program built on DMAR (SIEVER, a simulation runner) reads a result’s estimator, standard error method, test, missing data method, interval method, reported version and correction, cases and groups, two-stage row counts, auxiliary variables (the reliability family’s aux record and fa_confirmatory()’s two-stage record included), eligibility (eligible, or qualified by an unavailable H1 model or by a two-stage fit that could not be computed again with every case, with the text of the warning the function gave), and bootstrap counts from one list with fixed names, whatever family the table came from, instead of from attributes that differ by family. Refusals a program handles are classed: an unavailable unrestricted model (dmar_h1_unavailable, now the class of the error as well as of the qualifying warning; inherits(cnd, "error") tells them apart) and a two-stage fit that could not be computed again with every case (dmar_two_stage_rows_unavailable) can be caught by name, inherit dmar_refusal, and carry a code and their diagnostic or row counts, so an application need not match the wording of a message; the wording of these two did not change. The refusals of the SEM fit family are classed the same way: an inadmissible solution (dmar_inadmissible), a two-stage fit conditional on observed exogenous variables (dmar_two_stage_fixed_x), and the refusals of sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() (dmar_exact_fit_bootstrap_scope, dmar_pattern_too_small, and dmar_transformation_undefined), each with the fields the help of dmar_metadata() lists. The message of an inadmissible solution names what failed (the variable with a negative variance estimate, or the matrix that is not positive definite, with its group and level), and the two-stage refusal says on which rows to refit to keep the fit’s estimates (and, for a fit made with conditional.x = TRUE, to refit with conditional.x = FALSE as well). Every other error DMAR signals is a dmar_refusal with its own class as well; the help of dmar_metadata() lists them.

  • A misnamed item is refused with a class by fa_exploratory(), fa_confirmatory(), measurement_invariance(), measurement_alignment(), and the functions that share their checks. fa_exploratory(), factor_count(), and parallel_analysis() refuse items that cannot be read from the input (a name that is not a column of data or an item of S, a name given twice, a name that is NA, fewer than three items, or names that are not a character vector) with an error of class dmar_items_invalid, a dmar_refusal whose reason element names the check that failed ("form", "unknown", "duplicate", "count", or, for raw data whose column names repeat a name or, with items = NULL, that have a column without a name, "data_names") and whose items element holds the names at issue. An item that the factors of fa_confirmatory() name (and so those of cfa_k(), cfa_1(), cfa_2(), fa_bifactor(), and fa_second_order()), or that the model of sem_sam() names, and that the input lacks is the same mistake and is refused with the same class and the reason "unknown" ("form" for a name that is NA). So is an indicator that the model of measurement_invariance() names, whether as a named list of factors or as lavaan syntax, and the items of measurement_invariance() and measurement_alignment() are refused with the class and the reasons of fa_exploratory()’s. The messages and the calls refused are unchanged, with two exceptions: measurement_invariance() now refuses an item named twice in items (see Changes to Earlier Results), with the message measurement_alignment() gives it (“‘items’ must not repeat an item.”); and in both functions an items that repeats a name and names fewer than three columns, such as c("x1", "x1"), is refused for the repeat, where it had been refused for the count. sem_sam(), new in this release, names an indicator its data lack (“Indicators not found in ‘data’: y7.”) rather than speaking of an items argument it does not have. The class is new, and a program catches the mistake by it rather than by the wording, which differs by function.

  • A rung of measurement_invariance() that lavaan’s optimizer does not converge on stops with an error that names it. Through 1.0.x the call ended with lavaan’s error from its fit measures (“fit measures not available if model did not converge”), which named no rung. Each rung is now checked before anything is read from it, and one that did not converge stops with an error of class dmar_not_converged, the class fa_confirmatory() gives such a fit, whose message names the rung and which carries it as level, with the lavaan code that reproduces the rung’s fit as syntax and lavaan_call. Three items whose correlations in one group have a negative product, with the factor scaled by a marker item (lavaan’s default), give such a rung.

  • A sufficient affine-collapse diagnostic replaces the ordinary blanket FIML case-count refusal. It uses every row observing the candidate support and distinguishes dimension-guaranteed collapse from numerical affine instability. EM convergence alone cannot establish a finite global H1 maximum. Analytic alpha, observed-denominator omega, FMI, and two-stage methods require eligible unrestricted moments. Proper identified constrained FIML estimates with H0-based errors can remain available when H1 fails; unavailable fit indices and residual correlations are withheld, and the reason stays in print, tidy(), and glance(). A separate distinct-case bootstrap screen remains an explicit estimability policy. H1-dependent bootstrap points apply the likelihood screen again to the selected resample. Fixed/conditional-X model diagnostics screen responses only; conditional design rank and exact Y-on-X relations remain unassessed.

  • The footers, warnings, and help of a fit by estimator = "ULS" state the multiplier lavaan uses to form the standard statistic from the ULS fit function, N - G for G groups, where they said N; the help’s sample size convention already had it. No value changed. The warning of a ULS fit tested by the standard statistic has the class dmar_uls_standard_statistic.

  • Continuous ULS now withholds all ML-derived robust indices, including CFI/TLI/RNI, consistently in fit summaries and invariance ladders. Qualified scaled diagnostics may remain; common-units invariance does not establish validity of an ML correction outside its derivation.

  • CFA uses estimator-matched SE defaults: standard for ML and Huber-White for MLR (DMAR 1.0.x passed se = "standard" under every estimator; see Changes to Earlier Results). Incompatible SE/test choices cannot silently change FIML to listwise deletion. Its RMSEA interval keeps lavaan’s 90 percent, as DMAR 1.0.0’s cfa_k(), cfa_1(), and cfa_2() reported it whatever conf_level was, and the new argument rmsea_conf_level sets it (see Every RMSEA Interval at 90 Percent by Default). A development version of 1.1.0 made the interval follow conf_level, .95 by default; that change, which no release carried, is withdrawn.

  • Saturated models retain lavaan’s RMSEA = 0, CI [0, 0], and TLI = 1 conventions. The explanation states that these are saturated-model descriptions without approximate-fit evidence or a fit-index SE; identified parameter SEs and intervals can still be meaningful.

  • sem_fit_measures() corrects eligible two-stage fits for auxiliary-only cases, so estimates, SEs, tests, indices, and sample size use every case the first stage read. The correction is recorded rather than reporting a smaller sample size beside first-stage moments based on all rows.

  • The bootstrap family requires at least half of attempted replications and at least two defined estimates for each target. AVE retains its additional 100-return minimum. Ineligible intervals are withheld while point estimates and counts remain available. Defined improper estimates are retained under the documented policy. These floors do not guarantee nominal coverage. Categorical omega now defaults to 20 imputations inside each bootstrap replication; its separate point-estimate rule already uses at least 20. No new calibration of the 20-imputation default is claimed.

  • Reliability sensitivity takes the width-target proportion, the widths, and the coverage over one denominator, the simulated studies that returned an interval; a study without one is counted in the simulation attribute (attempted, with an interval, without), where a binomial interval describes Monte Carlo uncertainty in the width-target proportion. (DMAR 1.0.0 took the proportions of intervals that missed the true value over all attempted studies; see the entry on the record of the simulation.)

  • Simultaneous-interval sentences use only a matching multiplicity-adjusted p-value and explicitly name it, or explain that no matching p-value is available. Equivalence sentences say TOST p. Correlation and coefficient- of-variation intervals accept supplied tail areas when conf_level was omitted and refuse an explicitly inconsistent level; one-sided CV bounds respect the parameter’s zero boundary.

  • The eight score columns of factor_scores() carry the prefix .derived_ (.derived_regression, .derived_regression_se, .derived_regression_ci_lower, .derived_regression_ci_upper, and the same four for .derived_bartlett), so that a score joined to the observed data cannot be taken for an observed variable or collide with one. The attribute derived_columns names them by what each holds. Valid regression conditional means are retained when a factor-disturbance relation with an observed conditioning variable invalidates Bartlett’s conditional unbiasedness; the Bartlett quantities are then unavailable with a reason. Ordered models outside the verified score likelihood retain their explicit refusals.

  • Every indefinite supplied covariance matrix is refused after unit scaling. A general loading fixed or constrained to zero is treated like an omitted loading by the bifactor-index eligibility rule. General CFA/SEM can fit such a model, but the current bifactor indices do not apply.

  • Welch simple effects retain their valid F tests and withhold the inherited partial-eta-squared interval: its estimand does not match the reported ordinary variance-ratio estimate. Parallel population plans require the supplied population to satisfy parallel-model restrictions. Congeneric complete-data plans below items + 1 are raised to that feasibility minimum before missing-information inflation, with an assurance-planning warning.

  • A factor analysis or structural equation model fit whose likelihood has no maximum stops. lavaan lets an error variance fall below zero, and for some models and data the likelihood then has no maximum: it keeps rising, by less and less, as one item’s error variance falls without bound and its loading grows to match, and lavaan’s optimizer stops where its steps stop gaining and reports convergence, at a point its starting values and tolerance set rather than the data. When an error variance is negative, DMAR now fits the model again with that variance held further out (at ten times its estimate, or one model implied variance below it, whichever is further; with several, all of them together and then each alone), and when the log likelihood there is higher, or lower by no more than 1e-6 per case (a likelihood that flat leaves the estimate as much to where the optimizer stopped as a ridge does), it stops, for every output (output = "fit" included), with an error of class dmar_no_maximum (a dmar_refusal). The message names the function and the item, says what the fit further out found, says that DMAR fits the model with lavaan, the estimation engine, and to see lavaan for more details, where bounds = "pos.var" or a different model are the choices, and prints the lavaan code that reproduces the fit (the model syntax DMAR built, less the lines that define its indices, and the call, with a placeholder for the data that selects the items where lavaan would otherwise read every variable it is given); a model whose syntax would carry the message past the 8,170 bytes R prints of an error has the call printed and the syntax left in the condition. The condition carries the syntax, the call, the items, their error variances, the two log likelihoods, the tolerance, and the number of cases. A finite negative estimate, at a maximum of the likelihood, is reported as before: the nine-test bifactor model of fa_bifactor()‘s help gives visual perception an error variance of -41, and the likelihood falls on either side of it, while a fourth group factor on the Woody-McCall, revised paper form board, and flags tests sends the error variance of paper form board to -1163 under FIML, where the likelihood is still rising, and that model now stops. The check covers fa_confirmatory() (with cfa_k(), cfa_1(), and cfa_2()), fa_bifactor(), fa_second_order(), fa_exploratory() (whose refusal is also a dmar_efa_no_solution, with the reason "no maximum", which factor_count() reports as that count’s status), measurement_invariance() (naming the rung and the group), the configural fit of measurement_alignment(), and the single-factor fits of reliability_omega() and reliability_H() (the tau-equivalent fit of reliability_alpha() has a maximum, since its equal loadings keep one item’s error variance from running off). It applies to maximum likelihood fits; least squares and WLSMV fits have no likelihood and are not checked. A solution with no negative error variance costs nothing more; one with a negative error variance costs a refit, or, with several, one with all of them held and then one for each until one shows a ridge (0.03 s for the nine-test model above, and 0.08 s for the model with the fourth group factor, whose own fit takes 5 s). Inside a bootstrap (the reliability family’s, ci_bifactor_indices()’s, and that of reliability_H() on a fit), a replication with no maximum is set aside and counted among the replications that raised an error, under a message that names the item, and the run goes on. The engine fits each such replication a second time to recover its message, with the second fits spread over the same ncpus processes as the replications, and a fit that runs off is among the slowest lavaan makes: on one process, 100 replications of the 15-test bifactor model of fa_bifactor()’s help, 8 of them with no maximum, took 143 s, against 99 s without the check. The warning of fa_bifactor() about an improper solution names sampling error, a model that does not describe the items, and a group factor the data barely separate from the general factor as the possible causes, where it named the last alone. The structural equation models DMAR fits with lavaan are checked the same way. The fit of the analysis model to the population moments, from which ss_aipe_composite_sem(), ss_power_composite_sem(), ss_aipe_sem_path(), and ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity() (to supposed_cov_matrix, and to true_cov_matrix, now fit before any replication is drawn) read their population values, stops the planner when it has no maximum, with the code that fits the model to the matrix given (or to cov_sem(true_model)$sigma_theta) and the model printed whole, its := lines included, since they define the user’s own quantities. So does the lavaan fit from which mediation_mbco() starts its OpenMx fits. Its code fits the summary statistics directly when they are one group’s (a covariance matrix given as a data frame converted by as.matrix()); for several groups, or a model whose product terms the function writes into columns, it fits the data the function builds from them, which the message describes exactly, seed included, since the moments of a product column depend on the rows drawn; and a lavaan fit given as model is refused without code. The message names a different model as the choice, since the OpenMx model carries no bounds. A replication of those planners’ Monte Carlo with no maximum, which lavaan reports as converged where its optimizer stopped, is set aside as one that did not converge, and a fresh sample is drawn in its place. ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity() and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() read only the chi square of a fit, and are not checked: along a ridge the likelihood levels off, so the chi square, unlike the estimates, does not depend on where the optimizer stopped (in 60 bootstrap samples of a factor with four weak indicators, the 7 that ran off had statistics of 0.37 to 3.96 that would move by 0.00005 to 0.0011 further out), and setting such a fit aside would change the reference distribution, or refuse a population RMSEA that is determined. A bootstrap sample with no maximum therefore stays among the improper ones, counted or set aside as improper says. In a structural model, lavaan carries an observed variable that enters a regression as a latent variable of its own: an outcome, a covariate, or an indicator that also enters a regression (with a direct effect on it, for example). The variance of such a variable is not held and its loading is not moved, so a ridge on such an indicator, or on an outcome regressed on a latent variable, is not looked for; on the ridges of that kind tried, lavaan reported no convergence, where the check does not apply. A ridge on which lavaan reports no convergence, as it often does with a marker item fixing the scale, was already a replication that did not converge. The examples of these pages, none of whose fits has a negative error variance, take no longer: the check reads each fit’s parameter table, 5 to 15 microseconds a fit (21 fits in each composite planner’s examples, a fraction of a millisecond), and refits only a fit with a negative error variance, which in a Monte Carlo at a small N costs one refit for each replication that has one.

Either Variance in the Denominator of Every Omega

  • reliability_omega_categorical() gains a denominator argument. "observed" (the default, and the only coefficient the function computed before) builds the variance of the summed categories from the unrestricted polychoric correlations, as Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016, Eq. 18) did; it is the categorical counterpart of robust omega. "model_implied" builds it from the latent-response correlations the fitted single-factor model reproduces, which is categorical omega as Green and Yang (2009) defined it: their appendix program takes “the reproduced (model-based) correlation matrix” as the input to the denominator. The help page had attributed the unrestricted denominator to Green and Yang’s Eq. 21; it now states which paper used which. Every interval method applies to both settings, and the bootstrap recomputes the coefficient with the chosen denominator on each replication. reliability() forwards denominator for type = "omega_categorical" as it already did for type = "omega". The model implied setting needs no unrestricted polychoric correlation, but its loadings rest on the correlations the data do determine. Those identify the loadings only when they connect every item to the others, directly or through other items, and include at least one cycle of an odd number of items (three items whose three correlations are all determined, for example). When they do not, the loadings are arbitrary. In 13 of 60 samples of 300 from Green and Yang’s mixed-skew design (the help page’s example with N <- 300 and seeds 1 to 60 in place of 113) they did not, and in 2 of those lavaan’s start values gave loadings of opposite signs and a categorical omega of 0.05 and 0.09, against a population value of 0.716. Both settings then stop with an error naming the undetermined pairs and either the blocks of items no determined correlation joins or, within one block, the two sets of items between which every determined correlation runs. A bootstrap replication or a completed data set in that state is set aside and counted as undetermined. The argument changes no existing result; what the observed setting now does with a correlation the data do not determine is under Changes to Earlier Results.

  • bifactor_indices() gains a denominator argument. The default, "model_implied", divides by the variances the fitted bifactor model reproduces (Rodriguez, Reise, & Haviland, 2016), now including any residual covariances the model specifies (see Changes to Earlier Results); "observed" divides omega, omega_H, and omega_HS by the composite variances estimated from the data, the denominator of robust omega carried to the bifactor coefficients. ECV, PUC, and H do not depend on the setting. The observed setting requires a single-group fit. For a fit to ordered items both settings describe the sum of the latent responses behind the categories, not the summed categories; a new metric attribute ("observed" or "latent_response") records which, and the printed line names it.

  • Every omega now names its denominator and reports its local dependence. The printed tables of reliability_omega(), reliability_omega_categorical(), and bifactor_indices() state in one line how the total variance in the denominator was estimated, so a reader need not know the default to know which coefficient is on the page. reliability_omega() and reliability_omega_categorical() also carry a residual_cor attribute (the residual correlations of the single-factor fit, the largest of them, the item pair it belongs to, and whether the fit is saturated) and print the largest under the table. The residual correlations come from a maximum likelihood fit whatever the interval method (the weighted least squares fit behind ci_method = "adf" has residuals of its own and is not used). With auxiliary variables, under FIML or two-stage estimation, the residual correlations are those of the items alone, under the items’ own names. With three items the single-factor model is saturated and a proper solution reproduces every correlation, so the attribute’s saturated element is TRUE, no pair is named, and the printed line says so. An observed denominator protects the denominator, not the numerator: a doublet or a method factor shared by a few same-signed items raises their loadings, and omega with them, under either setting while leaving the two denominators close. The residual correlations are where such structure shows, although when it sits on the items that dominate the factor the single factor absorbs it and the misfit appears among the other items. No row of any table changes; the additions are attributes and printed lines.

  • In a bootstrap, the model implied setting sets aside only the replications whose loadings are not identified or whose solution is improper. A resample often leaves out the few respondents who determine a polychoric correlation, so a bootstrap meets undetermined correlations far more often than the sample does (see Changes to Earlier Results for the observed setting). denominator = "model_implied" needs no unrestricted polychoric correlation, so it sets aside a replication only when the correlations left determined do not identify the loadings or, as the observed setting does, when its solution is improper. That was 1 of 200 in a percentile bootstrap of the help page’s complete data, of 1,000 respondents (seed = 1). In the 45 of the 60 samples of 300 above whose point estimate is identified and proper, a median of 42% of the replications was set aside (B = 50, seed = 1), and more than half in 15 of them.

  • Help pages name the denominator each paper used. fa_confirmatory() and cfa_1() described the categorical omega that fa_confirmatory() reports for ordered factors as Green and Yang’s (2009); it is their assembly with the unrestricted polychoric denominator of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016, Eq. 18), the default of reliability_omega_categorical(), and the pages and the message now say so. The example of reliability_omega_categorical() now reproduces Green and Yang’s mixed-skew design and sets their coefficient beside the one Kelley and Pornprasertmanit recommended.

  • **The categorical omega assembly is checked against Green and Yang’s

    1. population values.** A new test reproduces ten entries of the nonlinear SEM column of their Table 1. Nine agree to the third decimal; the tenth (binary items, two negatively and two positively skewed, loadings of .8; published .591) computes as 0.5904.

One Bootstrap Engine for the Reliability Family

  • The reliability bootstrap refits by maximum likelihood. Every replication of robust omega, of a bootstrap interval for the model implied omega, and of the model implied reliability_alpha() refit the single-factor model by robust maximum likelihood, whose estimates are those of maximum likelihood; only the standard errors and the test statistic differ, and a replication reads neither. The replications now refit by ML, with the same estimates to the last bit, so every interval is unchanged for a given seed, and the bootstrap is faster: the scaled test statistic had cost 1.3, 10, and 37 times an ML fit at 9, 24, and 40 items, and a 40-replication bootstrap of robust omega on 24 items now takes 1.5 s rather than 7.1 s. Robust omega also fit the model twice on every call, once for the estimate and once for the residual correlations, and now fits it once.

  • Every replication is counted where parallel workers keep the count, and the draws are returned. The bootstrap attribute gains improper_kept, not_converged, too_few_cases, improper_rule, caution, require_half, ncpus, t (the estimate of every replication), and status (its fate: proper, improper, error, non_finite, undetermined, or not_converged), and the result gains the B_used attribute that the package’s other bootstraps carry. No element changes meaning; not_converged is zero for the reliability coefficients, whose replications still count a fit that did not converge among the non-finite ones, and is used by ci_bifactor_indices(). Through 1.0.1 the counts were kept where a forked worker could not report them, so a session with options(boot.parallel = "multicore") lost every count.

  • ncpus spreads the replications over several processes. reliability_omega(), reliability_alpha(), reliability_kr20(), reliability_omega_categorical(), reliability_H(), and reliability() gain ncpus = 1L: forked workers where the platform allows them and a socket cluster on Windows, with the jackknife behind a BCa acceleration on the same workers. boot draws every resample before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same interval, counts, and draws whatever ncpus is.

  • progress follows a bootstrap and can stop it. reliability_omega(), reliability_alpha(), reliability_kr20(), reliability_omega_categorical(), reliability_H(), reliability(), and ci_bifactor_indices() gain progress = NULL, their last argument: a function that the bootstrap calls as progress(done, total), with the replications attempted so far and B, after each replication when ncpus = 1 and after each block of ncpus * ceiling(B / (50 * ncpus)) replications (about a fiftieth of B) on several processes. An application that runs a long bootstrap, a Shiny app above all, can show how far it has gone and let its user stop it: when the callback returns FALSE, the bootstrap stops before the next replication or block with an error of class dmar_bootstrap_cancelled that carries done and total, and any other value is ignored. A BCa acceleration comes from the jackknife when fewer replications than cases return a value or the regression on the resampling frequencies fails, and while the jackknife runs the callback is called after each leave-one-out refit, or each block of them on several processes, with done and total both B, so a stop is honored there too, and done equal to total does not mean that the bootstrap has finished; the bootstrap then impute replications of categorical omega under missing = "mi" report the same way. An error inside the callback stops the call with an error of class dmar_progress_error that carries done, total, and the callback’s own condition, its class intact, as parent.
