The callback runs outside the random number stream, so a given seed returns the same interval, counts, and draws with or without it, and the default NULL runs the bootstrap exactly as before. ?dmar_metadata lists both classes beside the refusals. sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() and average_variance_extracted() have no progress argument in 1.1.0: their bootstraps do not run through this engine, so an application that calls them cannot follow or stop them this way.

  • improper = c("keep", "drop") for the single-factor coefficients. reliability_omega(), reliability_alpha(), and reliability() gain improper. A bootstrap replication whose solution was improper (a negative error variance) but still yielded a coefficient was kept and not counted; it is now counted, kept by default, and set aside under "drop". Keeping is the default because setting such replications aside conditions the bootstrap distribution on admissibility and trims its upper tail; in a small coverage check (model implied one-factor omega, five items with loadings .95, .70, .60, .50, and .40, N = 60, 120 data sets per condition, B = 300), percentile intervals covered at .958 when they were kept and at .933 when they were dropped, a difference near the Monte Carlo standard error of about .02. Under "drop" an improper point estimate stops when a bootstrap is requested. When the replications set aside and the improper ones kept reach the tail area (1 - C)/2 of B, the warning and the printed line add a caution that the limits depend on how they were treated. Categorical omega and H are not defined for an improper solution, so they set such replications aside, and both record improper_rule = "drop".

  • Replications of three items with no single-factor solution are counted on their own. The bootstrap attribute carries no_solution: the replications set aside because the correlations of three items had a product that was not positive, which no loadings reproduce. It is a subset of improper, reported under the status "improper", and the warning and the printed line name these replications apart from the Heywood cases (“had no single-factor solution”). reliability_H() from data counts them the same way, and its warning says that setting aside a Heywood case can trim the upper tail of the bootstrap distribution while one with no single-factor solution belongs on neither side. The element is zero for categorical omega, the bifactor intervals, and H from a fitted model, whose refits are not checked for it, as the help of reliability_omega_categorical(), reliability_H(), and ci_bifactor_indices() says; the categorical page defines returned and non_finite as reliability_omega()‘s page does. The warnings describe an improper replication by its criterion, an error variance below zero (a standardized loading past one; on the items’ own metric a loading above one is routine in a proper solution), and the bootstrap then impute warnings of categorical omega describe an improper replication or completed data set the same way. A replication with no single-factor solution is set aside under either rule: on the estimator’s scale it continues the top of the bootstrap distribution, since one loading, and omega with it, grows without bound toward that boundary, while its correlations point to low reliability, so it belongs on neither side. When some are set aside, the caution adds that the lower limit is likely too high. In a coverage check of the three-item estimator (three items of unit variance with loadings .70, .60, .30 or .775, .645, .155; 500 samples of N = 60 drawn after set.seed(1); percentile intervals from B = 999 resamples), the lower limit exceeded the population omega in 11.6 and 13.1 percent of the samples that yielded an estimate (413 and 352 of the 500), against the nominal 2.5.

  • The analytic reliability_alpha() records the improper rule it was given in its bootstrap attribute rather than the engine’s default. It fits no model, so no replication can be improper.

  • The bootstrap reports no interval when most replications fail the distinct-case rule. The standard error and limits are NA when more than half of the replications have too few distinct cases for the coefficient. Near that rule’s bound, the resamples kept are selected for repeating the fewest rows; at the bound they are only reorderings of the data and give an interval with no width. The bootstrap attribute counts these refusals in too_few_cases, including in its jackknife record. This rule applies throughout the engine. The separate require_half rule withholds an interval whenever fewer than half return a value, whatever the reason; it holds for every caller (the element require_half of the bootstrap attribute is always TRUE), as the entry on the bootstrap family’s half-return requirement states. The number of replications a request must ask for is set by the rule of the next section, One Rule for Bootstrap Replications. A bias estimate for H is reported only when its interval is formed.

  • A bootstrap warning describes limits only when they exist. With fewer than two returned values, or when either rule above withholds the interval, the warning and printed line say that no interval is reported and give no caution about its limits. The caution names an improper solution only when one was kept. A refusal quoted with its count loses its trailing period inside the parentheses.

  • An unobserved column in a replication is named separately from a constant one. No observed value leaves its variance and covariances unidentified; a single value leaves its variance zero. Both are counted and quoted by name. A bootstrap of reliability_H(fit = ) follows the fit’s own missing data method: complete-data and listwise fits use the rank of the sample covariance matrix, FIML and two-stage fits use the saturated model’s case rule, and pairwise fits use neither case-count rule. Its messages describe the resample without claiming that the supplied fit’s data were refused.

One Rule for Bootstrap Replications

  • Every function that runs bootstrap or Monte Carlo replications requires a sufficient number of them, counts the ones it uses, and says so in the result. A percentile limit is a quantile of the B replications and is located by the replications that lie beyond it. An interval read from quantiles is now run only when B puts at least 10 replications beyond each limit, and never with fewer than 100: 200, 400, and 2000 replications at the 90, 95, and 99 percent levels. A BCa interval, whose limits the bias correction and the acceleration move farther into the tails, is run only with 50 beyond each nominal limit: 1000, 2000, and 10000. An interval built from the standard deviation of the replications ("bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic") needs 100, and so does a Monte Carlo p-value. A one-sided bound and a reference quantile need 10 beyond their one quantile (200 at the 95th percentile). A B below the number required is refused before anything is computed, with an error of class dmar_count_invalid whose message states the number and the count behind it: mediate(d, "x", "m", "y", B = 200), the call of the 1.0.x help example, returned 0.1816 [0.1163, 0.2684] and now stops with “‘B’ must be a single whole number of at least 400. A 95% interval read from the quantiles of the replications has 2.5% of them beyond each limit, and an interval is reported only when at least 10 replications lie beyond each limit (10 / 0.025 = 400). To run fewer for exploration or a demonstration, see ?dmar_bootstrap.”; with B = 400 it returns 0.1816 [0.1165, 0.2592], the numbers DMAR 1.0.0 returned for B = 400. The numbers of the rule were computed for DMAR (the tail area a limit cuts off has a relative standard deviation of about 30 percent with 10 replications beyond it, whatever the shape of the bootstrap distribution; at 400 replications a 95 percent limit of a bell-shaped distribution varies from run to run by about 0.13 bootstrap standard errors); no published source is cited for them, and the new help page ?dmar_bootstrap gives the reasons.
  • The functions and what each accepted before. The rule governs mediate() (percentile, BCa, and Monte Carlo intervals; the Sobel interval draws nothing and B is not read for it), mediation_mbco() and plot_mediation_mbco() (Monte Carlo), reliability_alpha(), reliability_kr20(), reliability_omega(), reliability_omega_categorical(), reliability(), reliability_H(), ci_bifactor_indices(), average_variance_extracted(), fraction_missing_information(), cohen_kappa(), fleiss_kappa(), krippendorff_alpha(), htmt(), ci_ratio_of_means(), ci_ratio_of_means_paired(), R2_mixed_effects(), ci_eta_squared_generalized(), mlmr(), mlmr_mv(), parallel_analysis(), factor_count(), and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(). Before, a B was accepted from 2 in the reliability family, ci_bifactor_indices(), parallel_analysis(), and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(); from 100 in mediate(), mediation_mbco(), the kappa functions, krippendorff_alpha(), htmt(), the ratio functions, average_variance_extracted(), and fraction_missing_information(); and was not checked at all in R2_mixed_effects(), mlmr(), and mlmr_mv(). A fractional B was accepted and truncated by cohen_kappa(), fleiss_kappa(), and average_variance_extracted() (cohen_kappa(B = 250.5) ran 250 replications) and is now refused. mediation_mbco() required a B of at least 100 whatever the interval and now reads B only for ci_method = "monte_carlo". ci_eta_squared_generalized() keeps its own minimum of 1000, which the rule raises to 2000 at the 99 percent level. htmt() needs 200 at the default level (100 to 199 were accepted), parallel_analysis() and factor_count() 200 at the 95th percentile (factor_count(B = 0) still omits the reference), and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() 100. The planners that run an interval inside each simulated study follow the rule too: ss_aipe_indirect_effect() and ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity() hold B to it under method = "monte_carlo" (400 at the 95 percent level, where 100 was accepted by the planner and the sensitivity function made no check; under method = "closed_form", which draws nothing, B need only be a whole number), and the default B of ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() is now NULL, resolved to the larger of 200 and one and a quarter times the number the interval method and the level require: 500 for "percentile", 2500 for "bca", and 200 for the two bootstrap standard error methods at the 95 percent level, where the default was 200 for all four. The quarter is room for replications that return no value: the number required is held to the request, so a simulated study that loses a few replications still reports its interval, and with the quarter its limits still rest on about the number required. Its run time is proportional to G times B, so a percentile check takes about two and a half times as long by default and a BCa check twelve and a half times. With the exploratory option the three planners give one warning for the call, not one for each simulated study, and their results carry the attributes B, B_used, n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status, which record the request each simulated study ran.
  • No default is changed, and some defaults do not serve every level. The default B = 1000 of average_variance_extracted(), fraction_missing_information(), krippendorff_alpha(), ci_bifactor_indices(), R2_mixed_effects(), mlmr(), mlmr_mv(), and of reliability_omega_categorical() under missing = "mi" serves the 90 and 95 percent levels and not conf_level = 0.99, which needs 2000; the default of ci_bifactor_indices() does not serve ci_method = "bca" (2000 at 95 percent); and the default B = 2000 of mediate() serves a 99 percent percentile interval exactly and not a 99 percent BCa interval (10000). In each case the refusal names the number to pass.
  • A replication that returns no value is dropped, counted, and reported, everywhere. Five functions removed such replications without a count or a warning: mediation_mbco() (a Monte Carlo draw at which an effect is not a finite number), R2_mixed_effects(), ci_eta_squared_generalized(), mlmr(), and mlmr_mv() (a refit that failed or a value that is not finite). They now give one warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped, as the others do. R2_mixed_effects(), mlmr(), and mlmr_mv() removed a missing value for one statistic only, so the intervals of one call could rest on different replications; a replication without a value for any statistic is now dropped for all of them (see Changes to Earlier Results). The warnings that were unclassed now carry the class, and every one carries the fields B, B_used, n_dropped, B_required, share_dropped, caution, and status. When the dropped replications number at least the share of B beyond one limit (2.5 percent at the 95 percent level) the warning adds a caution, the rule the reliability family already applied, because they could then decide by themselves where that limit falls.
  • The number required is counted on the request, not on the replications that remain. B is held to the count before anything is computed, and that is the whole of the count rule. A request that meets it and then loses replications still reports its interval: the warning states how many were dropped, and when those that remain are fewer than the number required it says so and says to request more (“The 400 required are counted on the number requested (400), not on the number that remained; the 397 that remained are fewer, so request more bootstrap replications where some can fail, enough that at least 400 remain.”). The two rules about shares then decide: more than half dropped withholds the interval, and dropped replications that reach the share of B beyond one limit bring the caution. A constrained bifactor model of six tests of holzinger_swineford with ci_bifactor_indices(B = 400, seed = 63) and one improper replication set aside reports the intervals of its 15 indices from the 399 that return a value. Where replications can fail, ask for more than the minimum; the defaults do at the 95 percent level.
  • The warnings of the reliability family’s bootstrap name the function that was called. reliability_alpha(), reliability_kr20(), reliability_omega(), reliability_omega_categorical() (with and without missing = "mi"), reliability_H(), and ci_bifactor_indices() share one bootstrap engine, whose warnings began with the count (“3 of 400 bootstrap replications were set aside …”) and now begin with the function (“reliability_omega(): 3 of 400 bootstrap replications were set aside …”), as the warnings of the other functions under the rule do. The condition carries the name in the field fun. reliability() passes its call on, so its warning names the function that ran the bootstrap.
  • The bootstrap warnings of average_variance_extracted(), parallel_analysis(), and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() name the function too. These three compose their own account of a run (the factors, the reference data sets, the reasons a sample was set aside), and it began with the count (“2 of 200 bootstrap replications were set aside …”). It now begins with the function (“average_variance_extracted(): 2 of 200 …”), so every warning under the rule says where it came from. A note that factor_count() prints from its parallel analysis begins “parallel_analysis():”.
  • The messages about Monte Carlo draws say “draws” throughout. mediation_mbco() and plot_mediation_mbco() draw the estimates from their estimated sampling distribution. Their caution and their note on an exploratory run spoke of “replications” and of “the bootstrap distribution”; they now speak of draws and of the distribution of the draws, as the rest of each message does.
  • Too few usable replications withhold the interval; they no longer stop the call. When more than half of the replications were dropped the limits are NA, the estimate and every other row are returned, and the warning has the new class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. mediate(), cohen_kappa(), fleiss_kappa(), krippendorff_alpha(), htmt(), and the two ratio functions stopped with an error when fewer than 100 replications remained, and fraction_missing_information() when fewer than two did. With a predictor that is nonzero in one of 20 cases, mediate(B = 150, seed = 113) stopped with “Only 91 of 150 bootstrap replications returned a finite indirect effect”; the same call with B = 400 now returns the indirect effect 0.5959 with limits from the 240 replications that remain and the warning that 240 is fewer than the 400 required, and with B = 2000 it returns [0.1319, 0.9613] from 1267 replications, as before.
  • Every result that ran replications records them the same way. The attributes B (requested), B_used (the number the interval rests on), n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share") are on every such result; cohen_kappa(), fleiss_kappa(), htmt(), krippendorff_alpha(), and average_variance_extracted() had no B attribute, and mediation_mbco(), R2_mixed_effects(), ci_eta_squared_generalized(), parallel_analysis(), and factor_count() recorded no counts under these names. mlmr() and mlmr_mv() carry them as elements of the fitted object, and print() and summary() state them in one line. The rows B and B_used of mediate() and the row B_used of krippendorff_alpha() are kept. The bootstrap attribute of the reliability family keeps every element and gains required, bootstrap_status, and B_used; sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() gains B_required and bootstrap_status in its sem_fit list. dmar_metadata() returns required and status in its bootstrap element. The line under a table of the ratio functions reads “Bootstrap: 2000 replications, 1283 used (717 dropped; at least 400 must be requested). A dropped replication had a denominator of zero”; mediation_mbco() prints the corresponding line for its Monte Carlo interval, and the tables of mediate(), cohen_kappa(), fleiss_kappa(), krippendorff_alpha(), htmt(), R2_mixed_effects(), and ci_eta_squared_generalized() print “Bootstrap: 400 replications, 400 used (0 dropped; at least 400 must be requested)” beneath them when a bootstrap was run.
  • A BCa interval is held to the count where its limits finally sit. After the replications are run, the count of 10 is applied at the two quantile positions the bias correction and the acceleration give, and, like the count of the request, it is held to the number requested. When B puts fewer than 10 replications beyond one of them, no BCa interval is reported (limits NA, class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient, with the positions as positions and a suggested B as B_suggest). This applies to mediate(), the kappa functions, the ratio functions, and the reliability family. In the probe behind the rule this happened in at most 14 percent of data sets at B = 2000 (an indirect effect with 50 cases and small paths) and in 0 to 3 percent of the other conditions; the positions asked for more than 10,000 replications in about 1 percent of the data sets of that hardest condition (4 of 400, the largest count 32,909) and in none of the others. The count the positions take is what the result records as B_required and what the warning carries, in every family; the reliability family recorded the 2,000 of the request beside a message that stated the larger count, and printed no reason under the table, and now records and prints the count at the positions (“5105 are required where the bias correction and the acceleration place the limits, so no BCa interval is reported”).
  • What a withheld interval, a single bound, and a note look like. A bootstrap interval of ci_ratio_of_means() or ci_ratio_of_means_paired() that the rule withholds prints “Percentile bootstrap interval: no interval is reported.” in place of a line that called the missing interval “the whole line”, and its confidence_set attribute and tidy() column are NA. The messages call a one-sided bound a bound and the reference quantile of parallel_analysis() and factor_count() a reference quantile; a BCa interval with unequal tail areas is refused with a sentence that names the smaller nominal tail area, where it named two positions the request did not have; factor_count() gives the exploratory mark under its own name; parallel_analysis(percentile = 50) and factor_count(percentile = 50) stop with a message that names percentile, where it named conf_level. A warning about a run in which nothing was dropped (in the reliability family, a BCa interval replaced by the percentile interval, or replicates that are all the same value; in average_variance_extracted() and parallel_analysis(), the function’s account of improper replications kept or of reference fits that warned) was unclassed and has the class dmar_bootstrap_note. The B attribute of the reliability family is an integer, as the other counts are (it was a double when B was given as one). In an exploratory run below the required number the reliability family no longer passes on “extreme order statistics used as endpoints” from boot::boot.ci() beside its own warning, which already says how few replications each limit rests on, and mlmr() and mlmr_mv() no longer pass on lavaan’s count of bootstrap runs that failed beside the classed warning that reports the same replications with the counts. plot_mediation_mbco() returns a plot, which carries no attributes, and its warnings no longer say that the counts are recorded in the result.
  • cohen_kappa() and fleiss_kappa() refuse a BCa interval that is not defined. The acceleration needs kappa with each case left out. A leave-one-out kappa that is undefined (chance agreement 1) was removed without a word and the acceleration computed from the rest. The call now stops with an error of class dmar_bca_undefined (a dmar_refusal) that names the cases, as mediate() does; the same class is given when every bootstrap estimate falls on one side of the sample estimate or the acceleration is not finite. ci_method = "percentile" does not need these quantities.
  • options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) runs fewer replications, and marks the result. A first look, a help page example, and a simulation over many data sets do not need a reportable interval from each run. Under the option a B from 2 up is accepted; the result records B_required and has bootstrap_status "exploratory", the line under the table says that the interval is below the number required for a reported interval, and every call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory. The share rule still applies. The examples of R2_mixed_effects(), mlmr(), mlmr_mv(), ci_bifactor_indices(), reliability_omega(), and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(), whose replications each refit a model, set the option, run their small B, and restore it; the examples of mediate() and krippendorff_alpha() (now B = 400), of parallel_analysis() and factor_count() (B = 200), and the BCa example of reliability_alpha() (B = 2000) meet the requirement. The vignettes missing_data (six intervals, B = 200 before) and DMAR (factor_count(), B = 50 before) run the required numbers.
  • sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() gives one warning about the samples it sets aside. It gave two when no p-value was formed, one for the samples set aside and one for the missing p-value; it gives one, with the class that says which case it is.
  • New help page ?dmar_bootstrap. It states the rule and its reasons, what is recorded and where, the treatment of BCa intervals, the exploratory option, the conditions with their fields, and a table of the functions with their kind, default B, and the number required at the 95 percent level.

Coefficient H From a Fitted Model

  • reliability_H() computes coefficient H from a fitted model, raw data, or a covariance matrix, and its interval now uses the full covariance matrix of the estimates. In 1.0.0 the function took standardized loadings and, for an interval, their marginal standard errors, the diagonal of the covariance matrix of the loading estimates. Those estimates are correlated in any fitted factor model, so that interval could be too narrow or too wide: on one-factor ML and MLR fits (std.lv = TRUE) of seven blocks of holzinger_swineford tests (1, 2, 4; 6, 7, 9; 10, 12, 13; 1–4; 5–9; 14–19; and 20–24) the standard error from the full matrix is 0.75 to 1.29 times the one from the diagonal under ML and 0.69 to 1.16 under MLR. H is now computed from the fitted loadings, residual covariances, and factor variance. It does not depend on how the factor was identified, and when residuals inside the block are correlated it is the maximal reliability of Gabler and Raykov (2017). Its delta method variance runs over every free parameter with the fit’s own covariance matrix of the estimates (standard, robust, FIML, or WLSMV), under either ceq.simple setting of a fit whose equality constraints come from labels or group.equal, and it reproduces the H_<factor> row of fa_confirmatory() and lavaan’s own delta method for H defined with :=. The new arguments come after the 1.0.0 ones: fit (any factor of a lavaan confirmatory or structural model measured by observed items, named with factor, and any group, named with group); data (the single-factor model fitted as reliability_omega() fits it, with missing and aux); S and N; vcov_loadings; ci_method; B; seed; and ncpus. The default interval is the Wald interval on the logit scale, with the robust maximum likelihood standard error for data, the maximum likelihood one for S, the fit’s own for fit, and for loadings the one their vcov_loadings (or se_loadings) gives; standardized loadings with neither carry nothing an interval can be formed from and give the estimate alone (ci_method = "none"), with a line under the table saying what an interval needs. The four bootstrap methods refit the model on every replication, and their bootstrap attribute carries the estimated bias of the sample H, which runs upward (Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, & McIntosh, 2019). On the fit path the model is refitted to the fit’s own rows before any resample is drawn, and the call stops unless that refit reproduces the estimate; every refit starts from the fit’s estimates. A fit with sampling weights or a cluster variable, which a resample of rows cannot carry, is refused, and the delta method interval, which uses the fit’s own standard error, is named in its place. The refits of a fitted model are not checked for three items whose correlations admit no single-factor solution, so such a resample is counted as improper when lavaan stops at a solution that has run away and as non-finite when it does not converge; from data it is counted in improper and in no_solution, as reliability_omega() counts it. A fit for which H is not defined stops with the remedy named: an item that also loads on another factor or is regressed on another variable, a higher-order factor, an observed covariate predicting the factor, an improper solution, or three items whose correlations admit no single-factor solution. A loading or regression fixed or constrained to zero is not one: a model written with 0*item, or with a*item and a == 0 (directly or through a chain such as a == b with b == 0), gets the H of the model written without it. A bifactor fit, whose items load on more than one factor, is refused with a message that names the index bifactor_indices() reports, its maximal_reliability attribute, and ci_bifactor_indices(). Every call but the 1.0.0 form (see Changes to Earlier Results) returns the reliability family table (estimate, se, ci_lower, ci_upper, conf_level, N, N_complete, n_items; class dmar_reliability, coefficient "H"). Attributes name the factor, the group, the metric ("latent_response" for ordered items), the basis of the standard error, what came with standardized loadings (vcov_supplied), and the standardized loadings, and the printed table says which factor of a model it describes. reliability(type = "H") dispatches to it; auto-detection never chooses it. From data, a fit that lavaan stops with an error is reported with lavaan’s message, as reliability_omega() reports it.

The Bifactor Model

  • fa_bifactor() is new. It fits the bifactor model, a general factor on every item and two or more group factors, each on its own items, with every factor uncorrelated with the others and its variance fixed at 1, described as fa_confirmatory() describes a model: the items of each group factor are named in factors, the general factor’s name in general, and items on the general factor alone in general_only. It shares fa_confirmatory()’s engine, interface, and fit rows: raw data (by full information maximum likelihood, the default, or after listwise deletion) or a covariance matrix with its N, ML or MLR, equal_loading, equal_error, and equal_intercept within a factor, and the five outputs, "fit" returning the lavaan fit that bifactor_indices(), ci_bifactor_indices(), and factor_scores() take. Beside the loadings, error variances, and intercepts the table reports, with a delta method standard error and a confidence interval each, omega and omega_H for the total score; omega and omega_HS for each subscale; ECV, H, and the maximal reliability for every factor; and PUC, which depends on the structure alone and has no interval. Omega, omega_H, and omega_HS are the reliabilities of sums of the items as scored, the coefficients fa_confirmatory() and semTools::compRelSEM() compute, where bifactor_indices() keeps the standardized metric (on the help page’s 15 Holzinger and Swineford tests, omega_H is 0.552 for the sum of the scores and 0.577 for the sum of the standardized scores); ECV, H, the maximal reliability, and PUC are bifactor_indices()’s. The standard errors of the indices lavaan can define are its own; the maximal reliability’s is the delta method’s with numerical derivatives, and every limit is formed on the logit scale and lies within (0, 1). A structure outside the model, or one that is not identified, is refused before anything is fit, with an error of class dmar_bifactor_unidentified (a dmar_refusal) that names the factors or items and says in its reason element which kind of refusal it is: fewer than two group factors and an item on two group factors are outside the model ("scope"; a general factor beside one group factor, with items on the general factor alone, is identified, but the subscale indices need two or more); an item listed twice, under one group factor or under a group factor and in general_only, and names that clash are "names"; and a group factor of one item or of two with free loadings, and two group factors whose general loadings the data fix only up to a scale (two groups of three items each with nothing on the general factor alone, as on six of the Holzinger and Swineford tests, where lavaan cannot invert the information matrix), are "unidentified". Every model with two group factors that is fit gives a warning of class dmar_bifactor_empirical on empirical underidentification (Green & Yang, 2018), once the arguments and the data have passed their checks, so a call that then fails does not get it. When lavaan’s information matrix is singular, whether the observed information of a FIML fit or the expected information of a listwise fit or of a covariance matrix, every standard error, test, and interval is NA, the maximal reliability’s included, with a warning; lavaan inverts such a matrix without complaint, and the maximal reliability’s delta method would otherwise give a standard error of 0. Ordered items are refused with a pointer to bifactor_indices() for the latent response metric, and wald_df = "missing_information", calibrated on one factor models, is refused as well. An improper solution leaves the maximal reliabilities, and the H and omega rows it makes undefined, NA with a warning.

  • bifactor_indices() and ci_bifactor_indices() take items on the general factor alone. An item that loads on the general factor and on no group factor, which DMAR 1.0.x refused, now counts in the general factor’s ECV, omega, omega_H, H, and maximal reliability and in PUC, whose pairs with it are uncontaminated, and in no subscale, when the fit has two or more group factors. A fit with one group factor is refused by both (see Changes to Earlier Results).

The Second-Order Model

  • fa_second_order() is new. It fits the second-order factor model, first-order factors on their own items and one or more second-order factors on their own first-order factors, named in factors and second_order; several second-order factors are always correlated (uncorrelated second-order factors are not offered). The model is identified as lavaan’s std.lv = TRUE identifies it, every second-order factor’s variance and every first-order factor’s disturbance variance fixed at 1, and it shares fa_confirmatory()’s engine, interface, and fit rows: raw data (by full information maximum likelihood, the default, or after listwise deletion) or a covariance matrix with its N, ML or MLR, equal_loading, equal_error, and equal_intercept within a first-order factor and equal_second_order_loading within a second-order factor, and the five outputs. The table reports the first-order and second-order loadings, the error variances, and the intercepts; then, for each second-order factor, omega and omega_H for the sum of its items and its ECV, H, maximal reliability, and PUC, and for each first-order factor omega and omega_HS for its subscale score and the ECV, H, and maximal reliability of its disturbance, each with a delta method interval whose limits are formed on the logit scale (PUC has none); then the fit rows. The indices are those of fa_bifactor() computed from the Schmid-Leiman loadings the estimates imply (Schmid & Leiman, 1957; Yung, Thissen, & McLeod, 1999), which the schmid_leiman attribute gives in the standardized metric, item by item. Structures outside the model or not identified, and names that clash, are refused before anything is fit with an error of class dmar_second_order_unidentified (a dmar_refusal) whose reason element says which, as for fa_bifactor(): a first-order factor of one item, a second-order factor of one first-order factor, and one second-order factor over two first-order factors without equal loadings are "unidentified"; an item on two first-order factors and a first-order factor under two second-order factors are "scope"; and an item or factor listed twice under one factor, a first-order factor under none, and clashing names are "names". With exactly three first-order factors under one second-order factor (or two with equal loadings) the second-order structure is just identified, and a line under the table states that condition in words and says that the model then fits as the correlated factors model of fa_confirmatory() does whenever the factor correlations have a positive product and imply standardized loadings below one (on nine Holzinger and Swineford tests, a chi square of 85.31 on 24 degrees of freedom under both). Incomplete data under FIML in which no case observes two first-order factors together are refused when the pairs observed together do not identify the second-order loadings (three first-order factors under one second-order factor with one such pair), and fit when they do (four). In this parameterization a standardized second-order loading reaches one only as its loading runs off toward infinity, and lavaan’s optimizer can stop on the way short of the maximum, with other second-order loadings drifted far off, or not converge; so the model is fit a second time in a parameterization whose boundary is a point (each first-order factor on the scale of its second-order factor, the variance of its disturbance there bounded below at zero, every equality constraint of the call imposed exactly), and the larger likelihood is reported, two log likelihoods within 1e-6 per case being taken as the same maximum whatever the number of cases. On one second-order factor over spatial, verbal, and speed tests and t24, t25, and t26 of holzinger_swineford, the first fit stopped at a chi square of 251.77, where the maximum is 169.77. A standardized second-order loading of one at the maximum, a Heywood case at the second order, leaves that factor’s second-order loading and its loadings on its disturbance without a finite estimate and the rows of its disturbance undefined, all NA, while the other rows and the fit rows are those of the maximum (the standard errors holding the loading at one, and absent, with a warning, under se = "bootstrap"); and a correlation of two second-order factors beyond one leaves every maximal reliability NA. Each gives a warning that names it, with the values in the improper_second_order attribute, as a negative error variance is handled in fa_bifactor(). Under FIML, output = "summary" of a fit with a loading at one shows lavaan’s robust CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and GFI as NA, since lavaan cannot form them for a fit computed without the optimizer, with one warning in place of lavaan’s three. Each first-order factor is reported with loadings that sum to a positive value, and then each second-order factor with second-order loadings that do. The help shows the likelihood ratio test of the second-order model against the bifactor model in which it is nested (Yung et al., 1999; Chen, West, & Sousa, 2006), through lavaan::lavTestLRT() on the output = "fit" objects of fa_second_order() and fa_bifactor(). The function is named for the structure it fits because the sources call the orthogonal layered model of the bifactor family the hierarchical factor model.

Intervals for the Bifactor Indices

  • ci_bifactor_indices() is new. It gives nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals for the indices bifactor_indices() reports: ECV, omega, omega_H, omega_HS, and coefficient H for each factor they apply to, and the maximal reliability of each factor, which bifactor_indices() returns beside its table. PUC depends only on which items share a group factor and has no interval. Each replication resamples the rows the fit used (under full information maximum likelihood, every incomplete row with its missing data pattern), refits the model with the fit’s own parameter table and options, and reads every index from bifactor_indices() on the refit, so the intervals rest on the same replications (under improper = "keep", those of the maximal reliability on the proper ones among them); before any resample is drawn, the call checks that such a refit reproduces the point estimates. The percentile interval is the default (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016) and the BCa interval is available. B = 1000, seed, and ncpus work as in the reliability family, and the draws and the fate of every replication travel in the bootstrap attribute. Improper replications are set aside by default (improper = "drop"), unlike the reliability family’s default. A solution, the fit’s or a replication’s, is improper when bifactor_indices() flags it or lavaan’s post-estimation check fails, a check made on the model’s own parameters for a fit with auxiliary variables (lavaan’s aux), as sem_fit_measures() makes it: lavaan’s own check also tests the residual covariances of an auxiliary variable, which are not positive definite once it is related to the general factor strongly enough, however proper the bifactor solution. On a bifactor model of 15 Holzinger and Swineford tests (a general factor on tests 1 to 9 and 14 to 19, with spatial, verbal, and memory group factors on tests 1 to 4, 5 to 9, and 14 to 19; seed = 113), 212 of 1,000 replications were improper and their omega ran as high as 26.5; keeping every one of them would have put the upper limit of the 95 percent interval for omega at 13.7 rather than 0.902. improper = "keep" uses an improper replication only when every index it gives but the maximal reliability is defined and a proportion. The maximal reliability, which is not defined for an improper solution, rests on the proper replications under either rule, so its interval is the same under both, and an improper point estimate reported under "keep" has none. Coefficient H is not defined when a standardized loading reaches one (see Changes to Earlier Results), and such a replication is set aside under either rule. Every replication set aside is counted and named (improper, not converged, an error, an ordered item that lost a category in the resample), and a caution is printed when they reach the tail area of an interval. As throughout the bootstrap family, an index’s interval requires at least half of the B replications, and at least two, to return a value for it; otherwise its se and limits are NA, and the warning and the printed line say so. Multiple-group, clustered, and weighted fits, fits to a covariance matrix, and fits that did not converge are refused. So are the fits bifactor_indices() refuses, among them a fit with an item on two group factors. The H it bootstraps is the index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), not the maximal reliability of the factor, which has rows of its own (on the help page’s model run with B = 50 in place of its 10 and seed = 113, the general factor’s maximal reliability is 0.678 [0.646, 0.734] beside the index’s 0.769 [0.741, 0.808]). The sample values of both run upward (Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, & McIntosh, 2019), so the bootstrap attribute carries the bootstrap estimate of each index’s bias (the mean of the replicates its interval uses minus the estimate), and the printed table gives it for H and the maximal reliability. On the same example with B = 200 (the same seed) it is 0.031 for the first group factor’s maximal reliability and 0.019 for its H, against 0.005 for its omega. The printed table says what ECV and omega mean for a group factor. The table has one row per index and factor, with estimate, se, ci_lower, and ci_upper; tidy() and glance() give one row per index and one row of counts and settings.

Categorical Omega Without mvtnorm, and With Incomplete Items

  • Categorical omega no longer needs mvtnorm. reliability_omega_categorical() and the per-factor categorical omega of fa_confirmatory() sum a bivariate normal probability over every pair of thresholds of every pair of items (Green & Yang, 2009, Eq. 21). Through 1.0.1 each probability was its own call to mvtnorm::pmvnorm(), so categorical omega stopped for a user without mvtnorm, a suggested package, and those calls took most of the time of a bootstrap replication. DMAR now computes the probabilities itself, all at once, by the method of Drezner and Wesolowsky (1990) as refined by Genz (2004), the algorithm mvtnorm applies in two dimensions. The two agree to within 4e-16 on a grid of 2,873 points. Every categorical omega checked is unchanged to the rounding of its sums, by at most 9e-16: Green and Yang’s ten population designs, six to 24 Holzinger and Swineford tests cut into two to seven categories under both denominators, fa_confirmatory()’s per-factor omega, and a seeded bootstrap. Within about 1e-7 of a correlation of one mvtnorm loses accuracy, and within about 1e-10 it returns the limit at one (an error of up to 2.2e-6, at both limits zero); DMAR’s computation matches the exact values there. Only a communality or a polychoric correlation that close to one reaches that region. At 12 items with 7 categories the assembly takes 0.002 s rather than 0.37 s, so a bootstrap replication takes about 0.07 s rather than 0.43 s, and a BCa interval at the default B = 10000 about 12 minutes rather than 70 on the machine where this was measured. No argument, default, or output shape changes, and mvtnorm leaves Suggests.

  • reliability_omega_categorical() analyzes incomplete items by pairwise deletion or by multiple imputation. Through 1.0.1 it analyzed only the complete rows. It gains missing = c("listwise", "pairwise", "mi"), aux, impute = c("pmm", "polr"), and imputations = 5, appended after ncpus. "listwise" stays the default and returns the same results as before.

    "pairwise" estimates each threshold from the rows that observe its item and each polychoric correlation from the rows that observe both items (lavaan’s pairwise deletion). With no covariates in the model it is consistent only when values are missing completely at random, as listwise deletion is (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010). Under missingness at random it is biased (Shi, Lee, Fairchild, & Maydeu-Olivares, 2020), and the printed table says so.

    "mi" imputes the items by chained equations with mice (now in Suggests): predictive mean matching by default, or the proportional odds model. Auxiliary variables named in aux are predictors in the imputation model only, and a row with no observed item is imputed when an auxiliary variable is observed on it, and N counts it. The estimate is the mean of categorical omega over the imputations of the observed data. Its interval is the bootstrap then impute interval of Schomaker and Heumann (2018): each of B bootstrap samples of the incomplete rows is imputed imputations times, and the percentile interval of the replicate means is the confidence interval. BCa is refused. The items reach mice as plain integer codes, so a column read with haven, which carries value labels, and a factor whose labels are whole numbers are imputed as those numbers. Every incomplete item is imputed, including one observed together with another on only two or three rows, as in a planned missing design with a small overlap; the check by which mice sets aside a variable almost perfectly correlated with another would otherwise leave it with its missing values. An item with a single observed value is refused, and an item mice still does not impute stops the call by name. Turning that check off would also keep an auxiliary variable that duplicates another, so the auxiliary variables are screened first. One whose multiple correlation with the columns observed on every row that observes it (the items and the auxiliary variables kept before it) reaches .999, mice’s own threshold for a pair, carries no information beyond the predictors already in the model and is left out, with a message. Kept together, two or more such variables would make mice fall back to a ridge penalty and impute unstably. When mice still applies its ridge penalty, the warning says how often (ridge in the imputation attribute).

    The point estimate is formed from at least 20 imputations, and more when von Hippel’s (2020) quadratic rule asks for more, and averages those that return a value. The rule is applied to the upper limit of the fraction of missing information that the replications themselves estimate. A call with a bootstrap makes the most imputations the rule can ask for (201) and fits every one before the bootstrap runs, so nothing found in a completed data set of the observed data can discard a finished bootstrap.

    A completed data set with no categorical omega, an improper (Heywood) solution above all, is set aside and counted, as a bootstrap replication is, and the estimate averages the rest. The call stops only when fewer than half return a value, the criterion of Lim and Cheung (2022) for a failed analysis. Stopping on any one would fail with probability 1 - (1 - p)^M, for a share p of improper sets among M imputations. Imputation produces such solutions when the observed data have none, if two items are skewed in opposite directions and values are missing among the few respondents who determine their polychoric correlation. On the help page’s incomplete items under the model implied denominator (missing = "mi", ci_method = "percentile", B = 200, seed = 1), 26 of the 201 completed data sets of the observed data were improper, while the complete data and pairwise fits were proper (the complete rows leave two polychoric correlations undetermined and the loadings unidentified, so listwise deletion stops). An improper set has the largest loadings, so setting it aside lowers the estimate a little. The warning, the printed lines, and the imputation attribute (imputations_returned, imputations_set_aside, status) say how many were set aside and why.

    A bootstrap replication computes the same statistic as the point estimate: it averages those of its completed data sets that return a value, and it is set aside only when fewer than half do. A rule requiring every completed data set to return a value would set a replication aside with probability 1 - (1 - p)^M for a share p of sets returning none, which grows with imputations. Under this rule the share goes to zero as imputations grows when fewer than half of the sets fail. It does not fall steadily, though: an odd number of imputations needs one more set to return a value than the even number below it, so it sets more replications aside. The warning therefore names an even number when any set was set aside. In the bootstrap of the help page’s incomplete items above, a quarter of the replications’ completed data sets returned no value. Applied to the first two, three, four, and five imputations of each replication (the replicate_estimates element of the imputation attribute), the rule set aside 12.5, 21, 14.5, and 20% of the replications, where requiring every set would set aside 35.5, 45.5, 48.5, and 52.5%. The replicate by imputation estimates form an unbalanced one-way analysis of variance (Searle, Casella, & McCulloch, 1992). The warning and the imputation attribute (replicate_sets_set_aside) count the completed data sets set aside within the replications kept. As for the other treatments, no interval is reported when fewer than half of the replications return a value.

    The result’s imputation attribute carries the imputations, the fraction of missing information, and how much imputation noise widens the interval. A replication whose imputation fails is set aside and counted under a new reason, imputation, and a seed gives the same result for any ncpus. A completed data set whose fit lavaan stops with an error is set aside under "error", and the warning quotes lavaan’s message.

    In a Monte Carlo simulation described on the help page (10 items at n = 300, about a fifth of the values missing at random), predictive mean matching came closest to the complete data estimate, ahead of the proportional odds model, pairwise deletion, and listwise deletion.

  • B defaults to NULL in reliability_omega_categorical() and reliability(). For every existing call it means 10000, the default written before. Under missing = "mi", where each replication imputes the data and refits on every completed data set, it means 1000. When no item value is missing, missing = "mi" has nothing to impute and returns the complete data result, whose bootstrap takes that path’s default of 10000; the message says so.

  • reliability() forwards each family function’s missing data treatment. missing is now NULL by default and forwarded as given, so each family function checks it against its own choices (listwise, FIML, or two-stage for alpha and omega; listwise or FIML for H; listwise, pairwise, or multiple imputation for categorical omega). missing, aux, and the new impute and imputations reach reliability_omega_categorical(). KR-20 still refuses missing and aux.

Fit, Precision, and Comparison of Structural Equation Models

  • CFA help states the standard errors each estimator receives. se = "standard" supplies inverse-information standard errors: normal theory for ML, MLR, and GLS, and Browne’s asymptotically distribution free ones for WLS. Ordered items request robust.sem in its place. MLR otherwise needs se = "robust.huber.white" for sandwich standard errors under FIML. From a covariance matrix, robust.sem with ML needs the asymptotic covariance of the moments in NACOV. This corrects the description; no result changes.

  • sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() is new. It gives the chi square test of exact fit a reference distribution that does not assume normal data: the model based bootstrap of Bollen and Stine (1992), which transforms the data so that the fitted model holds in them exactly, resamples the transformed rows B times, refits the model to each sample, and reports the share of bootstrap statistics at least the observed one as p_bootstrap, with the Wilson interval for its Monte Carlo error (its limits print to the four decimal places of the p-value) and the counts of samples used, improper, and failed. With complete data it is lavaan’s bootstrapLavaan(type = "bollen.stine"), resample for resample when the seed given here is passed to lavaan as its iseed (with lavaan run serially; lavaan called without iseed draws its own seed from the caller’s random number stream). With incomplete data fitted by FIML it transforms the rows so that the saturated FIML estimates on the transformed data are the model implied moments, by the two transformations of Savalei and Yuan (2009): one matrix for every missing data pattern (the default) or pattern by pattern with each pattern’s own moments. Both are solved on the variables divided by their saturated standard deviations, so the result does not depend on the units of the variables; it differs element by element from the same transformations solved in raw units (as semTools’ bsBootMiss() solves the common one), though both make the model hold exactly. Every bootstrap sample keeps the missing values of the rows it draws, so the model is refitted by FIML. The transformed data are checked: the largest saturated estimating equation and the largest mean residual at the model implied moments are recorded, and cov_fiml() on the transformed data returns the fitted moments. Replications are drawn before any refit, so a seed gives the same result whatever ncpus is. A sample’s solution is improper when lavaan’s post-estimation check finds a negative variance estimate or a covariance matrix that is not positive definite; for a fit with auxiliary variables (lavaan’s aux) the check is made on the model’s own parameters, as for the fit itself (see the sem_fit_measures() entry). Fits to summary statistics, ordered indicators, non-ML estimators, two-level and clustered models, sampling weights, two-stage fits, fits conditional on observed exogenous variables, fits whose analysis data keep missing values without FIML (pairwise deletion), and fits without a standard test statistic are refused with the reason, as an error of class dmar_exact_fit_bootstrap_scope (a dmar_refusal) whose reason element names it (a fit whose cases lavaan removed by listwise deletion is bootstrapped on its complete cases, as it was fitted, with a warning); a missing data pattern too small for the pattern transformation is refused with class dmar_pattern_too_small, which carries the pattern, its counts, and its group, and a transformation that is undefined for the data with class dmar_transformation_undefined.

  • sem_fit_measures() is new. It reports the fit of a structural equation model in one table of twenty-four rows: the chi square test of exact fit; the RMSEA with its confidence interval and the tests of close fit (Browne & Cudeck, 1993) and not close fit (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996); CFI, TLI, NFI, IFI, and RNI; the covariance SRMR; and gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat with their intervals, with NA where the input does not determine a row. It takes a fitted lavaan model or the summary statistics a paper reports. With a fitted model the default version = "auto" gives lavaan’s robust measures for a fit with a corrected test statistic (MLM, MLR, WLSMV, a sampling weighted fit; Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, & Li, 2012; Brosseau-Liard & Savalei, 2014; Savalei, 2018, 2021), the FIML corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023) for a FIML fit (which approximate the complete data RMSEA and CFI and are not corrections for nonnormality), and the standard measures for a normal theory ML fit of complete data; with auxiliary variables (lavaan’s aux under FIML) the SRMR is over the model’s own variables, since lavaan’s SRMR averages in the auxiliary variables, whose residuals of about zero make it lower for the same model; the printed footer names the version and why it was chosen. A fitted model keeps lavaan’s sample size multiplier, so its values equal lavaan’s (for the scaled version, those lavaan gives under rmsea.scaled.mplus = TRUE); summary input takes sample_size_convention = "N-1" by default, the convention of ci_rmsea() (pass "N" for a statistic from lavaan or Mplus), and n_groups for Steiger’s (1998) multiple group RMSEA. The default conf_level is 0.90, the conventional level of the RMSEA interval, whose two limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 that the table reports beside it; the help page explains why, and conf_level = 0.95 gives a 95 percent interval. A fitted model that did not converge is refused with an error of class dmar_not_converged, and one whose solution is inadmissible with a refusal of class dmar_inadmissible that names the negative variance estimate, or the covariance matrix that is not positive definite (that of the latent variables, of the residuals of the observed variables, or of the residuals of the structural part of the model), as lavaan’s post-estimation check finds them. With auxiliary variables (lavaan’s aux under FIML) the check is made on the model’s own parameters: lavaan’s own check also tests the residual covariances of the auxiliary variables, which it models as saturated correlates, and that block is not positive definite once an auxiliary variable is related to a factor strongly enough (for one factor whose items have uncorrelated residuals, and an auxiliary variable related to them only through the factor, a correlation above .33 between the two when the maximal reliability of the items is .9), however proper the model’s solution. Auxiliary variables are recognized when they are given through lavaan’s aux; saturated correlates written into the model by hand are judged with the rest of theta. sem_residual_fit(), sem_information_criteria(), compare_sem(), ecvi(), and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() share the check, and ci_bifactor_indices() judges a fit with auxiliary variables by it.

  • sem_fit_measures() reports the robust measures of a mean and variance adjusted statistic, a CFI of 1 for a saturated model, and no measure of a ULS fit of continuous data that changes with the units of the variables. In the examples, the three-factor model of nine Holzinger and Swineford tests is visual perception, cubes, and lozenges; paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning; and addition, counting groups of dots, and straight and curved capitals, fit to holzinger_swineford by lavaan::cfa() with std.lv = TRUE.

    • MLMVS. lavaan computes no robust measures beside the older mean and variance adjusted statistic (estimator = "MLMVS", or test = "mean.var.adjusted"). Savalei (2018) shows that the robust RMSEA and CFI of Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, and Li (2012) and Brosseau-Liard and Savalei (2014) do not depend on which corrected statistic accompanies them. Each subtracts c df from the ML statistic, with c = tr(U Gamma)/df, which is that statistic’s scaling constant times its degrees of freedom over df. So "auto" reports the robust version of such a fit, computed by DMAR, with the interval and close fit tests of Brosseau-Liard et al. (2012, Eq. 10) and a robust gamma hat. The values equal lavaan’s for the same model fitted by MLM. For the three-factor model by MLMVS the RMSEA is .091 with 90 percent interval (the default) [.070, .113], the CFI .932, and gamma hat .958, where the scaled measures version = "scaled" gives are .089 [.066, .113] and .734. A saturated fit with this statistic is reported in the robust version as well. Nothing is computed from its undefined scaling constant there, and the footer attributes the corrections to Brosseau-Liard et al. without saying DMAR computed them.
    • Continuous ML without robust measures. Where lavaan offers a scaled statistic but no robust measures for a continuous ML fit, "auto" reports the standard version, with a warning; a bootstrap test, which carries no scaled statistic, gets the standard version without one. The standard version estimates the population values of the ML measures, as the robust one does and the scaled one does not (Savalei, 2018).
    • Saturated models. A model with no degrees of freedom and a statistic of zero has a CFI and an RNI of 1 in every version, and in the standard and scaled versions its NFI and IFI take their values at a statistic of zero (the robust version has none). lavaan’s robust CFI and RNI are formed with a scaling constant of 0/0 and come out NA, or a value only by rounding.
    • ULS with continuous data. The ULS statistic, (N - G) times the ULS fit function, is in the units of the squared covariances, and a measure of fit must not change when every variable is multiplied by the same number. lavaan forms the robust RMSEA of a ULSM or ULSMV fit of continuous data by putting that statistic into a correction derived for the ML fit function, so multiplying every variable by k multiplies it by k^2: 16.1 for the three-factor model by ULSM on the raw scores, and 0.161 with every score divided by 10. That RMSEA, its interval, and its close fit tests are NA. So are those of the standard version, whose CFI, TLI, RNI, and IFI set the degrees of freedom against the same statistic and are NA too (lavaan’s standard CFI is .977 for the raw scores and .979 for the scores divided by 10); its NFI, a ratio of two such statistics, is reported. When the model restricts the means, the ULS fit function adds the squared mean residuals to the squared covariance residuals, which are in other units, and every RMSEA row and incremental index of every version is NA: with the intercepts of paragraph comprehension and word meaning constrained equal in the same model (meanstructure = TRUE), lavaan’s robust CFI is .979 for the raw scores and .972 for the scores divided by 10, and its scaled RMSEA .160 and .181. The chi_square row and the SRMR are kept. The robust CFI, TLI, and RNI and the scaled measures of a model with free means do not depend on the units and are reported, though no cutoffs have been developed for them (Savalei, 2018). So are the measures of a fit by estimator = "ULS" alone, tested by Browne’s residual statistic, when its estimates do not change with the units. When restrictions link the means and covariances through shared parameters, as equal loadings and intercepts do through latent means, ULS estimates change with the units. Browne’s statistic at those estimates and its indices change too; RMSEA and incremental indices are withheld. The valid test statistic and SRMR remain. A warning, the uls element of the sem_fit attribute, and a line of the printed footer say which rows are NA and why.

  • The scaled version of sem_fit_measures() puts the scaled statistic in the standard formulas. Its RMSEA interval and its tests of close and not close fit are computed from the chi_square and df rows of the same table (Brosseau-Liard, Savalei, & Li, 2012, Eqs. 11 and 13; Savalei, 2018, Table 1). These are the values EQS and Mplus report, and the ones lavaan gives under rmsea.scaled.mplus = TRUE. lavaan’s default for a Satorra-Bentler, Yuan-Bentler, or mean and variance adjusted statistic refers the unscaled statistic to the noncentral chi square on tr(U Gamma) degrees of freedom, c df with c = tr(U Gamma)/df as in the previous entry (for a Satorra-Bentler or Yuan-Bentler statistic, whose degrees of freedom are df, c is the scaling constant itself): the same point estimate, but an interval and p-values that the rows beside them do not imply. The two differ little when c is near 1: for the three-factor model by MLR, c = 0.98, and the 90 percent interval is [0.0728, 0.1150] against lavaan’s default [0.0726, 0.1152]. They differ much when c is not near 1: for the same model on multivariate t data with 4 df (each pupil’s centered scores multiplied by sqrt(4 / rchisq(301, 4)) after set.seed(1)), c = 1.80, the interval is [0.0506, 0.0950] against [0.0562, 0.0892], and the p-value of close fit .046 against .013. A scaled and shifted statistic (MLMV, WLSMV) gets lavaan’s own values. For an MLMVS fit, whose scaled measures version = "scaled" reports, the interval is [0.0659, 0.1125] against lavaan’s default [0.0684, 0.1098]; "auto" reports the robust measures of such a fit, which DMAR computes.

  • Gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat come with intervals, and gamma hat has a robust version. The rows gamma_hat_ci_lower, gamma_hat_ci_upper, adjusted_gamma_hat_ci_lower, and adjusted_gamma_hat_ci_upper of sem_fit_measures() are the noncentrality limits of the RMSEA interval mapped to each index (Steiger & Fouladi, 1997, pp. 251–252, whose 90 percent interval of .972 to .997 for the adjusted index in their worked example the tests reproduce). For a robust ML fit of complete continuous data (MLM, MLR, MLMV, and MLMVS, whose robust measures DMAR computes since lavaan does not), the robust version reports gamma hat from the robust noncentrality, with limits from the robust RMSEA interval: 0.956, with the 90 percent interval [0.935, 0.973] that the default conf_level gives ([0.931, 0.976] at conf_level = 0.95), for the three-factor model by MLR. The help page says that gamma hat is lavaan 0.7-3’s gfi_lrt, which lavaan reports only when asked by name, and not the gfi lavaan prints, which is computed from Browne’s residual based statistic (for the same fit, the standard gamma hat, lavaan’s gfi_lrt, is 0.957 and its gfi 0.959). Only NFI and IFI have no robust version.

  • Gamma hat is NA where Steiger’s result does not reach. The result is for covariance structures. A fitted model that restricts the means gets NA, with the reason recorded in the sem_fit attribute. Examples are a growth model, or intercepts constrained equal (under either ceq.simple setting), constrained to a constant, entered in a linear constraint, tied to a loading, or held at the bound of an inequality constraint, which lavaan’s degrees of freedom do not count. Whether the means are restricted is read from the derivatives of the model’s moments, with the constraints that bind at the estimates imposed. Free means change nothing. Summary input whose df exceeds p(p + 1)/2, which only restricted means can produce, gives NA with a warning, where the formula would give an adjusted gamma hat above gamma hat. Below that bound summary input carries nothing that shows restricted means, and supplying p states that the model is a covariance structure. A sampling weighted fit gives NA too, since its statistic is a weighted pseudo likelihood ratio statistic.

  • A fit without a corrected statistic is described from lavaan’s options. "auto" reports its standard measures under a reason that names the estimator and the data. Some standard statistics have no chi square reference distribution: an ordered fit by DWLS or ULS with the standard test alone (the default test of those estimators, which WLSMV and ULSMV extend with a corrected one) and a DWLS or ULS fit of continuous data whose test was set to "standard" (lavaan’s default for continuous data adds Browne’s residual based statistic, which is chi square under normality), to which lavaan gives no p-value, and a sampling weighted fit whose test was set to "standard", a weighted pseudo likelihood ratio statistic whose p-value lavaan reports all the same. For such a fit a warning says that the statistic is not chi square distributed and names the remedy (a corrected test, or for continuous data leaving out test = "standard"), and version = "robust" refuses the fit with the same advice. Full WLS for ordered data is the exception. Its statistic is asymptotically chi square (Browne, 1984; Muthén, 1984) and lavaan reports its p-value, so its standard measures are reported without a warning, and a request for the robust version says that they are the ones to report. A continuous fit tested by a chi square statistic is described by its estimator (a normal theory ML or GLS fit, an asymptotically distribution free WLS fit, or a least squares fit tested by Browne’s residual based statistic) rather than as a normal theory fit.

  • equivalence_rmsea() is new. It tests whether the population RMSEA is below a bound chosen in advance: the test of not close fit (MacCallum et al., 1996) read as an equivalence test by Yuan, Chan, Marcoulides, and Bentler (2016). It reports the 1 - 2 alpha interval, whose upper limit is their T-size RMSEA, with the p-value and a verdict, and takes n_groups and sample_size_convention (default "N-1").

  • sem_residual_fit() is new. It reports the unbiased SRMR of Maydeu-Olivares (2017) with its standard error and confidence interval (90 percent by default, as lavaan’s, which pairs with the test of close fit at .05), the test of exact fit (with the standard error that holds under exact fit only), an optional test of close fit, the SRMR of the mean residuals, and the largest standardized residual (Maydeu-Olivares, Shi, & Rosseel, 2018). The residual covariance it used (normal theory, or distribution free for MLM and MLR) is recorded on the result. A FIML or pairwise fit of complete data gives the residual inference of a listwise fit with the same mean structure and information setting; missing values, two-stage fits, and fits with auxiliary variables (which change nothing in the model’s fit when no value is missing, but lower lavaan’s SRMR) are refused, and the message says which.

  • sem_information_criteria() is new. It reports AIC (Akaike, 1974), BIC (Schwarz, 1978), the sample size adjusted BIC (SABIC; Sclove, 1987; lavaan’s bic2), Haughton’s (1988) HBIC, and the IBIC and SPBIC that Bollen, Ray, Zavisca, and Harden (2012) proposed and Bollen, Harden, Ray, and Zavisca (2014) evaluated for structural equation models, then the log likelihood, the number of parameters, and N, in one table in which a criterion not requested is NA. It takes a fitted lavaan model, or as summary input the log likelihood, the parameter count, N, and (for IBIC and SPBIC) the information matrices, so that a published comparison can be reproduced; all four rows of Table 6 of Bollen et al. (2014) are reproduced to within 0.015. A fit whose fit function is not the normal log likelihood is refused with the reason (ordered indicators, an estimator other than ML, the Wishart likelihood, or sampling weights, whose pseudo log likelihood has no justification for these penalties; Asparouhov, 2005), a two-level model gives AIC only, and automatic IBIC and SPBIC are refused for fits whose information matrices are not the ones the criteria are defined on. The help page explains that IBIC depends on the units of the observed variables and on how the latent variables are identified, and that SPBIC under its default prior depends on the identification; it also notes that the worked example of Bollen et al. (2012, Table 1) counts log N twice in IBIC.

  • compare_sem() is new. It ranks models fitted to the same data by one criterion (BIC by default) and reports each model’s difference from the best, its relative weight within the set (Burnham & Anderson, 2004), and, for the BIC family, the approximate log Bayes factor of the best model over it. It first checks that the log likelihoods are comparable: the same cases and data values (or the same summary statistics), the same observed variables in any order, the same groups, missing data method, and mean structure, and the same exogenous observed variables (with fixed.x = TRUE, the default of lavaan::sem(), the log likelihood is conditional on them, and two saturated models of the same three variables that condition on different variables differ by hundreds of BIC points). A refusal names the two models and what differs. The two two-stage settings count as one missing data method, since they fit the same EM moments by the same likelihood and differ only in their standard errors and test, which no criterion uses; the comparison attribute records each setting used. For IBIC, and SPBIC under its default prior, a refusal states the rule: one identification for every latent variable of every model, which two models that each mix the two identifications in the same way do not meet. ?sem_information_criteria says the same. Weighted fits are refused; multiple group models (configural against metric invariance, for example) are compared by AIC, BIC, SABIC, and HBIC. tidy() and glance() methods come with it.

  • results_sentence() reads an interval held in <estimate>_ci_lower and <estimate>_ci_upper rows, and gains term. A sem_fit_measures() table holds the RMSEA’s interval in rows named for the estimate, and gamma hat’s and adjusted gamma hat’s the same way. results_sentence() writes the one term names or, when the table holds no interval in another form, the first such estimate, with no p-value: the table’s p-values are the tests of exact, close, and not close fit. The level is the interval’s own when the table records it, and otherwise the table’s. For the three-factor model of nine Holzinger and Swineford tests (visual perception, cubes, and lozenges; paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning; addition, counting groups of dots, and straight and curved capitals) fit by lavaan::cfa() with its defaults, results_sentence(sem_fit_measures(fit), digits = 3) is “rmsea = 0.092, 90% CI [0.071, 0.114]”, at the default level. term = "rmsea" also reaches the RMSEA of a fa_confirmatory() table, whose rmsea_ci_level row records the level of its RMSEA interval (its rmsea_conf_level, .90 by default), and gives the same sentence for the same model. The level is also read from the table’s rmsea_conf_level attribute, so a selection of the rmsea, rmsea_ci_lower, and rmsea_ci_upper rows, which leaves the rmsea_ci_level row out, keeps the level of its interval: for the model above the selection reads “rmsea = 0.092, 90% CI [0.071, 0.114]”, as the full table does. The same holds for the tables of fa_bifactor() and fa_second_order(). A term that names no estimate with such rows is refused with the names of those that have them. term is appended after digits, and reading such rows changes no sentence written before.

  • A vignette, “SEM Fit and Model Comparison” (vignette("sem_fit_measures")), teaches these measures on one running example, the nine tests of Jöreskog (1969) in holzinger_swineford: the chi square test of exact fit; the RMSEA with its interval, the tests of close and not close fit, and why the RMSEA is reported with a 90 percent interval; the equivalence test and the T-size RMSEA; the sample size convention and the multiple group RMSEA; the incremental indices and gamma hat; the standard, scaled, and robust version of each measure and which one a robust or FIML fit reports; the unbiased SRMR and reading the residuals; the information criteria, including a worked example in which rescaling one variable reverses an IBIC verdict while BIC, HBIC, and SPBIC do not move; ranking candidate models with compare_sem(); and the ECVI. Every number in its text is computed from the fits.

Missing Data: What the Missing Values Cost

  • fraction_missing_information() is new. For each free and each defined parameter of a full information maximum likelihood fit (a lavaan fit with missing = "ml" or "ml.x", for example from fa_confirmatory(..., missing = "fiml", output = "fit"), or an mlmr() or mlmr_mv() fit) it reports the fraction of missing information, 1 - SE_C^2 / SE_O^2 (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012), the proportion of the sampling variance of the estimate that is due to the missing values, with the effective N, N(1 - FMI), the target N, N / (1 - FMI), and the interval width inflation factor, 1 / sqrt(1 - FMI), which state in AIPE terms the precision the missing values cost. Both standard errors come from refits at the fit’s estimates with the optimizer off and one information type for both, the complete data side fit to the EM (unrestricted) moments with the same N and no (N - 1)/N rescaling of the covariance matrix, as lavaan computes them. information chooses among the three estimators of Chen and Savalei (2021): "unstructured", the default, which cannot be negative and broke down least in their simulations; "structured"; and "hessian", lavaan’s default, which agrees with lavaan’s parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE) to about 1e-7 when the fit runs lavaan’s EM as far (em_h1_args = list(tol = 1e-10)), and otherwise only to the precision of lavaan’s EM (see the first example below). The default therefore differs from lavaan’s. An MLR fit gets the normal theory FMI at its estimates, which is the ML fit’s. Multiple groups are supported, each row’s N following its group and its equality constraints, whether a constraint names labels or defined parameters (ind1 == ind2 with ind1 := a1*b1 and ind2 := a2*b2 gives the rows it ties the summed N, as a1*b1 == a2*b2 does), and the omega, H, and AVE that fa_confirmatory() defines get their FMI through their delta method variances. A percentile bootstrap interval is opt-in (ci_method = "percentile", with B and seed), and the printed table says that a sample FMI is imprecise unless N is several hundred (Chen & Savalei, 2021). Fits with ordered items, an estimator outside the ML family, listwise, pairwise, or two-stage missing data handling, conditional.x = TRUE, more than one level, sampling weights, or no convergence are refused with the reason, as are lavaanList objects and rotated EFA solutions. tidy() and glance() methods come with it. The examples below use the data sets of tests/testthat/test-fraction_missing_information.R in the source package.

    • Units. Both refits are made with every observed variable divided by the power of two nearest its standard deviation, the factors lavaan divides by when it rescales a badly scaled fit; the parameter table, defined parameters and constraints included, is carried through the same exact map, and the standard errors are mapped back. The FIML refit runs lavaan’s EM estimate of the unrestricted moments until no mean or covariance changes by more than 1e-10 times the smallest variance, where lavaan’s default stops at an absolute 1e-5. Take lavaan’s nine Holzinger and Swineford tests in three factors, with x5 and x9 missing at random (set.seed(11), then x5[runif(301) < plogis(-1 + x4)] and x9[runif(301) < 0.25] set to NA). lavaan’s own FMIs move by up to 5e-6 when its EM is run to 1e-14 rather than 1e-5, and those of the same model by school, whose solution has a negative residual variance, by up to .0014. With the fit’s estimates held (the fit to the rescaled data made at the rescaled estimates with optim.method = "none"), the FMIs of the three estimators agree with those in the original units to within 1e-9 in one group and 5e-8 by school when every variable is multiplied by .001, .01, 10, 1000, 10,000, or 1,000,000. Take next a regression of y on three predictors with values missing at random (200 cases of four standard normal variables correlated .5, drawn after set.seed(3), with x3[runif(200) < plogis(1 + 2 * x1)] and x2[sample(200, 3)] set to NA), fit by lavaan::sem("y ~ x1 + x2 + x3", missing = "ml", fixed.x = FALSE).
