Fit anew to the rescaled data, its FMIs agree with those at a standard deviation of 1 to within 1.3e-7 when y, x1, or x3 alone, or every variable, is multiplied by .001, 10,000, or 100,000, when x2 alone is multiplied by 10,000 or 100,000 (by .001 its standard deviation lies just above the .001 at which lavaan rescales a fit, and lavaan’s fit does not converge), and when the outcome is multiplied by 100,000,000, where mlmr(wald_df = "missing_information") gives the degrees of freedom it gives at 1. lavaan’s own parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE), which refits in the variables’ own metric, is off by up to .93 (by .04 to .07 for the slopes) with every standard deviation near 100,000, and returns NA with every standard deviation near 300,000 or with that of y near 10,000,000.
    • Estimates that are not at the maximum. The FMI is computed at the fit’s estimates. lavaan rescales a fit only when a standard deviation is .001 or less or 1000 or more, or two differ by a factor of 1000, and between those limits it can stop short of the maximum while it reports convergence. With every standard deviation of the regression near .003 the FMIs are off by up to .001. In the three factor model, identified by marker indicators, with every test multiplied by 100 they are off by up to .011, and by .12 multiplied by 500. In lavaan 0.7-3 a fit made with ov_order = "data" and rescaled by lavaan is not the maximum likelihood fit when the columns of the data are not in the model’s order: with x3, y, and x1 of the regression multiplied by .004, .03, and .5 and the columns ordered x3, x2, x1, y, the slopes’ FMIs are .28, .22, and .70 in place of .06, .19, and .70. The computation takes one Newton step in the refit metric. When an estimate moves by more than 1e-4 of the larger of 1 and its size, the FMIs are computed again one step on. A warning is given only when an FMI changes by more than 1e-4. It names the parameter, likelihood gain, and largest FMI change. Units and rescale_data = TRUE are named only for a fit lavaan did not rescale whose standard deviations indicate that cause; variable order is named only for a fit lavaan rescaled. A flat small- sample likelihood can trigger the warning without either cause, and the warning does not prescribe a remedy already applied. The FIML refit estimates the unrestricted moments in its own order of the variables, so a fit made with ov_order = "data" that lavaan does not rescale gets the FMIs of the same fit in the model’s order.
    • Models kept in their own metric, and refits that fail. A model the refits cannot carry to that metric (one with composites or product terms, which lavaan does not rescale either) keeps its own; there the Hessian estimator warns when a standard deviation falls outside .01 to 1000, and the check for a maximum is not made. A refit whose information cannot be inverted stops the computation with a message that names the likeliest cause, in place of lavaan’s warning that the model may not be identified: variables too badly scaled for a model kept in their own metric, a predictor so far from zero relative to its standard deviation that its coefficients and the intercept are nearly collinear. Centering is named as the remedy only when the same model with that predictor centered has invertible information; an indicator or outcome’s location is not blamed. Where centering changes an intercept the model fixes or constrains, both causes are named, or a model that is not identified. The messages name the variables of an mlmr() or mlmr_mv() fit as its formula does.
    • Solutions lavaan’s checks flag. A fit with auxiliary variables entered as saturated correlates (lavaan’s aux, which fa_confirmatory(..., aux = ) passes on) is supported. Every refit keeps the fit’s estimates whatever lavaan’s checks of a solution say of them, except for the run-away Heywood case described next. This covers an auxiliary fit, whose augmented residual covariance matrix is not positive definite by construction, two factors correlated above 1, and a residual variance a little below zero. lavaan’s own parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE) shrinks such a covariance to a correlation below 1 before it refits, and so reports the FMIs of other estimates: -1.62 against .25 for the covariance of two factors correlated 1.08 in a sample of 60. The computation stops with a message that says why when the refit at the estimates moves them. Besides a rotated solution, this happens with an improper one: lavaan (0.7-3) will not take as a starting point the estimates of a Heywood case whose negative residual variance exceeds the variable’s observed variance in size, and restarts from its simple starting values, and lavaan’s own parameterEstimates(fmi = TRUE) then reports FMIs computed at those values (NA for some rows, negative for the intercepts), warning only that the covariance matrix of the estimates is not positive definite. The computation also refuses data with no unrestricted estimate of their means and covariances: a pair no case observes together, or a saturated likelihood without a maximum. The pair or singular subset is named, and the checks precede every refit. An EM iteration limit where the maximum exists instead gives a warning in DMAR’s words. The conditions have classes dmar_fmi_never_together and dmar_fmi_saturated_singular; wald_df = "missing_information" gives the same reason and names numeric degrees of freedom as the alternative. Refits do not repeat lavaan’s notice of low pairwise coverage.

  • missing_patterns() and missing_coverage() are new. They describe the missing values before any model is fit: the distinct patterns of observed and missing items with their counts (the pattern with nothing observed kept as a row, since lavaan sets those cases aside), and the number and proportion of cases that observed each pair of items, with lavaan’s denominator, the cases with at least one observed item. Both return tables of the same shape whatever the number of items.

  • df_missing() is new. A Wald interval from full information maximum likelihood refers the estimate to the normal distribution; von Hippel (2016) showed that in small samples with missing values this reference distribution, not the estimate or its standard error, is what makes the interval too short, and that a t reference on degrees of freedom that shrink with the parameter’s fraction of missing information brought his intervals for regression coefficients and moments near nominal coverage. df_missing() computes both of his rules from a vector of FMIs or from the table fraction_missing_information() returns: method = "effective_n", N(1 - FMI) - k (his Eq. 31), and method = "complete_df", df_complete(1 - FMI)(df_complete + 1)/(df_complete + 3) (his Eq. 32), each bounded below at 3, as he recommends (floor). Neither k nor df_complete has a default, because the right value depends on the parameter: for a regression coefficient k counts the slopes and the intercept, and for a factor loading or omega DMAR’s calibration study chose k = 1 (see the wald_df items below). A clearly negative FMI, which the structured and Hessian estimators can return, is refused. Its example takes the FMIs from fraction_missing_information() on an mlmr() fit and sets the t interval beside the Wald interval it replaces.

  • df_barnard_rubin() is new. It gives Barnard and Rubin’s (1999) degrees of freedom for an estimate pooled over imputations, with the total variance, the imputations’ estimate of the FMI, the relative increase in variance, and both components of the formula, vectorized over parameters. floor = 3 is von Hippel’s bound; floor = 0 reproduces mice’s barnard.rubin(), and df_complete = Inf gives Rubin’s (1987) degrees of freedom. The between-imputation variance is passed as between, not B, which DMAR keeps for bootstrap counts. Both df functions return fixed-column tables with tidy() and glance() methods, and print beneath the table a line naming the rule that made the df column (with the m and df_complete used, for df_barnard_rubin()) and the value it is bounded below at, which a knitted table carries as well.

  • wald_df refers Wald intervals to a t distribution. reliability_omega(), reliability_alpha(), reliability(), fa_confirmatory() (with cfa_1() and cfa_2()), mlmr(), and mlmr_mv() gain wald_df = Inf, appended after their existing arguments (after the ... that fa_confirmatory(), its wrappers, and the mlmr pair forward to lavaan, so it must be named in full): the degrees of freedom of the t distribution their Wald intervals refer to. The estimate and its standard error are unchanged and the normal quantile is replaced by the t quantile (von Hippel, 2016); in fa_confirmatory() and the mlmr pair the p-values refer to the same t distribution, so the interval and the test agree, and the ratio is reported in the column test_statistic (z_value in 1.0.x; see the breaking changes). The default reproduces every interval and p-value of 1.0.x exactly (qt() and pt() at infinite degrees of freedom are qnorm() and pnorm()): results gain a wald_df attribute and their tidy() rows a wald_df column, Inf by default; a finite value adds a line under the printed table. summary() of an mlmr() or mlmr_mv() fit then heads its coefficient table t value and Pr(>|t|), as summary.lm() does, with that line beneath the table’s significance codes. A number applies to every Wald interval of the call: the "ml", "mlr", and "adf" intervals of alpha and of the model implied omega and their _logistic variants (on the logit scale), every parameter row of the fa_confirmatory() tables including the standardized solution, and every coefficient of the mlmr pair. A finite value where the interval is not a Wald interval (the closed forms, the profile likelihood, a bootstrap, robust omega, fa_confirmatory(output = "fit"), se = "none") is an error. mlmr() and mlmr_mv() also accept wald_df = "missing_information", von Hippel’s (2016) rule for regression coefficients, max(3, N(1 - FMI) -

    1. for each coefficient, with the FMI estimated from the fit as fraction_missing_information() estimates it and k the slopes and intercept of the coefficient’s outcome; with complete data it gives the N - k of lm(). Its computation does not depend on the units of the variables. It warns when the fit’s estimates are not at the maximum of the likelihood, as lavaan’s can be for variables measured in small units: with every standard deviation of the regression of the fraction_missing_information() entry near .003 (mlmr(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, ci_method = "wald")), the intercept’s degrees of freedom move by .15, and rescale_data = TRUE, passed through ..., is the remedy. A coefficient whose fraction of missing information cannot be computed stops the call with the reason rather than receive NA degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom and the df_missing() table they came from are attributes of the fit, and summary() lists each coefficient’s FMI and degrees of freedom. As von Hippel published it, the interval pairs the maximum likelihood standard error with the t quantile, so on complete data it is shorter than the interval of lm() by sqrt((N - k)/N). fa_confirmatory() and reliability_omega() accept the keyword as well, for the loadings and omega, on the rule DMAR’s calibration study chose (next item); reliability_alpha() takes a number only.

  • wald_df = "missing_information" for factor loadings and omega. Von Hippel’s (2016) evidence for his degrees of freedom covers regression coefficients and moments, not factor loadings or reliability coefficients, so DMAR ran a calibration study of its own. It lives in the source repository, methodology/missing_data, with the plan (the design and the decision rule, fixed before the run), the script, the results, and the per parameter summary from which every verdict can be recomputed; it is not in the package.

    • Design. The study simulated one factor models as fa_confirmatory() writes them: 6 items at N from 30 to 200 and 12 items at N = 50 and 100, normal data fit by ML and nonnormal data by MLR with Huber-White standard errors, and no missing values or 15 or 30 percent of the values of half the items missing completely at random or at random, with 2000 replications in each of 60 cells. It compared the normal interval with t intervals on four of von Hippel’s rules under a decision rule fixed before the run, and a repetition of his own design reproduced his Tables 4 and 5 to within .012.
    • Verdict. His effective sample size rule with k = 1 was the simplest rule to pass for the loadings: over the small samples with missing values its coverage was .0171 from .95 on average, against .0247 for the normal interval; averaged over a cell’s loadings it was never above .9502. With missing values no single loading’s coverage exceeded .96 (the highest was .9595); without them the t reference on N - 1 reached .963, where the normal reference reached .962. It also passed for omega (.0180 against .0242, never above .9550), with normal theory and robust standard errors alike.
    • Where it applies. fa_confirmatory() (with cfa_1() and cfa_2()) and reliability_omega() accept the keyword. In fa_confirmatory() the loadings of the "verbose" table take the t reference, each on its own degrees of freedom, and every other row keeps the normal reference, since the study evaluated neither factor correlations, intercepts, error variances, nor the AVE and H; omega passed on its own scale, but fa_confirmatory() now forms omega’s limits on the logit scale, where the t reference overcovered (.9645), so omega keeps the normal reference there, and the "measurement" table, which has no loading, refuses the keyword. In reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied") it applies to the "ml" and "mlr" intervals. With complete data, listwise deletion, or a covariance matrix every FMI is 0 and the degrees of freedom are N - 1.
    • Example. On the five spatial tests of holzinger_swineford (visual perception, cubes, lozenges, the second paper form board, and flags), two of which only the Grant-White pupils took (156 of the 301 values missing), fa_confirmatory(missing = "fiml", wald_df = "missing_information") gives the loadings of those two tests 139.8 and 143.7 degrees of freedom (FMI .53 and .52), the other three 246.0 to 274.9, and omega 214.6 (FMI .28); omega’s 95% interval moves from [.6946, .8061] to [.6942, .8064]. In a pilot of 60 of the pupils (set.seed(113); sample(301, 60)), the model implied omega’s FMI under reliability_omega(missing = "fiml", ci_method = "ml", denominator = "model_implied") is .23, its degrees of freedom are 45.5, and its interval [.665, .888] becomes [.662, .891], 2.7% wider.
    • Where it is refused. The keyword is refused, with the reason, where the study did not reach: the _logistic intervals (on the logit scale the t reference covered up to .9645 with normal data, where the normal interval was already within .0044 of .95 on average), the ADF intervals, robust omega, the standardized solution, estimators other than ML and MLR, ordered items, pairwise deletion and two-stage estimation, standard errors other than the normal theory and Huber-White ones (robust.sem is accepted only under listwise deletion, or from a covariance matrix with the required NACOV; it and Satorra-Bentler tests passed through ... are refused under FIML whether values are missing or not, because lavaan falls back to listwise deletion), and, under full information maximum likelihood, standard errors from any information but the observed information computed from the Hessian, lavaan’s default there and the study’s.
    • Alpha. reliability_alpha() refuses it too, since no rule passed the study’s decision rule for alpha: the t reference brought alpha’s FIML interval barely closer to .95 than the normal one, which was already close (.0042 against .0043), and covered .966 in one cell, the one where the study’s fit of the saturated model converged in only 53 percent of the replications. Without that cell the rule would have passed (.0035 against .0042), but the rule was fixed before the run and its verdict stands; a number of degrees of freedom remains available.
    • Attributes. The degrees of freedom are the wald_df attribute, the df_missing() table they came from is the wald_df_table attribute, and a line under the printed table names the rule, N, and the rows it applied to.

  • cov_fiml() returns the maximum likelihood covariance matrix and means of incomplete continuous data. These are the estimates of the saturated model fitted by full information maximum likelihood, the moments the EM algorithm converges to, computed with lavaan’s EM, run on the variables centered at their means and divided by their standard deviations, with the estimates transformed back. They are the unrestricted moments lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "sampstat.h1") returns for any FIML fit to the same variables. They are consistent when values are missing at random given the variables included, where the complete case matrix is consistent in general only when values are missing completely at random. lavaan’s EM stops when no mean or covariance changes by more than 1e-5, a criterion on the absolute change, so run in the raw metric its estimates depend on the units: on the regression data of the fraction_missing_information() entry with every variable multiplied by .001, lavaan::lavCor(missing = "ml") returns correlations off by up to .16, with no warning that its EM stopped short (it warns only that the matrix is near singular, its variances being near zero). Multiplying a variable by a constant multiplies the mean cov_fiml() returns, and its row and column of S, by that constant, and the estimates agree with lavaan’s own to about seven digits. A warning lavaan raises about the variables names them as data does. Columns named in aux enter the saturated model as auxiliary variables and are left out of what is returned, and a case observed only on its auxiliaries is used, as the reliability family uses it under FIML (see Changes to Earlier Results). The result is a list, like that of cov_sem(), because every use of it takes the matrix: S (divisor N), mu, N, N_complete, patterns, and converged. A non-numeric column, a column with fewer than two distinct observed values, a pair of variables never observed together, and a pair observed together only in rows where one of them takes a single value (or in one row only), whose rows in common say nothing about how the two vary together, are refused by name. cov_fiml() and the reliability family refuse such pairs in the same words, from shared checks: the message names the method that needs the covariance, says what an estimate of it would rest on (lavaan only warns about a pair never observed together, and its estimate of that covariance is arbitrary), and advises leaving out one variable of each pair, an auxiliary variable where the pair has one. The help page explains why N is not an effective sample size for a method that treats the matrix as complete data (Enders & Peugh, 2004; Savalei & Bentler, 2009). The matrix is the basis for an exploratory factor analysis or a parallel analysis of incomplete items.

  • A vignette, “Missing Data: What the Missing Values Cost” (vignette("missing_data")), teaches the missing data family on the six spatial tests of holzinger_swineford, two of which were given only at the Grant-White school. It covers the patterns of missing values and the cases behind each covariance; why listwise deletion needs values missing completely at random and FIML needs them missing at random given the model’s variables, shown on the real data (where listwise deletion analyzes one school) and on a deletion made missing at random whose complete data answer is known; auxiliary variables as saturated correlates through fa_confirmatory(..., aux = ), and what lavaan’s warning about the residual covariance matrix means there; the fraction of missing information of every parameter, with the effective sample size, the target sample size, the width inflation factor, the three estimators of Chen and Savalei (2021), and a bootstrap interval for the FMI; the EM covariance matrix of cov_fiml() as the basis of an exploratory factor analysis, and why its N is not an effective sample size; t reference distributions in small samples through wald_df = "missing_information", df_missing(), and df_barnard_rubin(); two-stage maximum likelihood with its residual based statistic and corrected fit indices; omega, alpha, and categorical omega (pairwise deletion and multiple imputation) from incomplete items; factor scores and their determinacy for each missing data pattern; and a sample size plan for omega made with the FMI and checked by simulation. Every number in its text is computed from the analyses.

Two-Stage Maximum Likelihood for Incomplete Data

  • fa_confirmatory(), cfa_1(), cfa_2(), and measurement_invariance() gain missing = "two_stage" and missing = "robust_two_stage" (lavaan’s spellings "two.stage" and "robust.two.stage" are accepted too). The model is fit to the EM estimates of the means and covariances, computed from every partially observed case and from any auxiliary variables passed as lavaan’s aux, which enter that first stage only (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Bentler, 2009). A case observed on an auxiliary variable but on no variable of the model is used too. The first stage estimates the items and the auxiliaries jointly and sums its likelihood over every case (Savalei & Bentler, 2009, Eq. 10), which is what makes the estimates consistent when the items go missing together at random given the auxiliaries.

    lavaan’s two-stage estimator reads such a case in its first stage but leaves it out of its N. That N turns the per case quantities of the two stages into:

    • every standard error, each too large by sqrt(N_read / N);
    • the naive statistic, and the scaled statistic, corrected indices, and RMSEA interval built on it;
    • the log likelihood;
    • in several groups, the weight of each group in the discrepancy function the second stage minimizes, on which the estimates of a model that constrains parameters across groups depend.

    The fit is therefore computed again with the sample size set to the cases the first stage read, group by group. lavaan’s own formulas then give every value on that N, in the table and in the lavaan fits of output = "fit" and of the "fits" attribute.

    • In one group, and at the configural rung, the estimates do not depend on the count and stay lavaan’s.
    • A rung that constrains parameters across groups is estimated again with the counts of the cases read. These are the two-stage estimates with every case read, whose estimates and naive statistic semTools’ twostage() gives.
    • lavaan’s summary() of such a fit counts the cases as used, and lavTestLRT() warns that a difference test between it and a fit lavaan made of the same data on its own N is invalid.
    • A message counts such cases, and a line under the table names the N. When the fit cannot be computed again, a warning says instead what rests on lavaan’s N.

    Example: six Holzinger and Swineford tests, a spatial factor of visual perception, cubes, and lozenges and a verbal factor of paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning, with the whole block missing for 77 of 301 pupils at random given general information, the auxiliary (set.seed(113), then the six tests set to NA in the rows sample(301, 77, prob = plogis(-1.5 + 1.2 * z)), with z the standardized general information score).

    • A verbal loading of 2.840 has a standard error of .190 rather than lavaan’s .220 (sqrt(301/224) = 1.159).
    • The robust two-stage chi square is 24.83 rather than 18.48.
    • BIC is formed with N = 301.
    • By school, 130 and 94 pupils with an observed test grow to 156 and 145 cases read. At the scalar rung the common intercept of lozenges is 18.00 (SE .697) rather than lavaan’s 18.21 (SE .782). The scalar difference test is 14.97 on 4 df, against 10.86 from lavaan’s own ladder, 16.46 under FIML with the same auxiliary, and 17.44 after listwise deletion.
    • Setting the 77 cases aside instead would condition the analysis on an observed item. On the same data it moves the loading to 2.796 and the intercept of paragraph comprehension from 9.21 to 8.75 (9.18 with complete data). Over 60 bootstrap resamples of the 301 pupils (set.seed(2026)), each with the block deleted in the same way, the intercept’s mean error against the resample’s complete data estimate is -0.49 with the cases set aside and -0.01 with them kept.

    The standard errors are the two-stage sandwich, normal theory or robust to nonnormality. After normal theory two-stage estimation the chi_square row is the residual based statistic of Savalei and Bentler (2009). DMAR computes it from the observed information of the saturated model over every case the first stage read, and their simulations found it to hold its rejection rate near the nominal level. After robust two-stage estimation the row is lavaan’s scaled statistic (Savalei & Falk, 2014). Simple equality constraints that lavaan keeps under ceq.simple = TRUE, passed through ..., are read: the residual based statistic of such a model is that of the same model without ceq.simple.

    The cfi and rmsea rows are lavaan’s robust indices, the corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023). They subtract from the naive statistic an estimate of its expectation, built from the asymptotic covariance matrix of the EM moments.

    • After robust two-stage estimation that matrix is the sandwich of the observed and first order information of the saturated model, and the indices are their TS V2, the version they recommend.
    • After normal theory two-stage estimation it is the inverse of the observed information, the form the sandwich takes under normality. The indices are then the normal theory analog of TS V2, which they did not study.
    • On nine Holzinger and Swineford tests in three factors (the spatial and verbal tests above, and addition, counting groups of dots, and straight and curved capitals), with 90 values each of sentence completion and straight and curved capitals deleted completely at random (set.seed(1), then sample(301, 90) for each in turn), the RMSEA is .0869 after normal theory and .0859 after robust two-stage estimation.
    • Zhang and Savalei define only the RMSEA and the CFI; the tli and nnfi rows and the RMSEA interval are lavaan’s extension of the correction. A line under the table says which version it holds.

    The rung-to-rung tests of measurement_invariance() are the scaled difference tests (Satorra & Bentler, 2001). AIC and BIC are the two-stage criteria of Lai (2021), the values sem_information_criteria() reports. The printed table says which statistic, indices, and criteria it reports. fa_confirmatory() frees the item intercepts under two-stage estimation as it does under FIML; through bare lavaan() lavaan would fix them at zero. An estimator other than ML, a robust se, ordered items, and covariance input are errors that name the option to use. fa_confirmatory()’s table gains a test attribute naming the statistic in its chi_square row, and measurement_invariance() a model_test attribute. No existing value changes.

  • reliability_omega(), reliability_alpha(), and reliability() gain missing = "two_stage", appended to the choices; the default is full information maximum likelihood when a value is missing (see Changes to Earlier Results). The model implied coefficients take the normal theory two-stage standard error under ci_method = "ml" and the robust one under "mlr". Their fits go through fa_confirmatory(), so a case observed on an auxiliary variable alone is counted as above.

    Robust omega divides the squared sum of the two-stage loadings by the sum of the EM covariance matrix, with a bootstrap interval that refits both stages. No delta method interval is offered for it, since none has been studied. Each bootstrap replication fits the second stage to the EM moments of the resample, without the two-stage standard errors and scaled statistic that lavaan computes for every two-stage fit and no replication reads. The bootstrap replications of the model implied coefficients do the same. The estimates are those of a full two-stage fit, to rounding error, wherever the likelihood has a well defined maximum. On a small, heavily incomplete resample, whose likelihood is nearly flat or has no proper maximum, the two optimizers can stop at different points. A replication’s value can then differ at the optimizer’s tolerance, and a solution that runs away can be counted as not converged rather than improper, or the reverse; under either verdict it is among the replications the bootstrap counts as set aside or improper.

    Analytic alpha, a function of the first stage alone, equals its FIML value and interval. Two-stage estimation uses the cases FIML uses, every case with an observed item or an observed auxiliary variable, since its first stage reads a case observed on an auxiliary variable alone. A message counts such cases, once per call rather than once per bootstrap replication. When the fit of a model implied coefficient cannot be computed again with every case, a warning says that its analytic standard error is too large and that a bootstrap interval counts every case. On visual perception, paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning, with the block deleted as in the example above and general information as the auxiliary, alpha (ci_method = "ml") is .773 (SE .0235) on 301 cases, the FIML value. Setting the 77 aside would give .769 (SE .0242) on 224.

    aux names auxiliary variables of the first stage, and aux without missing still means FIML. The intervals refused under FIML are refused here too, the profile likelihood also because no likelihood of the observed data is maximized.

  • sem_fit_measures() reports a two-stage fit with the statistic and indices fa_confirmatory() reports, and compare_sem() compares two-stage fits by their two-stage criteria. sem_fit_measures() reports the robust version, the corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023). After robust two-stage estimation these are their TS V2. After normal theory two-stage estimation they are its normal theory analog, which lavaan forms with the inverse of the observed information of the saturated model where TS V2 takes the sandwich of the observed and first order information, and which they did not study. The chi_square row is the residual based statistic, or the scaled statistic after robust two-stage estimation, and the printed footer names the version of the indices, as fa_confirmatory()’s does. It refuses version = "standard" (the naive statistic, which is not chi square distributed) and "scaled".

    The residual based statistic is refused, with a message that says what to do instead, for a fit with:

    • sampling weights or clustered cases;
    • an observed exogenous variable under fixed.x = TRUE or conditional.x = TRUE. Refit with fixed.x = FALSE (and with conditional.x = FALSE, since lavaan does not take fixed.x = FALSE beside conditional.x = TRUE), which leaves the estimates as they are when the exogenous variables are complete and otherwise also keeps the cases lavaan deletes for a missing exogenous variable when it conditions on them (robust two-stage estimation included), so the estimates then differ; to keep the fit’s estimates, refit on the rows the fit used, those on which every exogenous variable is observed, which lavInspect(fit, "case.idx") lists. The refusal is an error of class dmar_two_stage_fixed_x (a dmar_refusal) that carries the exogenous variables;
    • inequality constraints;
    • a parameter on a bound.

    Its listwise deletion warning counts only the cases lavaan deletes listwise; the empty cases lavaan drops under FIML or two-stage estimation, which carry no information, draw none.

    It warns when a two-stage fit made with lavaan has cases observed on an auxiliary variable but on none of the model’s variables. lavaan’s first stage reads such cases and its N leaves them out. The naive statistic, the scaled statistic and corrected indices built on it, the RMSEA multiplier, and the N row then rest on fewer cases than the EM moments, while the residual based statistic uses every case. The table reports lavaan’s values. The warning points to fa_confirmatory() and measurement_invariance(), whose fits keep and count such cases, and to FIML. On the six tests above (lavaan::cfa(model, data, std.lv = TRUE, missing = "two.stage", aux = "t5_general_information")), lavaan’s N is 224 and its robust RMSEA .095; the fit fa_confirmatory(missing = "two_stage") returns for the same model counts 301 cases and gives .103.

    compare_sem() reports no log evidence for two-stage criteria, which approximate no marginal likelihood, and refuses two-stage fits whose auxiliary variables differ.

  • sem_information_criteria() and compare_sem() count every case the first stage of a two-stage fit read. lavaan forms the two-stage log likelihood as its N times the complete data log likelihood per case at the EM estimates, and BIC, SABIC, and HBIC take the same N into their penalties. A case observed on an auxiliary variable but on none of the model’s variables moves the EM estimates and is left out of that N. The log likelihood and N are taken instead from the fit computed again with every case the first stage read.

    • In one group, and in several groups that no constraint holds together, the estimates stay, and each group’s log likelihood is its value per case times the cases read.
    • In several groups held together by a constraint, such as equal loadings or intercepts, the estimates move with the groups’ counts, and the log likelihood is the one at the two-stage estimates with every case read.
    • A line under the table says which, and the sem_information attribute records the counts.

    On the six tests above, fit by lavaan as in the previous entry, lavaan’s N for the two-factor model is 224 and its log likelihood -4040.25. That is 224/301 of the -5429.09 reported with N = 301, and BIC is 10966.61 (8183.32 from lavaan’s values). With the two schools as groups and equal loadings and intercepts (group = "school", meanstructure = TRUE, group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts")), the log likelihood is -5393.34 and BIC 10957.89, against -5393.52 and 10958.25 at lavaan’s estimates and -4020.79 and 8203.92 from lavaan’s values. A fit fa_confirmatory() or measurement_invariance() returns already counts the cases and gives the same criteria, and compare_sem() compares it with a lavaan fit of the same data. A warning names what rests on lavaan’s N only when the fit cannot be computed again.

Factor Scores

  • factor_scores() is new. It returns both standard factor scores of a fitted lavaan model for every row and factor: the regression score (the posterior mean) and the Bartlett score, or for ordered items lavaan’s empirical Bayes modal and maximum likelihood scores. Each comes with a per-case standard error and a conf_level interval, beside the number of the factor’s items the case answered, its missing data pattern, and, for continuous items in a fit not conditional on exogenous covariates, the determinacy of each score for that pattern, in one long table with one row per row of the data and factor. An item listed under a factor with its loading fixed or constrained to zero (0*item, or a*item with a == 0) is not one of that factor’s items. print(), tidy(), and glance() methods come with it.

    Under FIML each case is scored from its own observed items, and the determinacy for each pattern shows what a missing item costs; for one factor its square is coefficient H. Beside the regression score’s determinacy rho, the display and the determinacy and patterns attributes give 2 rho^2 - 1 (min_score_correlation), the lowest correlation two sets of scores equally consistent with the model can have (Guttman, 1955), reported without a line drawn. Rows the fit did not score (deleted listwise, with no observed item, without a group) stay in the table with the reason when data is supplied, and a frame that is not the rows given to the fit is refused. A row deleted listwise from an ordered fit is told that missing = "pairwise" scores it, since lavaan has no FIML for ordered items. A row deleted for a missing exogenous covariate is told, whatever the fit’s treatment of missing values, that missing = "ml.x" scores it (with conditional.x = FALSE for a fit conditional on the covariates), or with ordered items that no fit lavaan can score keeps it. Without data, where the two cannot be told apart, the reason in a one-group fit by listwise deletion names what scores each; in any other fit that deletes such rows it names missing = "ml.x" and says that supplying data identifies the reason. A case that answered none of a factor’s items has no Bartlett score and keeps a regression score that comes only from its other observed variables (the items of correlated factors, a covariate that predicts the factor, an outcome it predicts). A factor that a pattern’s observed items do not separate from another (a case that answered only an item two factors share) has no Bartlett score, rather than the minimum norm solution of lavaan’s generalized inverse; a factor the pattern does identify keeps its score.

    A fit of continuous items that keeps the incomplete cases without FIML is scored as a FIML fit is, each case from its own observed items, with the fit’s estimates. That covers a two-stage fit (lavaan’s missing = "two.stage" or "robust.two.stage", or fa_confirmatory(missing = "two_stage")), whose estimates are consistent when the values are missing at random, as the FIML estimates are (Savalei & Bentler, 2009). It also covers a fit by pairwise deletion (missing = "pairwise" or "available.cases"), whose estimates require values missing completely at random. lavaan’s lavPredict() scores such a fit as complete data and leaves every case with a missing value without a score, so factor_scores() computes these scores itself, by the closed forms lavPredict() applies pattern by pattern under FIML. Such a fit conditional on exogenous covariates is refused.

    Without a mean structure (the default for one group under listwise or pairwise deletion), a factor that a covariate predicts is centered where lavaan and FIML center it, at the slope times the covariate’s mean. In such a fit without an exogenous covariate, lavPredict() counts twice the mean of an observed variable that lavaan holds among the latent variables, which shifts by a constant every score whose weights involve it (the regression score of every factor related to it, the Bartlett score of a factor that predicts it); factor_scores() computes those scores itself, and a higher order factor keeps lavaan’s Bartlett score less that constant. An observed variable regressed on others, such as an item with a direct effect of a covariate (the MIMIC model of differential item functioning) or an outcome the factor predicts, is held by lavaan among the latent variables, with its loadings among the regressions. The scores, their standard errors and determinacies, the check of the ML score, and the check of the solution take its loadings and residual variance from there, as lavPredict() does, so an item with a direct effect enters its factor’s Bartlett score. An observed variable that lavaan holds the same way but regresses on nothing, such as a criterion that covaries with a factor (f ~~ z) or a covariate of a factor that also covaries with another variable, is conditioned on, as an exogenous covariate is.

    Without regressions among the variables lavaan holds as latent, a variable regressed only on exogenous covariates is conditioned on as well, also when it covaries with a factor. With such regressions, lavPredict() gives an observed variable regressed on nothing a row of zeros among the loadings, leaving its covariances with the factors out of the scores. factor_scores() scores these fits itself and refuses one conditional on the covariates. A fit with such regressions is refused when the disturbance of an observed variable regressed on others covaries with a factor or a variable the scores condition on: lavaan’s Bartlett score is then not conditionally unbiased, and where a factor is involved its regression score is not the conditional mean. The remedy carries the variable as a single indicator latent variable without fixing its loading, with its observed residual variance fixed at zero. This preserves the model under std.lv = TRUE as well. In multiple groups the refusal also names the intercept and residual variance and covariance equalities needed to preserve the constraints.

    For ordered items a factor has an ML score only where the likelihood of the case’s responses has a finite and unique maximum in it, which an exact check decides for any loading structure, cross-loadings, bifactor models, and observed variables regressed on the factors included (by Farkas’ lemma, through nonnegative least squares). Each of these has an NA ML score with the reason and keeps its EBM score: a factor whose observed items all sit at the end of their scales that their loadings point to (all in the lowest category, or all in the highest, for positive loadings), one whose likelihood rises without bound together with others, one its items cannot separate from another, and a higher order factor. Every other factor keeps its ML score, also one that shares items with a factor whose likelihood rises without bound: its maximum is then that of the case’s other items, which lavaan’s optimizer reaches within its tolerance. When lavaan’s default optimizer stops on the other factor and returns no score, the score comes from lavaan’s nlminb optimizer. With ordered items, lavaan’s EBM and ML scores omit terms from each case’s likelihood or prior. A fit is scored when the omitted term is constant in the factors: a covariate’s effect on an outcome that depends on no factor directly, or a fully mediated chain of continuous observed variables. A fit is refused for a direct effect of a covariate on a variable that depends on a factor directly, a regression of such a variable on an observed variable, or a regression on an ordered item. It is also refused when an observed variable lavaan holds among the loadings has a disturbance covarying with a factor, or a row lacks a predictor whose path reaches a factor without an observed mediator cutting it. A fit with exogenous covariates that is not conditional on them is refused because lavPredict() cannot score it. A fit of ordered items with residual covariances is scored with a warning, since lavaan’s EBM and ML scores leave those covariances out of each case’s likelihood; the help page gives the size of these errors in an example. Ordered items require lavaan 0.7-3 or newer: lavaan 0.7-2 counted the intercepts of ordered indicators twice in its EBM and ML scores, which were then wrong in any model where those intercepts are not zero (a multiple group model with equal thresholds, for one), so factor_scores() refuses an ordered fit under an older lavaan.

    Auxiliary variables carried as saturated correlates are set aside, and the scores are computed from the indicators with the fit’s estimates, since conditioning on them removes true score variance. A fit that carries them with ordered items is refused (refit without them), as is one that carries them and is conditional on exogenous covariates (refit with conditional.x = FALSE). A higher order factor has no Bartlett score, and its reason says so, where the scores are computed from the indicators (auxiliary variables set aside), where the data have missing values and the scores are computed here for a two-stage fit or one by pairwise deletion ("pairwise" or "available.cases"), or in a fit in which lavaan gives an observed variable regressed on nothing a row of zeros among the loadings, since lavaan’s construction of that score is not repeated there. Elsewhere it keeps lavaan’s score (less the constant above where lavaan counts a mean twice), and its Bartlett standard error from lavaan is in the pattern table.

    An improper solution is scored with a warning: a negative variance (the residual variance of an observed variable regressed on others included), a covariance matrix of the factors that is not positive definite (a factor correlation beyond 1, for one), a residual covariance matrix of the continuous items that is not, or, when none of these holds, a residual covariance matrix of the structural part of the model that is not, the conditions lavaan’s post-estimation check flags. For ordered items lavaan computes no score for a solution with a negative residual variance, and the warning and the reasons say so.

    The help page says which score belongs where: regression scores for a predictor and Bartlett scores for an outcome, each from its own measurement model (Skrondal & Laake, 2001), and one-step SEM or structural after measurement (lavaan::sam(); Rosseel & Loh, 2024, which includes Croon’s correction) as the route to relations among factors. Scores under missing data are discussed with Estabrook and Neale (2013). The help says that the Bartlett score’s conditional unbiasedness and the coverage of its interval hold under missing data only when whether an item is observed does not depend on the residuals of the items scored (Rubin, 1976), so not when it depends on the factor’s own observed items, with an example. It also says that the regression score’s posterior interval keeps its coverage when the missingness depends on the items scored, but not when it runs through an auxiliary variable set aside.

    A loading or regression held at zero, directly or through a chain of plain equalities, is read as absent. It makes no item, does not keep a saturated correlate from being set aside as an auxiliary variable, and gives the scores and reasons of the model written without it.

Planning Under Missing Data

  • ss_aipe_reliability() gains fmi and seed. A reliability coefficient estimated by full information maximum likelihood from incomplete data has a wider interval at a given N than a complete data plan assumes. fmi (default 0) is the fraction of missing information anticipated for the coefficient, supplied by a pilot study or a comparable data set through fraction_missing_information(); it is not the proportion of missing values. Missing information multiplies the sampling variance by 1 / (1 - fmi) (Savalei & Rhemtulla, 2012). The planner’s variance is V / (N - 1), so the plan divides the complete data N - 1 by 1 - fmi: N = (N_c - 1) / (1 - fmi) + 1, and an FMI of .5 doubles N - 1, not N. With an assurance, the Monte Carlo search runs at the complete data (effective) size and its answer is mapped back the same way, a first-order approximation that the sensitivity function checks. The table keeps its rows; the attributes fmi and necessary_N_complete record the plan, and a line under the table names both. The help page explains where a planning FMI comes from, why a pilot’s FMI is imprecise (Chen & Savalei, 2021), and why the upper limit of its interval is the conservative planning value. The plan maps the unrounded complete data solution, so the formula applied to the printed complete data N can give a case or two more than the plan (the first example of the help page, six parallel items that correlate .6 planned for a width of .10, needs 38 complete data cases and 42 at an FMI of .1, where the formula on 38 gives 43); the help says so. It also says that a pilot FMI from fraction_missing_information() refers to the cases the fit used, and that when the planned N counts every case recruited, those who will answer no item are folded in as 1 - (N_used / N)(1 - fmi). seed (default NULL) makes the assurance search reproducible and restores the caller’s random number stream on exit; without it the search draws from and advances that stream, as before. With fmi = 0 the plan is the complete data plan and no attribute is added; the planner’s other changes are under Changes to Earlier Results.

  • ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() gains fmi, missing_prop, and B. fmi is the planning value passed to the planner; missing_prop deletes each simulated item score completely at random with that probability and analyzes every replication by full information maximum likelihood, so a plan made with fmi is judged by the widths that incomplete data actually deliver. For four parallel items with reliability .80, a width of .15, and missing_prop = .2, the FMI of the coefficient is .184 relative to every case and .182 relative to the cases a fit keeps, since a share .2^4 = .0016 of the cases loses every item (the realized FMI, described below, of one FIML fit to 200,000 simulated cases: ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(true_reliability = .8, n_items = 4, width = .15, specified_N = 200000, missing_prop = .2, G = 1) after set.seed(113)). In 1,000 replications, with set.seed(113) before each call, the complete data plan (N = 74) gave "ml" intervals averaging .170 wide, and the plan made with fmi = .184 (N = 91) gave .152, against .153 for the complete data plan with complete data. Under missing data the default interval is "ml", as with complete data, and intervals whose standard errors ignore the missing values are refused. With missing_prop above 0, each replication that returns an interval also estimates the fraction of missing information its simulated data realized for the coefficient (the unstructured FMI of fraction_missing_information(), from alpha’s saturated model or omega’s single-factor model). The mean is reported beside the planning fmi as the attribute mean_realized_fmi, with the number of replications behind it in n_realized_fmi, a second line under the table, and a realized_fmi column in the per-replication file. A single sample FMI is too imprecise at the sizes a plan resolves to check a plan by (Chen & Savalei, 2021), and the mean over replications is the figure to carry into fmi. Computing it draws no random numbers, so the table’s rows are those of a run without it; it costs a fit and two refits per replication. The realized FMI is relative to every simulated case, the footing of the planner’s fmi: lavaan sets aside a case that loses every item, and the FMI relative to the cases it kept is folded back as 1 - (n_used / n)(1 - fmi_used). With three items at missing_prop = .5, a share .5^3 = .125 of the cases loses every item, so the FMI relative to the cases lavaan keeps understates the FMI the plan needs. B is the number of bootstrap resamples behind each replication’s interval, which was fixed at 200 whatever the interval; its default is the larger of 200 and the number the interval method and the level require, and a smaller value is refused (see One Rule for Bootstrap Replications). For alpha, with fmi and missing_prop at 0, B at its default, no assurance, and ci_method = "bonett", the results are those of 1.0.x, except for replications whose interval lies wholly below zero (see the entry on clamped limits under Changes to Earlier Results); the default interval is now "ml" (see the entry there on the interval its plan was made for).

  • ss_aipe_rmsea() does not take fmi. RMSEA is a function of the test statistic, not a model parameter, so no parameter’s FMI governs the noncentrality its interval is built on, and Savalei and Rhemtulla (2012) leave global measures of missing information to future research.

Sample Size Planning for a Mean

  • ss_aipe_mean() plans the sample size for the confidence interval for a single mean, the mean of one sample or the mean of paired differences, which DMAR could not plan before: ss_aipe_sm() plans the standardized mean, and ss_aipe_c() requires contrast weights that sum to zero. Without an assurance the plan makes the expected width no wider than width, and the expected width is exact under normality: it uses E(S) = c4(N) sigma, where ss_aipe_c() sets S equal to sigma, and so needs the same N as that rule or one fewer. With an assurance the realized width is no wider than width with that probability. true_kurtosis, on the excess scale of kurtosis() so that a pilot’s value can usually be passed as it is, adjusts the assurance through a scaled chi square with the exact mean and variance of S^2; the expected width plan does not use it and warns when one is supplied. A pilot whose scores take nearly two values can give a kurtosis() of -2 or less, which is refused, and the help page says what to pass instead. With a large kurtosis the assurance can be met at a very small N, missed over a stretch above it, and met again, so the plan is the smallest N from which the assurance holds at every larger N, and the search finds that N exactly. The answer row is necessary_N, beside the expected width at that size and the inputs.

  • ss_aipe_mean_sensitivity() checks such a plan by Monte Carlo, under a normal population or by resampling a vector of observed scores (population), which is how a plan meets the tails and skewness of real data, such as a pilot’s difference scores. It follows the sensitivity family’s arguments and rows, reports mean_mean, median_mean, and sd_mean for the realized means, and takes seed (default NULL), which makes a run reproducible and restores the caller’s random number stream on exit. For the help page’s pilot (the IQ gains of the control children in pygmalion, excess kurtosis 1.2), a plan for 90 percent assurance made under normal theory gave intervals no wider than the target of 4 points in .870 of 1,000 replications, and the plan made with the pilot’s kurtosis, six children larger, in .913.

Assurance When the Errors Are Not Normal

  • ss_aipe_c() gains true_kurtosis. With an assurance, the planner takes the pooled variance to follow the chi square law of normal theory, which holds only for normal errors. Errors lighter tailed than the normal, as bounded outcomes such as proportions and rating scale scores often are, make the pooled variance less variable than that law says, so a plan (for any assurance above one half) delivers more assurance than was requested; heavy tails make it deliver less. true_kurtosis (default 0) is the population excess kurtosis of the errors, a planning value on the scale kurtosis() reports, and it replaces the error degrees of freedom df = J(n - 1) in the chi square quantile with the effective degrees of freedom 2 / (2 / df + true_kurtosis / (n J)), which match the variance of the pooled variance (Box, 1953). The default reproduces the plans of earlier releases exactly, and the expected width plan (no assurance) does not use the argument. An assurance plan made with a nonzero true_kurtosis keeps its one row, carries the value as the attribute true_kurtosis, says in a line under the table that its assurance allows for that excess kurtosis, and reports it as the column true_kurtosis of glance(); with true_kurtosis = 0 no attribute or line is added. In a Monte Carlo check with two groups and an assurance of .80 (10,000 replications per condition), the plans made with the kurtosis supplied met the width target in .811 of the replications under uniform errors (excess kurtosis -1.2) and .811 under t errors on 10 degrees of freedom (excess kurtosis 1), where the normal theory plans met it in .915 and .776. The help page describes the approximation and its limits, and says that ss_aipe_c_sensitivity(), which is unchanged, simulates normal errors.

Common Method Variance: The Marker Adjustment With Its Interval

  • common_method_adjusted_r() gives every marker adjusted correlation with a confidence interval and the t test of Lindell and Whitney (2001), over one or more marker correlations. common_method_marker() works from the correlation matrix alone and does not take N, so its page left the test to the user. The new function takes N and returns one row per marker value and variable pair: the correlation, the adjusted correlation, its interval, and the t test on N - 3 degrees of freedom. The interval is the Fisher’s Z interval of ci_r() carried through the adjustment, conditional on the marker correlation. A grid of values for marker_r is how the dependence of a conclusion on that correlation is read. With marker_r = NULL the smallest positive correlation serves as the proxy marker, as in common_method_marker(). common_method_marker() is unchanged, and its page now points to the new function. A lower limit that the adjustment carries below -1 is set to -1; that happens exactly when the Fisher’s Z lower limit for the correlation falls below 2 r_M - 1, which with a positive marker correlation a small sample can produce whatever the sign of the correlation.

  • The missing-information t reference checks the fitted method. With missing values, mlmr() and mlmr_mv() refuse the keyword when lavaan fell back to listwise deletion, including under a Satorra-Bentler test. Complete data retain N minus the regression parameter count. fa_confirmatory() refuses robust.sem and Satorra-Bentler tests under FIML whether values are missing or not, and checks the fitted method for other fallbacks. The help correctly states that its default se = "standard" is normal theory for ML and MLR; an MLR test needs se = "robust.huber.white" for sandwich standard errors under FIML. With a covariance matrix, robust.sem needs the asymptotic moment covariance in NACOV. Alpha keeps its calibrated refusal of the keyword. The loading coverage maximum is qualified by whether values are missing; complete-data coverage uses t on N minus one.

  • Reliability’s missing-information diagnostics use the caller’s item and auxiliary names. The warning about a fit short of its likelihood maximum names the parameter in words. It recommends dividing every item by one common constant, which preserves omega, and each auxiliary by its own, rather than an unavailable refit option.

  • Categorical MI diagnostics describe the interval actually formed. Under bootstrap then impute, no widening or imputation-count advice is given for an interval that was not formed. An FMI estimated from the minority of replications that returned a value is labeled as such. An even imputation count is named only for completed data sets that failed, rather than an imputation failure alone.

Multiple Comparisons

  • ci_dunnett_t3() gives Dunnett’s T3, the pairwise comparisons SPSS reports when the variances are not assumed equal. Each pair has its own separate-variance standard error and Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, as in ci_games_howell(), and its critical value is the studentized maximum modulus for all a(a - 1)/2 comparisons at those degrees of freedom (Dunnett, 1980), the value cv_smm() returns. The adjusted p-value is that distribution’s tail beyond |t|, so it is below alpha when the interval excludes zero and not otherwise, to numerical precision; neither is simulated, and the degrees of freedom are not rounded. The table has the columns and class of the other post hoc intervals (contrast, mean_difference, se, df, t_value, the limits, and p_adjusted, class dmar_post_hoc_ci), and its display names the adjustment. It reproduces the Dunnett’s T3 output of SPSS for Chapter 12, Exercise 25 of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) and agrees with PMCMRplus::dunnettT3Test(). The help explains why the formula that raises the single t probability to the power C is Tamhane’s T2 (Tamhane, 1979), a different procedure whose intervals are never narrower, and when T3 is preferred to Games-Howell. ci_games_howell() and cv_smm() link to it.

Two Proportions Measured on the Same Units

  • ci_proportion_paired() gives a confidence interval for the difference between two proportions measured on the same units, and equivalence_proportion_paired() the score tests of noninferiority and equivalence on that difference. Two diagnostic procedures applied to the same patients, or a pass rate before and after instruction for the same students, give correlated outcomes, and only the discordant pairs inform the difference, so the methods for independent proportions do not apply. ci_proportion_paired() takes either the two 0/1 vectors or the counts n_10, n_01, and N, and returns the score interval of Tango (1998), which inverts the score statistic of Nam (1997). The interval stays inside [-1, 1], is defined when no pair is discordant, and excludes 0 exactly when McNemar’s test without a continuity correction rejects. The Wald interval is available for comparison; the help shows, from the exact coverage of every possible table, how far short of its level it can fall when discordant pairs are rare. equivalence_proportion_paired() reports in the shape of equivalence_c(), with the flag nonsuperior (the upper limit is below prop_diff_upper) as the last row and the verdict “Not relevantly superior only” among its outcomes. prop_diff_upper alone gives symmetric bounds; prop_diff_lower alone is a noninferiority test, whose table leaves the rows that would need an upper bound NA rather than reading them against a mirrored one. The tests reproduce Nam’s restricted estimates and score statistic (2.795) for the liver scan data he takes from McNeil, Keeler, and Adelstein (1975), and the limits match PropCIs::scoreci.mp(), against which a live comparison joins tools/oracle_checks.R.

The Ratio of Two Means

  • ci_ratio_of_means() and ci_ratio_of_means_paired() give a confidence interval for the ratio of two means, for independent groups and for two variables measured on the same units, from the raw data or from summary statistics. The default is Fieller’s confidence set, which inverts the t test of mu_1 - rho mu_2 = 0 and is reported as what it is: a bounded interval, the complement of an interval (whose gap is in the excluded_lower and excluded_upper rows), or the whole line, with the denominator’s t that decides which beside it. Independent groups default to unequal variances, inverting the Welch-type test with degrees of freedom that change with the ratio, so that the interval agrees with the test; var_equal = TRUE gives Fieller’s pooled interval. The paired function takes cluster for the cluster-robust covariance on Q - 1 degrees of freedom. A baseline argument gives the ratio of two advantages over a baseline, the retained fraction of a three-arm noninferiority design, and mean_baseline, sd_baseline, and n_baseline give it from the three arms’ summary statistics; noninferiority at a fraction f holds exactly when f is below the lower limit of a bounded interval with a positive denominator, and the help says so rather than testing chosen fractions. The log-scale interval of the response ratio, and percentile and BCa bootstrap intervals (B = 10000, seed = NULL, written in base R), are offered for comparison; the line under a log or bootstrap interval says when the Fieller set at the same level is unbounded, where a bounded interval can undercover. tidy() carries the gap and the form of the set, so a complement is not read as the whole line, and results_sentence() writes such a set as what it is (“99.5% confidence set: every value except those between 0.90 and 147.05”) rather than as “99.5% CI [-Inf, Inf]”; the sentence of every other table is unchanged. The log interval of a ratio whose terms are not both positive, and a bootstrap from summary statistics, are refused with conditions of class dmar_log_ratio_undefined and dmar_bootstrap_needs_data, which inherit dmar_refusal. The paired page works Fieller’s (1954) own example, whose set takes all three forms at three confidence levels.

Equivalence and Noninferiority of a Contrast

  • equivalence_c() reports nonsuperiority. A nonsuperior row, the last of the table, is 1 when the upper confidence limit is below contrast_upper: the contrast is then shown to be smaller than the smallest advantage that would matter, the mirror of noninferior and the decision of the upper one-sided test (p_upper, which reproduces emmeans::test() with side = "nonsuperiority"). The verdict gains a sixth outcome, “Not relevantly superior only”, checked after “Noninferior only” and before “Inconclusive”, which now means an interval that contains both bounds. This is the claim a study needs when contrast_upper is the improvement that would justify a change. plot_equivalence() applies the same rule through one shared helper, draws the sixth verdict in the palette’s sixth color, and keeps the colors of the other five; its legend sets each one-sided verdict beside the stronger one that implies it.

  • Noninferiority is planned without an upper bound, and paired designs are planned. power_equivalence_c() and ss_power_equivalence_c() require contrast_upper only for side = "equivalence". For side = "noninferiority" they take the margin, contrast_lower, and a call that gives only contrast_upper, as 1.0.x required of its delta_upper, still uses it as the margin, so no earlier call changes but for the names of the bounds. Both take a new last argument, design = c("independent", "paired"), and c_weights now defaults to NULL (it is still required for independent groups). With "paired", true_sd is the standard deviation of the per-unit contrast scores (for two conditions, the difference scores), and the standard error is sigma / sqrt(N) on N - 1 degrees of freedom, where N is the number of units. Each design has its own size, because the two are different quantities: power_equivalence_c() takes n_per_group for independent groups and N, the number of units and so the total sample size, for a paired design, and refuses the size of the other design with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid. The planner answers in the same terms: the rows of an independent plan are necessary_n_per_group, total_N, and actual_power, as in 1.0.x, and the rows of a paired plan are necessary_N and actual_power; tidy() reports the planned size and the power in the same columns for both. At 50 units, a difference score SD of 1, and a margin of .5, the noninferiority power is .9672, and 36 units reach .90. Independent designs give the results they did.

A Crossed Design of Units and Raters

  • ss_aipe_crossed() plans the numbers of units and raters for a fully crossed design, every rater scoring every unit, so that the interval for the mean is narrow enough at the least cost. Units and raters are both random, so the variance of the grand mean is var_unit / n_u + var_rater / n_r + var_residual / (n_u n_r), and with n_r raters no number of units brings the half-width below z sqrt(var_rater / n_r); the plan reports that rater floor. A design costs unit_cost per unit, rater_cost per rater, and judgment_cost per score (by default the number of scores), and the search prices the smallest feasible number of units for every number of raters up to max_raters (or for a panel fixed by n_raters). quantile = "t", the default, plans the interval ci_crossed() computes, with Satterthwaite (1946) degrees of freedom from the planning values; quantile = "normal" reproduces planning that uses the normal quantile. With the t quantile the planned width is not monotone in the number of units (the degrees of freedom eventually fall toward n_r - 1, and past a point the larger quantile outweighs the smaller variance), and the search takes the first feasible design. An assurance rests on the chi square approximation to the plug-in variance, and a plan with an assurance is never smaller than the plan without one, which already meets the width somewhat more than half the time; an assurance at or below one half returns that plan. A target no design within the limits meets is refused with a message naming the limit that binds, max_units or the number of raters. With judgments as the only cost the plan lies near the ratio n_u / n_r = var_unit / var_rater of Marcoulides and Goldstein (1990). The help gives the mapping to an information retrieval evaluation, in which the units are topics and the raters are relevance assessors.
  • ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity() draws complete arrays from the true components at a planned or specified design and reports the realized widths, the proportion at or below the target, and the coverage of the true mean, in the return schema of the sensitivity family, with seed = NULL and filename = NULL. The planner’s arguments, its search limits included, pass through to it.
  • ci_crossed() gives the interval for the mean of a complete units by raters array: the ANOVA estimates of the three components, a negative one set to zero, plugged into the variance of the grand mean, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Its var_unit, var_rater, and var_residual rows are the planning values ss_aipe_crossed() takes. On the four judges and six targets of Shrout and Fleiss (1979) it reproduces their mean squares and shows how much wider the interval for the mean over a population of judges is than one that treats the four judges as fixed.
  • tidy() and glance() read necessary_n_units as the planned size of a crossed design, with necessary_n_raters (or specified_n_raters) kept beside it.

Two-Phase Sampling: A Costly Measurement With an Inexpensive Proxy

  • A family for the mean of a target measurement that is costly to obtain, when an inexpensive proxy is available on a large pool of units. The design is two-phase, or double, sampling (Neyman, 1938): the proxy is measured on the whole pool and the target on a random subsample of it, the labeled units. ci_two_phase() gives the interval for the population mean of the target from the regression estimator, with standard error from the residual variation among the labeled units and the proxy’s variation over the pool, optional cluster standard errors whose degrees of freedom count the clusters among the labeled units, and units with a missing value set aside one by one; it refuses a target that is constant on the labeled units rather than report an interval of zero width. method = "prediction_powered" gives the prediction-powered estimate of Angelopoulos et al. (2023), which fixes the proxy’s weight at 1 where the regression estimator learns it. The table reports the estimate as mean_Y, named for its estimand, the population mean of the target, with its standard error, degrees of freedom, and limits, and the weight the estimate gives the proxy mean of the unlabeled units as proxy_weight (the slope times N / M for the regression estimate, 1 for the prediction-powered one), beside slope, correlation, proxy_bias, se_ratio_target_only, n_labeled, and n_pool. ss_aipe_two_phase() plans the number of labeled units for a given pool, for the expected width or with assurance, always leaving at least one unit with the proxy alone; it reports beside the plan the number needed without the proxy, which is the plan ss_aipe_mean() makes, and refuses a width the pool cannot deliver rather than returning a missing value. ss_aipe_two_phase_cost() chooses both sizes: given the cost of a proxy measurement relative to a target measurement, it returns the least costly design in whole numbers whose ci_two_phase() interval has an expected width no larger than the one asked for. The width is that of the interval as it is reported, with the t quantile on n - 2 degrees of freedom, which is the criterion ss_aipe_two_phase() uses for a given pool, so that planner, given the returned pool, returns the returned number of labeled units; the alternative of measuring the target alone is the necessary_n_target_only plan of that function, and a two-phase design is returned only when it costs less. The search is exact: for each number of labeled units the smallest pool follows from the width, a convex lower bound on the cost (from the normal quantile, which the t quantile is never below) says which numbers of labeled units can still beat the best design found, and those are all examined. In 2,200 planning sets drawn at random the result equaled an exhaustive search over pairs of sizes every time. The rows are necessary_n_labeled, necessary_n_pool (0 when the design measures the target alone), relative_cost (the cost of the returned design over that of the target alone, both in whole numbers), relative_cost_continuous (the same ratio for fractional sizes under the normal quantile, which is a lower bound and is 1 at or below threshold_cor), expected_width, necessary_n_target_only, threshold_cor, and the inputs. threshold_cor is exact for fractional sizes only; above it the least costly design in whole numbers can still be the target alone, and is then returned. Planning values whose sizes cannot be represented as whole numbers, or whose search would examine more than 1e8 numbers of labeled units, stop with an error of class dmar_two_phase_no_design. For a width of 0.20 with a standard deviation of 1, a correlation of .90, and a cost ratio of .05, the design is 109 labeled units in a pool of 1,011, at a cost of 159.55 target measurements against 387 for the target alone, with an expected width of 0.19999. ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity() evaluates a design by simulation under the family’s return schema, from a bivariate normal population or by resampling observed pairs; it reports the population target mean as true_mean_Y, the simulated estimates of it as mean_mean_Y, median_mean_Y, and sd_mean_Y, and the estimate in its per-replication file as mean_Y. ss_seq_two_phase() evaluates the sequential stopping rule, which needs no planning values, in the form of ss_seq_c(); it asks for more labeled units while the target is constant on them or is an exact linear function of the proxy on them, where the rule could stop on no evidence. The vocabulary is that of measurement (target, proxy, labeled units, pool); each help page says in one sentence how the terms map onto the evaluation of an AI system’s outputs.

  • ss_seq_c()’s help page says when to use it and how it differs from the balanced procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018).

  • ss_aipe_two_phase_cost() refuses a cost_ratio that is not a single number above 0 and below 1 with a condition of class dmar_cost_ratio_invalid, which carries the value given.

One Notation for the Regression and Correlation Functions

The regression, correlation, and coefficient of variation functions now name the total sample size, the number of predictors, a planner’s planning values, and the desired width one way. No function is renamed and no result changes for a given model. The DMAR 1.0.x names are not accepted; Breaking Changes in 1.1.0, at the top of this section, lists every old and new name.

  • p is the number of predictors in the partial and semipartial correlation family, as it is in ss_power_R2(), ci_R2(), and ci_reg_coef(). var_partial_r(), var_semipartial_r(), expected_partial_r(), ss_aipe_partial_r(), ss_aipe_semipartial_r(), ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity() took J, the number of variables partialed out. They now take p, the number of predictors in the regression of Y on X and the variables partialed out, so p - 1 variables are partialed out, p is at least 2, and p = J + 1: a partial correlation of Y and X given two other variables was J = 2 and is p = 3. A categorical variable with a levels counts as a - 1 predictors. The degrees of freedom are then the regression ones: the raw-scale variance of a partial correlation divides by N - p, Fisher’s Z variance is 1 / (N - p - 2), the squared standard error of the t test of a semipartial correlation is (1 - R2_full) / (N - p - 1), and the planners return N = p + ceiling(z^2 V / h^2) for a half-width h. p holds the place J held, so a 1.0.x call that gave the count by position must add 1 to it (see Breaking Changes in 1.1.0). In the notation of a model comparison, q is the number of predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model (q = p_full - p_restricted, the predictors being tested) and the number of variables partialed out is p - q; a partial or semipartial correlation concerns one predictor, so q = 1 and p - 1 variables are partialed out. The help pages of the family and of ss_power_R2_change() say so, and ss_power_R2_change() reports a row q. No result changes for a given model.

  • N is the total sample size. var_partial_r(), var_semipartial_r(), expected_partial_r(), ci_r(), var_r(), expected_r(), equivalence_r(), ci_cv(), and var_cv() took n and take N, as ci_R2(), ci_R(), cv(), and the regression functions already did; ci_r() and ci_R(), which share a help page, now document one N. A size per group is n_per_group and a size per cell is n_per_cell; n alone remains only for one size per study or per plotted effect (meta_r(n = ) is a vector of study sizes). The second position is unchanged, so ci_r(.3, 100) runs as it did; ci_r(r = .3, n = 100) stops with “unused argument”. The other functions that took a total sample size as n take N too (var_alpha(), var_icc(), ci_proportion(), ci_eigenvalue(), and the rest of the table in Breaking Changes in 1.1.0). The divisor of ecvi() was n and is multiplier, because it is the multiplier of the fit function (N, or N less the number of groups), not always the total.

  • A planner names its planning value as its sensitivity function names the data generating value, true_X. The planner treats the value as the truth; the sensitivity function shows what the plan delivers when the truth (true_X) differs from the value planned with (supposed_X, which was estimated_X).

    The planners are ss_aipe_cv(), ss_aipe_R2(), ss_power_R2(), ss_aipe_r(), ss_power_r(), ss_aipe_partial_r(), ss_aipe_semipartial_r(), and ss_aipe_equivalence_r(); the sensitivity function ss_aipe_equivalence_r_sensitivity(), which took true_r and estimated_r, takes true_cor and supposed_cor. The planners for a regression coefficient take true_reg_coef_j (ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), ss_power_reg_coef(), ss_power_rc()) or, for the standardized coefficient, true_std_reg_coef_j (ss_aipe_src()) for the coefficient the plan is made for, and ss_aipe_cv() takes true_mean and true_sd where it took mu and sigma; the mean that ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() generates data from is true_mean, as in ss_aipe_mean_sensitivity(). ss_aipe_cv(true_cv = .25, width = .10, conf_level = .99) is the worked example of Kelley (2007, pp. 759–760; the call is printed on p. 765), which gives 99; with the exact noncentral t distribution the function returns 101 (see Changes to Earlier Results). The full-model planning value that ss_aipe_semipartial_r() gains in this release is true_R2_full. var_r(), expected_r(), and expected_partial_r(), which evaluate a formula at a population correlation, take it as true_cor (rho), the name in the planners, and var_R2() and expected_R2() take the population squared multiple correlation as true_R2 (population_R2), as ss_aipe_R2() and ss_power_R2() do; expected_R2() reports its value in the row expected_R2 (expected_value_population_R2), as var_R2() reports var_R2. The null value of ss_power_r() was rho_0 and is null_cor, as null_R2 and null_rmsea are the null values of their planners.

  • width is the desired width. ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() took w and take width, as their planners do.

  • true_cor_YX and true_cor_XX. ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity() and ss_power_R2_sensitivity() took rho_yx and rho_xx, the correlations their data are generated from, and take true_cor_YX and true_cor_XX, the names in the coefficient planners.
