  • Every population value of a coefficient planner carries true_. ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), ss_aipe_src(), ss_power_reg_coef(), and ss_power_rc() took rho2_Y_X, rho2_j_X_without_j, rho2_Y_X_without_j, sigma_Y, sigma_X, rho_XX, and rho_YX beside b_j or beta_j; each now has the prefix the coefficient has and names its quantity: true_R2_Y_X, true_R2_j_X_without_j, true_R2_Y_X_without_j, true_sd_Y, true_sd_X, true_cor_XX, and true_cor_YX, beside true_reg_coef_j or true_std_reg_coef_j. Cohen’s f squared was cohen_f2 in ss_power_R2(), ss_power_reg_coef(), and ss_power_rc() and is true_f2, the name of the row that reports it in ss_power_R2() and ss_power_R2_change(); the row of the two coefficient planners that holds its square root, Cohen’s f, was effect_size and is true_f.

  • specified_N in ss_power_r(). The sample size at which power is wanted was N and is specified_N, the name in ss_power_R2() and ss_power_reg_coef() and the name of the row the function returns.

  • The wrappers spell their arguments as the functions they call do. ss_aipe_rc() and ss_aipe_src() took Rho2_j_X_without_j and sigma_X_j and take true_R2_j_X_without_j and true_sd_X, the names in ss_aipe_reg_coef(); ss_power_rc() took Rho2_j_X_without_j and takes true_R2_j_X_without_j, the name in ss_power_reg_coef().

The row for the full-model planning value of ss_aipe_semipartial_r(), new in this release, is true_R2_full. A row that echoes an argument has the argument’s name, and one quantity has one row name: the desired width is the row width (seven planners and design_consequences() called it width_target or target_width), the expected width is expected_width (three planners called it ci_width_expected), and the null value of ss_power_r() is null_cor. necessary_N, specified_N, and total_N keep their names.

Power for the Change in R Squared When Predictors Are Added

  • ss_power_R2_change() plans the sample size for the test that predictors added to a regression model contribute nothing, the model comparison F test of a restricted model with p_restricted predictors against a full model with p_full, and returns the power at a specified_N. DMAR could plan the omnibus test of all predictors (ss_power_R2()) and, with fixed predictors, the test of one coefficient (ss_power_reg_coef()), and had no planner for a set of added predictors or for one added predictor when the predictors are random. The effect is given as any two of true_R2_full, true_R2_restricted, and true_R2_change, or as true_f2 alone. The change in R^2 is the squared semipartial correlation of the added predictor when one is added and the squared multiple semipartial correlation of the added set when several are; divided by one minus the restricted model’s R^2 it is the squared multiple partial correlation, and Cohen’s f^2 is that partial value divided by one minus itself, (rho^2 full - rho^2 restricted) / (1 - rho^2 full). The help page sets these relations out, with the error degrees of freedom of the two models in the notation of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027).

    With fixed predictors (random_predictors = FALSE) the test statistic is noncentral F with p_full - p_restricted and N - p_full - 1 degrees of freedom and noncentrality N f^2. With one added predictor that is the calculation of ss_power_reg_coef() (the two agree to 1e-8 on 81 combinations, and both give 50 for a change from .30 to .40 with five predictors and power .80), and with no predictors in the restricted model it is ss_power_R2() (agreement to 1e-12 on 54 combinations, both predictor models). For five predictors that explain .25 and four added predictors that raise that to .30, at an alpha of .01, the power at N = 90 is .2413 and the sample size for power .80 is 242, the values the G*Power 3.1 manual prints for that design (.241297 and 242).

    With random predictors, the default, the power comes from the distribution of the sample squared multiple partial correlation, which is that of a squared multiple correlation with the added predictors alone and a sample size reduced by the number of predictors in the restricted model (Gatsonis & Sampson, 1989, p. 518), computed with Lee’s (1971, Section 5.1) approximation as in ss_power_R2(). The same design needs 250, and the power at N = 90 is .2202. Against the exact distribution, the power by Lee’s approximation differed by at most .0043 over the combinations examined (squared partial correlations up to .95, an alpha from .001 to .10, and one or more error degrees of freedom) and by at most .0004 with 25 or more error degrees of freedom; the necessary sample size differed from the one the exact distribution gives, by one case, in 20 of 1,500 searches, and in those the power by the exact distribution at the size returned was within .0011 of desired_power. The same holds for ss_power_R2(), which shares the search. In a Monte Carlo with raw data (20,000 replications in each of twelve conditions, six with random and six with fixed predictors) the rejection rate under the null hypothesis was within 2.0 standard errors of alpha_level and the power within 1.9 standard errors of the value returned.

    Cohen’s (1988) noncentrality, f^2 (u + v + 1), is f^2 (N - w) for an increment with w predictors in the restricted model, where this function uses N f^2 for fixed predictors; Cohen’s value is the fixed-predictor call with no restricted model at a sample size of N - w, which the last example of the help page shows (noncentrality 6.071 and power .2225 where N f^2 gives 6.429 and .2413), and the necessary sample size by Cohen’s form is at most w above the fixed-predictor answer (247 against 242 in that design). The result has nine rows: necessary_N or specified_N, actual_power, noncentral_f_parm (NA with random predictors), true_f2 (the planning value of Cohen’s f^2), true_partial_R2, true_R2_change, q (the number of predictors removed from the full model to give the restricted model, p_full - p_restricted), df_1, and df_2.

  • A change of zero is refused with a classed condition. ss_power_R2_change() and ss_power_R2() stop with a refusal of class dmar_effect_zero when the planning values give an effect of exactly zero (no sample size gives a test of a true null hypothesis power above alpha_level); the message says what to give instead.

The Semipartial Correlation: Its Variance, Its Plan, and the Check of the Plan

  • var_semipartial_r() gives the first-order variance of a semipartial correlation, which depends on the full-model R2. Under multivariate normality, N times the variance of the sample semipartial correlation tends to (1 - rho_sp2)2 - q (1 - 2 rho_sp^2), where q is the full-model R2 minus rho_sp^2, the squared multiple correlation of the outcome with the variables partialed out. DMAR 1.0.x gave (1 - r_sp2)2 / (N - p), which is that variance only when q = 0. When the variables partialed out explain some of the outcome, the 1.0.x value is too large if rho_sp^2 is below 1/2 and too small if it is above: at r_sp = .3 with a full-model R2 of .59 the numerator is .4181 where 1.0.x used .8281, and at r_sp = .8 with a full-model R2 of .94 it is .2136 where 1.0.x used .1296. At r_sp = 0 the 1.0.x value was 1 / (N - p) whatever the R2, while the same function with R2_full = .64 returned .36 / (N - p - 1). The new argument under_null (default TRUE) chooses between the two quantities that need R2_full: under_null = FALSE returns the first-order variance with the divisor N - p, the quantity for a Wald interval and for planning, and the default returns (1 - R2_full) / (N - p - 1) as before. The help page now describes that default as what it is, the squared standard error in the t test of X’s coefficient, which equals the first-order variance at rho_sp = 0; it is not a variance for an interval about a nonzero r_sp. No value an existing call returned has changed. A call without R2_full returns what it did and now warns (class dmar_semipartial_r_no_R2_full) that the value holds only when the variables partialed out explain none of the outcome. An R2_full smaller than r_sp squared, which no data can produce and which 1.0.x accepted (the 1.0.x call var_semipartial_r(.9, 100, 1, R2_full = .10) returned .0093), is refused with an error of class dmar_semipartial_r_incoherent, a dmar_refusal, that says what to pass when the two values were rounded. The help page states the limits of the approximation found in simulation: it understates the variance when |rho_sp| is large and N - p is small, and the sample semipartial correlation is biased toward zero by roughly rho_sp (p - 1) / (2N).

  • The help pages no longer credit (1 - r_sp2)2 to Olkin and Finn (1995) or to Algina and Olejnik (2003). Olkin and Finn (1995) do not treat the semipartial correlation; their Model A is the difference between a squared multiple correlation with two predictors and a squared simple correlation, from whose delta method variance the result above follows for one variable partialed out (Alf and Graf, 1999, give the difference between two squared multiple correlations with any number of predictors), and the pages now say so. The Yuan and Chan (2011) entry leaves the references of var_semipartial_r(), since the sentence that cited it is withdrawn. Algina and Olejnik (2003, p. 317) are cited for what they state, that for the squared semipartial correlation the required sample size is largest when the squared multiple correlation of the restricted model is zero. The sentences that described the 1.0.x form as Fisher’s (1924) result applied by analogy, and as matching the leading 1/N behavior of the variance in Aloe and Becker (2012), are withdrawn; Aloe and Becker (2012) are cited for the effect size.

  • ss_aipe_semipartial_r() takes true_R2_full, a planning value of the full-model R2, and plans from the first-order variance at that value: N = p + ceiling(z^2 V / w^2), with V as above and w the half-width. For a planning value of .2, three variables partialed out (p = 4), and a width of .10, necessary_N is 714 with true_R2_full = .54, where the plan without it (and DMAR 1.0.x) gives

    1. The result gains a last row, true_R2_full, which is NA when none was given. Without true_R2_full the plan uses the largest V over every full-model R2 that is possible with true_r_sp, so the sample size is sufficient whatever that R2 is (see Changes to Earlier Results for the cases in which this differs from 1.0.x). The count of predictors must be a whole number, where the 1.0.x call ss_aipe_semipartial_r(r_sp = .3, J = 1.5, width = .2) had returned a necessary_N of 321.5. A plan with true_r_sp = 0 and true_R2_full = 1 is refused: the first-order variance is zero there.

  • ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity() simulates a population in which the variables partialed out can explain part of the outcome, through the new arguments true_R2_full (the population’s full-model R2; by default true_r_sp squared, the population 1.0.x simulated) and supposed_R2_full (the planning value passed to the planner). Under normality the distribution of the sample semipartial correlation depends on the population only through the semipartial correlation, the full-model R2, p, and N, so the two values describe every normal population. Its result gains the rows true_R2_full and supposed_R2_full. Each interval is now the Wald interval the planner plans for (see Changes to Earlier Results). In 20,000 replications of a plan for a width of .10, the intervals missed the true value in .053 of samples at r_sp = .8 with a full-model R2 of .94 (N = 331, mean width .0995) and in .051 at r_sp = 0 with a full-model R2 of .64 (N = 556, mean width .0998); the Monte Carlo standard error of each rate is .002. The pages of ss_aipe_semipartial_r() and var_semipartial_r() name two further conditions in which the interval misses too often: a full-model R2 near 1 with a small N, at any r_sp (.13 at r_sp = .1, a full-model R2 of .99, p = 4, and the planned N of 12), and |r_sp| above about .9 with variables partialed out that explain some of the outcome, where the misses fall mostly on one side even with several hundred observations (.064, .051 of it on one side, at r_sp = .95, a full-model R2 of .97, p = 2, and N = 395).

  • ss_aipe_partial_r() with assurance returns the smallest sample size that attains it, computed from the distribution of the sample partial correlation. At a given sample size the width of either interval the function plans depends on the sample only through r and narrows as |r| grows, so the interval is no wider than the target exactly when |r| is at least a value r* that the function solves for. The probability of that event is taken from the distribution function of the sample partial correlation, which under multivariate normality is that of a simple correlation from N - (p - 1) observations, written as an integral of a central t probability against a beta density (R’s noncentral t is an approximation above a noncentrality of 37.62, which plans for narrow intervals reach). The function returns the smallest sample size, at or above the one planned without assurance, at which the probability is at least assurance, and two rows are appended to the table: assurance and assurance_attained, the probability at the returned sample size. The search does not go below the plan without assurance, because below it the probability is not monotone in the sample size. DMAR 1.0.x multiplied the sample size by qchisq(assurance, df) / df, the step for an interval whose width is proportional to a standard deviation; here it gave too few cases when the correlation is large in absolute value and too many when it is small. With one variable partialed out (p = 2), a width of .10, and an assurance of .80:

    rho 1.0.x now attained now
    0 1586 1539 1.000
    .30 1318 1310 .807
    .50 902 915 .803
    .70 426 448 .804
    .85 135 151 .807
    .95 23 28 .805

    The page’s example (true_cor = .30, p = 3, width = .20, assurance = .80) returns 338, where it returned 344. In 16 further conditions simulated from regression data (20,000 data sets each, the variables partialed out by least squares; Monte Carlo standard error .0015 to .0025), the 1.0.x sample sizes delivered from .139 below the request to .145 above it (.711 for a requested .85 at rho = .80, and 1.000 for a requested .95 at rho = .20), and the sample sizes now returned from .002 to .012 above it, each within .004 of assurance_attained. At rho = 0 the plan without assurance already meets the width in every sample, and assurance adds nothing. No argument restores the earlier sample sizes.

  • ss_aipe_semipartial_r() with assurance finds the sample size by simulation, and takes G and seed. The width of this interval depends on two statistics, the sample semipartial correlation and the sample full-model R2, so the function simulates them: for each sample size tried it draws G (default 20,000) samples from a multivariate normal population with the planning values, through the entries of the triangular factor of the Wishart matrix that the two statistics depend on, and takes the share of intervals no wider than the target. It returns the smallest sample size found, at or above the one planned without assurance, at which that share is at least assurance. Three rows are appended: assurance, assurance_attained (the share in a fresh set of G draws at the returned sample size, which had no part in choosing it), and G; the Monte Carlo standard error of the attained share is the attribute assurance_mc_se. The answer has Monte Carlo error: without seed two calls can differ by a few cases (eight unseeded plans for one condition gave 252 to 254; 40 seeded plans of each of two other conditions gave 470 to 473 and 306 to 310, and the probability at the smallest of those sizes was .897 and .895 for a requested .90), and assurance_attained can fall below the request by a few of its standard errors (the standard error is .003 at the default G and an assurance of .80; in 200 seeded plans the lowest value was .009 below a request of .90). The sample size returned is therefore the one at which the probability is about the request, and assurance_attained is an unbiased estimate of the probability at it. Without true_R2_full the simulated population is the one the plan without assurance is made for (variables partialed out that explain none of the outcome when true_r_sp squared is at most 1/2, a full-model R2 of 1 otherwise). G and seed are checked and used only with assurance; G must be at least 100, because the step estimates a probability from those samples (G = 1 returned an attained assurance of 0 or 1). DMAR 1.0.x multiplied by the same chi square factor as the partial correlation planner. With an assurance of .80 (now with seed = 113):

    true_r_sp true_R2_full p width 1.0.x now attained now (fresh draws)
    .25 not given 4 .15 635 621 .802
    .30 .09 3 .20 344 337 .814
    .70 .49 3 .15 197 214 .808
    .85 .7225 3 .15 65 89 .798
    .80 not given 2 .10 219 370 .824

    (DMAR 1.0.x had no true_R2_full; it planned every row with variables partialed out that explain none of the outcome. In the last row, where true_r_sp squared is above 1/2, this release plans without true_R2_full for the full-model R2 at which the variance is largest, which accounts for most of the change from 219.) In 11 further conditions checked from data with ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity() (5,000 data sets each; Monte Carlo standard error .003 to .006), the earlier sample sizes delivered from .37 below the request to .02 above it (.530 for a requested .90 at a semipartial correlation of .90 and true_R2_full = .81; .574 and .623 for a requested .80 at .80 and -.70 with true_R2_full equal to true_r_sp squared), and the sample sizes now returned delivered .798 to .819 for .80, .854 to .858 for .85, .906 to .908 for .90, and .953 for .95. No argument restores the earlier sample sizes. The page still says that a plan whose sample size is small (a large |r_sp| with true_R2_full near true_r_sp squared) should be checked with the sensitivity function, because the first-order variance is too small there.

  • The count of variables partialed out must be a whole number in the seven functions of the partial and semipartial correlation family (var_partial_r(), var_semipartial_r(), expected_partial_r(), ss_aipe_partial_r(), ss_aipe_semipartial_r(), and the two sensitivity functions). A fractional count (J = 1.5 in 1.0.x) had been accepted and carried into the result. The count is now given as the number of predictors, p, a whole number of at least 2 (see “One Notation for the Regression and Correlation Functions”). The two sensitivity functions also check G (a whole number of at least 1) and specified_N (a whole number of at least p + 3 for the partial correlation on Fisher’s Z scale, whose interval needs N - p - 2 > 0, and p + 2 for the raw-scale interval and for the semipartial).

  • ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity() simulates the interval that was planned, and takes fisher_z. The planner plans the raw-scale interval, r plus or minus z (1 - r^2) / sqrt(N - p), unless fisher_z = TRUE; the sensitivity function planned that interval and then formed Fisher’s Z interval in every replication, so its pct_ci_less_width did not describe the plan. It now takes fisher_z (appended after filename), passes it to the planner, and forms the same interval in each replication; the raw-scale limits are not truncated, and the smallest sample size is p + 2 for the raw-scale interval and p + 3 for Fisher’s. The table carries the attribute interval ("raw" or "fisher_z") and prints a line that names the interval. For true_cor = supposed_cor = .70, p = 3, width = .20 (N = 103), 2,000 replications under set.seed(7): mean width .203, pct_ci_less_width .470, and non-coverage .046 in DMAR 1.0.0 (Fisher’s interval at the raw-scale plan, with J = 2), and .200, .516, and .062 now; with fisher_z = TRUE the plan is 107 and the three are .199, .521, and .050. No argument restores the 1.0.x results of this function or of ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity().

  • A full-model R2 that falls below the squared semipartial correlation only by rounding is accepted, with a warning. A semipartial correlation reported as .46 has a square of .2116, and the full-model R2 beside it may be reported as .21. The 1.0.x call var_semipartial_r(.46, 100, 1, R2_full = .21) (one variable partialed out, J = 1 by position) returned .00814433 in DMAR 1.0.0. The pair is checked in this release, since a full-model R2 cannot be below the squared semipartial correlation. A pair that two-decimal rounding can produce, R2_full + .005 >= max(0, |r_sp| - .005)^2, passes with a warning of class dmar_semipartial_r_rounded (fields R2_full and r_sp): var_semipartial_r(.46, 100, p = 2, R2_full = .21) returns .00814433, as it did (p = 2 is the 1.0.x count of 1 plus 1). What the warning says follows what is computed. The squared standard error of the t test (the default, under_null = TRUE) is (1 - R2_full) / (N - p - 1), which does not involve r_sp, so the warning says that the value uses R2_full as given. The first-order variance (under_null = FALSE), the planner, and the sensitivity function compute from the part of the full-model R2 that the partialed variables explain, which is then taken as zero, and their warning says that the variables partialed out are taken to explain none of the outcome. A pair further apart (R2_full = .15 with r_sp = .46) is refused as before, with the class dmar_semipartial_r_incoherent. The same rule applies in ss_aipe_semipartial_r() and ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity().

  • The variance on ?var_partial_r and ?ss_aipe_partial_r is named for what it is, and the variance of the semipartial correlation is credited to the article that prints it. The pages called (1 - rho2)2 / (N - p) the “Olkin-Finn (1995) asymptotic variance”. Olkin and Finn (1995, Equation 3, p. 157) give the first-order variance of a simple correlation, (1 - rho2)2 / N; the article has no variance of a partial correlation and no N - p form. The pages now say “first-order variance”, state that the sample partial correlation given p - 1 variables is distributed as a simple correlation from N - (p - 1) observations, and say that the divisor N - p is the package’s and differs from that at order 1/N^2; the message of var_partial_r() for too small an N reads “Need N > p for the first-order variance of the partial correlation.” ?var_semipartial_r and ?ss_aipe_semipartial_r name the first-order variance of Aloe and Becker (2012, Equation 4, p. 284), which they obtain from Alf and Graf (1999), with N - p in place of their n, and show that its numerator is the one the functions compute. No number changes.

The Order-Based Effect Sizes Share One Contract

  • vargha_delaney_A(), cliff_delta(), and probability_of_superiority_paired() read their observations through one check, and say what they will not order. The three statistics depend on the data only through the order of the observations. They accept numeric and logical vectors, and now ordered factors with the same levels in the same order, which are read through their order: a five-category item supplied as an ordered factor gives the value its integer codes give, and the value any increasing rescoring of the categories gives. A one-column matrix (the result of scale()) and a one-dimensional array (the result of tapply()) are read as the vectors they are, and Date and POSIXct vectors are ordered by their numeric values. vargha_delaney_A() did so before; cliff_delta() and probability_of_superiority_paired() refused logical vectors and dates (“must both be numeric vectors”) and now accept them. Infinite values have their place in the order in all three functions. When an infinite value was compared with an equal infinite value, cliff_delta() stopped (“missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”) and the paired function returned a table of NA; a single infinite value was already ordered correctly. Input with no common order is refused with an error of class dmar_scores_not_ordered, a dmar_refusal (see ?dmar_metadata): an unordered factor, an ordered factor beside anything else or beside an ordered factor with other levels, two difftime objects in different units or one beside anything else, a Date beside a POSIXct, and character, complex, list, and matrix input.

  • Missing values are removed and counted in all three. vargha_delaney_A() has always removed them group by group. cliff_delta() stopped on a missing value with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, and probability_of_superiority_paired() returned a table in which every row was NA, with no message. cliff_delta() now removes them group by group and the paired function removes every pair with a missing member. Each result carries the numbers removed in its n_missing attribute: c(group_1 = , group_2 = ) for the two-group functions (through the formula interface of vargha_delaney_A() as well), one count of pairs for the paired function. A conf_level that is missing or not a single number gets the worded error in all three; cliff_delta(x, y, conf_level = c(.90, .95)) stopped with “‘length = 2’ in coercion to ‘logical(1)’”.

  • A grouping factor with an unused level is accepted by the formula interface of vargha_delaney_A(). The two groups are the two levels observed with an outcome; vargha_delaney_A(y ~ g, data = d) with levels(d$g) of "a", "b", "c" and no row in "c" stopped with “Grouping variable must have exactly two levels.”

  • An estimated variance of 0 is reported the same way by all three, with a classed warning. The estimated variance is 0 exactly when the groups are completely separated (every observation in one group exceeds every observation in the other; for pairs, every pair favors the same member) or every observation has the same value. cliff_delta() already reported both limits at the estimate with a warning under complete separation. vargha_delaney_A(c(4, 5, 6), c(1, 2, 3)) returned A = 1 with limits [1, 1] and no warning, and probability_of_superiority_paired(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(4, 5, 6, 7)) returned NaN limits and no warning. All three now report both limits at the estimate and warn, with class dmar_interval_degenerate and a reason element ("complete_separation" or "no_variation"), that the limits are degenerate and are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage. The warning of cliff_delta() keeps its 1.0.x opening words through “completely separated (|delta| = 1)” and gains the class; cliff_delta() and the other two also warn when every observation has the same value, where the limits are both at 0 (0.5 for A and the paired probability). Each help page has a paragraph on the case.

  • The pairwise comparisons are computed from ranks, not from a matrix of every pair. vargha_delaney_A() and cliff_delta() built the matrix of all pairwise comparisons with outer(), about 36 bytes a pair. The placements and the proportions of pairs won, lost, and tied now come from the mid-ranks, minimum ranks, and maximum ranks of the pooled and the separate samples. The estimators, the variance estimators, and the tie conventions are the same, and the results agree with the earlier ones to rounding (see “Changes to Earlier Results”). With 6,000 observations per group, vargha_delaney_A() took 0.52 s and about 1,240 MB, and now takes 0.03 s and under 30 MB; cliff_delta() took 0.57 s and about 960 MB, and now takes 0.02 s and under 30 MB.

  • vargha_delaney_A() refers its test to Student’s t by default, and offers a studentized permutation test. The new argument test = c("t", "permutation", "z") chooses the reference distribution of the statistic W = (A - 1/2) / SE, which is the same under all three and is reported in the column test_statistic (z_value in 1.0.x, a name that is wrong under the t and permutation references; see the breaking changes). "t", the default, uses Student’s t with the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of the two placement variances, the Brunner-Munzel test as Schüürhuis, Konietschke, and Brunner (2025, Equations 7 and 8) give it. "z" uses the standard normal distribution, as DMAR 1.0.x did. "permutation" recomputes W over reassignments of the pooled scores to the two groups, with the arguments exact, n_resamples, and seed of randomization_test() and its rules: every reassignment when there are at most 50,000, random ones otherwise, and a p-value that is the share of reassignments at least as extreme in absolute value. The three arguments are read and checked only under "permutation". Two columns are added after the nine of 1.0.x, df and test; tidy() and glance() give them after p_value; the table records the reassignments in a resampling attribute and prints “Permutation test: all 252 reassignments” or “Permutation test: 10000 random reassignments”. The function reproduces the statistic 3.1375 on 17.683 degrees of freedom, p = 0.005786, of the pain score example in the help of lawstat::brunner.munzel.test(), and the estimate 0.8 and p = 0.0239 of Table 2 of Schüürhuis et al. The permutation p-value equals a brute-force enumeration in 400 small data sets with and without ties. The normal reference rejects a true A = 1/2 too often in small samples. At a nominal .05 with normal data (10,000 samples a condition for z and t, Monte Carlo standard error .002; 2,000 for the permutation test, standard error .005) the rates for z, t, and the permutation test were .086, .071, and .047 with 5 per group; .073, .056, and .047 with 10 per group; .090, .062, and .063 with 8 and 20 and the larger standard deviation, three times the other, in the smaller group; and .060, .052, and .046 with 20 per group. The permutation test is exact when the two distributions are equal and approximate when they differ in spread with A = 1/2. With completely separated groups it is the only one of the three that gives a p-value (2/252 for 5 and 5 untied scores). The help has the formulas, the table, and a paragraph on why the test and the logit interval can disagree. See “Changes to Earlier Results”.

  • Each refusal of input with no common order says why, what would have been computed, and what to supply. The class is still dmar_scores_not_ordered. For an unordered factor the message names the argument and shows the levels of the object and the codes R stores for them (“here the levels are high, low, mid, stored as 1, 2, 3”), says how the statistic would have ranked them, and gives the call that states the order. A character vector has a message of its own (“10” sorts before “9”); it was told only that it was of class character. An ordered factor beside anything else is told what the other group is and that the comparison would be of positions in a list of levels with scores. Two ordered factors with different levels are shown both lists and, where the two share a label under two codes, that label and its codes. Every message says “Nothing was computed.” The condition of an unordered factor or a character vector carries the argument at fault as arg. Each help page has a paragraph “What is refused, and why”, and ?vargha_delaney_A and ?cliff_delta an example: for the ratings low, mid, high, high against low, low, mid, high, the codes of the unordered factors give A = 0.406 where the ordered levels give 0.656.

  • The warning of an estimated variance of 0 explains the case, and states the limit Feng and Cliff (2004) give for it. The class is still dmar_interval_degenerate, and the reported limits do not change. The message now says what the two reported limits are, why a sample without overlap gives a variance estimate of 0, that this describes the sample and not the population, how large the samples are, what to report, and that the randomization test remains valid. For completely separated groups cliff_delta() and vargha_delaney_A() state the limit of Feng and Cliff (2004, p. 324, Equations 6 to 8), (n_b - z^2) / (n_b + z^2) for a delta of 1 with n_b the smaller group size: 0.131 at the 95 percent level with five in the smaller group, and 0.566 on the scale of A. That limit is not the one the functions report. The condition carries estimate, n, and limit_feng_cliff beside reason. The help of each function has a section “When the estimated variance is zero” that names every case and what is returned: complete separation, no variation, separation produced by infinite values, two constant groups, groups that only touch (an ordinary, wide interval), and, for pairs, wins with ties and fewer than three pairs.

  • A table whose limits are not a confidence interval carries the mark with it. When the estimated variance is 0 the three functions set the attribute interval_degenerate to "complete_separation" or "no_variation"; dmar_metadata() returns it in a field of that name; the printed table adds “Limits are not a confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0.”; and tidy() and glance() have a logical column interval_degenerate, so that a stack of rows keeps the mark. cliff_delta() and probability_of_superiority_paired() return tables of the classes dmar_cliff_delta and dmar_probability_of_superiority_paired (before dmar_tbl) for this. results_sentence() reads the mark; see “Changes to Earlier Results”.

  • The help of vargha_delaney_A(), cliff_delta(), and probability_of_superiority_paired() is rewritten in full. Each page states the estimand, the sampling unit, and the kind of interval; the assumptions; the estimator and the variance estimator with their formulas and sources; how the interval is formed; what each column or row is; what is refused; every case of a zero variance; and a reading of an example in words. ?cliff_delta states that the variance is the sample version of Feng and Cliff’s (2004) Equation 2 (p. 323), whose printed coefficients (n_1 - 1) and (n_2 - 1) are transposed, with the argument that shows it, and that their Equation 4 is not used; it no longer cites Cliff (1996) or says what other R implementations do. ?vargha_delaney_A no longer calls the DeLong, DeLong, and Clarke-Pearson (1988) estimator “the standard nonparametric variance (Brunner & Munzel, 2000)”; it says that Schüürhuis, Konietschke, and Brunner (2025) state the two estimators to be identical. The two pages show that their intervals are the same construction on two scales with different variance estimates: for 1:5 against 3:7, A = 0.18 with limits 0.034 and 0.576, which are -0.931 and 0.151 on the scale of delta, where cliff_delta() gives -0.64 with limits -0.935 and 0.177. ?probability_of_superiority_paired derives its variance as that of a mean of independent scores and no longer attributes it to Brunner and Munzel (2000).

  • randomization_test() gives the degenerate-interval warning under its own name. When the Cliff’s delta rows have no variation or the groups are completely separated, the warning of class dmar_interval_degenerate began “cliff_delta():”, a function the user did not call. It now begins “randomization_test(): for the Cliff’s delta rows (computed by cliff_delta()),”, with the same class and elements.

  • The examples of vargha_delaney_A(), cliff_delta(), randomization_test(), and randomization_test_paired() show the accepted call. The call that is refused is described in a comment and is no longer run under try().

Mediation: Resamples in Which the Indirect Effect Is Defined

  • mediate() codes its covariates once and decides in each resample whether the indirect effect is defined. The two regressions were refit in every bootstrap resample from a formula, so the columns of a factor covariate were recoded from the rows drawn. Three things followed, and each is repaired. A covariate category with few cases stopped the call with R’s contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or more levels whenever a resample held no case of it; with 2 of 60 cases in a category and B = 400 the call failed as a factor or a character covariate and returned 0.1857 [0.0644, 0.3222] as a 0/1 column. All four codings now return that table. A resample of this kind leaves the covariate column redundant, the paths a and b keep unique values, and the resample is kept; the new attribute "n_covariate_redundant" counts them. A resample in which a or b is not estimable (the predictor constant, or the predictor or the mediator a linear combination of the other predictors in the rows drawn) has no indirect effect. It is dropped and counted: the table has a new row B_used after B (the number of replications the interval rests on; B for the Monte Carlo interval, NA for Sobel), the attributes "B", "B_used", and "n_dropped" hold the counts, dmar_metadata() now records the bootstrap of a mediate() result, and the one warning has the class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped and carries B, B_used, and n_dropped. When too few replications remain the limits are withheld (see One Rule for Bootstrap Replications); through 1.0.x the call stopped when fewer than 100 remained. The interval then describes resamples in which the effect is defined; that is the package’s rule for a replication that returns no value, not a result that gives the interval its nominal coverage, and the help page says so. The decision does not depend on the units or the origin of a variable: a predictor with a large mean relative to its spread (x + 1e9) stopped with missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed and now returns the table of the unshifted predictor.

  • mediate(ci_method = "boot_bca") refuses the interval when it is not defined. The acceleration is estimated by the jackknife, which needs the indirect effect with each case left out in turn. When one of those was not estimable the value was removed without a word and the acceleration computed from the rest. The call now stops with an error of class dmar_bca_undefined (a dmar_refusal) that names the cases, and likewise when the bias correction or the acceleration is not finite; ci_method = "boot_percentile" does not need these quantities. This is DMAR’s rule for its jackknife acceleration.

  • mediate() takes column names as they are. The names given as x, m, y, and covariates were pasted into a formula, so a name was read as formula syntax. A column named predictor score stopped the call with a parse error and one named outcome$score with object 'outcome' not found; a covariate column named w^2 beside w was read as w a second time and the square left out of the model with no message (in the data of the independent check, N = 120, the path a was 0.831 where the model with the square gives 0.451); a column named w:x, I(w), or log(w) was evaluated as an expression and could use an object w that was not in data; and a column named . put every analysis column, the outcome included, among the predictors of the mediator. No name reaches a formula now, and every such column is the column it names.

  • mediate() says what it cannot use. A factor or character x, m, or y, and a logical x or m, stopped with subscript out of bounds; the message now says the column must be numeric and that a predictor with two categories is supplied coded 0 and 1. A logical y, which was read as 0 and 1, is refused with the same message (see Changes to Earlier Results). A one-column matrix, such as scale() leaves in a data frame, is read as its column, as before. A column named in two roles (x and m the same column, y among the covariates, a covariate named twice) stops with the name. An infinite value among the analysis variables stops with a message, as does a predictor that is constant or a linear combination of the covariates, and a model that leaves the outcome regression no residual degrees of freedom. A covariate with a single value in the complete cases, which stopped the call when it was a factor or a character column, is left out with a message. A Date, date-time, or time difference predictor is read as a number, as before; a mediator or an outcome of these classes, which stopped the call (“‘^’ not defined for”difftime” objects”), is now read the same way. B must be finite: B = Inf was accepted with ci_method = "sobel".

  • mediation_mbco() gives at most one warning per call for its Monte Carlo intervals. A call in which several effects lost draws gave one warning for each effect. It now gives one: of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient if the interval of any effect is withheld, otherwise dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped if any effect lost draws, otherwise dmar_bootstrap_exploratory. The message has one line for each affected effect and then the full account of the effect with the fewest usable draws, and the condition carries the data frame effects (term, B_used, n_dropped, formed, status).

Total and Partial Eta Squared and Omega Squared

  • eta_squared(), omega_squared(), ci_eta_squared(), and ci_omega_squared() take estimand = c("all", "total", "partial"). The default, "all", reports every estimand; "total" or "partial" selects one. These four functions replace eta_squared_partial(), omega_squared_partial(), and ci_eta_squared_partial(), which are removed (see One Function for Each ANOVA Effect Size for the call that replaces each and the columns of the tables).

  • Total eta squared and total omega squared. eta_squared() reports, beside the partial value SS_effect / (SS_effect + SS_error), the total value SS_effect / SS_total, with the corrected total sum of squares, and omega_squared() reports the total omega squared (SS_effect - df_effect MS_error) / (SS_total + MS_error) beside the partial value (SS_effect - df_effect MS_error) / (SS_effect + (N - df_effect) MS_error) (Olejnik & Algina, 2000, Table 10; Maxwell, Delaney, & Kelley, 2027, Eqs. 7.40 to 7.47). In a one-way design the two are the same number. For a fitted model the total uses the sums of squares of anova(); for an aovlist fit the total eta squared divides by the corrected total over every stratum, and the total omega squared, which is defined for designs whose factors are all between subjects, is NA.

  • Sums of squares from a published table. eta_squared() takes SS_effect with SS_total (the total) and SS_error (the partial); omega_squared() takes SS_effect, df_effect, and the error mean square (MS_error, or SS_error with df_error), with SS_total (the total) and N (the partial). SS_effect, df_effect, and F_value may hold several effects of one analysis, named for the effects, and the table has a row for each: the 2 by 4 table of Kim (2016, Table 3) is eta_squared(SS_effect = c(LIGHT = 34.716, MATERIAL = 1996.998, "LIGHT:MATERIAL" = 1570.389), SS_error = 2261.612, SS_total = 5863.715, df_effect = c(1, 3, 3), df_error = 72). Each interface takes exactly its own inputs: sums of squares with F_value, MS_error with SS_error, and a SS_total smaller than SS_effect + SS_error are refused, and so are summary statistics given with a fitted model (see Calls That Are Now Refused).

  • An estimand the inputs do not determine is NA, with the reason. An F statistic and its degrees of freedom determine the partial value only, since the total also depends on the design’s other effects. With estimand = "all" such an estimand is NA, the estimand_notes attribute gives the reason, and the console prints it beneath the table. Asked for by name, it is refused with an error of class dmar_estimand_undetermined, which carries estimand and reason.

  • The interval functions report the total where an interval exists. The noncentral F interval from an effect’s F is an interval for its partial value, which in a one-way design is the total, so ci_eta_squared() and ci_omega_squared() of a fitted one-way model report it for both. For an effect of a design with other effects, and for an aovlist fit, the total is reported with NA limits, and estimand = "total" is refused.

  • ci_omega_squared() takes an aovlist fit, computing the partial value of each effect and converting its limits with the size of its stratum, as ci_eta_squared() and omega_squared() do; through 1.0.x it took only a single-stratum fit.

  • results_sentence() reads an interval held in columns named for its estimate, such as eta_squared_partial_ci_lower and eta_squared_partial_ci_upper in a row of ci_eta_squared(). A row with one interval gives its sentence; for a row with two (a one-way model reports the same interval for the total and the partial value), term names the one to write. plot_ci() draws each estimate of such a table that has limits, labeling the rows with the effect and the estimand when there are two.

  • The estimand changes no value: every partial eta squared, partial omega squared, and interval is reported as the other entries of this release describe, under the column names of One Function for Each ANOVA Effect Size; the total values are new.

The Assurance Method of the Sample Size Planners

  • assurance_method in ss_aipe_smd(), ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_rc(), ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_src(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), and their sensitivity functions. With assurance it says how the planner finds the probability that the realized interval is no wider than width; without assurance it changes nothing. "analytic", the default, computes without simulation.

    • Where that probability has an exact form, in ss_aipe_smd(), ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_rc(), and ss_aipe_reg_coef() with its default noncentral = FALSE, the plan is the smallest sample size, not below the plan without assurance, at which the exact probability is at least assurance, and the row assurance_attained reports that probability. These plans differ from those of DMAR 1.0.x (see Changes to Earlier Results).
    • Where it has none, in ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_reg_coef() with noncentral = TRUE, and both intervals of ss_aipe_src(), the plan is the published approximation: that of Lai and Kelley (2012) for the ANCOVA contrast, that of DMAR 1.0.x and MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef() for the noncentral interval, and the chi square plan of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3) for the central interval for the standardized coefficient. It starts from this release’s plan without assurance (see Changes to Earlier Results) and draws no random numbers. It does not compute the probability it attains, which can be less than the request, so assurance_attained is NA, and the printed footer says so.
    • "simulation", offered only where the probability has no exact form, returns the smallest sample size, not below the plan without assurance, at which the probability estimated from G simulated samples, with seed, is at least assurance. It reports the estimate as assurance_attained, with the row G and the Monte Carlo standard error of the estimate as the attribute assurance_mc_se. The same samples serve every sample size tried, so the estimate changes smoothly with the sample size, and the plan can be a case or two from the one the probability itself would give.
    • Where the probability is exact, a simulated estimate would only add Monte Carlo error, and "simulation" is refused, with or without assurance, with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid (arg = "assurance_method") whose message names where it is offered: ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_reg_coef() with noncentral = TRUE, ss_aipe_src(), and their sensitivity functions, among them ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity() with noncentral = TRUE. Any other value is refused the same way, and an abbreviation is not matched.
    • The attributes assurance_method and assurance_probability ("exact", "simulation", or "not computed") and a line of the printed footer record how assurance_attained was found. The sensitivity functions pass the argument to the planner they plan through. In the planners G and seed are used and checked only with assurance and assurance_method = "simulation".

  • The exact probability in ss_aipe_smd() and ss_aipe_sc(). The interval is no wider than width when the noncentral t statistic falls between the two values at which the width equals the target. In ss_aipe_smd() the probability of that event is an integral of the normal distribution function over the chi square, which does not depend on R’s noncentral t; in ss_aipe_sc() it is the noncentral t probability, computed exactly (see Exact Noncentral t and Studentized Range Distributions). With equal tails it depends on the effect only through its magnitude. The plan is found by doubling a step upward from the plan without assurance and then bisecting. At true_smd = 0, width = .8, and assurance = .95 it is 50 per group (.994636), where the published plan of DMAR 1.0.x, 49, attains .949878, and at true_smd = 1, width = .5, and assurance = .99 it is 149 (.990260), where the published plan, 150, attains .994302. ss_aipe_sc() at true_std_contrast = 0 and c_weights = c(1, -1) gives the same 50. In 45 planning sets of ss_aipe_smd() (|true_smd| of 0 to 2, widths of .25 to 1, assurances of .80 to .99) and 96 of ss_aipe_sc() (contrasts of -1 to 2, weights for two, three, and five groups, widths of .5 and 1, equal and unequal tails) the plan is the smallest sample size found by raising the sample size one case at a time from the plan without assurance, and the probability does not fall at any sample size from that plan to ten past the returned one. With assurance, ss_aipe_sc() adds the rows assurance and assurance_attained to the one row DMAR 1.0.x returned.

  • The simulated step of ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), assurance_method = "simulation" with G (default 10000) and seed, returns the smallest sample size per group, not below the plan without assurance, at which the ci_sc_ancova() interval is no wider than width with at least that probability, for normal errors and a normal covariate distributed alike in every group. The probability is simulated from the exact sampling distribution of the five statistics the width depends on, so the covariate means term of the standard error and, with divisor = "s_anova", the sampling of s_ancova / s_anova enter it, which the published plan of Lai and Kelley (2012, pp. 358–359) leaves out. This is the a priori simulation Lai and Kelley (2012, pp. 360–361) gave for the ANOVA divisor. A contrast and its negative get the same plan. Sample sizes per group, with the probability that the interval is no wider than the width:

    standardized contrast, correlation, weights, width divisor assurance 1.0.x and the default of 1.1.0 "simulation", seed = 1
    .5, .5, c(1, -1), .5 s_ancova .80 129 (.772) 130 (.872)
    the same s_ancova .90 130 (.872) 131 (.933)
    the same s_anova .80 98 (.547) 104 (.842)
    the same s_anova .90 100 (.658) 106 (.906)
    .8, .6, c(.5, .5, 0, -1), .6 s_anova .90 47 (.691) 51 (.937)

    The simulated plan can differ by one from the smallest sample size at which the probability itself reaches the request (in the third row 103 already gives .803). With assurance, ss_aipe_sc_ancova() returns the rows assurance and assurance_attained (NA for the published plan) and, for the simulated plan, G; DMAR 1.0.x returned one row. In ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity() the draws of the simulated step come from the stream before the replications, so under set.seed() the replications differ from those of the default even where the two plans agree.

  • The plans of the regression coefficient planners with assurance. For the central interval for the coefficient in the units of the data, the plan of ss_aipe_reg_coef() with noncentral = FALSE and of ss_aipe_rc(), the probability is an exact F probability for random predictors from a multivariate normal population. For the standardized coefficient, the noncentral interval of ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE) and ss_aipe_src() and the central one of ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE), assurance_method = "simulation" estimates it from G (default 20000) samples of the exact Wishart sampling distribution, with seed. Given squared multiple correlations, which leave the correlation of Y with the predictor open, the simulated step uses the least favorable value. The plans, and what they attain, are in Changes to Earlier Results. In ss_aipe_src_sensitivity(), which now plans for the standardized coefficient at unit standard deviations, the default plan is the 1.0.x step only when the supposed variances of Y and of the targeted predictor are equal (for the noncentral interval, when both are 1; DMAR 1.0.x refused the noncentral plan otherwise): for true_var_Y = 4, true_cov_YX = c(.8, .6), and unit predictor variances correlated .3, supposed correctly, width = .3, noncentral = FALSE, and assurance = .9, it gives 181 where DMAR 1.0.x planned 657 (see Changes to Earlier Results). DMAR 1.0.x stopped with an error on every plan of the three sensitivity functions with one predictor, so there is no 1.0.x plan for such a call to return.

  • G and seed in ss_aipe_reg_coef() and ss_aipe_src(), for assurance_method = "simulation"; G must be a whole number of at least 100.

  • noncentral in ss_aipe_src(). TRUE by default, the noncentral interval for the standardized coefficient that ss_aipe_src() planned in DMAR 1.0.x; FALSE plans the central interval for the standardized coefficient of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 1), whose standard error is formed from the two sample squared multiple correlations: their plan for the expected width without assurance (Equation 2), with assurance their chi square plan (Equation 3) by default, and with assurance_method = "simulation" the smallest sample size that attains it, simulated as the noncentral step is.

  • New rows in the result of the three regression coefficient planners: assurance (the request) and assurance_attained (the probability at the returned sample size, NA for a published approximation) whenever assurance is given, and G when the step simulated.

Calculators Given Population Values or Sample Summaries

  • cohen_f(), ci_srsnr(), and covmat_from_cfa() say what they compute from each kind of input. Each computes the same quantity from population values or from sample summaries and estimates, its help page says what the result is in each case, and its arguments carry quantity names without true_ (see Renamed Arguments and the paragraph on these calculators under Old Names That R Still Matches). The values are unchanged: every call that still runs, with the arguments renamed, returns what it returned, and ss_aipe_reliability(), which builds its population covariance matrix with covmat_from_cfa(), plans the same sample sizes.

Exact Noncentral t and Studentized Range Distributions

  • The noncentral t distribution is computed exactly wherever R’s pt(), qt(), and dt() are not accurate. R’s pt() sums a series up to a noncentrality of 37.62 and returns a normal approximation beyond it (and beyond 400,000 degrees of freedom), which was off by as much as .14 with one degree of freedom, .008 with 38, and .001 with 1,000; below one degree of freedom it is not accurate even inside 37.62. DMAR now takes the probability, quantile, or density from pt(), qt(), or dt() where they are accurate (within 1e-9 of the exact probability up to a noncentrality of 37.62 with at most 2,000 degrees of freedom, and up to 33 with more) and otherwise from an integral of the normal distribution function against the distribution of the chi square (below one degree of freedom, against the standard deviation raised to the power df). ci_nc_t() and every interval and planner built on it, the critical values of cv_t(), the individual intervals of limits_of_agreement(), the power of the ss_power_*() planners whose test is a t test (of ss_power_indirect_effect(), only the power of the test of a with X fixed; its other powers average the noncentral t power over the sums of squares of its predictors) and of design_consequences(), and the likelihood of the Bayesian t tests use these routines. Inside the range of pt() the results are those of pt() and qt() (to 1e-13 for probabilities and powers). No warning about the range is given, since no limit is approximate. A limit outside the range takes about ten times as long to compute as one inside it: ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = 3, width = .3, assurance = .9) took 0.5 seconds and takes 2.1. Below one degree of freedom, should the integral or a search fail, the call stops with a condition of class dmar_computation_failed that names df. The values that change are in Changes to Earlier Results.

  • The studentized range is computed exactly wherever R’s qtukey() and ptukey() are not accurate. There cv_tukey_hsd(), ci_tukey_kramer(), ci_games_howell(), contrast_test(adjust = "tukey"), qbryant_paulson(), pbryant_paulson(), cv_bryant_paulson(), and ci_c_ancova_bp() integrate the probability integral of the range against the chi square distribution of the error variance, take each critical value as its root, and take the adjusted p-values from the same distribution function; elsewhere the values are those of qtukey() and ptukey(), as before. Where the exact computation is used and the values that change are in Changes to Earlier Results.

Teaching

  • A new vignette, “Classical Tests as Path Models in lavaan” (vignette("anova_as_path_model")), fits the single sample and paired t tests, the one way and two way analyses of variance (balanced and unbalanced), and the analysis of covariance as path models, and shows exactly where they reproduce the classical answers: a factor enters as a set of code variables tested jointly, and the likelihood divides by N where the classical test divides by the error degrees of freedom. It uses the depression_bdi and pygmalion data and draws its path diagrams with base graphics.
  • The reliability vignette shows alpha falling below omega on the four spatial tests of holzinger_swineford in place of the first five mtcars columns, which are not a scale. The tests are scored on different scales, so their raw-score loadings on one factor are far from equal and the sum of the raw scores carries that inequality; the vignette prints the test standard deviations, the loadings, and the fit with the loadings free and constrained to be equal, then standardizes the tests and shows alpha and omega nearly agreeing on the sum of the standardized scores, so the reader sees that tau-equivalence is a property of the composite as scored. A second example, labeled as hypothetical, simulates six items that each have variance 1, three loading .9 on the factor and three loading .1; the vignette computes the population alpha (0.626) and omega (0.718) from the loadings and then estimates both from a sample of 300, so the reader sees a gap larger than the spatial tests’ on items that already share one variance, where standardizing leaves the gap in place. The vignette no longer draws on a data set from outside the package.
  • Three more vignettes now use the package’s own data in place of base R’s. “Introduction to DMAR” (vignette("DMAR")) fits its one-way ANOVA, for omega squared and for the Tukey pairwise comparisons, to the drinks_trial outcome on its log scale in place of PlantGrowth, pooling the trial’s two cohorts and saying that the pooling is a simplification, and screens six spatial and verbal tests of holzinger_swineford in place of attitude, the same six its measurement model takes up. “Reading DMAR Result Tables” (vignette("dmar_output")) and “Visualizing Effect Sizes and Distributions With DMAR” (vignette("effect-size-visualization")) show their two-factor table, and in the second its forest plot, on pygmalion, expectancy condition crossed with grade, in place of ToothGrowth and warpbreaks. Both say that the rows come from sequential (Type I) sums of squares, which with these unequal cells differ from Type II or III sums of squares for the earlier terms, and point to the help page that describes how to supply those statistics. The visualization vignette also shows the bloomers’ advantage grade by grade, concentrated in grades 1 and 2, which the omnibus interaction spreads over 5 degrees of freedom.
  • The hypothetical example of the reliability vignette (six items, three loading .9 and three .1) is now a section of its own, “A Hypothetical Example: Items With Widely Unequal Loadings”, so it appears in the table of contents; its code and numbers are unchanged. “Introduction to DMAR” (vignette("DMAR")) shows anova_within() on pygmalion in place of nlme::Orthodont, with the pretest and the two follow-up IQ scores as three occasions of a within-subjects factor, reports the partial eta squared for occasion with its confidence interval from ci_eta_squared(estimand = "partial") on the same analysis fitted by aov() with an Error() term, and says that the analysis pools the two expectancy conditions. DESCRIPTION, the package citation (citation("DMAR")), the README, and the vignettes “Introduction to DMAR”, “Moving From MBESS to DMAR” (vignette("mbess_to_dmar")), and “Visualizing Effect Sizes and Distributions With DMAR” now describe DMAR in one phrase, as a more general and greatly expanded reimagining of MBESS. DMAR 1.0.x called it, in different places, a more modern, more general, and greatly expanded reimagining, the modern, more general reimplementation and expansion, and a modern and greatly expanded reimagining. The help pages of ci_eta_squared(), ci_omega_squared(), eta_squared(), and omega_squared(), which suggest car::Anova(object, type = 3) for Type III statistics, now say that Type III main-effect tests compare unweighted marginal means only when the factors are coded with sum-to-zero contrasts (contr.sum, set in the fit or with options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))), as the help page of car::Anova() warns, and that factorial_anova() applies that coding itself.
  • The README’s Related packages section gives the title of BUCSS as published, “Bias and Uncertainty Corrected Sample Size” (it read “Bias-Corrected Uncertainty Adjusted Sample Size”), and names its authors, Kelley, Anderson, and Maxwell.

Every Function That Draws Random Numbers Takes a Seed

  • Every function that draws random numbers takes seed. seed = NULL is now the last argument of the sensitivity functions that lacked it (ss_aipe_c_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_c_ancova_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_equivalence_r_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_icc_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_mixed_effects_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_omega_squared_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_r_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sm_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_src_sensitivity(), ss_power_R2_sensitivity(), ss_power_reg_coef_sensitivity(), and, described in their own entries, ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity()), of procrustes_phi(), of ss_aipe_equivalence_r() (whose assurance step is a simulation), and of the data generators simulate_ancova_data(), simulate_ancova_factorial_data(), simulate_longitudinal_polynomial(), simulate_longitudinal_gompertz(), simulate_longitudinal_logistic(), simulate_longitudinal_negative_exponential(), and simulate_longitudinal_richards(). Where a function ends in ..., seed follows it and is given by name. With the default every one of them draws from the caller’s stream exactly as before: for each of the 30 functions other than the six with entries of their own, a call under set.seed() returns the result it returned before the function had the argument, where no other entry of this release changes that result, and leaves the stream at the same point. A number makes the call reproducible, gives what set.seed() with that number followed by the call gives, and leaves the caller’s stream as it was. A seed that is not a single number is an error. For those six sensitivity functions the same holds wherever their results did not change for another reason (1,314 values of four of them compared under a common set.seed(), largest difference 0, every run of ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity() without separated replications, and, for ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity(), whose interval changed, the mean_smd, median_smd, and sd_smd rows and the stream after the call in 4 of 4 cases). In ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() the seed is set before the plan, so it also fixes the simulated assurance step of the planner. With assurance and assurance_method = "simulation", ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_src_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity() with noncentral = TRUE take that step from the caller’s stream when seed is NULL, so the stream after the call is not where 1.0.x left it; the default, "analytic", draws nothing for the plan. vargha_delaney_A() takes seed for its permutation test, and ss_aipe_semipartial_r(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_src(), and ss_aipe_reg_coef() with noncentral = TRUE for their simulated assurance steps.

Tests and Maintainer Tools

  • tools/release_checks.R fails when an export that can draw random numbers has no seed = NULL argument. tools/precompute_vignettes.R optimizes the PNG figures without loss after a knit, with oxipng or optipng when one is installed and otherwise, when python3 can import Pillow, with tools/optimize_png.py. That script rewrites a figure only when the new file decodes, with Pillow and with the script’s own decoder, to the values and channels of the original, and it copies the iCCP, eXIf, and pHYs chunks byte for byte; it leaves 16-bit images, APNGs, and files with other chunks (gAMA, cHRM, sRGB, sBIT, and others) as they are, and prints a line for each figure. The step says so when none of the three is available. The 42 vignette figures and man/figures/logo.png were passed through it: the figures went from 2,112,862 bytes as knitr wrote them to 1,380,358, and the logo from 90,909 bytes to 75,027. tools/doi_audit.py compares every DOI in the help with the metadata registered for it; tools/release_gate.R prints the number of references that disagree and does not fail on it.

  • tests/testthat.R runs every test file only when NOT_CRAN reads as true the way testthat’s skip_on_cran() reads it (isTRUE(as.logical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN")))), and the curated CRAN subset otherwise. In DMAR 1.0.0 any nonempty value selected every file, so NOT_CRAN = "false" (or "F", "1", "yes") ran the whole suite while skip_on_cran() still skipped its Monte Carlo blocks.

  • tools/release_gate.R runs R CMD check on the CRAN path whatever the shell that starts it has set: NOT_CRAN unset, TESTTHAT_CPUS = 2, and one thread for OpenMP, OpenBLAS, MKL, and vecLib, for the check’s process only. In 1.0.0 the check inherited the caller’s values: from a shell with NOT_CRAN = true and TESTTHAT_CPUS = 8, the check’s tests ran the full suite on eight workers instead of the curated subset on two, and the gate timed that run.

  • The release gate fails the full local test suite when a test was skipped, when a test file ran no test, when no expectation passed, or when the result cannot be read. A skip at the top of a file (eleven test files open with skip_if_not_installed() for lavaan or boot) leaves no result for that file, so the gate counts files as well as tests and its line says how many of the test files ran. It fails the oracle harness when a snippet was skipped, when none ran, or when the harness printed no summary line. In 1.0.0 only failures, errors, and warnings failed the suite, so an empty suite, a skipped test, and a file skipped from its top level all passed. Only a nonzero exit status failed the harness, and the harness exits 0 when an oracle package is missing (“oracle checks: 2 ok, 1 skipped, 0 failed” passed).

  • When every gate passes, the release gate checks the copy it hands off against the sha256 on its record and writes DMAR_<version>.tar.gz.sha256 beside it, in the form shasum -a 256 -c reads (the hash, two spaces, the file name). A sidecar an earlier run left there is removed first (emptied where the folder allows no removal), so a failed delivery leaves no sidecar that vouches for an older tarball. A copy that fails or does not match, or a sidecar that cannot be written, ends the run with status 1, prints “DELIVERY FAILED”, and rewrites the record’s Result line as “ALL GATES PASSED, DELIVERY FAILED; the hand-off is not certified”. In 1.0.0 the result of the copy was not read: with an unwritable or missing destination the gate printed “ALL GATES PASSED” and exited 0 with no tarball delivered, and no sidecar was written.

  • The release gate’s NOTE gate is named for what it allows: “no NOTE beyond incoming feasibility (new submission, spelling in DESCRIPTION, a URL server error that a re-probe clears) and HTML validation skipped by an old local HTML Tidy”. It reads each item of the feasibility NOTE against those three and fails on any other, naming it (an invalid DOI, a Title not in title case, a URL check that could not run, a CRAN URL not in canonical form). It allows the HTML manual NOTE only when its whole text is R’s message that the local HTML Tidy is too old. It lists every NOTE with its text, so a PASS shows what it tolerated; it judges a NOTE whose result R printed on a line of its own (after a network warning, say) with the step it belongs to; and a NOTE the Status line counts but the log does not show fails it. In 1.0.0 the gate was “no NOTE beyond new-submission and spelling” and passed the old-Tidy NOTE with no detail. It failed a feasibility NOTE only on five phrases (invalid file URIs, Non-FOSS, Insufficient package version, Size of tarball, Days since last update) or on a URL that stayed bad, so an invalid DOI, a Title not in title case, and a URL check that could not run all passed. It also passed an HTML NOTE that said math rendering was skipped as well, and, unlisted, a NOTE whose result was on a line of its own.

  • Both R CMD check gates of the release gate (no ERROR or WARNING, and the NOTE gate) fail when the check printed no Status line. Given a tarball that does not exist, R CMD check warns (“is neither a file nor directory, skipping”), prints no Status line, and exits 0. In 1.0.0 a check log with no feasibility step, that one among them, stopped the gate with the R error “‘from’ must be a finite number” before any record was written.

  • The timing limits of the release gate are raised. The whole check may now take 720/403 (about 1.79) times the accepted release’s local time, the ratio that projects 720 s on the r-devel Linux flavor of the CRAN farm, and the CRAN-path tests may take 60 s; the limits were 600/403 (about 1.49) and 30 s. The 1.1.0 candidate checked in 316 s locally (ratio 1.71), with the CRAN-path tests at 46 s; in 284 s (ratio 1.54, a projected 619 s) after the first trimming of the CRAN-path tests and examples; and in 250 s (ratio 1.35, a projected 545 s) after the cuts below, which take the CRAN-path tests to 16 files, prebuild the vignettes, and shorten twenty example pages, three of them for the second time. The anchors of the closed-form planners, added after those measurements, bring the subset to 40 files and add under a second to the CRAN-path tests. The gate still prints the 600 s line of the incoming pretest, which returned the package for overall check time on 5 September 2026, and says when the projection is over it.

  • On CRAN the curated test subset runs in one process and holds 40 of the 362 test files. The promised detectors (test-rd_hygiene.R and test-ss_sensitivity_filename.R) run whole. Fourteen files each carry a published-value or oracle anchor for one family, which pins the package’s numerics across platforms: the pinned MBESS values, metafor, multcomp, car, lavaan, Equation 5.14 of Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley, the example of Kelley (2007), for which the exact noncentral t gives the plans of 101 and 142 where the article reports 99 and 141 from R’s approximation, the exact noncentral t against its oracle, SIEVER’s recorded numbers, the published studentized maximum modulus, Yuan et al. (2016), Shrout and Fleiss (1979), Kelley and Rausch (2011), and Raudenbush and Liu (2001). Twenty-four more files each keep one block of a closed-form sample size planner (one that runs no Monte Carlo and fits no model) on CRAN: the G*Power 3.1 manual for ss_power_R2_change(), Kelley and Maxwell (2003) for ss_aipe_src() and ss_aipe_reg_coef(), the pinned plans of the published approximation of Lai and Kelley (2012) in ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), the exact probability of an ss_aipe_sc() plan computed apart from the package, the exact noncentral t past the range of pt() for ss_power_c(), ss_power_smd(), ss_power_indirect_effect(), and ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(), and, for the others, a closed form, a scan, or an integral written in the test file. Closed-form planners that no file of the subset tests are tested in the full local suite only, among them ss_aipe_c() against the 1.0.0 search over a grid (4.5 s) and ss_aipe_R2() against MBESS (0.2 s), whose blocks take more than 150 ms, ss_aipe_reliability() against lavaan, ss_power_equivalence_c() against the noncentral t, and ss_aipe_rc(), which calls ss_aipe_reg_coef(). In each anchor file but test-numerical-correctness.R, whose pinned values all run on CRAN except the ss_aipe_R2() search, the anchor comes at or near the top, and a top-level skip_on_cran() after it skips the rest of the file there with one skip; a skip_on_cran() inside a block costs about 8 ms under the check’s reporter, more than most blocks take to run. The per-family smoke files left the subset, and with them the published-value anchors of other functions (those of combine_p(), omega_squared(), and fleiss_kappa() among them). They, and every block the CRAN check skips, run in the full local suite and the release gate, which are unchanged. In the local check the CRAN-path tests take 5 to 6 s with 527 expectations, where they took 23 s with 4,678, and 47 s (93 s of CPU on two testthat workers) with 13,578 before the first trim. The \donttest{} detector collects the tags of the manual in 0.25 s rather than 0.7 s, with the same result on every page. The tests load lme4 only for the full suite. The release gate’s floor on CRAN-path expectations is the subset’s count, 527 (it was 2000), so a file that loses its anchor fails the gate.

  • The vignettes go to CRAN as prebuilt HTML. Every vignette has been a precomputed twin since 1.0.0, so the check ran no vignette code, but its step “checking re-building of vignette outputs” still rendered the 21 twins through rmarkdown and pandoc: 17 to 18 s of the local check, which win-builder has run at about three times the local time. tools/release_gate.R now runs tools/asis_vignettes.R on its archive of the commit before R CMD build. In that copy only, the script renders each twin by the call R CMD build makes, writes <name>.html.asis beside the HTML for the R.rsp::asis engine, and removes the twin and its figures. The check then copies the HTML instead of rendering it: the step takes 7 s locally (5 to 6 s of CPU) in place of 17 to 18 s (13 to 14 s of CPU). The HTML is byte for byte what the check rendered before, and the 21 vignettes keep their titles. Each vignette’s executable source, vignettes/<name>.Rmd.orig, ships in the tarball beside its .html.asis entry: it is the source that tools/precompute_vignettes.R knits to the twin from which the HTML is rendered. No vignette engine claims a file whose name ends in .orig, so R CMD build and R CMD check neither run nor render it, and vignette(package = "DMAR") lists the same 21 vignettes. The tarball is 1.5 MB smaller (7.2 MB against 8.7 MB), because the figures, and the twins’ markdown, no longer ship beside the HTML that holds them. A vignette’s source link in browseVignettes() now shows its R.rsp::asis entry; the twins are in the GitHub repository. The source tree keeps the twins, and its .Rbuildignore still leaves out the HTML and the .Rmd.orig sources, so devtools::build() (with R.rsp installed) and pkgdown work as before, and no rendered output is committed. R.rsp joins Suggests and VignetteBuilder. The gate fails in each of these cases:

    • the tarball’s vignettes/ holds anything other than one .html.asis entry and one .Rmd.orig source for each twin, or a shipped .Rmd.orig is not the committed one byte for byte;
    • an HTML in inst/doc is not the one rendered from its twin, or does not record the MD5 of its .Rmd.orig as committed;
    • the vignette index lacks a twin or its title, or lists anything else;
    • the check’s vignette step takes more than 10 s of CPU, which only rendering would take.

    A tarball built by hand goes through the same script, and the script’s header gives the commands.

  • Twenty-seven help pages run their examples faster than in the first builds of 1.1.0, every demonstration kept and each comment still giving the count a reported analysis deserves. They were trimmed in two rounds, ten pages in the first and twenty in the second (three in both); six of the twenty-seven are new in 1.1.0, and for the other twenty-one the earlier counts below are those of 1.0.0. The bootstrap and Monte Carlo counts are lower: ci_bifactor_indices() and reliability_omega() with B = 10 (were 50 and 40), mlmr() and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap() with B = 10 (were 20), ss_power_composite_sem(), ss_aipe_composite_sem(), ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity() with G = 10 (were 20), ci_eta_squared_generalized() with B = 100 under options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) (was 1000, the fewest it accepts otherwise), htmt() with B = 500 (was 1000), randomization_test() with n_resamples = 2000 (was the default 10,000), ss_aipe_reliability() with G_initial = 20 and G = 100 (were 50 and 200), ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() with G = 100 (was 200), and ss_aipe_c_ancova_sensitivity() with G = 25 (was 50); the permutation test of vargha_delaney_A() draws 2,000 reassignments, and the FIML check of ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() runs G = 3. Where a page fitted the same model twice to show two settings, one call now shows both: the per-factor descriptor call of fa_confirmatory() carries the equal loadings and its parallel call the tau-equivalent constraints, fa_exploratory() shows the target rotation on the ULS solution, the covariance matrix call of cfa_1() also names its items, the raw data figure of plot_smd() carries the group labels and the title, and the 90 percent limits of limits_of_agreement() use the individual method. Fits that feed another function skip what it does not use: point_estimates_only = TRUE in the factor_congruence() example, effect_sizes = FALSE in the df_missing() example, and a fit to the covariance matrix of the complete tests in the covmat_from_cfa() example. plot_trajectories() panels six children (was twelve), and now() waits a twentieth of a second (was a fifth). The examples took 36 s of page time, where they took 44 s in the first builds. The comments of the ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_pcm_sensitivity() examples no longer say that the share of intervals narrower than the target is about one half and that the mean width is at or under the target, which their output did not show, and the bias figures of ?ci_bifactor_indices say they are from the example run with B = 200.

  • The interval and the plans for the coefficient of variation are tested against values computed apart from the package. ci_cv() is checked against the interval Kelley (2007, p. 758) prints, against limits computed to 30 digits, and at each one-sided bound.
