The probability that the interval at an ss_aipe_cv() plan is no wider than the width is computed in base R from the noncentral t distribution, by integration over the normal variate: .5307 and .9966 at the two plans of the article’s worked example (101 and 142), and .7436 at a plan that the assurance step leaves below a request of .80 (5, where Table 1 prints 6). tools/kelley2007_table3_row.R reruns the five plans of the Table 3 row that shows a misprint, which take about six minutes of processor time (about two and a half minutes on five cores) and are not in the suite.

References in the Help

  • Every author-year mention in a help page now has its entry on the same page. A check of the release tooling parses every built page and finds the mentions in its text and examples (“Name (1970)”, “(Name, 1970)”, with chains of authors, et al., possessives, and particles such as von). The pages its first run flagged are fixed: ten gained the entries they name (cfa_1() and cfa_2(), for example, carry the seven estimator and interval references their inherited arguments cite), and on the others the mention was reworded instead (example comments that named the Holzinger and Swineford study now name the holzinger_swineford data, whose page carries the reference).

  • The five-group example of the noncentral F interval pages (ci_pvaf(), ci_snr(), ci_srsnr(), ci_eta_squared(), ci_omega_squared(), eta_squared(), and omega_squared(), and in 1.0.x omega_squared_partial(), now removed) and of the one_way_anova_power vignette, which 1.0.0 credited to Bargmann (1970) with his name spelled as Venables (1975) spells it, with one n, now spells it Bargmann; Venables, Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004) used the example in turn. Each of the seven pages gains the Bargmann (1970) entry, with its editors and pages, and the Venables (1975) entry, neither of which any of them carried in 1.0.0. The Fleishman (1980) entry gains its DOI, and eta_squared() and omega_squared() gain the entry itself. In the vignette the Bargmann entry gains its editors and pages, and Fleishman and Venables entries are added. A test pins ci_nc_F() to the .90 limits of Venables (19.381, 71.551) and of Steiger (19.380, 71.549).

  • The release tooling fails when a citation form corrected for this release appears again. It keeps a list of the wrong forms, each beside the form that replaced it, and first confirms that the pattern for each form finds examples of the wrong text and passes examples of the right. It then reads the R sources (help sources, comments, and messages), the help pages, the vignette sources, the tests, DESCRIPTION, the package citation, the spelling word list, and the README. The list holds the journal and subtitle of Kelley, Maxwell, and Rausch (2003), the title of the Steiger and Fouladi (1997) chapter, and the editions of Rencher and Christensen (2012) and of Anderson (2003) (all four under Changes to Earlier Results), the spelling of Bargmann above, and, on pages new in 1.1.0, the DOI of the Kiers (1994) entry and of the Saunders (1961) entry, the year and pages of Fieller’s (1941) insulin study, the equation number given for the incremental fit index of Bollen (1989), and the description of DMAR as a “reimplementation and expansion” of MBESS, replaced in the package citation, the README, and the MBESS vignette as described under Teaching. The list also holds seven forms corrected on 1.0.0 pages: the DOI of the Owen (1968) entry, the first page of the Phillips (1990) entry, and the pages of the Hofmann (1977) entry (all three under Changes to Earlier Results), the citation of Sokal and Rohlf (1995) for the expected value of the sample coefficient of variation, which is Expression 3 of Sokal and Braumann (1980), and the entries for Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), for Lachowicz, Preacher, and Kelley (2018), and for Tofighi and Kelley

    1. without their issue numbers.

  • ?ss_power_R2 credits the random-predictor approximation as Lee’s (1971, Section 5.1) three-moment noncentral F approximation. The help called it a two-moment Patnaik (1949) approximation; the code is Lee’s Equation 25, which fits three moments, and Lee (1971) does not cite Patnaik. The Patnaik (1949) reference is removed from the page. The pages of ss_power_R2(), ci_R2(), and ci_correlation() said the distribution of the sample R^2 under random predictors “is given by Lee (1971)”; Lee (1971, p. 117) credits it to Fisher (1928), and the pages now do, with Lee credited for the approximation they use.

  • ?vargha_delaney_A no longer calls the DeLong, DeLong, and Clarke-Pearson (1988) variance estimator unbiased. The estimator is consistent; it is not unbiased in general. Its expectation exceeds the variance of the estimate of A by a nonnegative term of order 1 / (n_1 n_2), which is zero when both variables take only two values; with three continuous observations per group from one distribution the variance is 7/108 and the estimator averages 8/108 (a test enumerates the 20 allocations). The page now says that A = 0.5 is stochastic equality (Vargha & Delaney, 2000, p. 102), which is weaker than equality of the two distributions, and that the reported test is of A = 0.5; cites Equation 14 on p. 107 for the rank formula, where it cited p. 109; says that the samples must be independent and points to probability_of_superiority_paired(); and says that the limits of cliff_delta() and of vargha_delaney_A() do not map onto each other exactly, since the two use different variance estimators. The sentence that credited Newcombe (2006a, 2006b) with showing better coverage for the logit interval is removed with its two references, as the claim was not verified against the papers; the page cites Pohar Perme and Manevski (2019, doi:10.1177/0962280218814556), who conclude that the DeLong variance estimator is reliable and that the interval should be formed on the logit scale. The Hanley and McNeil (1982) entry, which no sentence cited, is removed, and the DeLong et al. reference gains its DOI. ?cliff_delta says that its analytic interval is “valid in large samples” where it said “exact in the large-sample limit”.

  • The help of cv() describes the unbiased = TRUE value as Kelley (2007, Equation 4) does, as a nearly unbiased estimate, and no longer as unbiased or as a first-order bias correction, and its title is now “Coefficient of Variation (Sample Value or Nearly Unbiased Estimate)”. The page gives the expected value of the sample coefficient from Expression 3 of Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 51), which Kelley (2007) reproduces, in place of the expansion with the single term 1/(4N) that 1.0.0 credited to Sokal and Rohlf (1995), and it bounds the statement that the sample coefficient is biased downward: that holds when the population coefficient is below about one half, and above it the sample coefficient is too large on average. The multiplier (1 + 1/(4N)) is credited to Haldane (1955), as both papers credit it. The page now says what the multiplier leaves (a relative bias of about kappa^2/N - 9/(32 N^2), the second term derived for the page), gives the bias of both values at a coefficient of 0.1 and of 0.3 with 10 cases, and says that the corrected value is the more biased of the two once the coefficient exceeds about 0.35 to 0.4. The sentence that called the interval of ci_cv() “the McKay (1932) noncentral t based interval” and the comparison with Vangel (1996) that 1.0.0 attributed to Kelley (2007), which does not cite Vangel, are replaced: ci_cv() inverts the noncentral t distribution (Johnson & Welch, 1940; McKay, 1932; Kelley, 2007), and the chi square approximations of McKay (1932) and Vangel (1996) are ones it does not use. Where 1.0.0 pointed to “the corresponding asymptotic variances” in var_cv(), the page names the one variance that function returns, the first-order variance of the sample coefficient under normality. The sample coefficient is written k = s / M, as on ?var_cv and ?ss_aipe_cv, and the entry for Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) no longer points to Chapter 3. The page gains the Haldane (1955), Johnson and Welch (1940), and Sokal and Braumann (1980) entries and drops the Sokal and Rohlf (1995) entry, which nothing on it cites. ci_cv() describes its cv_unbiased row (c_of_v_unbiased in 1.0.x) as the nearly unbiased estimate, and the table of the mbess_to_dmar vignette describes ci_cv() as the noncentral t interval. No value changes.

  • DESCRIPTION no longer says that every estimation, inference, and planning function returns one data frame. Most do; the regression functions for incomplete data (mlmr(), mlmr_mv()) and a few others (correlations_test(), cov_fiml()) return a list suited to their task, as ?DMAR and the README already said.

  • ?ss_aipe_crd_es opens with what the six planners take and return, and its width argument is described as the width of the interval for the standardized difference (the text said unstandardized).

  • ?var_cv says where its variance comes from and how accurate it is. The 1.0.x page said the first row was McKay’s (1932) noncentral t based approximation, that Vangel (1996) showed the second gave better coverage, and that the first is what most planning tables use. McKay (1932) and Vangel (1996) give chi square approximations to the distribution of a function of the sample coefficient of variation, which ci_cv() does not use, and the variance the function returns is not taken from them. The page now gives the value as the first-order (delta method) variance under normality, kappa^2 (1/2 + kappa^2) / (N - 1), with its derivation. Expression 5 of Sokal and Braumann (1980, p. 52) without its third-order term is kappa^2 / (2 (N - 1)) + kappa^4 / N; the function has N - 1 under both terms, so its value is larger by kappa^4 / (N (N - 1)). The page states how close the value is to the variance of the sample coefficient under normality, computed with the sample mean kept away from zero: for a population coefficient of .30 or less and 10 or more cases it is too large, and the largest excess is 3.0 percent to one decimal place; at .50 with 10 cases it is 5.7 percent too small. It also states how far the value can be from the large-sample variance of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equation 30) when the population is not normal: in the limit it is 39 percent too large for a gamma population with a coefficient of variation of .80 and 56 percent too small for a Laplace population with a coefficient of .30. The page gains the Sokal and Braumann

    1. and Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018) entries, and its entry for Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) no longer points to Chapter 3. Its example prints the variance to six decimal places and sets its square root beside the standard deviation of simulated coefficients, for normal data and for gamma data. The argument and the row have new names and the second row is removed (see Renamed Arguments, Renamed Output Rows and Columns, and Changes to Earlier Results).

  • ?ss_aipe_crd has a title and a first paragraph that say what the six planners take and return (“Sample Sizes for a Cluster Randomized Design: Accuracy in Parameter Estimation for the Difference Between Condition Means”), in the words ?ss_aipe_crd_es uses for the standardized difference. No number changes.

  • ?ss_seq_c credits each part of the procedure to its source. The stopping rule is that of Chow and Robbins (1965) applied to a contrast, and the allocation of the groups is the cost-optimal allocation of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025, Theorem 1). The page credited the whole fixed-width procedure to the 2025 article, which plans for noninferiority and equivalence tests under a budget and has no fixed-width interval; ?ss_seq_c_sensitivity is corrected the same way.

  • ?mr_cv gains the entries for Bao (2009) and for Bao’s erratum to it, which its part on Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) cites, and it cites Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2017) and Kelley (2007), which the page listed without citing. ?mr_cv and ?mr_smd give the issue of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), 23(2); ?ss_aipe_indirect_effect and ?var_indirect_effect that of Lachowicz, Preacher, and Kelley (2018), also 23(2); and those two pages and ?ss_aipe_indirect_effect_sensitivity that of Tofighi and Kelley (2020), 25(4). Both minimum risk pages state the range of m0 and of gamma, and ?mr_smd describes A as the structural cost divided by the square of epsilon (it said that the maximum allowable difference was the square of epsilon).

  • ?ci_cv states that its interval assumes a normal population. The interval is exact for a random sample from a normal population with a positive mean and is not robust to departures from normality, which a larger sample does not repair: in simulations of the 95 percent interval (coefficients of variation of .3 and .5, sample sizes of 30 and 200) coverage was .81 to .85 for Laplace data, .90 to .94 for lognormal data, and .96 to .97 for gamma data. The page says when the upper limit is infinite and why that interval has the stated coverage, and describes the tail columns as the requested tail areas. Its references gain Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), whose large-sample interval the page mentions, and lose the Journal of Statistical Software article, which the page does not cite. ?ss_aipe_cv writes Equation 3 of Kelley (2007) as the approximation it is (Sokal & Braumann, 1980, p. 51, Expression 3; for a coefficient of .25 it is above the expected value of the sample coefficient by 3.1 percent at N = 5 and 0.1 percent at N = 20), and it and ?ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity say what the plans deliver for gamma and lognormal populations. On the three pages the pointers to Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027) name what they point to: Chapter 3 on confidence intervals for effect sizes, and on ?ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity Sections 3.9.1.5 and 4.9 in place of Section 3.5. No number changes.

Bug Fixes

  • Sizes given as R integers no longer overflow. R multiplies two integers as an integer, and the product becomes NA, with the warning “NAs produced by integer overflow”, once it passes 2^31 - 1 = 2,147,483,647: with 46,341 or more in each of two groups, and also with unequal groups such as 40,000 and 60,000. ci_smd(), ci_smd_c(), ci_mahalanobis(), convert_d_r(), convert_r_d(), convert_delta_lambda(), convert_lambda_delta(), cles(), nnt_from_smd(), proportion_of_superiority(), meta_smd(), ss_power_smd(), var_smd(), and bayes_independent_t() multiplied the two group sizes this way when they were given as integers (such as 50000L, or a count from length()), and plot_smd() and ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity() pass their sizes to ci_smd(). In DMAR 1.0.0, at 50,000 in each group and at 40,000 and 60,000, ci_smd(smd = .2, n_1 = 50000L, n_2 = 50000L), ci_smd_c(smd_c = .2, n_C = 50000L, n_E = 50000L), cles(), nnt_from_smd(), proportion_of_superiority(), and plot_smd(smd = .2, n_1 = 50000L, n_2 = 50000L) then stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, ci_mahalanobis() stopped with a message that its limits “could not be computed for the observed F-statistic NA”, meta_smd() with “Supply a positive sampling variance for each effect size.”, and bayes_independent_t() with “‘from’ must be a finite number”, while ci_smd() and ci_smd_c() given ncp, the four conversion functions, and var_smd() returned NA. ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_smd = .1, specified_n_per_group = 50000L, G = 3) (true_delta and n_per_group in 1.0.x), which uses its one size for both groups, stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, as it did with 46341L (with 46340L it gave its table). ss_power_smd() overflowed even with sizes given as doubles, since it turned a given size into an integer, and reported the power as NA. randomization_test() and plot_smd() count the group sizes of raw data as integers (randomization_test() with sum() of a logical vector, plot_smd() with length()), so they stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” for any data whose two group sizes have a product above 2^31 - 1 (46,341 scores in each group, or 100,000 and 21,475), whatever the type of the scores. The sizes are now multiplied as doubles, and the results are those for the same sizes given as doubles: ci_smd_c(smd_c = .2, n_C = 50000L, n_E = 50000L) gives the limits 0.188 and 0.212, convert_r_d(.2, n_1 = 50000L, n_2 = 50000L) gives 0.408, ss_power_smd(.02, n_1 = 50000, n_2 = 50000) gives the power .885, randomization_test() reports the standardized mean difference with its interval, plot_smd() draws the interval that ci_smd() gives for the sizes as doubles, and ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_smd = .1, specified_n_per_group = 50000L, width = .03, G = 3, seed = 1) gives the table of the same call with 50000 (mean interval width 0.0248). The specified-size paths of ss_power_reg_coef() and ss_power_R2() turned a size above 2^31 - 1 into NA (“NAs introduced by coercion to integer range”): in DMAR 1.0.0 ss_power_reg_coef(true_f2 = 1e-9, p = 3, specified_N = 3e9) (cohen_f2 in 1.0.x) returned NA for the power, and ss_power_R2(true_R2 = 1e-9, p = 3, specified_N = 3e9) (population_R2 in 1.0.x) stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. Such a size is now used as given: the first call gives the power .410, and the second .275.

  • krippendorff_alpha() gives alpha for 46,342 or more pairable values. It formed N (N - 1), where N is the number of pairable values counted with length(), as a product of integers, which becomes NA from N = 46,342 on (46,342 times 46,341 is 2,147,534,622). Take 23,171 units rated twice on three nominal categories, drawn after set.seed(7) as r1 <- sample(1:3, 23171, TRUE) and r2 <- ifelse(runif(23171) < .7, r1, sample(1:3, 23171, TRUE)). In DMAR 1.0.0 krippendorff_alpha(cbind(r1, r2)) summed the distances over all 1.07e9 pairs of values and then stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, after the warning “NAs produced by integer overflow”. The product is now formed as a double, and the same call, after the same sum over pairs, gives alpha .698 (D_expected .667), the values from the frequencies of the ratings.

  • The Paule-Mandel estimate of tau2 and the Q-profile interval for tau2 no longer depend on the units of the effect sizes. meta_es(), meta_smd(), meta_r(), and plot_forest() with method = "pm" found the PM estimate, and every estimator found the limits for tau2 and I2, by root searches that stopped within 1.5e-8 of the root in the units of tau2, a distance larger than tau2 for effect sizes in small units. For y = (-1, 0, 1) with sampling variances .01 the PM estimate is 0.99 and the interval 0.2611 to 39.49; for the same effect sizes times 1e-6 (variances times 1e-12) the estimate, divided by 1e-12, was 10.1 and the interval 101 to 101. The searches are now made on tau2 divided by the scale of the data, as the REML search already was, and stop at a distance relative to the root, so the results for effect sizes multiplied by c are those for the original ones times c squared (tau2 and its limits) or c (the pooled estimate, its standard error, and the prediction limits). For the 12 simulated studies of the package’s tests the PM tau2 was 0.0431063198 and is 0.0431063219; metafor at its default tolerance gives 0.04310566, so a comparison with its default output can differ in the sixth significant digit.

  • ss_aipe_smd() no longer passes on the warnings of R’s pt() in its assurance step. For a negative true_smd it asked pt() for the lower tail of a probability near 1 (15 warnings full precision may not have been achieved in 'pnt{final}' at true_smd = -1, width = .5, and assurance = .90). Each tail is now computed directly as a small probability, and those plans give no warning.

  • equivalence_smd() and ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity() give their intervals when the product of the two group sizes passes 2^31 - 1. The product of the two group sizes, stored as integers, overflowed R’s integer range (“NAs produced by integer overflow”). equivalence_smd() with integer n_1 and n_2, or with raw data, whose two sizes had a product above 2,147,483,647 (46,341 or more in each group, or 40,000 and 60,000) returned NA for the t statistics, the p-values, the limits, and equivalent; it now returns them (equivalence_smd(smd = .1, n_1 = 46341L, n_2 = 46341L, smd_lower = .2, smd_upper = .2) gives the limits 0.089 and 0.111). The sensitivity function, whose sizes are integers, stopped there with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” (at 54,112 per group, the plan for width = .02 at a 90 percent level) and now returns its table.

  • ss_aipe_equivalence_smd() and ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity() check their numeric arguments on entry. A missing, not-a-number, or infinite true_smd or supposed_smd, a missing or vector-valued equivalence bound, a specified_n_per_group that is missing, fractional, or below 2, and a missing width are refused with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid that names the argument. DMAR 1.0.0 stopped on most of these with R’s “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, refused an infinite planning value as “Required n exceeded 1e6 per group; check inputs”, and truncated a per-group size of 10.7 to 10 without a word.

  • reliability_H() with fit checks the covariance matrix of the estimates as the factor analysis tables do. Where that matrix comes from an information matrix that is singular in the directions the fit’s equality constraints leave free, the standard error and limits are NA, with the warning of class dmar_result_qualified that fa_confirmatory() gives for the same fit; a two-item factor uncorrelated in the sample with the other factor had H = .853 with a standard error of 533.8 and the interval [0, 1], with no warning. Where lavaan computed no standard errors, reliability_H() stopped with “argument is of length zero” and now returns the estimate with the same warning (the vcov_basis attribute is then "none").

  • The check of the information matrix in fa_confirmatory(), fa_bifactor(), fa_second_order(), and reliability_H() reads a fit with ceq.simple = TRUE correctly. Parameters that share a label then share one free number and carry no equality constraint, and the check took the information of the unconstrained parameters for that of the model, so models identified by their labels (a two-item factor with equal loadings, two groups with loadings equal by label, a group.equal fit) were reported singular.

  • fa_confirmatory() and fa_bifactor() with output = "standardized" and se = "none" return the standardized estimates, with the se, z, pvalue, ci.lower, and ci.upper columns NA; they stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. fa_second_order(), which returned the estimates without those columns, has them too.

  • bifactor_indices() no longer asks lavaan for the standard errors of the standardized solution, which it does not use, so lavaan’s warning “Could not compute standard errors!” no longer reaches the caller beside the Heywood warning of an improper fit. The indices are unchanged.

  • htmt() refuses blocks that are not disjoint sets of distinct items under distinct names. An item listed twice in a block, an item placed in two blocks, or two blocks under one name gave a ratio without a word: for nine simulated items whose blocks A = x1, x2, x3 and B = x4, x5, x6 give .615, listing x1 twice in A gave .544, placing x3 in both blocks .944, and naming both blocks A 1.533. These, and an item whose name belongs to two or more columns of data, are refused before anything is computed, with an error of class dmar_htmt_blocks_invalid whose reason element names the check ("repeated", "shared", "construct_names", or "data_names") and whose blocks and items elements name what is at issue. Disjoint blocks give the same ratios and bounds as before.

  • The standardized cluster randomized planners (ss_aipe_crd_es_*()) count and report the simulated data sets that give no usable interval, and pass on the warnings of their fits. The counts, the reasons, and the first error message are in the new attribute simulation (also read with dmar_metadata()) and on the printed line “Replications”; a warning of class dmar_replications_without_interval gives the counts when data sets failed, and a design at which no data set gave an interval, or at which an assurance cannot be reached, is refused with an error of class dmar_computation_failed, where the width had been NaN or the search had stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. The planners wrapped their search in suppressWarnings(); each kind of warning a fit gives is now given once, as a warning of class dmar_result_qualified that counts the data sets that gave it. A fit of optimizer status 0 or 1 is used, and any other status counts as a failed data set. The models are built with mxExpectationRAM(), mxFitFunctionML(), and mxFitFunctionAlgebra() in place of the deprecated mxRAMObjective() and mxAlgebraObjective(), with identical limits, and the socket cluster used on Windows is stopped however the simulation ends.

  • The searches of the standardized cluster randomized planners end. The search upward for the cluster size at a fixed number of clusters had no end when the width leveled off above the target. It now simulates cluster sizes up to 100 above the size the unstandardized difference needs (above its own start when that size is beyond 100,000) and never above 500 (a search that would start above 500 is refused with reason "cluster_size_beyond_reach", whose field lower_bound says whether the start is a lower bound on the size the target needs), and a width still above the target is refused with reason "width_not_reached", the narrowest width found, and its Monte Carlo interval. Three designs in a row with no finite width end either search (reason "no_finite_width"), and a call simulates at most 500 designs (reason "search_budget"); each is an error of class dmar_computation_failed. The two planners over both sizes pick the first of tied widths or costs, where a tie stopped them with an error from if().

  • The cluster randomized searches meet a budget or a width equal to the end of a bracket. A cost or a width equal to the target at the end of a bracket of the coarse search stopped ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 20000, cluster_size = 20, cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1), ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_budget(budget = 10000, n_clusters = 10, cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1), and the two width planners at the width of 1000 clusters of 20 (0.1216020) and of 100 clusters of 1000 (0.3557016) with “‘from’ must be a finite number” in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0. Each now returns 1000, at a cost equal to the budget or a width equal to the target; their ss_aipe_crd_es_*() counterparts share the budget searches. In a grid of 480 budget searches the 51 (number of clusters) and 29 (cluster size) that stopped now return a size, and no other result changed; in 1,152 cluster size searches from a width, at targets that are not the width of a design, no result changed. A width equal to the target inside a bracket also meets it now (see “Changes to Earlier Results”).

  • ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width() returns a numeric value column. The cluster size search gave the string “> 100000” for a number of clusters that cannot reach the width, which made the whole column character whenever one of the numbers of clusters tried could not: ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width(width = .5, cluster_cost = 10, individual_cost = 1, pr_treat = .5, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8) returned the strings “80”, “7”, “0.499131775130474”, and “1360” in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0 (the development versions also “0.5”, the width asked for). The search gives Inf internally, and the plan is the same numbers (80 clusters of 7, budget 1360), now numeric in the table and in tidy() and glance(): in 720 calls the number of clusters, the cluster size, and the budget are identical, and the width differs only where the development versions returned strings, by at most 2.5e-15 relative. Given back as width, the width a plan reports now gives that plan: ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_cost = 30, individual_cost = 1, pr_treat = .5, ...) plans 20 clusters of 10 for a budget of 800, and the string “0.994337792651072” that DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions reported for its width is below that width and, given back, gave 19 clusters of 13 for 817. Every cluster randomized planner returns a numeric value column. ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_width() refuses a width no cluster size up to 100,000 reaches with reason "width_not_reachable" (class dmar_argument_invalid, as in the development versions), the width the interval falls toward as the clusters grow as width_limit, and whether a larger cluster size would reach it; the message said only that the target was “impossible to achieve”. ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width() gives its refusal of a search whose unstandardized start is beyond 100,000 the reason "cluster_size_beyond_reach", with start = Inf.

  • The searches over both sizes no longer stop with an error from R. ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_budget(budget = 20000, cluster_cost = 1000, individual_cost = 1, pr_treat = .1, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8) stopped with “invalid ‘type’ (list) of argument” in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0, because no number of clusters it tried was within the budget, and pr_treat = .005 stopped with “wrong sign in ‘by’ argument”, because the floor of two clusters in each condition (400) was above the end of the search (200). Both are refused with reason "budget_infeasible" (20 clusters of 2 cost 20,040; 400 cost 400,800). In 720 calls of the budget planner the 92 that stopped this way are refused, and the 628 plans are identical. ss_aipe_crd_es_both_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_cost = 5, individual_cost = 1, true_es = .5, true_icc = .9, pr_treat = .5, G = 2, seed = 113) simulated one more cluster than the budget buys, with a cluster size of NA, and stopped with “invalid ‘times’ argument” in both; that design is no longer simulated, and the call returns 142 clusters of 2.

  • The documented variance pairs (between, ICC) and (within, ICC) plan in the six unstandardized cluster randomized planners. ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_size = 20, pr_treat = .5, true_var_between = .2, true_icc = .2) and the same call with true_var_within = .8, true_icc = .2 stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0; both return 18 clusters, as the other pairs do. The variances are resolved once per call, where they had been resolved at every number of clusters tried; every call with consistent inputs gives the same plan (36 calls over the six planners and six pairs, identical but for the string rounding of ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width() above).

  • mediation_mbco() refuses a joint hypothesis one of whose expressions adds no restriction to the others, before any model is fit, with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid (arg = "hypotheses") whose redundant and kept elements name the expressions. The degrees of freedom of a joint test were the number of expressions, so a repeated expression, a multiple or combination of others, or one that is 0 wherever the others are counted as a restriction: in the single mediator model fit to 100 simulated cases (seed 731), hypotheses = list(h = c("a", "a")) gave the statistic of "a", 4.980, with 2 degrees of freedom (p = .0829, where "a" gives p = .0256), and c("a*b", "b"), whose null set is that of "b", gave p = .0316, where "b" gives .00858. The rank of the Jacobian of the constraints at the unrestricted estimates, and points of the null set of the other expressions found branch by branch, find such an expression. c("a*b", "a*cp"), whose null set is a = 0 or b = cp = 0, is still tested with 2 degrees of freedom. See Constraints that add no restriction in ?mediation_mbco.

  • mediation_mbco() fits badly scaled variables in a rescaled metric. When the standard deviations of the observed variables differ by a factor of 1000 or more (the rule of lavaan’s rescale_data option), each variable is divided by a power of 2 near its standard deviation for the OpenMx fits, and every result is returned in the original metric; the divisors are in the new "rescale" attribute. The optimizers had stopped far from the maximum: with the seed-731 data, x multiplied by 1000, and m divided by 1000, the statistic for "a" was 1316.2 and is 4.980, the least squares value, and that of the indirect effect 7.56 and now 4.980.

  • mediation_mbco() fits the null model of a conditional indirect effect at a probe value branch by branch ((a0 + a1*w)*b is 0 where b = 0 or where a0 + a1*w = 0): in a first-stage moderated mediation of 300 simulated cases (seed 3812) the statistic at a moderator value of 1 was 37.294 and is 33.631, the smaller of the two branch statistics. When every branch fit is valid, the smallest is the constrained minimum and the constrained searches, which could end just off the null set, are not run.

  • mediation_mbco() reports the test of a total effect (and of other sums and differences of effects) where its null fit had failed (reported as NA with a warning in 10 of 100 simulated data sets of 150 cases with every coefficient 0). A constraint without branches is now also started from the full-model estimates moved onto its null set.

  • ?mediation_mbco states the conditions under which the likelihood ratio statistic has its chi square reference, and that the null hypothesis of no indirect effect is not regular where both coefficients are zero. There, in the single mediator model with observed variables, the test at the .05 level rejects with probability .05 squared, .0025, in large samples (between .0025 and .05 when the estimates are correlated), so it is conservative. The page gives this limit beside the rejection rates of .025 to .075 that Tofighi and Kelley (2020) report from simulations in which one coefficient of the indirect effect is zero, and says what each describes.

  • ss_power_reg_coef() and ss_power_rc() check p on every route: a single whole number of at least 1. p = 2.5 returned necessary_N = 47.5 (true_f2 = .2), p = 0 and p = -1 returned 47, and the route through true_reg_coef_j stopped with “argument is of length zero” when p was left out. Each is now refused with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid (arg = "p").

  • ss_power_reg_coef() and ss_power_rc() plan for a single predictor given through true_cor_XX and true_cor_YX. ss_power_reg_coef(true_cor_XX = matrix(1, 1, 1), true_cor_YX = .3, which_predictor = 1) stopped with 'a' is 0-diml and returns necessary_N = 93, the result of true_f2 = .09 / .91 with p = 1. which_predictor must be a whole number from 1 to p, true_cor_XX a correlation matrix, and true_cor_YX possible with it (a squared multiple correlation below 1); each is checked by name.

  • ss_power_reg_coef() and ss_power_rc() refuse at once a sample size for an effect of 0 when desired_power is above alpha_level, with a condition of class dmar_effect_zero, since the power is then alpha_level at every sample size; the search ran to N = 10,000,000 (about 40 seconds) and stopped with class dmar_computation_failed. An effect too small for any sample size up to 10,000,000 to reach desired_power is refused at once with that class. Both inherit dmar_refusal.

  • ss_aipe_reg_coef() plans for one predictor on the covariance structure path. true_cor_XX = matrix(1) with p = 1 stopped with “the condition has length > 1” (and, with true_reg_coef_j given, object 'b_j_tmp' not found); it now returns the plan of the direct path (327 for a correlation of .4 and width = .2), and p and which_predictor follow from a 1 x 1 matrix.

  • ss_aipe_reg_coef() and ss_aipe_rc() check a supplied true_reg_coef_j on the covariance structure path against the coefficient on the scale true_sd_Y and true_sd_X describe. With true_sd_Y = 2 and true_sd_X = 1 the correct coefficient .681 was refused and the standardized .341 accepted. The plan is unchanged; the refusal now gives both values.

  • ss_aipe_rc(), ss_aipe_src(), and ci_src() state the conditions of the function they call in their own argument names (for example true_std_reg_coef_j, not true_reg_coef_j, in ss_aipe_src()). ss_aipe_src() refuses true_sd_Y or true_sd_X other than 1 itself, saying that it plans for the standardized coefficient and ss_aipe_rc() for the unstandardized one; the refusal had spoken of ‘noncentral=TRUE’, which the user had not given.

  • ci_src() without a coefficient is refused by name, where it stopped with “argument is of length zero”; it takes the coefficient from t with its standard error, from t with R2_Y_X and R2_j_X_without_j, or from the three squared multiple correlations. The warning that a standardized coefficient is unusually large applies beyond 1.1 in either direction, not only to positive values. ci_rc() and ci_reg_coef() take reg_coef_j = NULL by default, for the routes on which the other inputs determine the coefficient, and ci_rc() reports that coefficient between its limits.

  • ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity() refuses a missing true_var_Y (with noncentral = FALSE it built a covariance matrix of the wrong size), a which_predictor outside 1 to p, and a specified_N that is not a whole number of at least p + 2.

  • ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() differs from DMAR 1.0.0 when the variances of Y and of the targeted predictor differ. For true_var_Y = 4, true_cov_YX = c(.8, .6), unit predictor variances correlated .3, supposed correctly, width = .3, and noncentral = FALSE, DMAR 1.0.0 planned 610 (657 with assurance = .9) and judged the intervals against .681; this release plans 156 (with assurance = .9, 181 by default and 171 with assurance_method = "simulation" and seed = 1) and judges them against .341. A call with one predictor and specified_N, which DMAR 1.0.0 answered, changes as well: with true_var_Y = 4, true_cov_YX = .8, true_cov_XX = matrix(1), and specified_N = 100 it judged the intervals against .8, where this release judges them against .4. With equal variances of Y and of the targeted predictor (unit ones, or every variance 4), whatever the variances of the other predictors, and two or more predictors, the calls without assurance and those with assurance and the default assurance_method return the 1.0.0 table, to rounding error, with the same draws at the same sample size, plan a case below 1.0.0 (156 and 181 here, 157 and 182 in 1.0.0; see Changes to Earlier Results). ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity() plan with the supposed standard deviations, as 1.0.x did (609 here without assurance and 672, the exact central plan, with assurance = .9, where 1.0.x planned 610 and 657), and need no such change; for their plans with one predictor see the next entry.

  • The regression sensitivity functions plan the calls DMAR 1.0.x refused. In ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() a noncentral plan (the default) from a supposed variance of Y or of the targeted predictor other than 1 was refused by DMAR 1.0.0 (“Since you’ve specified ‘noncentral=TRUE’, all variances should be one”); for true_var_Y = 4 and assurance = .9 this release plans 179 (176 with assurance_method = "simulation" and seed = 1). (DMAR 1.0.0 answered a call in which only a predictor that is not targeted has a variance other than 1.) DMAR 1.0.0 also stopped on every call of ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity(), and ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() that planned the sample size with one predictor, for either interval and with or without assurance (“argument is of length zero”, or, for a noncentral plan from a supposed variance of Y other than 1, the refusal above). This release plans these calls: for true_var_Y = 1, true_cov_YX = .4, true_cov_XX = matrix(1), width = .3, noncentral = FALSE, assurance = .9, and seed = 1, ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_rc_sensitivity() plan 178 and ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() 171 (159 with assurance_method = "simulation"), and the noncentral plans are 172 (165 with "simulation"). With true_var_Y = 4 and true_cov_YX = .8, ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() plans the same sample sizes, and the central plans of the other two functions are 639.

  • The upper quantiles of the intervals and plans of a regression coefficient, a contrast, and a correlation are taken in the upper tail. ci_reg_coef() with noncentral = FALSE, ci_c(), ci_r(), the central plans of ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), and ss_aipe_src() and the exact central assurance step of the first two, the simulated central step of ss_aipe_src(), ss_aipe_sc(), and ss_aipe_sc_ancova() formed an upper quantile as qt(1 - alpha, df) or qnorm(1 - alpha). 1 - alpha rounds a small tail area away, and it is exactly 1 for a tail of 2^-54 or less, where the quantile is Inf. That is how ci_c() and the central ci_reg_coef() returned an upper limit of Inf, and ci_r() a limit of 1 or -1, at a tail of 1e-20 in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0. Each quantile is now qt(alpha, df, lower.tail = FALSE) (or the qnorm() counterpart), exact at any tail. A tail that small is now refused (see Calls That Are Now Refused); above the floor the change is in the last digits at the usual levels and in about the eighth or ninth significant digit near the floor (see Changes to Earlier Results).

  • The help of the regression coefficient planners describes what they plan for. In ?ss_aipe_reg_coef, ?ss_aipe_src, and ?ss_aipe_rc, the plan without assurance was called the plan for the expected width. It is the plan for the width at the expected values of the two sample squared multiple correlations, which is not the mean width over samples, as Details already defined it. On the squared multiple correlations path, the noncentral and standardized assurance step was said to take the smallest probability over every value of the correlation of Y with the targeted predictor that the planning values allow, “so the sample size suffices whatever it is”. It takes the smallest over 21 equally spaced values across that range, an approximate minimum: between two of them the probability can be a little lower, and the plan a little short of the request. With p = 2 the two ends are the only possible values. The help also said the simulated estimate rises with N. The search assumes that it does not decrease, which held in every set checked, although single simulated intervals were wider at N + 1 in 3,208 of 95 million comparisons. No result changes.

  • ss_aipe_R2() plans for an abbreviated which_width. The function checked which_width with char.expand() and discarded the expanded value, so an abbreviation matched none of the three plans and the function returned NULL. In DMAR 1.0.0, ss_aipe_R2(true_R2 = .5, width = .15, which_width = "L", p = 5, random_predictors = FALSE) (population_R2 in 1.0.x) returned NULL, as did "F", "Fu", "Lo", "U", and "Up". It now gives 117, the plan of "Lower"; "F" gives 264, the plan of "Full", and "Up" gives 13, the plan of "Upper". An abbreviation is expanded as match.arg() expands it in the other planners whose which_width lists the three values.

  • cohen_f() refuses a specification it cannot read as one. It computes f from means with var_within, from eta_squared, or from sd_means with sd_within, and an argument of one of these given with an argument of another was ignored: in DMAR 1.0.x, cohen_f(eta_squared = .10, mu = c(1, 2)) returned .333, the f of eta squared. Such a call, one half of a pair given alone, n_per_group without means, a vector where one number is needed, and a missing value among means are refused with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid that names the arguments.

  • ci_srsnr() with means refuses df_1, df_2, or N that disagree with the group sizes, and group sizes that are not whole numbers. They were replaced without a word: ci_srsnr(means = c(94, 91, 92, 83), var_within = 67.375, n_per_group = 6, N = 100) ran with N = 24, and n_per_group = c(7.5, 8, 9) ran with 21.5 denominator degrees of freedom. var_within or n_per_group without means, which was ignored, is refused, and the refusal of equal group means (an F of 0) names means, not F_value.

  • omega_squared() returns a DMAR table of class dmar_anova_es, as eta_squared() does, so it prints with the package’s display and has tidy() and glance() methods; through 1.0.x it returned a plain data.frame.

  • omega_squared() and ci_omega_squared() accept F_value = 0 and report 0; through 1.0.x they refused it.

  • plot_ci() draws the estimates of ci_eta_squared_generalized(), where it plotted the midpoint of each interval.

  • ci_proportion() keeps every Wilson limit in [0, 1], with a lower limit of exactly 0 at 0 successes and an upper limit of exactly 1 at N successes. In floating point those limits came back a few units in the last place either side of 0 or 1 (as low as -5.6e-17, as high as 1 + 2.2e-16). Every other limit is unchanged. The Wald interval is not clamped.

  • ci_games_howell() gives limits and a p-value for a pair whose Welch degrees of freedom fall below 2, where R’s qtukey() and ptukey() return NaN. With groups a = (1.2, 2.9), b = (3.1, 5.5), and c = (4.0, 7.9, 6.1), the b - a pair (1.80 df) had NA limits and p-value and has [-7.516, 12.016] and p = .4499. With two groups the interval and p-value equal those of t.test(var.equal = FALSE) below 2 df as well. cv_tukey_hsd(), ci_tukey_kramer(), contrast_test(adjust = "tukey"), and qbryant_paulson(n_covariates = 0) likewise return the critical value below 2 error df (cv_tukey_hsd(.05, df = 1.5, n_groups = 4) is 10.189), and a critical value R’s qtukey() fails to find (qtukey(.25, 51, 32) stops with “convergence failed”) is computed as the root of the exact distribution function.

  • contrast_test() no longer returns NA standard errors when a group has a single observation, whose variance is NA in R though its weight in the pooled error variance is zero. For 20 groups of which two have a second observation (2 error df), the standard error of the “2 - 1” contrast was NA and is 0.2008, from the residual mean square of the one-way fit.

  • format_p() refuses a digits_p that is not a whole number from 1 to 324, with a condition of class dmar_argument_invalid; format_p(.123456, digits_p = 3.9) returned “0.123”. Its help page says that it formats and does not check its input. A refusal that names the value given shows it to 15 significant digits when 7 would show a different number (a digits_p of 1 + 1e-12 was named as “1”).

  • ci_sc() judges contrast weights by their values. It compared the sum of the positive weights with 1 by identical(), which also compares the storage type and every bit: c_weights = c(1L, -1L) or -1:1 stopped with “Please use fractions to specify the contrast weights”, and c(.7, .2, .1, -1) was refused while c(.1, .2, .7, -1) was accepted. ci_sc(), ss_aipe_sc(), and ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity() now apply one rule to the values of the weights (the positive values sum to 1 within 1e-8), with one set of messages, and weights given as text are refused with class dmar_argument_invalid (they stopped with “invalid ‘type’ (character) of argument”).

  • ss_aipe_sc() with assurance plans a negative contrast with unequal tails as its magnitude with alpha_lower and alpha_upper exchanged, since the ci_sc() interval at -t is the reflection of the interval at t with the tails exchanged. It kept the tails as given, so the interval could be too wide more often than the request allowed (see Changes to Earlier Results).

  • ss_aipe_sc_ancova() plans wide targets and correlations near 1. Its plan without assurance let the sample size fall below 2 per group, where the error degrees of freedom are 0 or below: ss_aipe_sc_ancova(true_std_contrast = .5, true_cor = .5, divisor = "s_anova", c_weights = c(1, -1), width = 3.6) did not return, and width = 5 with divisor = "s_ancova", or true_cor = .999 with divisor = "s_anova" and width = .5, stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. The plan is now at least 2 per group, and these give 2, 2, and 6, the smallest sample sizes that meet the widths (see Changes to Earlier Results).

  • ss_aipe_sc() and ss_aipe_sc_ancova() find the plan without assurance by doubling a step and bisecting, not by raising the sample size by one, so a narrow target no longer takes seconds or minutes, and a plan the 1.0.0 search did not finish, such as width = 1e-5 (about 3e11 per group), is returned. The plans of ss_aipe_sc() are unchanged: ss_aipe_sc(true_std_contrast = .5, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .01), 316,921 per group, took 3 seconds and takes under a second. ss_aipe_sc_ancova() starts the search at 2 per group, and some of its plans are smaller (see Changes to Earlier Results).

  • ss_power_indirect_effect() returns a sample size that attains desired_power in data drawn from the model it plans for. It took the power of each path test with the noncentrality fixed at the population standard error, as if the sum of squares of X were N and the residual sum of squares of the mediator given X were its expectation, and took the joint significance power as the product of the two path powers. In a study both sums of squares vary from sample to sample (that of the mediator in every design, since the mediator is measured, and that of X when X is measured), and the two tests are not independent, since the residual sum of squares of the mediator is the error sum of squares of the test of a and the predictor sum of squares of the test of b. So the reported power was too high: its plan of 65 for paths of .39 and power .80 has a power of .7675. The power of each path test is now its noncentral t power averaged over the chi square distributions of those sums of squares, and the joint significance power is the probability that both tests reject, computed given the residual sum of squares of the mediator, given which the two tests are independent; the plan is 69, with power .8010. The new argument random_predictors, TRUE by default as in ss_power_R2_change() and ci_R(), makes X random (normal), as when it is measured; FALSE fixes X by design, with variance 1 computed with divisor N (two groups of equal size, for example). The mediator is random under either setting, and the setting is recorded in the "random_predictors" attribute. The help said that the tests validated the result against raw-data simulation; the test then allowed a relative error of 6 percent, and it now requires agreement within four Monte Carlo standard errors, at the plan and at one case fewer, for either test and either predictor model.

  • The Sobel power of ss_power_indirect_effect() is the probability that the Sobel test rejects. DMAR 1.0.x referred |ab| / se_ab, with population standard errors, to the normal distribution. The first-order Sobel statistic that mediate() uses is t_a t_b / sqrt(t_a^2 + t_b^2), in the t statistics of the two paths; it is not normal with unit variance, and the approximation erred in either direction: at N = 96 with paths of .39 it gave .8026 where the power is .8818, so its plan for .80 was 96 where 84 suffice, and at N = 12 with paths of .6 and .5 and a direct effect of .2 it gave .3165 where the power is .1226. The power is now the probability that 1 / t_a^2 + 1 / t_b^2 is below 1 / z^2 under the joint sampling distribution of the two statistics.

    The probability is an integral over |t_a| that integrate() computes in pieces, and development versions of 1.1.0, which no release carried, computed it with three faults that are now fixed. First, they stopped with an error of class dmar_computation_failed whenever integrate() returned a piece with a roundoff status, as it does for pieces next to the critical value z that are worth almost nothing (less than 1e-45 in this call): ss_power_indirect_effect(.2, .1, specified_N = 10, alpha_level = .999, method = "sobel") stopped with “The power of the Sobel test at N = 10 could not be computed reliably: the numerical integral over the distribution of the path t statistics failed (roundoff error is detected in the extrapolation table).” and is .9983 (DMAR 1.0.x gave .9990; see Changes to Earlier Results). In a grid of 5,760 Sobel powers (alpha_level from .000001 to .99999, paths from .02 to .95, N from 10 to 1,000,000, X random and fixed) they refused 664, at alpha_level .995 (two, both at N = 1,000,000), .998, .999, .9995, .9999, and .99999, and a path near 1 brought the refusal to ordinary levels: ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .999999, specified_N = 10, alpha_level = .5, method = "sobel") was refused and is .7457. A piece with either roundoff status (“roundoff error was detected” or “roundoff error is detected in the extrapolation table”) is now accepted when its estimated absolute error is finite and at most its share of 1e-9 and its value is at least minus that share, so the power carries an estimated quadrature error below 1.2e-9; the largest such piece in the grid was worth 2.9e-19. A piece returned “OK” is accepted whatever its error estimate, as before. A roundoff piece over its share is refused with class dmar_computation_failed and the message “… failed (<status>, with an estimated absolute error of <e> against a budget of <b> for this piece). The joint significance test (method =”joint_significance”) does not need this integral.”; every other status of integrate() is refused as before. Second, at alpha_level of .99999 and above, the lower end of the integral can round to just below z, where the integrand was NaN: 40 of the 664, among them ss_power_indirect_effect(.95, .3, specified_N = 10, alpha_level = .99999, method = "sobel"), stopped with “… failed (non-finite function value).” and the warning “NaNs produced”. The Sobel test cannot reject at |t_a| <= z, so the integrand is now 0 there, and that call gives .999991. Third, with X random and |a| near 1, the density of |t_a| has a separate peak at each node of the distribution of the sum of squares of X, and integrate() stepped over some of them: ss_power_indirect_effect(.999999, .5, specified_N = 10, alpha_level = .5, method = "sobel") gave .3521 where the power is .5216, and the plan ss_power_indirect_effect(.999999, .5, desired_power = .52, alpha_level = .5, method = "sobel") stopped at ten million where it is 10. Once two neighboring peaks stand more than 2 standard deviations apart, which takes |a| above about .9, each peak gets pieces of its own. No call in the grid is now refused or warns, and none of 270 plans at alpha_level up to .99999 is refused (126 were). In the grid of 5,760 the powers that both computed agree within 3e-15. In a second grid of 2,520 powers with X random (|a| from .85 to .999999, b from .02 to .999999, N from 10 to 100,000, alpha_level from .001 to .999), of which they refused 130, the powers that both computed agree within 5e-14 at |a| up to .999; at |a| = .9999 they move by up to 2e-7, and at .99999 and .999999 by up to .23 and .97, and the plan ss_power_indirect_effect(.99999, .2, desired_power = .80, method = "sobel") moves from 9,418,685 to 9,418,684. The new values agree with independent integrals that share no code with the function to 3e-11 or better (alpha_level up to .999999, paths up to .999999), and with 2,000,000-draw Monte Carlo estimates within 4 standard errors in 360 settings with |a| from .9999 to .999999.

  • The Bryant-Paulson distribution with covariates is computed at large error df and with many covariates. From about 4 x 10^7 error df with one covariate (5.6 x 10^7 with six, 10^8 with 30), pbryant_paulson() returned about 0 (pbryant_paulson(3.7, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 4, df = 1e8) was 5.6e-25, where the probability is .956), and qbryant_paulson(), cv_bryant_paulson(), and ci_c_ancova_bp() stopped with uniroot()’s “f() values at end points not of opposite sign” or, at the edge of that range, returned a critical value that was too large (qbryant_paulson(.95, n_covariates = 1, n_groups = 4, df = 4.09e7) was 4.5327, where it is 3.6332). df = Inf stopped with “non-finite function value”. With 40 or more covariates the same failures began at smaller df: about 3 x 10^6 with 40 covariates, 10^6 with 150, 1.3 x 10^5 with 200, and 1.6 x 10^4 with 300. At large df the weight of the integral over the covariate shrinkage factor lies within a few multiples of sqrt(p / df) of one end of its range, where the quadrature over the whole range did not find it, and with many covariates the factors of the weight overflowed and underflowed apart. The integral now stops where all but 1e-15 of the weight lies, the weight is computed on the log scale, and with df = Inf the functions return the studentized range at infinite df, as they do with no covariates.

  • The help of seed in the standardized cluster randomized planners, mediate(), plot_mediation_mbco(), ci_eta_squared_generalized(), mediation_mbco(), ss_aipe_indirect_effect(), and measurement_alignment() says what seed = NULL does: it draws from the current random number stream and advances it. The help said that it left the generator’s state unchanged.

  • Help pages state what the code computes and attribute claims to their sources. Documentation only; no function, argument, output row, or value changed. ?ci_src and ?ci_reg_coef say that the standard error of a standardized coefficient treats the sample standard deviations as fixed (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, pp. 315–316), so it is approximate, and give the coverage of the intervals in simulations; ?ci_c_ancova_bp says how much wider the Bryant-Paulson intervals are than Tukey’s (84 percent with three covariates and 2 error df at alpha = .05); ?var_alpha attributes the N - 1 form to van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel

    1. and the N - 2 form to Bonett (2003), as the rows now do; and ?ss_aipe_pcm, ?irt_grm, ?irt_information, ?mr_cv, ?mr_smd, ?skewness, ?kurtosis, ?descriptives, and the pages of four power functions define their arguments, columns, and formulas. Statements the code, the data, or the cited source do not bear out are corrected or attributed on the pages of correlations_test(), ci_ratio_of_means(), ci_ratio_of_means_paired(), ci_smd(), expected_smd(), var_smd(), var_r(), expected_r(), ci_proportion(), krippendorff_alpha(), gwet_ac(), equivalence_c(), fa_confirmatory(), obrien_test(), manova_split_plot(), welch_t(), summary_t_test(), randomization_test_paired(), teacher_expectancy, prime_time_achievement, and holzinger_swineford, and ?DMAR and the pages of more than thirty functions and data sets describe the package without praise or unsupported claims (“modern”, “easy to use”, “the most general”, and the like).

  • Refusal messages state the requirement instead of the user’s error. ci_reg_coef() said “You have not properly specified ‘alpha_lower’ correctly.” and says “‘alpha_lower’ must be between 0 and .5.”; convert_R2_f() and convert_f_R2() say “Specify both ‘df_1’ and ‘df_2’, or omit both and specify ‘N’ and ‘p’.”; and reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() say that DMAR offers no ADF interval under that treatment of missing data, rather than that none exists. The condition classes are unchanged.

  • The vignettes, the README, and DESCRIPTION are corrected. Documentation only. Rd markup that pandoc left out of the HTML of four vignettes is Markdown now. The vignettes and the README no longer say that every ci_*() function inverts a noncentral distribution, that every plot shows a confidence interval and the sample size, or that every result is a data frame of term and value rows; their tables of argument names give the 1.1.0 names; they and the DESCRIPTION describe the package and MBESS in factual terms; and the README’s suggested citation gives the version as 1.1.0.

  • The refusals of ci_cv() name the argument at issue. With cv and no N, the condition’s arg is N, the argument that is missing. data given together with cv is refused with “Give either ‘data’, or ‘cv’ with ‘N’, not both.”, where DMAR 1.0.0 asked for the sample size. A mean or an sd that is not a single finite number is refused by name; ci_cv(mean = 5, sd = "a", N = 30) (n in 1.0.x) stopped with “non-numeric argument to binary operator”. A sample mean that is not positive has one message, whether it was given as mean or computed from data, which states the value and that the interval requires a positive mean and a positive standard deviation; it no longer asks whether taking the absolute value of the mean makes sense.

Changes to Earlier Results

  • ss_aipe_cv() plans on the expected value of the sample coefficient of variation again, as Kelley (2007) does. The method (Kelley, 2007, p. 758) evaluates the width at E[k | kappa, N] of the paper’s Equation 3 at each candidate sample size. DMAR 1.0.x evaluated it at the population value multiplied by (1 + 1/(4N)), the nearly unbiased estimate of Equation 4, which is above the population value where the expected value is below it. The cause is inherited: MBESS through 3.3.3 computed Equation 3 inside cv(unbiased = TRUE), which the planner called; cv() was later changed to the Equation 4 multiplier and the planner followed it without being edited. Of 34 expected-width conditions of the paper’s Table 1 the earlier value was the tabled one in 10 and one larger in 24; of 16 conditions with assurance .99 it was one to three larger in all 16. The function now returns the tabled value in 39 of the 50 (24 of the 34 and 15 of the 16), and 101 and 142 for the paper’s worked example (true_cv = .25, width = .10, conf_level = .99, without and with assurance = .99), where the paper gives 99 and 141 and DMAR 1.0.x returned 100 and 142. The tables were computed with R’s approximation to the noncentral t distribution, and the function now plans for the exact interval of ci_cv() (see the entry on that change below). The help states how the returned sample size relates to the expected width itself. ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(), which plans through ss_aipe_cv() when no sample size is given, changes with it.

  • The population coefficient of variation in ss_aipe_cv() is the argument true_cv (it was C_of_V), the name the data generating value has in ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(). C_of_V is not accepted. See Breaking Changes in 1.1.0.

  • ss_aipe_cv() with assurance is the published procedure of Kelley (2007), for any assurance strictly between 0 and 1. Two rows of the tables of that article show a misprint. Table 1, assurance .80, width .125, coefficient of variation .40 prints 127, between 69 and 122 in its row; the procedure gives 93. Table 3, assurance .80, width .010 prints 14,279; 28,321; 50,209; 38,120; and 82,817 for coefficients of variation of .30 to .50, which do not increase; the procedure gives 14,279; 20,475; 28,321; 38,120; and 50,209 with R’s approximation to the noncentral t distribution, with which the tables were computed. How the plans of the exact distribution compare with the printed values is in the entry on the exact interval below. The help page describes the step as it is computed: the search is run for the value of the article’s Equation 3 at the quantile of the sample coefficient, and applies Equation 3 to that value again at each sample size. With R’s approximation this computation gives the printed value in 524 of the 528 assurance cells (the other four are the misprints), where the search for the quantile itself, as the article’s text words the step (p. 759), gives it in 365. The result has one row, necessary_N, with or without assurance, as in 1.0.x. assurance had to be above .50 and may now be any probability strictly between 0 and 1; a value such as .50 asks that the realized interval be no wider than width in about half of the studies that could be run. A malformed assurance (a vector, a character string, NA) or one outside (0, 1) stops with one refusal, of class dmar_assurance_invalid, that states the value given, why neither 0 nor 1 is accepted, and what to give, where R’s own errors appeared. The procedure is a close approximation and not an exact search. With the exact distribution, in the 488 printed cells with an assurance and at most 5,000 cases, the probability that the realized interval is no wider than width at the returned sample size is .744 to .902 where .80 was requested (below .80 in 37 of 244) and .9916 to .9997 where .99 was requested, and away from the published tables it can fall below the request (.587 for a requested .60 with true_cv = .22, width = .09, and a 95 percent interval, where the function returns 57). The shortfall grows as the request falls toward .50: in 105 plans at 95 percent confidence the probability is below the request by at most .038 for .50, .036 for .55, .058 for .60, .032 for .70, and .001 for .80, and by nothing for .90 and .99; and a request of .50 returns one fewer than the plan without assurance in 12 of 15 plans (17 against 18 for true_cv = .05 and width = .0375, where the probability at 17 is .462). The help gives these numbers, and ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() estimates the probability for any plan by simulation.

  • ss_aipe_sm() takes any assurance strictly between 0 and 1. The assurance step plans for the value that the sample standardized mean exceeds in magnitude with probability 1 - assurance, the one-sample form of the procedure of Kelley and Rausch (2006, Equations 18 to 20 and 25 to 31), and that value is defined for every probability in (0, 1). DMAR 1.0.x refused an assurance at or below .50. A value such as .50 asks that the interval be no wider than width in about half of the studies that could be run, and a value below about one half returns a smaller sample size than the plan without assurance: for true_sm = 1, width = 0.5, and a 95 percent interval the function returns 93 without assurance, 87 at .20, 93 at .50, 100 at .80, and 105 at .90, where the probability that the interval is no wider than 0.5, from the noncentral t distribution, is .228, .519, .812, and .925. An assurance that is not NULL or a single number strictly between 0 and 1 stops with the refusal of class dmar_assurance_invalid that ss_aipe_cv() gives. No result for an assurance above .50 changes for this reason (the exact interval of ci_nc_t() changes a few plans by one or two; see the entry on the AIPE planners built on ci_nc_t()).

  • ss_aipe_cv() plans for the exact interval of ci_cv(), so it no longer returns every value printed in Kelley (2007). The noncentrality of the interval, the square root of N over the coefficient of variation, passes 37.62 whenever the interval is narrow, and the assurance step also takes the noncentral t quantile exactly where R’s qt() inverts pt() (see Exact Noncentral t and Studentized Range Distributions). The tables of Kelley (2007) were computed with R’s approximation. Apart from the four misprinted cells (127 in Table 1; 28,321, 50,209, and 82,817 in Table 3; see the entry above on ss_aipe_cv() with assurance), the function returns the printed value in 468 of 788 cells (the procedure computed with the approximation gives all 788), one to three fewer cases in 232, and one to three more in 88; it returns every printed value with a width of .125 or more at 90 and 95 percent confidence and 9 of the 120 with a width of .075 or less at 99 percent. The worked example of the article (true_cv = .25, width = .10, conf_level = .99) gives 101, and 142 with assurance = .99, where the article gives 99 and 141 and DMAR 1.0.x gave 100 and 142: at 99 the interval at the expected value of the sample coefficient is .1006 wide, and .0999 by the approximation. For true_cv = .10, width = .10, and 99 percent the plan is 20 (printed 19); for .05, .05, and 99 percent, 19 (printed 21). The help page’s numbers on the assurance step are recomputed with the exact distribution (see the entry above on ss_aipe_cv() with assurance). The warning ss_aipe_cv() gave when its search passed a noncentrality of 37.62 is gone.

  • ci_cv() no longer warns when its upper limit is infinite, and the tail columns at that limit hold the requested areas. DMAR 1.0.0 warned “The computed confidence interval does not have the same coverage as the specified confidence interval.” and reported prob_less 1 and prob_greater 0 on the upper limit. The interval does have the stated coverage. The upper limit is infinite when the square root of N over the sample coefficient is at most the 1 - alpha_upper quantile of the central t distribution on N - 1 degrees of freedom, and the infinite limit is part of the exact interval: in the 19,975 of 20,000 normal samples with a positive mean, for a coefficient of variation of .8 and N = 6, the upper limit of the 95 percent interval was infinite in 31 percent and coverage was .952, and with .5 and N = 5 it was infinite in 9 percent and coverage was .948. ci_cv(cv = 1.2, N = 6) returns 0.571 and Inf without a warning, with prob_less .975 and prob_greater .025 on the upper limit. No limit changes. The functions that call ci_cv() are quiet with it: ss_aipe_cv(true_cv = .45, width = .10, conf_level = .99) (C_of_V in 1.0.x), whose search starts at a sample size where the limit is infinite, gave the warning once in DMAR 1.0.0 and gives none, with the plan unchanged by this; and ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() gives one warning of its own for the replications with an infinite limit (see the entry on the replications it summarizes).

  • A fit whose likelihood has no maximum now stops, where DMAR 1.0.x reported a table or stopped with an unrelated error. When an error variance has run off below zero along a ridge of the likelihood, which is flat or still rising there, lavaan’s optimizer stops where its steps stop gaining and reports convergence, and DMAR 1.0.x reported that point’s estimates, omega, and fit rows, with a warning about a Heywood case. fa_confirmatory(), cfa_k(), cfa_1(), cfa_2(), measurement_invariance(), and measurement_alignment(), and the single-factor fits behind reliability_omega(), now stop instead, for every output, with an error of class dmar_no_maximum that prints the lavaan code of the fit (see “A factor analysis or structural equation model fit whose likelihood has no maximum stops” above). On three items whose correlations have a negative product (the sample of the reliability tests, population correlations .4, .3, and -.05, N = 300), DMAR 1.0.0’s cfa_1(), which deleted incomplete cases listwise by default, returned the table of the point where lavaan stopped, with an error variance of -1899 and an omega of 442; cfa_1(missing = "listwise") now stops. With that sample as one group and a sample of 300 from a population in which three items correlate .5 as another, DMAR 1.0.0’s measurement_alignment() aligned a configural fit that had stopped with a loading of 21.8 and an error variance of -475 in the first group and gave the second a factor variance of 1282; it now stops. ss_aipe_reliability() counts a simulated sample with no maximum as an interval wider than width, and ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() sets such a replication aside, whatever its error variances sum to; DMAR 1.0.x used the interval of the point where lavaan stopped. A bootstrap replication with no maximum, whose estimate DMAR 1.0.x used, is set aside and counted among the replications that raised an error. A finite negative error variance, at a maximum of the likelihood, is reported as before. ss_aipe_composite_sem(), ss_power_composite_sem(), ss_aipe_sem_path(), ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity(), and mediation_mbco() stop the same way when the fit they read their result from has no maximum: a planner’s fit of the analysis model to the population moments, or the lavaan fit from which mediation_mbco() starts its OpenMx fits. DMAR 1.0.x went on from the point where lavaan stopped. Given a lavaan fit (std.lv = TRUE, meanstructure = TRUE) in which those three items measure a mediator between two other variables, mediation_mbco() reported an indirect effect of -0.0000008 with a likelihood ratio statistic of 0; and for a single factor with free loadings fit to their covariance matrix, ss_aipe_sem_path() stopped with R’s “incorrect number of dimensions” and the composite planners said that the loading “gives no sampling variability”, errors that did not name the cause. A replication of the Monte Carlo of ss_aipe_composite_sem(), ss_power_composite_sem(), or ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity() with no maximum, which DMAR 1.0.x kept, is set aside as one that did not converge. ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity(), which reads only the chi square of its fits, is not checked, and its results change only as its own entries below describe (its default level and how its intervals are formed).

  • ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity() passes the arguments in ... to every fit, and ss_aipe_sem_path() adjusts its own fit’s plan for assurance. The arguments in ... go to lavaan::sem(). DMAR 1.0.x passed them to the planning fit to supposed_cov_matrix alone, so the fit to true_cov_matrix, which gives the population value of the path, and the fit to each simulated sample used lavaan’s defaults: with std.lv = TRUE, the path of the help’s population was planned in the metric that argument sets, where it is 0.577, and simulated and covered in the metric of a marker item, where it is 0.5. With an assurance, ss_aipe_sem_path() adjusted a sample size it read from a second fit of the model made without ..., so the plan under std.lv = TRUE was adjusted from the plan of the default metric; it now adjusts the plan of the fit it reports, with one population fit fewer. Results change only when ... is used, and an argument such as bounds = "pos.var", which the refusal of a fit with no maximum names as a choice, now reaches every fit.

  • measurement_invariance() refuses an item named twice in items. DMAR 1.0.x built the model f =~ y1 + y1 + y2 + y3 from items = c("y1", "y1", "y2", "y3"), which lavaan (0.7-3) reads as the three-item model f =~ y1 + y2 + y3, so the ladder described one item fewer than the call named. The call now stops with an error of class dmar_items_invalid (reason "duplicate"), as measurement_alignment() and fa_exploratory() refuse such items. Only items is checked for a repeat, since DMAR writes the model from it. An indicator repeated in lavaan syntax given as model is read by lavaan as one indicator, as before, and a named list given as model that names an item twice is refused as before, without the class.

  • fa_confirmatory(), cfa_k(), cfa_1(), and cfa_2() take the standard errors that match the estimator by default. se now defaults to NULL, which gives Huber-White (robust) standard errors under estimator = "MLR" and "robust.sem" under "WLSMV"; DMAR 1.0.x defaulted to se = "standard" and passed it to lavaan under every estimator but with ordered items, so its MLR standard errors were the normal theory ones beside a robust test (for the second loading of a verbal factor of three Holzinger and Swineford tests, 0.249 then and 0.213 now). se = "standard" gives the 1.0.x standard errors (checked against DMAR 1.0.0’s cfa_k(): identical).

  • fa_confirmatory() fits by full information maximum likelihood by default, as fa_exploratory() does, and cfa_k(), cfa_1(), and cfa_2() follow it. missing = "listwise" gives the listwise deletion that DMAR 1.0.x applied by default, and fa_exploratory() accepts it as well. With incomplete items the default now uses every case with an observed item, so the estimates, their standard errors, and N change. With complete data the estimates are unchanged, and for estimator = "ML" so are the chi square, CFI, TLI, and RMSEA; the standard errors come from the observed information, which lavaan uses under FIML and Savalei (2010) recommends with incomplete data, rather than the expected information, and moved by at most about 2 percent on the two factors of the examples. The item intercepts (nu rows) join the table, and AIC and BIC count them. With estimator = "MLR" FIML on complete data leaves the standard errors as listwise deletion gives them (DMAR 1.0.x took other ones under MLR; see the entry on se below), and the robust CFI and RMSEA are the corrected version 3 indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), named under the table. Ordered items, the least squares estimators, se = "robust.sem", and the Satorra-Bentler kind of test, which FIML cannot accompany, are fitted as before when no item value is missing; when values are missing they ask for missing = "listwise" (or "pairwise" for ordered items) rather than deleting cases unasked, and fa_exploratory() now treats ordered items the same way. The srmr row is the SRMR of the covariance residuals alone whenever the model has a mean structure (lavaan’s srmr_bentler_nomean, as sem_fit_measures() reports it), so the intercepts, whose residuals are zero, do not lower it. With auxiliary variables (lavaan’s aux under FIML) the srmr row is over the items alone: lavaan averages the auxiliary variables in, whose residuals are also about zero, and for the three-factor model of the nine Holzinger and Swineford tests with 40 values missing per item the SRMR of .068 fell to .062 with one auxiliary variable and .058 with two. A fit whose observed information matrix is singular reports no standard errors, with a warning, as a listwise fit already did; lavaan inverts such a matrix without complaint and gives finite standard errors for parameters that are not identified. fa_exploratory() and factor_count() record the FIML method as "fiml" rather than lavaan’s "ml".

  • cv_smm() is right at very small degrees of freedom. In DMAR 1.0.0, with df below 1 at conventional levels (below about .8 at an alpha_level of .05, and below about .6 at .10) or with df of about 2 or less and an alpha_level of .02 or less, its integral over the chi squared variate missed a sliver of the integrand by the origin: the call stopped with “the integral is probably divergent”, or, at df = 2 and alpha_level = .001, returned a critical value whose tail area was 1.5 to 5 times alpha_level (32.80 rather than 40.43 for two comparisons). Each root is now checked against the upper tail computed by conditioning on the maximum modulus instead, and found on that tail when the two disagree. Every value that was right is returned unchanged, bit for bit.

  • design_consequences(), sd_unbiased(), and var_ete() are right at a very large df or N. Each uses E(S)/sigma = sqrt(2/df) Gamma((df + 1)/2) / Gamma(df/2), the mean of a standard deviation on df degrees of freedom relative to sigma, or the variance 1 - (E(S)/sigma)^2 that goes with it. E(S)/sigma is below 1 at every df and about 1 - 1/(4 df) for a large one, but each function computed it as a difference of two lgamma() values that nearly cancel there. design_consequences() multiplies the width it would have with the standard error known by E(S)/sigma for mean_ci_width and expected_half_width, and by the square root of the variance for sd_ci_width. The factor was off by 4e-11 at df = 1e5, first reached 1 at df = 10810066, and was 1 or more at about half of all df above 1e8, which put mean_ci_width above the fixed width and sd_ci_width at 0. sd_ci_width lost more, because one minus the square of a number near 1 keeps only the digits the two do not share: it was off by 1e-12 at the 118 df of 60 per group, by 8e-6 at df = 1e5, by 0.1 percent at df = 1e6, and was 57 times its value at df = 1e9. No other row involves them, and at the df of an ordinary design the mean rows move only in the last digits (by 4e-15 at 118 df). sd_unbiased() divides by the same factor and returned s unchanged at N = 1e8 and .998 s at N = 1e12, where the correction is upward; var_ete() with covariate_value = "sd" uses the variance and moves by 2e-13 or less at a few hundred cases and by 3e-6 at N = 1e6.
