Both are now formed from the logarithm of E(S)/sigma, the mean as its exponential and the variance through expm1() of twice it. From df = 100 on the logarithm is its asymptotic expansion, and below that the expansion carried down two df at a time by an exact recurrence whose terms all have one sign, so nothing cancels at any df. Against a 320-bit evaluation, both are right to a few units in the last place: over some 490,000 df from 0.05 to 1e15, the largest relative error found is 5.5e-16, about 2.5 times the machine epsilon. E(S)/sigma is never above 1, and it never decreases as df grows on grids as fine as 1e-13 apart, including across every even df from 2 to 100, where the computation changes form; from one double to the next it can step back by a unit in the last place, as any value computed with a rounding error can. ss_aipe_mean() and ss_aipe_two_phase(), both new in this release, use the same factor.

  • expected_r() and expected_partial_r() are right at a very large N. E[r] = rho 2F1(1/2, 1/2; (N + 1)/2; rho^2) Gamma(N/2)^2 / {Gamma((N - 1)/2) Gamma((N + 1)/2)}, and the gamma ratio is the square of E(S)/sigma on N - 1 df (the entry above). expected_r() formed it from three lgamma() values that nearly cancel at a large N, and it was off by 1e-11 at N = 1e5 and 1e-7 at N = 1e8. The bias rho - E[r] is only about rho (1 - rho^2) / (2N), so its error was larger in proportion: at rho = .5 the bias column was 0.2 percent too small at N = 1e6, 26 percent too large at N = 1e7, 31 times its value at N = 1e8, and of the wrong sign at N = 3e8, where E[r] came out above rho. The ratio now comes from the logarithm in the entry above, and the bias and relative_bias columns are formed directly rather than from rho - E[r]: relative_bias is one minus the product of the series and the ratio, formed from their logarithms, and bias is rho times it. The difference rho - E[r] keeps only the digits the two do not share, and with the ratio right to a few units in the last place it is still off by 3e-7, relative, at N = 1e8. Against a 320-bit evaluation the bias is now right to 2e-14, relative, for |rho| of .9 or less at N from 4 to 1e12. So that the series carries the digits the bias needs, the option DMAR.expected_r.tol now stops the sum once a term is below that fraction of the sum of the terms after the leading 1, rather than of the whole series, and the sum can run to more terms than in 1.0.x; the non-convergence warning still compares the last term with the whole sum, so it is given where it was. At N of 1000 or less, E[r] moves by less than 2e-12, relative. A rho so small that rho^2 is 0 in double precision, below about 1.6e-162, gave E[r] = 0 and a relative_bias of 1; it now gives E[r] = rho c4(N)^2. expected_partial_r() calls expected_r() at N - (p - 1) and moves with it.

  • manova_split_plot() tests the within-subjects main effect averaged over the groups, as Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027, Section 14.6) do. The default Type III B rows test whether the grand means of the within-subjects contrasts are zero. DMAR 1.0.x fitted the between-subjects factor under R’s default treatment coding, in which the intercept that Type III tests is the first group’s mean of each contrast, so its B rows were the simple effect of the within-subjects factor in the first group, tested against the error matrix pooled over the groups (the book’s Equation 14.66), rather than the main effect. The factor is now coded with sum-to-zero contrasts whatever options("contrasts") says, so Type III tests the unweighted grand means, which the book prefers and notes that SAS and SPSS test by default (Section 14.6.9 and note 6 of Chapter 14), and ss_type = 2 tests the weighted grand means, in which each group counts in proportion to its size. On the reaction times of the book’s Table 14.9 (10 young and 10 old participants at angles of 0, 4, and 8 degrees), DMAR 1.0.0 gave F(2, 17) = 36.22 for angle, the value the book reports for the simple effect of angle among the young participants (Equation 14.66, p. 810); the book’s angle main effect, F(2, 17) = 110.65 (Equation 14.54, p. 798), is what the function now returns. With only the 0 and 8 degree conditions (Table 14.7), DMAR 1.0.0 gave F(1, 18) = 75.77 where the book gives 233.41 (p. 792). The A and interaction rows are as before, as is every row under ss_type = 2, since none of them depends on the coding. The B rows were already the main effect whenever the contrasts in force for the between-subjects factor summed to zero: for an ordered factor under the default ordered coding, contr.poly, and for an unordered factor when options("contrasts") named contr.sum or contr.helmert. Under contr.SAS they were the simple effect in the last group. No argument gives the 1.0.x B rows. They are the Time rows of the call DMAR 1.0.x made under R’s default contrasts, car::Anova(lm(Y ~ g), idata = data.frame(Time = factor(within, levels = within)), idesign = ~ Time, type = 3), with Y the matrix of the within columns and g the between-subjects factor. The help no longer says that Types II and III coincide for a single between-subjects factor: they give the same tests of A and of the interaction, and the same test of B only when the groups are of equal size. The model is now fitted to objects of its own, so a between-subjects column named Time, for which DMAR 1.0.x reported the test of A in the B rows, is handled like any other, as are a between-subjects column named Y or with a name that is not syntactic and a within-subjects column named Y, with which it stopped with an error. The function no longer passes on car’s warning HF eps > 1 treated as 1, which comes from the univariate tests it does not report.

  • reliability_omega(), reliability_alpha(), reliability_H(), and measurement_invariance() take full information maximum likelihood as the default of missing as well, so that the omega of reliability_omega() and that of fa_confirmatory() agree on incomplete data, and reliability(), which passes missing on only when it is supplied, follows them. missing = "listwise" gives the listwise deletion that DMAR 1.0.x applied by default. The default resolves by one rule in the four functions: the analysis is FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise. That differs from fa_confirmatory(), which fits complete data by FIML too. Data in which no value is missing, and a covariance matrix, are analyzed as they stand, as DMAR 1.0.x analyzed them, because the complete-data intervals of alpha and omega (the closed forms, "adf", and "likelihood", none of which FIML gives) need that analysis, and so no complete data result changes: FIML would give the same estimates, but its standard errors come from the observed information and the Huber-White sandwich, alpha’s bootstrap would refit a saturated model on every replication, about 70 times as long, and an MLR ladder’s robust indices would be the corrected ones of Zhang and Savalei (2023). A row with every item missing (every model variable, in measurement_invariance()) does not count as a missing value, since listwise deletion and FIML both drop it, so data that are complete but for a blank row keep the complete data analysis. Incomplete items are analyzed by FIML, so the estimates, their standard errors, and N change; under FIML the analytic alpha’s default interval is "ml", since Bonett’s needs complete cases. An option FIML cannot accompany (the complete-data closed form intervals, "adf", and "likelihood" in alpha and omega; ordered items, estimators other than ML and MLR, se = "robust.sem", and the Satorra-Bentler kind of test in measurement_invariance()) is used as before when no item value is missing, and with missing values the call stops and names the options rather than deleting cases unasked; the checks of omega’s denominator and alpha’s estimator come first, so that neither option named meets another refusal. Auxiliary variables imply FIML, as before. reliability_H() takes data for the first time in this release, and reliability_omega_categorical() keeps listwise deletion as its default. In measurement_invariance(), under FIML by default or by name, a group that never observes a variable of the model, or never observes two of them together, is refused by name before any fit (an error of class dmar_group_coverage, a dmar_refusal carrying the variables and pairs), with what to do instead; lavaan stopped with “subscript out of bounds”, which the new default would have made the ordinary result for holzinger_swineford’s t25_paper_form_board_r and t26_flags by school. An explicit missing = "fiml" with se = "robust.sem" or a test of the Satorra-Bentler kind now stops, as in fa_confirmatory(), where through 1.0.1 lavaan fit the complete cases with a warning, and so does a ladder lavaan fitted by another treatment than the FIML asked for (it fits GLS, WLS, and ULS in two stages).

  • reliability_omega() forms the default interval of the model implied omega on the logit scale. The default ci_method is "mlr_logistic" where it was "mlr": the same robust standard error, with the limits formed on the logit scale and transformed back to the scale of the coefficient (Browne, 1982; Kelley, 2007), so that reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied") and the omega row of fa_confirmatory() give limits of the same form. It applies under listwise deletion, FIML, and two-stage estimation alike. The change rests on a Monte Carlo study (in the repository’s methodology/reliability_limits) in which the logit limits met every criterion fixed before the run, with normal data under listwise deletion and FIML and with nonnormal data fitted by MLR. The study formed both kinds of limits from the same standard error, the normal theory maximum likelihood one for normal data and the Huber-White one of MLR for nonnormal data, so it compared the scale on which the limits are formed: with normal data the logit limits covered from .939 to .956 in every cell, against .910 to .952 for the limits on the scale of omega, whose misses fell mostly on one side. No cell used the robust.sem standard error of "mlr_logistic" with complete data, which estimates the same asymptotic variance as the Huber-White one. ci_method = "mlr" gives the limits of DMAR 1.0.x; ci_method = NULL is the default, as it was through 1.0.x. Given a covariance matrix with denominator = "model_implied" and no ci_method, reliability_omega() now uses "ml_logistic", the maximum likelihood standard error with the limits formed the same way, as reliability_H() does, where through 1.0.x it stopped because its default needed raw data; reliability(), which chose "ml" on that path, follows it. Under wald_df = "missing_information", whose calibration covers the intervals on the scale of omega only, the default remains "mlr" ("ml" with a covariance matrix). The estimate and the se row do not change, nor do robust omega (whose default is no interval) and coefficient alpha’s defaults.

  • FIML and two-stage reliability fits count distinct cases that observe an item. A row observed only on auxiliary variables informs their distribution, but not the items given them; a repeated row adds no dimension. The count must exceed the items plus auxiliary variables, in the data, every bootstrap replication, and each jackknife deletion. Fitted coefficients under listwise deletion count distinct complete rows. Listwise alpha is offered as an alternative only when it would accept those rows, with Feldt’s interval named when exactly two are complete. A standard error lavaan could not compute is NA, rather than zero.

  • FIML and two-stage reliability coefficients refuse a constant composite. When complete rows outnumber the items, their sum is checked directly. A constant sum makes the saturated likelihood unbounded as its variance tends to zero. Otherwise the EM covariance estimate is checked with a tolerance reflecting EM convergence. Bootstrap replications follow the same rule. H’s weighted composite is exempt. For all Holzinger and Swineford pupils on visual perception, cubes, lozenges, and paragraph comprehension, center each pupil’s scores on that pupil’s mean, then delete the first ten visual perception scores. Version 1.0.1’s model implied FIML alpha was 1.49e-13 with limits [0, 9.23e-8]. The data are now refused because the composite is constant in the 291 complete rows.

  • An indefinite supplied S is named as not a covariance matrix when its composite variance is not positive. The message gives its negative eigenvalue, and the composite variance when clearly negative, rather than calling the matrix singular with a zero composite variance. For S <- matrix(-.9, 3, 3); diag(S) <- 1, version 1.0.1 returned alpha 3.38 with limits [4.31, 1] at N = 100 with ci_method = "feldt". This matrix is now refused; positive semidefinite ipsative matrices keep the constant-composite message.

  • The equal-loading factor analytic plan uses its fitted coefficient. Let S <- matrix(.3, 4, 4); diag(S) <- c(1, 1, 1, 4) and S[4, 1:3] <- S[1:3, 4] <- -.5. At width .20, ss_aipe_reliability(S = S, model = "True Score", type = "Factor Analytic", width = .20) plans 244 cases, against 786 in 1.0.1, whose plan used alpha of the correlation matrix. The Parallel model gave 1669 and is now refused as far from parallel. Conversely, S <- diag(c(10, 10, 1, 1)); S[1, 2] <- S[2, 1] <- 4; S[3, 4] <- S[4, 3] <- -.3 has positive alpha but a zero fitted loading. At width .30, 1.0.1 planned 202 for Parallel and 386 for True Score; both now refuse it. Highly reliable congeneric populations are checked at a feasible estimation size: four loadings of .99 with error variances 1 - .99^2 at width .20 still plan 2 cases, as in 1.0.1. The closed form can remain below the minimum estimation size. Every assurance plan carries no_interval, including zero, and glance() adds fmi, necessary_N_complete, and no_interval when present. The closed form’s tidy() width is NA, as in 1.0.1.

  • fa_confirmatory() refuses correlated factors no case observes together. Their covariance does not enter the observed-data likelihood; a third factor observed with both does not identify it. Split the four spatial and three verbal Holzinger and Swineford tests between forms using set.seed(3); form <- sample(1:2, 301, replace = TRUE), with the spatial block missing on form 1 and verbal on form 2. Version 1.0.1 reported the correlation at its starting value, zero, and omega_spatial .650 with a standard error of zero and limits [.650, .650]. The fit is now refused by name; fit each factor alone or link the forms with common items. Orthogonal factors are fitted, since their correlation is fixed, and their coefficients and standard errors equal the separate fits. More generally a fit whose information cannot be inverted reports NA for standard errors, tests, and intervals in every table output, with a warning.

  • Zero degrees of freedom with a nonzero statistic gives no TLI or RMSEA. A binding inequality can leave a positive statistic at zero degrees of freedom, which lavaan does not count as an equality. For a factor of three unit-variance variables correlated .8, .8, and .5, at N = 200 with bounds = "pos.var", the statistic is 32.8 and CFI .925. Version 1.0.1 reported TLI and NNFI 1 and RMSEA 0 [0, 0]; those rows are now NA, since they divide by the degrees of freedom. CFI keeps .925. The RMSEA and following delta_rmsea of such an invariance rung are also NA. A rung’s CFI decides the version of its indices independently of its test. An exactly fitting saturated model keeps its earlier convention.

  • CFA summaries carry the method and reference of their results. glance() adds estimator, missing, test, fit_indices, and rmsea_ci_level after its earlier columns. tidy() of CFA, reliability, mlmr(), and mlmr_mv() results carries wald_df per row, and reliability’s glance() carries it too. The default is Inf. Rows on a t reference can therefore be stacked with rows on the normal reference without losing which interval each has. measurement_invariance(group_partial = character(0)), refused in 1.0.1, now frees nothing, as NULL does. Empty group.partial passed through ... also frees nothing.

  • reliability_omega() refuses a single-factor solution that leaves no reliability coefficient. On three items whose correlations had a negative product, it returned an omega of 471, from a loading of 43.6 and an error variance of -1899, with only a warning about a Heywood case. A single factor implies that the product of the three correlations is the square of the product of the loadings, so no real loadings reproduce such correlations and the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist. The function now stops with a message that quotes the correlations, under either denominator, for covariance input, and under FIML. It also stops when the error variances of an improper solution sum below zero, so that the model implies a negative error variance for the composite and an omega above one, the signature of a solution that has run away (McDonald, 2004), and the model implied reliability_alpha() does the same for the tau-equivalent model. An improper solution whose coefficient is still a proportion is returned with a warning, as before, and the warning now names the item, its error variance, and its observed variance; the observed denominator, which gave no warning of its own, now gives it. In a bootstrap, a replication with no coefficient is set aside under either improper setting (on 80 cases with one loading of .95, one such replication in 200 had put the bootstrap standard error at 1.02 rather than 0.049), and a replication of ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() whose fit is now refused is set aside rather than returning an absurd interval. This is a deliberate, loud change for those samples: a number that described where the optimizer stopped is replaced by an error. lavaan’s own per-replication notices of improper solutions no longer reach the console.

  • Each confidence limit of a reliability coefficient is clamped into [0, 1], and a negative estimate is warned about. Through 1.0.1 the lower limit was raised to 0 and the upper limit lowered to 1, each on its own. So when a negative coefficient alpha or KR-20 had an interval lying wholly below zero, the limits came back inverted, with the estimate outside them. On four binary items, one nearly the reverse of another (set.seed(3); z <- rbinom(60, 1, .5); Xb <- cbind(i1 = z, i2 = 1 - z, i3 = rbinom(60, 1, .5), i4 = rbinom(60, 1, .5)); Xb[1:6, 2] <- z[1:6]), reliability_kr20(Xb) gave -0.821 with Feldt limits [0, -0.171], and reliability_alpha(as.data.frame(Xb)) gave Bonett limits [0, -0.196]. Both limits are now clamped into [0, 1], so they stay in order and that interval is [0, 0]. The estimate is returned as computed, with a warning (class dmar_negative_reliability) that it lies outside the range of a reliability coefficient and that an item keyed in the opposite direction is the usual cause. The _logistic intervals, which gave NA limits without a word, now say why. Only results whose upper limit, before clamping, was below zero change. In ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() such a replication now has a width of 0 rather than a negative one, and the warning is muffled inside the loop. At true_reliability = 0 such a replication also covers the true value, since [0, 0] contains zero, so none can miss high there; through 1.0.1 its inverted limits counted as a miss high. With four items, N = 40, and Bonett’s interval (ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(true_reliability = 0, n_items = 4, width = .3, specified_N = 40, ci_method = "bonett", G = 400) after set.seed(1)), the share of intervals missing zero goes from .0400, .0325 of it high, to .0075, all of it low. With the "ml" interval it goes from .0425, .0100 of it high, to .0350, all of it low; its low misses move from .0325 to .0350 because that interval’s standard error now comes from the covariance matrix (see the next entry). The function evaluates the interval a study would report, and a miss high at zero would place the reliability below zero; its help says so. Above zero the counts do not change.

  • The "ml" interval of reliability_alpha() and reliability_kr20() takes its standard error from the covariance matrix. The van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000) variance was evaluated on the correlation matrix of the items, which is the variance of alpha of standardized items, and paired with alpha of the raw items. The paper defines it on the covariance matrix, as do Terry and Kelley (2012, Eq. 8) and Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016, Eq. 20), and the help already said it was computed from the covariance matrix. Whenever the item variances differ, the standard error was wrong in either direction. With equal loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2 at N = 206 it was .0256 where alpha-hat varies with a standard deviation of .0339, and the 95 percent interval covered .863 of 4,000 samples; it now covers .952. With item standard deviations from .8 to 1.9 it covered .889 (.944 now), and with the large variances on the high loading items its standard error was twice the standard deviation and it covered .9998 (.945 now). Items of equal variance are unaffected. On six binary items of unequal difficulty KR-20’s standard error moves from .0311 to .0279 against a sampling standard deviation of .0242. The default Bonett interval and the FIML and two-stage "ml" intervals, which already used the covariance matrix, are unchanged, and on complete data the listwise and FIML standard errors now agree up to the divisor. The code came from MBESS, whose ci.reliability() (through its internal .interval.type31_32_type1()) still evaluates the variance on the correlation matrix, so the two packages’ "ml" alpha intervals now differ when the item variances do.

  • Item names lavaan cannot parse no longer stop the single-factor coefficients. Through 1.0.1, reliability_omega() (robust omega, the default, and the model implied omega), the model implied reliability_alpha(), and reliability() passed the column names to lavaan. lavaan stopped on a name such as “item 1” or “1a”, and the error was reported as a model that did not converge; under FIML the message also gave advice about small samples. The items now enter the fit as y1, …, yJ, and every result, message, and warning carries the user’s names. lavaan’s warnings, such as “some observed variables are perfectly correlated; … variables involved are”, are raised again with them. So are those of the saturated model behind FIML, which named the variables v1, v2, … or y1, y2, … even in 1.0.1, for analytic alpha under FIML and for the fits with auxiliary variables. reliability_H() from data, new in 1.1.0, works the same way. On the five verbal tests of holzinger_swineford (t5_general_information to t9_word_meaning) renamed “item 1” to “item 5”, robust omega is 0.900, the same as under the data’s names, where 1.0.1 stopped with “The single-factor CFA model did not converge.” A fit that lavaan stops with an error is reported with lavaan’s own message rather than as a convergence failure, and the message names the items and auxiliary variables as the data do, in reliability_omega(), the model implied reliability_alpha(), and reliability_omega_categorical(); a fit that ran and did not converge is still reported as one, with the advice for FIML and two-stage estimation. reliability_omega_categorical() had reported every failure of its fit as “The single-factor categorical CFA model did not converge,” which sent the user looking for a problem with the sample. Its bootstrap sets a replication without a fit aside and counts it as before, so no estimate, interval, or count changes. reliability_omega()’s advice on requesting the robust omega interval now comes after the estimate, so a call that stops on its fit gives no advice first.

    A name given to two columns is refused by name wherever the columns are selected by name. Through 1.0.1, under FIML the first of two same-named columns was analyzed twice, and the call reported a model that did not converge; with auxiliary variables the second was dropped without a warning. On t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t4_lozenges, and t6_paragraph_comprehension, with the t2_cubes column also named t1_visual_perception and t9_word_meaning as an auxiliary variable, reliability_alpha() returned 0.555 with J = 3, the alpha of the other three tests (0.606 with J = 4 when the columns are named apart). An auxiliary variable’s name given to an item column as well is refused too.

  • reliability() picks the coefficient from the items alone. Auto-detection read every column of data, auxiliary variables included. So ordered items with a continuous auxiliary variable, or an integer one with more than 10 values, went to continuous omega under FIML rather than categorical omega under multiple imputation, and a factor auxiliary stopped the call with a base R error. The rule now reads only the columns not named in aux.

  • fa_confirmatory() reports the average variance extracted and coefficient H as NA for a factor with a negative error variance, and omega as NA when the factor’s error variances sum below zero. An item whose error variance is negative has a communality above one. The AVE averages the communalities, and H, the largest reliability a weighted sum of the items attains, is at least that communality, since the item weighted alone attains it, so for such a factor neither is a proportion of variance. Through 1.0.1 both were reported beside the Heywood warning: on holzinger_swineford, a factor of visual perception and lozenges beside one of general information, paragraph comprehension, and sentence completion had H = 1.321 [0.166, 2.476] and an AVE of .726. Both rows are now NA, the estimate and its interval alike, with one warning that names the items and their communalities. Omega depends on the error variances only through their sum: while the sum is positive it is a proportion and is reported, as reliability_omega() reports it (.707 for that factor), and when the sum is negative the model implies a negative error variance for the sum score, so omega is NA too (visual perception and cubes beside three speed tests had omega 1.050, H 1.536, and an AVE of .788). For ordered items the communality is that of the latent response. Through 1.0.1 an improper ordered factor stopped the whole fit with the mvtnorm error “‘corr’ is not a correlation matrix”; its categorical omega, which is not defined for an improper solution, its AVE, and its H are now NA, named in the same warning. The classed Heywood warning is unchanged, and output = "fit" keeps lavaan’s defined parameters.

  • average_variance_extracted() reports NA, with a warning, for a factor whose solution is improper, as fa_confirmatory() does. An indicator whose error variance is estimated below zero has a communality above one, so the AVE of its factor, which averages the communalities, is not a proportion of variance. fa_confirmatory() now reports that factor’s ave row as NA, but average_variance_extracted(fit) averaged the squared standardized loadings regardless: for visual perception and lozenges beside a factor of general information, paragraph comprehension, and sentence completion in holzinger_swineford, where visual perception’s communality is 1.304, it reported .726. The factor’s ave, and its interval when one is requested, are now NA, with a warning that names each such indicator and its communality in the words of fa_confirmatory()’s. The check reads the sign of the error variance and takes the communality as one minus the standardized error variance, so it gives the same answer whatever the identification of the fit, for the latent responses of ordered items under either parameterization, and in every group of a multiple group fit. Proper factors are unchanged (.705 for the verbal factor there). When every factor of the fit is improper, ci_method = "percentile" forms no interval: no bootstrap is run, and no confidence level is recorded or printed.

  • average_variance_extracted() counts the improper replications its bootstrap keeps, and its warning gives the caution for each factor. A replication whose resample solution is improper for a factor that is proper in the observed fit (an indicator with a negative error variance) is kept, as the reliability family’s default improper = "keep" keeps one. Through 1.0.1 it was neither counted nor reported, though its AVE averages a communality above one and can exceed one.

    • The table now carries the reliability family’s bootstrap attribute (attempted, returned, failed, improper_kept, refit_failed, caution, improper_kept_by_factor, and the rest), and prints the family’s bootstrap line under the table, at the console and in a knitted report. When two or more factors have an interval, a second line gives the improper replications kept for each.
    • A caution is added when the replications set aside and the improper ones kept for a factor reach the tail area beyond a limit. With one factor the line keeps the reliability family’s wording; with two or more, it gives the share of each factor the caution holds for, counted for that factor alone. The bootstrap gives one warning, as the family does: the replications set aside, the improper ones kept, and the caution for each factor it holds for, with that factor’s count.
    • lavaan’s bootstrap cannot tell a refit that failed from one that did not converge. Such replications are counted among the non-finite ones and as refit_failed, and the line and the warning both say that they “failed to refit or did not converge” and were set aside, where 1.0.1’s warning said that they “failed to refit (or did not converge) and were dropped”.
    • Example: 80 pupils drawn from holzinger_swineford (set.seed(113); d <- holzinger_swineford[sample(301, 80), ]), fit by lavaan::cfa() with a verbal factor of paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning and a spatial factor of visual perception, cubes, and lozenges, then average_variance_extracted(fit, ci_method = "percentile", B = 200, seed = 113). The spatial factor is proper in the sample (AVE .449), yet 101 of the 198 replications that returned a value were improper for it, and its upper limit is 1.19. Version 1.0.1’s warning said only that 2 of 200 replications failed to refit (or did not converge) and were dropped. The warning now says that they were set aside, that 101 of the 198 used came from an improper (Heywood) solution and were kept, and that for spatial 103 of 200 replications (51.5%) came from a solution improper for it or were set aside, against the 2.5% beyond each limit of a 95% interval. The line under the table says “for spatial, 51.5% of the replications came from a solution improper for the factor or were set aside, at least the 2.5% beyond each limit”, and the second line “spatial 101, verbal 0”.
    • The table gains the class dmar_ave ahead of dmar_tbl on every path. No interval changes.

  • average_variance_extracted() reads a loading fixed or constrained to zero as none. Through 1.0.1 it averaged the squared standardized loading of every =~ row of a fit, so a loading fixed at zero (0*item) or constrained to zero (a*item with a == 0) entered the factor’s average as a loading of zero. On holzinger_swineford (lavaan::cfa(model, data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE)), a visual factor of visual perception, cubes, and lozenges written with 0*t7_sentence beside a verbal factor of general information, paragraph comprehension, and sentence completion is the same model as the one without that row (chi square 22.876 on 8 degrees of freedom for both), yet it had an AVE of .279 rather than the .371 of its three tests. The verbal factor written with 0*t1_visual_perception beside the same visual factor had .529 (.705 times 3/4) rather than .705. Such a row is now left out of the average and out of the check for an improper solution described above, as factor_scores(), bifactor_indices(), and reliability_H() read it. With a visual factor of visual perception and lozenges alone, whose visual perception error variance is negative, 1.0.1 gave the visual factor .726 and the verbal factor written with 0*t1_visual_perception .529. The visual factor’s AVE is now NA under that check, and the verbal factor’s is the .705 of the model without the row, since visual perception is not one of its indicators. Fits without such a row are unchanged.

  • fa_confirmatory(), cfa_1(), and cfa_2() refuse group passed through .... fa_confirmatory() labels every loading, error variance, intercept, and factor correlation, and lavaan holds a label shared by several groups equal across them. A group argument therefore fit one pooled model, every measurement parameter equal across the groups and each factor’s variance fixed at 1 in each: a model of complete invariance rather than a model by group. lavaan warned about the single labels, and the table repeated each labeled row once per group with the same estimate. The call is now an error that names the route: measurement_invariance(), whose configural model frees every parameter in each group and whose fit gives reliability_H(fit = , factor = , group = ) the H of one group, and reliability_omega() on one group’s rows.

  • fa_confirmatory() names the version of its fit rows after FIML, and its SRMR when the model has a mean structure. Under missing = "ml" (or "fiml"), the cfi, tli, nnfi, rmsea, and RMSEA interval rows have always been lavaan’s robust indices. For a FIML fit these are the corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), version 6 (version 3 with estimator = "MLR"), and they are not computed from the chi_square row beside them. The srmr row of a model with a mean structure is lavaan’s SRMR, which averages in the mean residuals, so it is not the SRMR sem_fit_measures() reports: .0229 against .0259 on the verbal and deduction tests of the help page (hs_factors) with 90 sentence completion scores deleted at random (set.seed(1), then t7_sentence[sample(301, 90)] <- NA) under missing = "ml". Lines under the table now say both, and the table carries them in a new fit_rows attribute, so a knitted report shows them too. When the robust indices of a fit are not available (lavaan computes none, and DMAR computes them only for the mean and variance adjusted statistic), every index row holds one other version and a line says which. That is the standard indices for a maximum likelihood fit of continuous items, and the scaled ones, or else the standard ones, after FIML or two-stage estimation, for ordered items, or by least squares. Another line names robust indices DMAR computed, for the mean and variance adjusted statistic. Whether the fit used FIML is read from the fit, so a fit lavaan made to the complete cases (with missing = "ml" and a test it cannot combine with FIML) is not labeled with the FIML corrected indices. An exactly fitting model with no degrees of freedom gets no version line under FIML or two-stage estimation; its SRMR and two-stage method lines stay. With a nonzero statistic the version line names CFI alone and another line explains the undefined TLI and RMSEA rows. A help paragraph says which version each fit row is. No number changes here; the next entry gives the rows that do.

  • fa_confirmatory() reports one version of its fit indices, and the robust indices of a fit with the mean and variance adjusted statistic.

    • Through 1.0.1 each of the cfi, tli, nnfi, rmsea, and RMSEA interval rows took the first of its robust, scaled, and standard versions that lavaan had computed, so a row whose robust version was NA could hold another version than the rows beside it.
    • With the older mean and variance adjusted statistic (test = "mean.var.adjusted" passed through ...), for which lavaan computes no robust indices, every row held the scaled version, whose population value changes with the kurtosis of the data (Savalei, 2018). The rows now hold the robust indices, computed by DMAR as Savalei (2018) shows they can be. They equal lavaan’s under estimator = "MLM", and a line under the table says that DMAR computed them.
    • On the verbal and deduction tests of the help page (fa_confirmatory(data = holzinger_swineford, factors = hs_factors, test = "mean.var.adjusted")), CFI .961 and RMSEA .046 [0, .089] become .993 and .047 [0, .091], both intervals at 90 percent, the level of 1.0.x and the default of rmsea_conf_level. On the three-factor model of nine tests (see the sem_fit_measures() entry on the mean and variance adjusted statistic), CFI .734 becomes .932 and RMSEA .089 [.068, .110] becomes .091 [.070, .113].
    • Where neither lavaan nor DMAR computes robust indices for a maximum likelihood fit of continuous items, the rows hold the standard indices, never the scaled ones, and a line under the table says so.
    • An exactly fitting model with no degrees of freedom keeps the values 1.0.1 gave it (CFI, TLI, and NNFI 1, RMSEA 0), under FIML and two-stage estimation as well, with no version line. A nonzero statistic keeps its CFI but gives NA for TLI, NNFI, and RMSEA, as the entry on zero degrees of freedom explains.

  • mlmr() and mlmr_mv() leave the covariances among the predictors free when auxiliary variables are supplied. The saturated correlates of auxiliary were written as a covariance of each auxiliary with each predictor. That made the predictors endogenous to lavaan, whose automatic covariances among exogenous variables then no longer reached them, and nothing else freed them, so with two or more predictors every covariance among them was fixed at zero and the model that should be saturated (Graham, 2003) was not. The covariance of every pair of predictors is now written, and the model over the outcomes, the predictors, and the auxiliaries is saturated, with chi square 0 on 0 df. Its coefficients are the regression implied by the full information maximum likelihood means and covariances of every variable, auxiliaries included (what cov_fiml() returns), and on complete data they and R squared are those of lm(). A fit with one predictor, or none, is unchanged. When a predictor has missing values, the coefficients, standard errors, intervals, and p-values change. On holzinger_swineford, with t6 regressed on t7 and t9, t9 made missing at random given t7 for 110 of the 301 students (set.seed(113)), and t13 as the auxiliary, the model had chi square 129.5 on 1 df and an implied covariance of 0 between t7 and t9, whose correlation is .69. The t7 slope was 0.449 (SE 0.031) and is now 0.362 (SE 0.044), against 0.362 without the auxiliary and 0.317 on the complete data, and the t9 slope moves from 0.096 to 0.143 (0.167 on the complete data). The auxiliary example on the mlmr() page, where t26_flags is missing for 156 students, had chi square 14.1 on 1 df; its intercept moves from -0.703 to -0.436 and its t7 slope from 0.488 to 0.476. When the predictors are complete, the coefficients and their standard errors were already right, since their maximum likelihood estimates do not depend on the predictors’ covariance there, but every quantity that uses the model implied variance of the outcome was not. For t6 on t7 and t9 with complete data, R squared was .471 and is now .602, the value lm() gives; the standardized coefficients move from .541 and .423 to .469 and .367, and the semi-partial R squared from .141 and .086 to .106 and .065. The log likelihood moves from -4123.6 on 13 parameters to -4013.7 on 14, and AIC and BIC with it. The likelihood ratio test of anova() for adding t9 in the first example was chi square 8.62 and is now 13.72. In mlmr_mv() the first example gives t6 a t7 slope of 0.362 rather than 0.450 and t26_flags a t9 slope of 0.104 rather than -0.050, and with complete data the R squared of each outcome is now that of lm() (.602 and .474 for t6 and t8, where they were .471 and .379). The auxiliary simulation in the mlmr vignette, whose predictors are complete, prints the same values. With the model saturated, the three estimators of fraction_missing_information() now agree on such fits as they do without auxiliaries: in the first example the t7 slope’s unstructured and Hessian estimates were .016 and -.559, and all three are now .254. wald_df = "missing_information" therefore gives that slope 221.5 degrees of freedom rather than 293.1.

  • mlmr() and mlmr_mv() refuse an auxiliary variable under listwise or pairwise deletion. lavaan’s listwise deletion drops every row missing any variable of the model, the auxiliaries included, so through 1.0.1 an incomplete auxiliary silently shrank the sample. mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning, data = holzinger_swineford, missing = "listwise", auxiliary = "t26_flags") fitted 145 of the 301 rows, with coefficients of 0.971, 0.313, and 0.178 where lm() gives 1.117, 0.317, and 0.167. An auxiliary carries information only through the full information likelihood, so the combination now stops and names the remedy (drop the auxiliary or set missing = "fiml"), as reliability_alpha() and reliability_H() stop. Under pairwise and available cases deletion (missing = "pairwise" or "available.cases") the moments are computed from each pair of variables on its own. With the model saturated, the coefficients then depend on the moments of the outcomes and predictors alone, so an auxiliary can change nothing, while the result recorded it as used. In mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning + t26_flags, data = holzinger_swineford, missing = "pairwise", auxiliary = "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals"), 1.0.1’s coefficients agreed with those of the fit without the auxiliary to within 5e-6; its standard errors differed only because the auxiliary also fixed the covariances among the predictors at zero (see the entry above), so the t7 slope’s was .0245 against .0355. That combination is now refused the same way.

  • Under missing = "fiml" with auxiliary variables, a case whose items are all missing is used when an auxiliary variable is observed on it. reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() set aside every case with no observed item, with auxiliary variables or without. The saturated correlates model estimates the items and the auxiliaries jointly, so such a case informs the item moments through its auxiliaries, and lavaan’s own FIML fit of the model keeps it, as cov_fiml() does. Setting it aside made the analysis conditional on having an observed item, which depends on the auxiliaries when the items go missing together at random given them, and the estimates were then biased. On the nine tests of the three-factor model (visual perception, cubes, lozenges, paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, word meaning, addition, counting groups of dots, and straight and curved capitals), with the whole block set to NA for 77 pupils at random given general information (set.seed(113), the rows sample(301, 77, prob = plogis(-1.5 + 1.2 * z)) with z the standardized t5_general_information, the auxiliary), N goes from 224 to 301, alpha from .610 to .613, model implied omega from .350 to .358, and robust omega from .228 to .234. reliability_H() from data, new in 1.1.0, uses such cases too. A result changes only when some case has every item missing and an auxiliary observed, and N now counts such cases. Two-stage estimation, new in 1.1.0, uses them as well: its first stage reads their auxiliaries, and the coefficients are computed on every case it reads, although lavaan’s two-stage estimator leaves such cases out of its N (see Two-Stage Maximum Likelihood for Incomplete Data). Under multiple imputation, also new, reliability_omega_categorical() imputes such a case from its auxiliaries.

  • The FIML item covariance matrix behind analytic alpha and robust omega is the EM estimate. Under missing = "fiml", analytic reliability_alpha() and the observed denominator of reliability_omega() apply their formulas to the maximum likelihood covariance matrix of the items under the saturated model. Through 1.0.1 that matrix came from lavaan fitting the saturated model from its default starting values, which on many items stops short of the maximum: on all 26 Holzinger and Swineford tests, with the Pasteur students missing the last two, it took 2484 iterations and left covariances up to 0.0105 from the maximum likelihood values, the log likelihood 3e-7 below its maximum. The matrix is now the EM estimate cov_fiml() returns, the unrestricted moments lavaan computes for every FIML fit to the same variables (the EM runs on the standardized items, as in cov_fiml(), so the matrix does not depend on their units, and agrees with lavaan’s to about seven digits), and the standard error of the "ml" interval is the delta method one from the saturated model evaluated at that estimate, with no optimization run. On the Holzinger and Swineford examples checked (6, 9, 23, and 26 tests, with the Pasteur students’ missing tests or with values deleted at random given general information, with and without an auxiliary variable), alpha changes by at most 1.5e-6, robust omega by at most 5.8e-6, and the standard error by at most 4.4e-8; on the 26 tests alpha is .8234684 rather than .8234689. The estimate no longer depends on the interval asked for, the FIML alpha of complete data equals the listwise one to machine precision (it differed by 2.3e-9 on nine tests), and the computation is faster: on 23 incomplete tests about three times for alpha with its interval and five to ten times for robust omega. Two-stage analytic alpha, which uses the same matrix, changes the same way, as does the fraction of missing information ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() records for alpha. Model implied alpha and model implied omega are unchanged.

  • Under FIML and two-stage estimation, a pair of variables never observed together is refused by name. reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() now stop, as reliability_H() from data and cov_fiml(), new in 1.1.0, do, naming each pair of items or auxiliary variables that no case observes together and pointing to missing_coverage(). Through 1.0.1 lavaan only warned, and the covariance it returned for such a pair was arbitrary: on t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t4_lozenges, and t6_paragraph_comprehension, with t1_visual_perception deleted in rows 1 to 150 and t2_cubes in rows 151 to 301, reliability_alpha(missing = "fiml") returned 0.536 with a standard error of 0 and the interval [0.536, 0.536]. In a bootstrap, a resample left with such a pair, or a jackknife deletion behind the BCa acceleration, is set aside with the message, under two-stage estimation as under FIML. A pair observed together only where one of them takes a single value, or by one row only, is refused the same way (see the next entry).

  • Under FIML and two-stage estimation, a pair of variables observed together only where one of them takes a single value is refused. Rows in which one of two variables is constant say nothing about how the two vary together, so the estimate of their covariance rests on the form of the normal model, or is not determined at all. reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() now name such a pair and stop, as they do for a pair never observed together, and so do reliability_H() from data and cov_fiml(), new in 1.1.0. A pair that only one row observes is refused the same way, and in a bootstrap a resample that leaves such a pair is set aside.

    • Example: rows 1 to 100 of t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t4_lozenges, and t6_paragraph_comprehension, with t1_visual_perception deleted in rows 91 to 100 and t2_cubes set to 25 in rows 1 to 90, the rows that observe t1_visual_perception. Under missing = "fiml", version 1.0.1 returned robust omega 1.06, the analytic alpha 0.113 with no interval, and the model implied omega 0.890 [0.281, 1].
    • Under listwise deletion 1.0.1 returned alpha 0.511, counting t2_cubes among the items. t2_cubes is now refused as constant in the 90 complete rows (see the entry on an item that does not vary), and the message says why FIML cannot help.

  • reliability_omega_categorical() refuses fewer than three items. With two ordered items the single-factor model is not identified: the one polychoric correlation determines only the product of the two loadings, while categorical omega depends on each. The value returned before depended on the start values of the optimizer and on the order of the columns, and its bootstrap interval reflected where the optimizer landed. The function now stops with the message reliability_omega() gives for two continuous items, and reliability(), whose automatic routing sends two integer items to categorical omega, lets the error through rather than substituting another coefficient.

  • Categorical omega no longer drops an undetermined polychoric correlation from its total variance. The unrestricted polychoric correlations behind the observed denominator came from a second, saturated fit (the approach MBESS also takes). When the data do not determine a polychoric correlation, as when two items are skewed in opposite directions and their bivariate table has empty cells, that fit gives the correlation no weight and returns its starting value, 0, so the pair was removed from the total variance without notice and the coefficient was too high, by about .035 for each such pair. In samples of 500 from the mixed-skew design of Green and Yang (2009), the help page’s example with N <- 500 and seeds 1 to 100 in place of 113, 45 of the 99 samples with a proper solution had at least one such pair. Against the coefficient with the model implied correlation in the pair, 1.0.1’s was .030 to .045 too high with one undetermined pair (38 samples) and .065 to .088 with two whose loadings are identified (3 samples). The correlations now come from the single-factor fit itself, which agrees with the saturated fit whenever every correlation is determined, so every other result is unchanged, and the computation needs one fit instead of two per bootstrap replication; that fit also no longer computes a test statistic it never used, which changes no number. Together the two cut the fitting time of a bootstrap replication by more than half. When a correlation is not determined, reliability_omega_categorical(denominator = "observed") stops with an error naming the pair. When the correlations the data do determine identify the single-factor loadings, it points to denominator = "model_implied", which does not need the pair. fa_confirmatory() reports that factor’s categorical omega as NA with a warning naming the pair. A bootstrap meets such pairs far more often than the sample does, since a resample often leaves out the few respondents who determine the correlation (about half the replications on the help page’s example, whose sample has no such pair). Those replications are set aside, counted in the new undetermined element of the bootstrap attribute, and named in the printed line and the warning. The warning says that the interval then conditions on the replications that redrew the respondents who determine the correlation (on the help page’s example, 80, 95, and 97 of 200 in percentile bootstraps with seed 1, 2, and 3; with the improper ones, 80, 96, and 98 were set aside, close to the half beyond which no interval is reported, as the entry on a bootstrap of categorical omega that returns fewer than half describes), and that denominator = "model_implied" sets aside only the replications whose determined correlations leave the loadings unidentified (see Either Variance in the Denominator of Every Omega). This is a deliberate, loud change for those samples only: a number that rested on an arbitrary 0 is replaced by an error.

  • An improper categorical solution is named. When the single-factor fit returns a standardized loading above one (a negative residual variance, a Heywood case), categorical omega is not defined, and the function failed with the error “‘corr’ is not a correlation matrix” from mvtnorm, under the model implied denominator only after a message advising that denominator. It now stops with an error naming each improper item and its loading, before anything is said about undetermined pairs. A bootstrap replication with an improper solution is set aside as a non-finite value and counted in the new improper element of the bootstrap attribute (it was counted as an error, with the message from mvtnorm), and the warning from lavaan about the negative variance no longer repeats once per replication.

  • reliability_omega_categorical() says which sum its coefficient describes. Categorical omega scores each item’s categories 0, 1, …, C - 1 in the order of its codes (Green & Yang, 2009, Eq. 11; Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016, Eq. 16), as MBESS and semTools do, and the help page now says so. When an item’s codes are not equally spaced, or items step by different amounts, the sum of the codes as given is a different composite, and a message names the items. In the examples behind the help page its reliability was 0.009 to 0.012 lower for codes -2, -1, 1, 2, and 0.034 lower for items coded 1, 3, 5 beside items coded 1, 2, 3. The coefficient is unchanged.

  • Listwise deletion that leaves too little to analyze says so. With no complete row, only one, or an item that takes a single value in the complete rows, reliability_omega_categorical() printed lavaan’s table of variables and stopped with “The single-factor categorical CFA model did not converge.” It now stops before any fit, names the cause, and offers missing = "pairwise" (when every pair of items is observed together) or missing = "mi". No estimate changes.

  • The reliability family treats SPSS user-defined missing values as missing. A column read by haven::read_sav(user_na = TRUE) keeps a code declared missing in SPSS (999 for a test not given, 9 for a refusal) as a value of class haven_labelled_spss, which SPSS and haven’s is.na() treat as missing. Through 1.0.1, reliability_alpha(), reliability_omega(), and icc() analyzed it as a score or rating. reliability_kr20() refused it as not 0/1, and reliability_omega_categorical() counted it as a further category. fleiss_kappa() summed it as a count. cohen_kappa() dropped such a pair only when haven was loaded, and otherwise counted the code as a further category. These functions and reliability() now set, as reliability_H() from data, new in 1.1.0, does, the declared values (na_values and na_range) to missing in every column before anything is deleted or fitted, as read_sav() does by default. A message names the columns and counts, and haven need not be loaded. icc() and fleiss_kappa(), which do not accept missing values, then refuse such a column as they refuse NA.

    • Five spatial tests of holzinger_swineford, t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t3_paper_form_board, t4_lozenges, and t25_paper_form_board_r, with the 156 missing scores of the last recoded to 999 and declared missing (x <- holzinger_swineford$t25_paper_form_board_r; haven::labelled_spss(ifelse(is.na(x), 999, x), na_values = 999)). Version 1.0.1 gave alpha 0.008 and omega 0.015; the functions now give 0.687 and 0.730 under listwise deletion (missing = "listwise", the default through 1.0.x), the values for the same data with NA.
    • Three raters of 60 subjects (set.seed(1); t <- rnorm(60), then round(3 + t + rnorm(60, sd = .5)) for each rater in turn), with the first six ratings of the third declared missing as 9. icc() gave ICC(2,1) 0.318, against 0.668 on the complete rows, and now refuses the data. cohen_kappa() of the first and third raters gave 0.170 on 60 pairs and seven categories when haven was not loaded. It now gives 0.196 on 54 pairs and six, as it did with haven loaded.
    • Data read with read_sav()’s default, which already makes these values NA, are unaffected.

  • reliability_omega_categorical() reads a factor’s labels as the numbers they name. Through 1.0.1 a factor item passed only when its labels were 1, 2, …, K in order. A Likert factor labeled 0 to 4, or one whose lowest category no respondent chose (levels “2” to “5”), was refused with “column 1 contains non-integer values”. The labels are now read as numbers, and the item is analyzed as those numbers under every treatment of missing. Listwise and pairwise deletion and multiple imputation therefore rank its categories alike, and the factor gives the result of its integer codes. For example, the items of the help page’s example recoded as factors labeled 0 to 4 (as.data.frame(lapply(as.data.frame(items - 1), factor))) were refused by 1.0.1 and now give 0.720, the value of their codes. Two kinds of factor are refused, with a message that names the column and says what to do: one whose labels are words, and an ordered factor whose levels are not in the order of the numbers they name.

  • A bootstrap of categorical omega reports no interval when fewer than half of its replications return a value. Through 1.0.1 reliability_omega_categorical() formed its interval from any two replications that returned a value. When most were set aside, the rest were a minority of the resamples, selected by whether they returned a value, and their spread described those resamples rather than the sampling distribution of the coefficient.

    • The standard error and the limits are now NA in that case, under every ci_method and every treatment of missing. A warning and the printed line say why.
    • This is the criterion by which the point estimate under multiple imputation stops when fewer than half of its completed data sets return a value (Lim & Cheung, 2022).
    • Example: six binary items of 60 respondents, one respondent alone endorsing the first item, so every resample without that respondent has a constant item (set.seed(113); eta <- rnorm(60); y <- 1 * (outer(eta, rep(.7, 6)) + matrix(rnorm(360), 60) * sqrt(1 - .7^2) > 0); y[, 1] <- 0; y[1, 1] <- 1). A percentile bootstrap (B = 200, seed = 113) set aside 106 replications in 1.0.1 and gave [0.660, 0.921] from the other 94. It now reports no interval.
    • A larger sample is the remedy. Other callers keep the floor of two returned values, except when most resamples fail the distinct-case rule described under the bootstrap engine.

  • Listwise deletion that leaves fewer than two complete rows stops alpha, KR-20, and omega before anything is computed.

    • Through 1.0.1, with no complete row, or only one, reliability_omega() (either denominator) and the model implied reliability_alpha() passed the data to lavaan, which printed its table of the variables and stopped on a variance it could not compute, and the call reported a model that did not converge. The analytic reliability_alpha() returned NA with a warning that NaNs were produced, and reliability_kr20() returned NA for the estimate and every limit with two such warnings. Example: the first 40 pupils of holzinger_swineford on visual perception, cubes, lozenges, paragraph comprehension, and sentence completion, with one score deleted from every row (d <- holzinger_swineford[1:40, c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges", "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence")]; for (i in 1:40) d[i, (i - 1) %% 5 + 1] <- NA).
    • Each function now stops, says that listwise deletion leaves nothing to analyze, and offers missing = "fiml", as reliability_omega_categorical() offers its own treatments for its items. FIML is offered only when it can use the rows; otherwise the message says why it cannot, as when a pair of items is never observed together. An item that no row observes is named instead. reliability_H() from data, new in 1.1.0, does the same.
    • For KR-20 the message offers reliability_alpha() with missing = "fiml", which computes the same coefficient (alpha of 0/1 items is KR-20) from the incomplete rows as well, when full information maximum likelihood can use them (otherwise the message says why it cannot). Example: the nine tests t1_visual_perception to t9_word_meaning, each scored 1 above its median (as.integer(x > median(x))), with each of the 301 pupils missing one test in rotation (pupil i misses test i %% 9 + 1). Version 1.0.1 returned NA; the call the message offers gives 0.752, 95% CI [0.709, 0.795], against 0.756 for KR-20 of the complete data.
    • With two or more complete rows alpha and KR-20 are computed as before, and the single-factor coefficients reach the fit when the complete rows outnumber the items; any error lavaan stops with is quoted. An item or a total that takes a single value in the complete rows is now refused by name, and at two rows the intervals not defined there are refused while Feldt’s remains, for KR-20 as for alpha (see the entries below).

  • An item that is not numeric, or that does not vary, is refused by name. reliability_alpha(), reliability_kr20(), and reliability_omega() now stop before computing anything when an item takes a single value in the rows analyzed, and name it, as does reliability_H() from data, new in 1.1.0. The rows analyzed are the complete rows under listwise deletion, and the rows that observe the item under FIML and two-stage estimation. A covariance matrix with a zero variance on its diagonal is refused the same way.

    • Such an item adds a constant to the composite, which leaves the composite’s variance and reliability as they are. Alpha and KR-20, however, counted it among the J items: with one such item, alpha is J(J - 2)/(J - 1)^2 times the alpha of the other items, which is the alpha of the same composite.
    • Examples. On the first 100 pupils of holzinger_swineford with t2_cubes set to 5, alpha of t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t4_lozenges, and t6_paragraph_comprehension was 0.487, against 0.548 for the other three. On the first 20 pupils, with the nine tests t1_visual_perception to t9_word_meaning each scored 1 above its 90th percentile among all 301 pupils (as.numeric(x > quantile(x, 0.9))), no pupil passes four of the tests, and KR-20 was 0.196, against 0.217 for the other five.
    • Through 1.0.1, omega (from data or from a covariance matrix) and the model implied alpha reported that the model did not converge; from data, lavaan first printed its table of the variables. The analytic alpha under FIML reported that the saturated model did not converge.
    • Under listwise deletion, the message says when the item varies in the rows deletion removed. It then offers missing = "fiml" (for KR-20, reliability_alpha() with missing = "fiml") only when FIML could use those rows, and otherwise says why it cannot. A shared column name is a condition to fix first, rather than an obstacle in the data; fitted coefficients refuse shared names before checking the rows. FIML is not offered when the composite is constant in the complete rows and they outnumber the items.
    • An item column that is neither numeric nor logical is refused by name, with its class. Through 1.0.1, listwise deletion stopped with stats::cov()’s “is.numeric(x) || is.logical(x) is not TRUE”, and FIML with the report about the saturated model. A logical item is still read as 0 and 1.

  • A bootstrap replication in which an item takes a single value is set aside, with the refusal. The rule above now holds in every bootstrap replication of every continuous coefficient, and in the jackknife behind the BCa acceleration. Categorical omega already set such replications aside, but passed them to lavaan first. It now refuses them by item name before fitting, without printing lavaan’s variable table; their reason is counted as an error with the refusal rather than as an unnamed non-finite value. The same check applies to completed resamples after imputation.

    • A resample that leaves out every case on which a rare item differs from the rest raises the refusal. The bootstrap counts and quotes it, and the caution reports the share.
    • A resample leaves out a given case with probability (1 - 1/N)^N, about 0.37, so an item passed by one respondent loses its variation in about a third of the resamples.
    • Through 1.0.1, KR-20 and the analytic alpha of such a resample counted the item, at J(J - 2)/(J - 1)^2 times the coefficient of the same composite without it, and the replication was kept. Omega and the model implied alpha reached lavaan, which printed its table of the variables to the console for each such replication.
    • Example: the first 60 pupils of holzinger_swineford, with the nine tests t1_visual_perception to t9_word_meaning scored 1 above their medians among all 301 pupils, and t20_deduction scored 1 at the highest score among the 60 (one pupil). KR-20 is 0.689. Its percentile interval (B = 1000, seed = 113) was [0.560, 0.779], with 370 of the 1000 replications computed with t20_deduction constant. It is now [0.564, 0.775], from the other 630, with the caution.

  • A composite that does not vary is refused. When the covariances of the items cancel their variances, the composite has no variance and no reliability. Ipsative items, whose scores sum to the same total in every row, are the usual case. reliability_alpha(), reliability_kr20(), and reliability_omega() now stop and say so.

    • Through 1.0.1, alpha divided the item variances by a composite variance of zero, or by the rounding error left in its place.
    • Example: t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, and t4_lozenges, each centered on the pupil’s mean of the three (x - rowMeans(x) for all 301 pupils). Alpha was returned as 1.42e16, with a standard error of -1.42e15 and NaN limits.
    • KR-20 of the two rows (1, 0, 1, 0) and (0, 1, 0, 1) was returned as -Inf, with the limits 0 and -Inf.
    • Omega and the model implied alpha reported that the model did not converge.

  • The coefficients fitted by the single-factor model need more complete rows than items. Under listwise deletion, N complete rows give a covariance matrix of rank at most N - 1. With no more complete rows than items it is singular, and the maximum likelihood fit is not defined. That fit lies behind robust and model implied omega and the model implied alpha, and behind reliability_H() from data, new in 1.1.0.

    • Through 1.0.1 the call reported a model that did not converge, as on pupils 1 to 5 of t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t4_lozenges, t6_paragraph_comprehension, and t7_sentence.
    • The call now stops before the fit and says why. It offers missing = "fiml" when FIML could use the incomplete rows, and otherwise says why it cannot, or that the model needs more cases.
    • Alpha and KR-20 need only the trace and the sum of the covariance matrix, and are computed from two or more complete rows (alpha is 0.351 on those five pupils, as in 1.0.1).

  • Full information maximum likelihood and two-stage estimation need more cases than variables. Both first estimate the saturated model over the items and any auxiliary variables.

    • The count is of distinct cases that observe an item. Auxiliary-only cases and repeated rows do not add dimensions. With n such cases, their missing values filled in any way, the data lie in a space of at most n - 1 dimensions. With no more cases than variables, the EM estimate of the covariance matrix is therefore singular or nearly so, and it depends on where the algorithm stops.
    • reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() now stop before any fit and say so, as does reliability_H() from data. For the analytic alpha, listwise deletion is offered only when it would accept the complete rows, naming Feldt’s interval when exactly two are complete. Bootstrap and jackknife resamples obey the same rule.
    • Example: pupils 1 to 5 of the five tests above, with t1_visual_perception missing for pupil 4 and t2_cubes for pupil 5. Version 1.0.1 reported for alpha that the saturated FIML model did not converge, and for omega that the model did not converge.

  • At two complete rows, the intervals of alpha and KR-20 that are not defined there are refused. Two rows give a covariance matrix of rank one, in which every pair of items correlates +1 or -1, whatever the items. Each interval is refused for its own reason, as "fisher" already is below N = 4:

    • Bonett’s variance, 2J/((J - 1)(N - 2)), is infinite at N = 2.
    • The "ml" and "adf" standard errors, and those of their _logistic variants, are zero for any data. The asymptotic variance of van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel vanishes at a matrix of rank one. Each case’s centered cross products are then proportional to the covariance matrix, which alpha does not change with.
    • Every bootstrap resample is one row drawn twice, or both rows.
    • Feldt’s interval remains, and every refusal names it. Its F reference is exact for any N of at least 2 under multivariate normality and parallel items; for KR-20’s 0/1 items it is an approximation (Feldt, 1965).
    • Hakstian and Whalen’s interval remains too, but at N = 2 its upper limit lies above one for every data set whose alpha is below one at any confidence level above about .90, and is clamped to one; at alpha = 1 its interval is [1, 1].
    • Example: rows 1 and 50 of holzinger_swineford (pupil ids 1 and
      1. on t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t4_lozenges, t6_paragraph_comprehension, and t7_sentence (alpha -0.475). Version 1.0.1 returned:
      • Bonett’s [0, 1], with an infinite standard error (alpha’s default interval);
      • NaN for "ml" and "adf" (a variance of zero, made negative by rounding error);
      • NA limits for their _logistic variants;
      • the inverted percentile interval [0, -0.475].
    • Feldt’s [0, 0.998] is unchanged.
    • KR-20’s default, Feldt’s interval, is computed from two complete rows as alpha’s is. An item the two rows answer alike is refused as constant, and two rows with the same total are refused as a composite that does not vary.

  • bifactor_indices() puts residual covariances in its model implied denominators and refuses correlated factors and multiple-group fits. Each model implied denominator is now the sum of the corresponding block of the item correlations the fitted model reproduces. For every orthogonal fit without residual covariances that equals the earlier formula to machine precision, so those results are unchanged; for a fit that specifies residual covariances the earlier formula left them out, and a positive one made omega, omega_H, and omega_HS too high (omega_H .646 against .635 on a test sample with one cross-group residual covariance). A fit that correlates any two of the general and group factors, which the help page always excluded, is now refused with an error naming the pair. A multiple-group fit took its loadings from the first group and its residual variances from the last, so its table described neither group: for nine items with general and group loadings of .5 in two groups of 200 (set.seed(11); the fixture of the package’s tests), the general factor’s omega was .865 and its omega_H .623, while the model fitted to the first group alone gives .862 and .621, and to the second group alone .874 and .674. Such a fit is now refused (see Calls That Are Now Refused); fit the model to each group’s data to obtain that group’s indices.

  • bifactor_indices() refuses an item on two group factors. The help page, the argument, and the error message all required each item to load on exactly one group factor, but only an item on none was refused. An item on two took the loading and the membership of the group factor listed last, so its other loading dropped out of ECV, omega, omega_HS, H, and PUC, and the result depended on the order of the model syntax. On the 15-test Holzinger and Swineford bifactor model with lozenges (t4) also on the verbal factor, the spatial row described three of its four tests (omega_HS .188, H .254), PUC counted lozenges as a verbal test, and ECV was .441, where every loading counted gives .432. Such a fit is now refused, with the items and factors named. A loading fixed or constrained to zero no longer counts, so a model written with 0*x3, or with a*x3 and a == 0, on a second group factor gets the indices of the same model written without that loading; through 1.0.1 the zero loading took the item from its real factor. An item listed under one group factor keeps that loading whatever its value, as before.

  • bifactor_indices() refuses a fit with one group factor. DMAR 1.0.0 refused a fit with no group factor (“No group factors found; a bifactor model needs a general factor plus two or more group factors.”) and required every item to load on a group factor (“Every item must load on exactly one group factor.”), so it described a general factor beside a single group factor when every item was listed under that factor (some of them with loadings fixed at zero, and with general named, since both factors then listed every item), giving a table whose indices divide the common variance between those two factors alone. Such a fit is not a bifactor model with subscales, and it is now refused, with a message that names the group factor and any items on no group factor, as fa_bifactor() and ci_bifactor_indices(), new in 1.1.0, refuse it. There is no warning period. The message for an item on two group factors now says that an item loads on one group factor at most, since an item on none is accepted when there are two or more group factors.

  • bifactor_indices() reports H as NA for a factor with a standardized loading at or beyond one. The index counts 1 - l^2 as each item’s error, so such a loading leaves an item an error variance that is not positive and the index is not defined, as reliability_H() treats an improper solution. Through 1.0.1 the loading was left out, and H described the factor’s other items, with only the general Heywood warning to show it. On nine simulated items (set.seed(7); n <- 150; lg <- c(.9, rep(.6, 8)); ls <- c(.42, rep(.5, 8)); g <- rnorm(n); f <- list(rnorm(n), rnorm(n), rnorm(n)), item i equal to lg[i] * g + ls[i] * f[[ceiling(i / 3)]] + sqrt(1 - lg[i]^2 - ls[i]^2) * rnorm(n)), fit as a bifactor model with three orthogonal group factors of three items each and std.lv = TRUE, the first general loading is 1.06, and the general factor’s H was .841, the H of the other eight loadings. That value was not a limit of nearby solutions: as that loading rose to .9999, H rose to .9998, and past one it fell to .841. It is now NA, and every other cell of the table is unchanged. In ci_bifactor_indices(), new in 1.1.0, such a replication yields no coefficient and is set aside under either improper rule.

  • bifactor_indices() says which H it reports and what its group rows mean, and gives the maximal reliability of each factor. The help page called H “the construct reliability (maximal reliability) of Hancock and Mueller (2001)”. The column is the index Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) report: Hancock and Mueller’s closed form on one factor’s standardized loadings, which treats the variance an item shares with the other factors as uncorrelated error. In a bifactor model that variance is correlated, so the index is not the maximal reliability of the factor under the fitted model, and it can lie on either side of it. In the help page’s example the general factor’s index is 0.769 and its maximal reliability 0.678, barely above omega_H (0.673), so no weighting of the items reaches the index; on the 15-test Holzinger and Swineford model they are .789 and .681; and with group loadings of mixed sign the maximal reliability is the larger. On a group factor’s row the maximal reliability is the larger when the items of the other subscales measure a strong general factor well, since the optimal weights remove it through them: with nine items in three subscales, general loadings .7, and group loadings .3, a group factor’s index is 0.229 and its maximal reliability 0.279. That maximal reliability belongs to the group factor’s regression score from all nine items, which weights the other subscales’ items negatively. No score of the subscale’s own items reaches it, and their best weighting reaches only the omega_HS of 0.125. The maximal reliability, l’ R^-1 l with R the item correlations the model reproduces, is the square of the regression score determinacy that factor_scores() reports. It is now returned in the new attribute maximal_reliability (NA for an improper solution), printed under the table, and given an interval by ci_bifactor_indices(); its sample value, like the index’s, runs upward, as the help page says. The ECV on a group factor’s row, which no page defined, is the general factor’s share of the common variance of that factor’s items. One minus it is the group factor’s own share, so .85 beside an omega_HS of .08 says the subscale is mostly general. The omega there is the reliability of the subscale’s total score. Both are now defined on the help page and in a line under the printed table, as they are for ci_bifactor_indices(). No value in the table changes.

  • reliability_H() returns the reliability family table for every call; the table of 1.0.0 is gone. In 1.0.0 the function took loadings, se_loadings, and conf_level and returned the row reliability_H, with ci_lower, ci_upper, and var_H when se_loadings was supplied. Such a call now returns the table every other input returns (rows estimate, se, ci_lower, ci_upper, conf_level, N, N_complete, n_items), with no warning period. With se_loadings it has the same estimate and the same logit interval, var_H being the square of se. Without se_loadings it has the estimate, with se and the limits NA, because standardized loadings alone carry nothing an interval can be formed from. Code that read x$value[x$term == "reliability_H"] reads x$value[x$term == "estimate"]. factor, group, missing, and aux do not apply to loadings and are refused. Every interval built from se_loadings warns, with class dmar_H_marginal_se, that it ignores the covariances among the loading estimates. The help page now attributes the logit interval to Browne (1982) rather than Browne (1968). It replaces the unverified statement that Hancock and Mueller proved H >= omega >= alpha, as does the function interactions vignette, which said that H is uniformly at least omega and omega at least alpha, with the bound that holds by construction: H is at least the model implied omega of the same single-factor fit; robust omega need not lie below it. Alpha is at most omega in the population for congeneric items with uncorrelated errors.

  • The bootstrap attribute names two causes. Every reliability coefficient’s bootstrap attribute, and its jackknife element, gains undetermined and improper: the replications among the non-finite ones that were set aside because the resample left a polychoric correlation undetermined or gave an improper solution (zero outside categorical omega). The reasons vector keeps its 1.0.1 shape.

  • A bootstrap whose returned replicates are all equal returns that value at both limits. When every item is an exact linear function of the same variable, every resample gives the same coefficient. The percentile and BCa intervals of reliability_alpha() and reliability_kr20() stopped with “argument is of length zero” (after boot printed “All values of t are equal”), or with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” when some replications were set aside. They now return the common value at both limits, as bootstrap_se already did (and so does bootstrap_se_logistic, whose limits at a value of one, identical items, were NA, or one where rounding left the replicates just below it, since the logit is infinite there), with a warning that the bootstrap distribution is a single point. A BCa request falls back to that percentile interval and says why in ci_method. The engine also warns whenever fewer than two replications return a value, not only when some were set aside.

  • B is validated by reliability_alpha(), reliability_omega(), reliability_kr20(), and reliability_omega_categorical().
