When a bootstrap is requested, B must be a single whole number of at least 2, the fewest replications from which a standard deviation or a pair of quantiles can be formed, as reliability_H() and ci_bifactor_indices() require. Through 1.0.1 B = 0 or 1 returned NA limits without a warning (categorical omega did not check B at all, and B = 1 returned its estimate with NA limits), and a fractional, negative, or missing B failed inside boot with an error that did not name it. Each function now stops before anything is computed, with one message. No estimate or interval changes.

  • A DMAR table prints to three decimal places, not to three significant figures. A value in a DMAR table that is not a whole number printed to digits significant figures, 3 by default, and format() dropped its trailing zeros and wrote a small value in scientific notation: 13.018 printed as 13, 0.5596 as 0.56, 233.4107 as 233, 0.041234 as 0.0412, 1.5 as 1.5, and 0.00001234 as 1.23e-05. It now prints to digits decimal places with its trailing zeros, never in scientific notation: 13.018, 0.560, 233.411, 0.041, 1.500, and 0.000. A value that rounds to zero prints as 0.000 whatever its sign. Whole numbers, such as degrees of freedom and sample sizes, print without a decimal part as before. A measured quantity that lands on a whole number, at the bound of its range or where it is fixed, printed as a whole number too, and where the table shows that it is measured it now prints to the decimal places of the values beside it (?dmar_tbl gives the rule):

    • the limits of an interval and the estimate they belong to, and the other bounds DMAR names with _lower or _upper, such as an equivalence margin: a lower limit of exactly 0, which printed as 0, prints as 0.000 beside an upper limit of 0.083, and a factor variance fixed at 1 prints as 1.000 beside its interval;
    • a fit index, a power, a proportion or probability (the pct_ rows of a sensitivity analysis among them), a mean, median, standard deviation, or other moment, a test statistic, a standard error, a noncentrality parameter, the delta and the weights of a model comparison, and a heterogeneity index, wherever they appear: a CFI of 1 prints as 1.000 beside a TLI of 1.012, a power of 1 as 1.000 beside a power of 0.840, and a standard deviation of the interval widths of 0 as 0.000 beside their mean of 1.176;
    • a whole value in a column that also holds values that are not whole, unless the column is named for a count: an F of 4 prints as 4.000 beside 4.270, and a standard error of 0 as 0.000 beside 0.050, while degrees of freedom adjusted for sphericity still print 2 beside 1.830;
    • the columns a function names as measured: the loadings, intercepts, and standard deviations of dmacs(), where an intercept given as 2 prints as 2.000 beside one of 2.300.

    Elsewhere a whole value prints as a count, as before, since nothing in a long table says which of its other whole numbers are counts: a planning value given as 15 prints as 15. p-values (digits_p, four decimal places, with the “< 0.0001” floor) and the information criteria a table names in its fixed_terms (digits_fixed, three decimal places) print as before. print(), format(), knit_print(), and as_kable() show the same table, and the displays that lay out cells of their own (those of fa_exploratory(), factor_count(), and factor_scores()) and the lines beneath a table print measured values the same way: a CFI of 1 prints as 1.000 in the display of factor_count() as it does in the table of sem_fit_measures(), and a congruence coefficient of 1 as 1.000 in the table of factor_congruence() and in the matrix beneath it. For code written against 1.0.x:

    • The digits argument of print() and format() for a DMAR table, and options(dmar.digits = ), now count decimal places, not significant figures: print(x, digits = 5) showed five significant figures and now shows five decimal places, in the table and in the numbers a display writes beneath it. digits must be a whole number of 0 or more; a fractional or negative value, which signif() accepted, stops with an error that says so.
    • format(x) returns the new display strings.
    • No stored value changes. x$value, the other columns, tidy(), and glance() return the numbers at full precision, as before; read the column, or print with more decimal places (print(x, digits = 8)), to see more of a number than the table shows.
    • results_sentence() keeps its own digits, two decimal places by default, which options(dmar.digits = ) does not change. It now writes a value that rounds to zero without a minus sign, as the table does: a lower limit of -0.004 reads “95% CI [0.00, 0.55]”, where it read “[-0.00, 0.55]”.

  • A knitted result table carries every line the console prints. knit_print() and as_kable() wrote only the sum-of-squares type and the confidence level, so a knitted omega lost its denominator and residual lines and a knitted bootstrap interval its replication count (missing since 1.0.1). The tables of sem_fit_measures(), equivalence_rmsea(), sem_residual_fit(), sem_information_criteria(), compare_sem(), fraction_missing_information(), and factor_scores() print lines of their own with the table (which version of a fit measure was reported and why, the sample size convention, the verdict of a test, what a model comparison checked, how a fraction of missing information was estimated), and a sample size plan for incomplete data prints the missing data it assumed. The console print and the knitr methods now read one footer, which every class extends through an internal generic; a knitted table sets each footer line as a paragraph beneath it (two lines no longer run together), and as_kable() joins them into the caption. A knitted fraction_missing_information() table leaves out the columns the console leaves out, and a knitted factor_scores() result is the summary the console prints (the first rows of each factor, the reasons values are missing or borrowed, the determinacy of each missing data pattern, how to read the intervals) rather than every row. The console’s confidence level is formatted by the same helper as the knitted one, which prints every conventional level as before, and a blank line now separates it from the lines after it. The lines above a fa_confirmatory() table (the measurement structure each factor’s constraints imply, also for cfa_1() and cfa_2()) and above a mediation_mbco() table (the effects and N, the groups, the full model’s deviance, AIC, BIC, and R squared, how to read each p_value), which print methods of their own wrote and knit_print() never called, are set as paragraphs before a knitted table and first in the as_kable() caption. No stored value changes.

  • as_kable() and knit_print() escape the lines they write for LaTeX and HTML. knitr escapes a table’s cells and column names but writes a caption as it is given, and as_kable() passed the table’s lines to it without escaping them. With format = "latex", or the default format in an .Rnw document, the “%” of “Confidence level: 95%” started a LaTeX comment that swallowed the caption’s closing brace: a LaTeX document did not compile, and an R Markdown PDF printed the table’s LaTeX source as text. An underscore in an item name (the residual correlation line of an omega) or an ampersand in a citation (the pairwise deletion line) stopped the compilation as well. The caption is now escaped for the format knitr renders, and knit_print() writes its lines in that format’s markup: escaped paragraphs and a verbatim block for LaTeX, where a “%” had silently cut the rest of its line, and <p> and <pre> elements for HTML. Markdown output, the default in R Markdown, is unchanged. A caption passed through ..., which R refused as an argument matched twice, is refused with a message that says how to caption the table otherwise.

  • Two DMAR tables knitted in one chunk stay apart. knit_print() wrote its output with no blank line before or after it, and knitr writes a chunk’s outputs with nothing between them. In a chunk with echo = FALSE that printed two tables, the second table’s header row was appended to the first table’s last footer line (“Confidence level: 95%|term |value |”). Pandoc then read that line as the second table’s header, in R Markdown’s HTML and PDF output alike: the footer became a header cell, the second table lost its last column name, and the first table lost its footer paragraph. The output is now set off by a blank line on each side, as knitr sets off a kable of its own.

  • results_sentence() reads an interval held as ci_lower and ci_upper, names the estimate the interval belongs to, and reports the interval’s own confidence level. In DMAR 1.0.x it read an interval only from rows or columns then named lower_limit and upper_limit, and told every table that held one as ci_lower and ci_upper (a row of contrast_test(), adjusted_means(), content_validity_index(), fa_confirmatory(), or the coefficient table of mlmr() or mlmr_mv(), and the tidy() results that hold their limits as ci_lower and ci_upper) that it “carries no confidence interval”. Every table now names its limits ci_lower and ci_upper (see Breaking Changes), so the rows of common_method_adjusted_r(), new in 1.1.0, are read as well, from the columns of a one-row table, a row beside a generic estimate column is labeled by its term (so results_sentence(tidy(ci_smd(...))) writes what results_sentence(ci_smd(...)) writes), and a table with neither pair is told what was looked for. Two earlier defects change sentences it wrote before. The estimate of a wide table was its first numeric column other than the limits, N, and the p-value, so the first row of the ?responder_analysis example read “n = 60.00, 95% CI [0.38, 0.62]” and the second row of simple_effects_AB(aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth)) “F_value = 13.33, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35], p = 0.0006”; the estimate is now the estimate or value column when there is one and otherwise the first numeric column that is not a limit, standard error, test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, confidence level, or count (“estimate = 0.50” and “eta_squared_partial = 0.20” there). And the confidence level was read from the table’s attribute alone, which the reliability family does not set, so a 90% interval for omega was written “95% CI”; it is now read from the attribute, the conf_level row, or the conf_level column. A tidy() row that the default method builds from a wide table was labeled “estimate” through 1.0.1 and is now labeled with the quantity it holds (see the entry on the default tidy() below). Every other change to a sentence is one of the entries that follow.

  • Every table that forms a confidence interval records its level, and results_sentence() states no level a table does not record. results_sentence() took 95% when a table recorded no level, and many recorded none:

    • ci_eta_squared() and ci_omega_squared() (and ci_eta_squared_partial(), which this release removes);
    • vargha_delaney_A() and pairwise_within();
    • every interval formed from alpha_lower and alpha_upper (ci_c(), ci_cv(), ci_mahalanobis(), ci_r(), ci_R(), ci_rc(), ci_reg_coef(), ci_rmsea(), ci_sc(), ci_sm(), ci_smd(), ci_smd_c(), ci_src());
    • and the tidy() and glance() results of every table the default methods handle.

    A 90% interval was therefore written “95% CI”. With fit <- aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth), results_sentence(ci_eta_squared(fit, conf_level = 0.90)[1, ], digits = 3) gave “eta_squared = 0.224, 95% CI [0.073, 0.350]”, where the 95% interval is [0.053, 0.377]. With set.seed(1); x <- rnorm(40, 0.5); y <- rnorm(40), results_sentence(vargha_delaney_A(x, y, conf_level = 0.90), digits = 3) gave “A = 0.674, 95% CI [0.565, 0.767], p = 0.0051”, where the 95% interval is [0.543, 0.782].

    Each of these tables now records its level: conf_level, or 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper when the tail areas are given, as ci_R2(), ci_pvaf(), ci_snr(), and ci_srsnr() already did.

    • The ANOVA intervals, vargha_delaney_A(), pairwise_within(), and the intervals formed from tail areas print that level beneath the table, which they did not.
    • vargha_delaney_A() and pairwise_within() return DMAR tables and print as the rest do; their columns are unchanged. vargha_delaney_A() gains tidy() and glance() methods whose row is named “A”.
    • pairwise_within(bonferroni_ci = TRUE) records conf_level, the level its Bonferroni intervals hold jointly, as contrast_test(adjust = "bonferroni") and the post hoc intervals record theirs. The line beneath the table of both functions names the adjustment and the level of each interval: “Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous across the 3 comparisons (Bonferroni: each interval at 98.33%)”. With set.seed(1); Y <- matrix(rnorm(60), 20) + rep(c(0, 0.3, 0.6), each = 20), the second row of pairwise_within(Y, bonferroni_ci = TRUE, conf_level = 0.90), whose interval [0.02, 1.07] is the 96.67% interval of that comparison, was written “95% CI”; it is written “90% CI”.
    • ci_eta_squared_generalized() recorded the default 0.95 beside the interval that alpha_lower = 0.05 and alpha_upper = 0.05 define; it records 0.90.
    • The default tidy() of a wide table with an interval adds a conf_level column (NA when no interval was formed). The default tidy() of a long table with an interval adds a conf_level column that holds the level on the rows of the interval and NA on every other row. Those rows are its estimate and its two limits, or an estimate’s <estimate>_ci_lower and <estimate>_ci_upper rows at that interval’s own level. The rows therefore carry their level when tidy() results are stacked with rbind(): the rows of tidy(ci_proportion(30, 60, conf_level = 0.99)) stacked under tidy(ci_proportion(12, 40, conf_level = 0.90)) give “proportion = 0.50, 99% CI [0.34, 0.66]”.
    • The default glance() of a long table with an interval adds estimand and conf_level columns (see the next entry): results_sentence(glance(ci_proportion(30, 100, conf_level = 0.90))) gives “proportion = 0.30, 90% CI [0.23, 0.38]”.
    • The tables results_sentence() reads for the first time in 1.1.0 carry their level as well. The coefficient tables of mlmr() and mlmr_mv() record it. The tidy() results of the reliability family, fa_confirmatory(), content_validity_index(), mediation_mbco(), fraction_missing_information(), mlmr(), and mlmr_mv() (with conf.int = TRUE) carry a conf_level column. For m <- mlmr(t6_paragraph_comprehension ~ t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning, data = holzinger_swineford, conf_level = 0.90), results_sentence(m$coef_table[2, ]) reads “t7_sentence = 0.32, 90% CI [0.26, 0.38], p < 0.0001”.

    results_sentence() now refuses a table that records no level, such as one assembled by hand, unless its new argument conf_level gives the level. It also refuses a conf_level that differs from the level the table records. No interval changes.

  • results_sentence() reports the estimate a long table’s interval belongs to. In a table that holds its interval in ci_lower and ci_upper rows, the estimate was the first other row, and two tables list another quantity first.

    • correction_for_attenuation(r = .3, reliability_x = .8, reliability_y = .7, N = 200) gave “correlation_observed = 0.30, 95% CI [0.22, 0.56]”: the observed correlation beside the interval of the corrected one, .401.
    • proportion_of_superiority(smd = .5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50) gave “smd = 0.50, 95% CI [0.54, 0.82]”, an interval that does not contain the estimate it names.

    The two tables now name the row their interval belongs to in a ci_estimate attribute, which results_sentence() reads: “correlation_corrected = 0.40, 95% CI [0.22, 0.56]” and “proportion_of_superiority = 0.69, 95% CI [0.54, 0.82]”. Their rows are unchanged. The tidy() of a long table names the estimate in its rows, through its conf_level column, and its glance() names the column that holds the estimate in an estimand column, so the sentence of either is the table’s own. Through 1.0.1 the glance() sentence of the attenuation table also named the observed correlation.

  • results_sentence() reports the TOST p-value of an equivalence test. It appended the first p-value row of a long table. The tables of equivalence_r(), equivalence_smd(), and equivalence_c() list the p-values of the two one-sided tests before the TOST p-value, so a result that is not equivalent was written with the p-value of one one-sided test.

    • equivalence_r(r = .15, N = 300, cor_lower = .2, cor_upper = .2), whose TOST p-value is .187 (not equivalent), gave “r = 0.15, 90% CI [0.06, 0.24], p = < 0.0001” (the p-value of the lower test, 5e-10). It now gives “r = 0.15, 90% CI [0.06, 0.24], p = 0.1870”.
    • For equivalence_smd(smd = .3, n_1 = 100, n_2 = 100, smd_lower = .5, smd_upper = .5) the sentence gives p = 0.0806 where it gave the lower test’s 3e-08.
    • For example 3 of ?equivalence_c it gives p = 0.0393 where it gave the lower test’s 3.9e-07.

    The three tables name p_tost in a p_sentence attribute, which tidy() and glance() carry, so their sentences give the same p-value. The meta-analysis tables, whose first p-value row is the pooled p-value, are unchanged.

  • results_sentence() writes “p < 0.0001”, not “p = < 0.0001”. A p-value below the floor of format_p() was appended as “, p =” and then “< 0.0001”. The sentence now writes the bound: summary_t_test(mean_1 = 2, sd_1 = 1, n_1 = 30, mean_2 = 0, sd_2 = 1, n_2 = 30) gives “mean_difference = 2.00, 95% CI [1.48, 2.52], p < 0.0001”. Larger p-values are written as before.

  • The default tidy() of a wide table with an interval takes as its estimate the column the interval belongs to, and its sentence names that quantity. It took the first numeric column. A row of simple_effects_AB() therefore gave its F statistic beside the limits for partial eta squared: for simple_effects_AB(aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth)), results_sentence() on its second tidy() row wrote “estimate = 13.33, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35], p = 0.0006”, where the estimate is 0.20. A table whose estimate column follows a count (responder_analysis()) lost the count.

    In a table that carries an interval, the estimate is now the table’s own estimate (or value) column. Otherwise it is the first numeric column that is not a limit, standard error, test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, confidence level, or count, the rule results_sentence() follows. The other numeric columns follow under their own names (the F statistic as F_value, the count as n).

    When the estimate comes from a column with a name of its own, an estimand column after estimate keeps the name, and results_sentence() labels the row with it; otherwise it labels the row with its term. The tidy() row’s sentence is then the table’s own. content_validity_index() also gains the estimand column "i_cvi": content_validity_index(matrix(c(4, 4, 3, 4, 3, 1, 4, 3), nrow = 2), conf_level = .90) gives “i_cvi = 1.00, 90% CI [0.47, 1.00]” on its first raw or tidy row, where 1.0.1 refused both as carrying no interval. A tidy FMI row labels its estimate fmi rather than the parameter’s name. For the existing examples:

    • “eta_squared_partial = 0.20, 95% CI [0.04, 0.35], p = 0.0006” for that row;
    • “D2 = 0.50, 90% CI [0.03, 1.03]” for ci_mahalanobis(D2 = .5, n_1 = 40, n_2 = 40, p = 3, conf_level = .9);
    • kappa for fleiss_kappa() and cohen_kappa(), mean_difference for pairwise_within(), and ave for average_variance_extracted();
    • the row’s term for icc() (“ICC(2,1)”), responder_analysis() (“control”), and adjusted_means() (the group).

    1.0.1 labeled the others “estimate”; it wrote no sentence for the tidy() rows of average_variance_extracted() and adjusted_means(), which hold their limits as ci_lower and ci_upper, and pairwise_within() had no tidy() method. The term column is unchanged. A table without an interval is tidied as before.

  • The intervals of ci_eta_squared() for the effects of a fit with an Error() term are converted with the size of each effect’s stratum. DMAR 1.0.x (in ci_eta_squared() and in ci_eta_squared_partial(), which this release removes) converted the noncentrality limits of every effect of an aovlist fit into limits for partial eta squared with the total number of rows, lambda / (lambda + N). Within subjects that put the interval on a smaller quantity than the one the partial eta squared beside it estimates: for the three IQ occasions of pygmalion analyzed in vignette("DMAR"), 930 rows against F(2, 618), the 95% interval was [0.111, 0.194] and lay below the estimate of 0.212. Each effect is now converted with the size of its own stratum. Within subjects that size is the stratum’s total degrees of freedom, here 2 + 618 = 620, which gives [0.157, 0.265]; the within-subjects example of ?ci_eta_squared goes from [0.015, 0.322] to [0.023, 0.417]. In the between-subjects stratum of a mixed design it is the number of subjects: with the expectancy treatment added to the pygmalion analysis as a between-subjects factor, the upper limit for treatment, converted with the 310 children rather than the 930 rows, goes from 0.018 to 0.052. Fits without an Error() term convert with the total sample size and the raw-argument interface with the N it is given, as before, and their results are unchanged; for an effect tested between subjects the total sample size makes the interval exact for the population partial eta squared that Steiger (2004), Kelley (2007), and Smithson (2001, 2003) define. Smithson’s conversion with the effect and error degrees of freedom plus one, which Fidler and Thompson (2001) also used, agrees with that definition only in a one-way design. The help of ci_eta_squared() gives the reasons and the literature, which does not settle the within-subjects case. The raw-argument interface now accepts an N as small as df_effect + df_error, the size of a within-subjects stratum that tests one effect, which DMAR 1.0.x refused. It does not warn when N is the number of rows of a within-subjects design, since it cannot tell that number from the total sample size of a between-subjects factorial design.

  • The parametric interval of ci_eta_squared_generalized() for the effects of a fit with an Error() term is converted with the size of each effect’s stratum. DMAR 1.0.x converted the noncentrality limits of every effect of an aovlist fit with the total number of rows, and within subjects the interval was for a smaller quantity than the one the estimate estimates: for the three IQ occasions of pygmalion, the 95% interval was [0.019, 0.037] against an estimate of 0.041. Each effect is now converted with the size of its stratum, as ci_eta_squared() converts it (the entry above), which gives [0.029, 0.054]. With that size the conversion maps each limit to the value of the population generalized eta squared of Olejnik and Algina

    1. when the ratio of the other sums of squares in its denominator to the effect’s error sum of squares is at the value it converges to. In the between-subjects stratum of a mixed design the size is the number of subjects: with the expectancy treatment added to the pygmalion analysis between subjects, the upper limit for treatment goes from 0.015 to 0.044. The within-subjects example of ?ci_eta_squared_generalized goes from [0.005, 0.145] to [0.008, 0.203]. Fits without an Error() term are converted with the number of observations, as before, and their intervals are unchanged. The help now sets out the quantity the conversion is made for and says that the interval cannot be exact when anything measured, or another stratum’s residual, enters the denominator: generalized eta squared then depends on a second parameter besides the noncentrality parameter, which alone determines the distribution of the effect’s F, and the interval takes that parameter’s sample value as known. The F interface now accepts an N as small as df_effect + df_error, the size of a within-subjects stratum that tests one effect, which DMAR 1.0.x refused.

  • eta_squared_generalized() and ci_eta_squared_generalized() stop when an effect of a fit with an Error() term is tested in more than one stratum. When observations are missing within subjects, or a covariate varies within them, aov() divides the effect’s sum of squares among strata and tests the effect in each of them. DMAR 1.0.x then returned a row for every stratum each time the effect’s name came up, each computed from the effect’s share in the first stratum: for 20 subjects in two groups observed three times, with four observations missing, aov(y ~ group * time + Error(subject / time)) gave nine rows for its five tests, time and group:time four times each, and the parametric interval stopped with an error from inside the noncentral F computation (“the condition has length > 1”). No one stratum’s share is the effect’s sum of squares, and Olejnik and Algina (2003) define the estimate for balanced designs, so both functions now stop and name the effects and strata involved. A fit in which every subject is observed equally often in every within-subjects condition, and every covariate is constant within subjects, tests each effect in one stratum, whatever the sizes of the between-subjects groups, and its results are unchanged.

  • ci_eta_squared_generalized() gives the parametric interval from sums of squares, and eta_squared_generalized() accepts the degrees of freedom that come with them. The interval needs df_effect, df_error, and N beside the sums of squares. Without them DMAR 1.0.x stopped and asked for them; with them it stopped with “‘F_effect’ must be a single non-negative number”, because eta_squared_generalized(), which computes the estimate, then read the call as the F interface as well; called directly with the same arguments, it stopped the same way. The sums of squares never gave an interval, and with the degrees of freedom present they gave no estimate either, whatever the method. Both functions now take df_effect and df_error with the sums of squares and read only F_effect, F_observed, and df_observed as the F interface. The estimate is computed from the sums of squares alone, which need no degrees of freedom, and the interval from the F they imply, (SS_effect / df_effect) / (SS_error / df_error), with N checked as the F interface checks it. That F is the effect’s test when SS_error is the sum of squares of the effect’s error term: the residual in a design without an Error() term, and otherwise the residual of the stratum in which the effect is tested, with the residuals of the other strata in SS_observed, beside the measured sources (Olejnik & Algina, 2003). The help of both functions now says so, and that each F of the F interface divides by the effect’s error mean square. For the one-way analysis of IQ gain by grade in pygmalion, the sums of squares of the anova() table, with N = 310, give 0.118 [0.048, 0.176], the row of the fitted model and of the F interface. Given no fitted model and both interfaces, ci_eta_squared_generalized() answers, as DMAR 1.0.x did, when they describe the same test: the F that the sums of squares imply for the effect, and the ratio of SS_observed to SS_error, agree with the F interface’s to a relative tolerance of 1e-6, the tolerance eta_squared_generalized() applies to the two estimates, and the interval is formed from the F-values. When they disagree it now stops, whatever the method, and so it does when only part of the F interface comes with the sums of squares; a fitted model still sets every raw argument aside with a warning, and eta_squared_generalized(), which computes no interval, still accepts the two interfaces together when they give the same estimate. DMAR 1.0.x accepted both interfaces whenever they gave the same estimate and built the interval from the F-values, but the two can agree on the estimate and still imply different F statistics for the effect. Sums of squares of 100 for the effect, 70 for the measured sources, and 200 for the error, on 2 and 50 degrees of freedom, imply an F of 12.5; an F of 25 for the effect and of 85 for a measured source on 1 degree of freedom give the same estimate, 0.270. With N = 53 the sums of squares give the interval [0.089, 0.413] and the F-values [0.127, 0.381], which DMAR 1.0.x reported for the two together. Both functions now also refuse a sum of squares, an F-value, or a number of degrees of freedom that is missing or infinite, and ci_eta_squared_generalized() an infinite N. DMAR 1.0.x stopped on most missing values with R’s “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, returned an estimate of 0 or NaN for an infinite value, and gave the F interface the interval [0, 0] for an infinite N.

  • The partial omega squared of each effect of a fit with an Error() term is computed with the size of its stratum, and the stratum is named. DMAR 1.0.x (omega_squared_partial(), which this release removes; omega_squared(fit, estimand = "partial") is its call) computed df_effect (F - 1) / (df_effect (F - 1) + N) with the total number of rows: for the three IQ occasions of pygmalion, 930 rows against F(2, 618), it gave 0.150, below the partial eta squared of 0.212 and its interval [0.157, 0.265]. With the stratum’s 2 + 618 = 620 the estimate is 0.209, an estimate of the quantity whose interval ci_eta_squared(estimand = "partial") gives; for treatment in the mixed design of the entry above, computed with the 310 children, it goes from 0.004 to 0.012. The value with the number of rows is the partial omega squared that Olejnik and Algina (2003) compute for a repeated measures factor, and the raw-argument interface given that number as N still returns it. The table of an aovlist fit gains a stratum column after the estimate, as in eta_squared(), which the description of the function promised; its N column still reports the number of observations, and the help says how to find the size of a stratum from summary() of the fit. Fits without an Error() term are unchanged. The raw-argument interfaces of omega_squared() and ci_omega_squared() now accept an N as small as df_effect + df_error, which DMAR 1.0.x refused, so that ci_omega_squared() gives a row’s estimate and its interval from the row’s F, its degrees of freedom, and the size of its stratum, and omega_squared() gives the same estimate. ci_omega_squared() now takes an aovlist fit itself (see Total and Partial Eta Squared and Omega Squared).

  • The tidy() of an ANOVA effect size table returns every effect. tidy() of ci_eta_squared(), ci_eta_squared_partial(), ci_eta_squared_generalized(), and ci_omega_squared() in DMAR 1.0.x returned the first row of the table alone, so the tidy() of a factorial fit dropped every other effect, and glance() was the same row. For fit <- aov(len ~ supp * factor(dose), data = ToothGrowth), tidy(ci_eta_squared_partial(fit, conf_level = 0.90)) gave one row, the supp effect (.224 [.073, .350]); tidy(ci_eta_squared(fit, estimand = "partial", conf_level = 0.90)) gives three, adding factor(dose) (.773 [.659, .814]) and the interaction (.132 [.011, .246]).

    The term names the effect size and, for ci_eta_squared() and ci_omega_squared(), its estimand (eta_squared_partial or eta_squared_total, where 1.0.1 named eta_squared; see One Function for Each ANOVA Effect Size), and an effect column after it names the effect; a stratum column follows it for a fit with an Error() term. A table of one effect and one estimand, as from summary statistics, therefore gives the row it gave with the effect column added. Its glance() is that row when tidy() gives one row. Otherwise it is one row with the effect size (term, the estimands separated by a comma when there are two), the number of effects (n_effects), N, and conf_level.

  • manova_split_plot(), mixed_anova(), and anova_within_two_way() return DMAR tables. DMAR 1.0.x returned each result as a plain data.frame, so class(x) was "data.frame" and the table printed through print.data.frame(), which formats a column of numbers as a whole: one small p-value put the whole p_value column in scientific notation. In the example on the help page of mixed_anova(), the three p-values printed as 2.148782e-05, 1.817787e-12, and 9.565106e-01. Each function now returns its table with the class c("dmar_tbl", "data.frame"), as anova_within() and factorial_anova() do, and it prints through the dmar_tbl display layer: whole numbers such as degrees of freedom without a decimal part, other values to 3 decimal places, and p-values to 4 decimal places, with one below 0.0001 printed as “< 0.0001” (in that example, < 0.0001, < 0.0001, and 0.9565). Adding the class changes nothing else in the object, and as.data.frame(x) returns the table as a plain data frame. For mixed_anova() and anova_within_two_way() that is the 1.0.x data frame itself (identical() to it): the columns, rows, and values are unchanged, as is the sum_of_squares_type attribute of mixed_anova(). For manova_split_plot() the columns and rows are those of 1.0.x, but not every value: its default Type III B rows now test the within-subjects main effect, where those of 1.0.x tested a simple effect (see the entry above on that test), and its other rows, with the B rows under ss_type = 2, agree with those of 1.0.x to rounding error (within 1e-12, relative, on the designs compared) rather than exactly. For code written against 1.0.x:

    • is.data.frame(x) and inherits(x, "data.frame") are TRUE as before, and x$p_value and the other columns hold the table’s numbers at full precision. Code that tests the class itself sees the new one: identical(class(x), "data.frame") is FALSE; class(x) == "data.frame" has length 2, so if () on it stops with “the condition has length > 1” in R 4.2.0 and later (earlier versions warn and use the first element, FALSE); and against a saved 1.0.x result of mixed_anova() or anova_within_two_way(), identical() is FALSE and all.equal() reports a difference in the class alone.
    • The data frame methods work on the table as they did on the plain data frame. x[i, ], subset(), and rbind() with x first keep the class, so their results print the new way too; merge() still returns a plain data frame, and summary() and as.matrix() return what they return for the plain data frame. print() and format() now dispatch to the dmar_tbl methods, so format(x) returns the display strings described above rather than those of format.data.frame(). In an R Markdown document a table that a chunk prints is set by knit_print.dmar_tbl() as a knitr::kable() table of those strings where 1.0.x showed console text; knitr::kable(x) called directly formats the numbers itself, as before.
    • tidy() and glance() answer through the default methods for a wide DMAR table (see ?dmar_tidiers). tidy() gives one row per row of the table, its term joining the label columns (effect with statistic_name, denominator, or adjustment), its estimate the first numeric column (statistic_value, ss, or F_value), and the other numeric columns after it under their own names. The last row of the tidy() of manova_split_plot() is the table’s record of the sum-of-squares type: its term is "sum_of_squares_type:NA" (the row’s statistic_name is NA), its estimate the type, 2 or 3, and its other columns NA, so code that summarizes the estimates of the tests leaves that row out, as it would from the table. glance() gives one row: the number of rows (n_terms), with conf_level and B_used NA, since no interval or bootstrap is formed. For the plain data frame of 1.0.x the generics package has no method, and where broom was loaded its data frame tidiers, which broom has deprecated, answered: tidy() stopped with an error on the character columns, and glance() gave nrow, ncol, complete.obs, and na.fraction. results_sentence() refuses these tables as before, since none holds a confidence interval. as_kable(), which stopped on the plain data frame of 1.0.x with “no applicable method”, now returns a knitr::kable() table of the display strings, and dmar_metadata(), new in 1.1.0 and taking only a DMAR table, accepts these tables.

    ancova() already returned a dmar_tbl in DMAR 1.0.x, and its result is unchanged.

  • ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(estimator = "omega") returns intervals. Since 1.0.0 it asked reliability_omega() for the "mlr" interval under the default observed denominator, for which no Wald interval is defined; every replication failed silently, and the table showed no widths and a non-coverage of zero. Omega is now computed with denominator = "model_implied", the coefficient the planner’s interval is built on, with the "ml" interval the plan describes (see the entry on the interval its plan was made for). A replication that returns no interval is now set aside rather than counted as covering the true value; the proportions are over the replications that returned one, one warning states how many were set aside and why, and a run in which none returned an interval stops with the reason. The rule changes nothing for alpha with Bonett’s interval, its default through 1.0.1.

  • ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() evaluates the assurance plan at the planner’s defaults. With an assurance, the plan whose N is simulated was searched at 50 and 200 replications (G_initial and G, then initial_iter and final_iter) against the planner’s defaults of 500 and 5000, and the noise let a size below the one the assurance needs pass by chance. For four parallel items of reliability .80, a width of .15, and an assurance of .80, the evaluated N ranged from 93 to 101 over seeds 1 to 30 (set.seed(s) before each call; mean 96.9) against 98 to 101 (mean 99.2) at the defaults, so a correctly specified plan seemed to fall short of its assurance. The plan now runs at the planner’s defaults, as the rest of the sensitivity family does, which adds about a second. With ci_method = "ml" the replications’ alpha intervals change as reliability_alpha()’s do, slightly for the unit variance items simulated here (mean width .1531 to .1527 in 1,000 replications at N = 74, after set.seed(113)); Bonett’s interval, the default through 1.0.1, is unchanged.

  • ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity() evaluates the interval its plan was made for. The plan is ss_aipe_reliability()’s for the parallel model with the normal theory interval, a Wald interval with the van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000) variance. The replications, however, computed Bonett’s (2002) interval for alpha and the "mlr" interval for omega, so a correctly specified plan was judged by an interval it was not made for. The default ci_method is now "ml" for both estimators, with complete or incomplete data. For alpha that is reliability_alpha(ci_method = "ml"), whose variance at a population of parallel items is the compound symmetry form the plan uses. For omega it is reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"), whose delta method variance equals that form there to machine precision. Under missing data these are the Wald intervals with the FIML standard error that the fmi adjustment plans for.

    • Take four items, a true and planned reliability of .80, a width of .15, and an assurance of .80, with set.seed(113) before each call (true_reliability = .8, supposed_reliability = .8, n_items = 4, width = .15, assurance = .8, G = 2000). The plan of 99 cases gives intervals no wider than .15 in 81.3 percent of the 2,000 replications, against 76.75 percent with ci_method = "bonett" on the same draws, and a mean width of .1312 against .1346.
    • For omega (estimator = "omega", G = 1000), which returned no intervals in 1.0.x, the default gives 83.3 percent against 81.9 with ci_method = "mlr".
    • The first example on the help page (G = 20) goes from a mean width of .1685 and a proportion of .40 to .1630 and .45.
    • For alpha, naming ci_method = "bonett" reproduces 1.0.x without an assurance, apart from the replications the entry on clamped limits describes. With an assurance the plan is now searched at the planner’s defaults (see the entry on the assurance plan), which draws other replications: the call above gave 78.65 percent and a mean width of .1337 in 1.0.1. Any other interval can still be named.

  • Noncentral chi square intervals stay right for a statistic in the millions. R’s pchisq() with a noncentrality stops its series after 10^6 terms, and above a noncentrality of about 2e6 it returns wrong probabilities (0 where the value is .19 at 3e6), with a warning that was suppressed. ci_nc_chisq(), and through it ci_rmsea(), ecvi(), and the intervals of sem_fit_measures() and equivalence_rmsea(), then returned limits collapsed onto one value below the statistic. For a statistic of 3e6 on 3000 df the 90 percent limits were 2979734 twice and are now 2991307 and 3002700; the RMSEA interval at N = 1e5, with the multiplier N, was [0.09966, 0.09966] around an estimate of 0.09995 and is now [0.09986, 0.10004]. Above a noncentrality of 1e5, the distribution function is now summed as the Poisson mixture of central chi square distributions it is, accurate to rounding. At and below 1e5 nothing changes. equivalence_rmsea() and the close fit tests of sem_fit_measures() use the same function: a bound of .10 at a statistic of 3e6 had a p-value of 0 and was declared met, where the p-value is .193. For a fitted model, sem_fit_measures() computes the limits and tests itself once the statistic, or the noncentrality of a close fit bound, exceeds 1e5. The robust limits and tests of a FIML, ordered data, or two-stage fit, which it cannot rebuild, become NA with a warning past 1e6.

  • ci_rmsea() gains sample_size_convention = c("N-1", "N"). It sets the multiplier with which the reported RMSEA was computed; lavaan’s default likelihood and Mplus use N. The default keeps every earlier result. The help page now says correctly that the lower limit of the 90 percent interval settles the test of close fit and the upper limit the test of not close fit (it had described the upper limit as the test of close fit), and that the function assumes one group.

  • ci_rmsea() refuses zero degrees of freedom and a sample size that leaves no multiplier. A saturated model (lavaan reports an RMSEA of 0 on 0 df) had returned limits of Inf with no warning, the lower one above the estimate. N = 1 under the default convention had given an upper limit of Inf, and N between 0 and 1 an NA. df must now be greater than 0; it need not be whole, since a mean and variance adjusted statistic has fractional degrees of freedom. N must make the multiplier positive. An invalid conf_level is refused in its own name rather than as alpha_lower and alpha_upper.

  • ci_rmsea() forms a 90 percent interval by default. The default conf_level is 0.90, where DMAR 1.0.x had 0.95, since a 100(1 - 2 alpha) percent interval decides the one-sided tests of close and not close fit at level alpha (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996, p. 136), so the limits of the 90 percent interval are those tests at .05 (see Every RMSEA Interval at 90 Percent by Default). For an RMSEA of .035 on 40 df with N = 425, the interval of the help page’s first example, the limits were .008 and .055 and are .015 and .052. conf_level = 0.95 restores the 1.0.x interval. An interval given by alpha_lower and alpha_upper is unchanged.

  • ss_aipe_rmsea() plans a 90 percent interval by default. The default conf_level is 0.90, where DMAR 1.0.x had 0.95, so that the plan is for the interval ci_rmsea() now forms by default. A lower level needs a smaller sample for the same width: for an RMSEA of .045 on 5 df and a width of .060, necessary_N was 1068 and is 802. conf_level = 0.95 restores the 1.0.x plan.

  • ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity() simulates 90 percent intervals by default and forms each as lavaan does, from the replication’s statistic with lavaan’s multiplier.

    • The default conf_level is 0.90, where DMAR 1.0.x had 0.95, as in ss_aipe_rmsea() and ci_rmsea(). conf_level = 0.95 restores the level.
    • Each replication’s interval was formed from lavaan’s RMSEA, which lavaan computes with the multiplier N under its default likelihood, as though it had been computed with N - 1, the default convention of ci_rmsea(). The interval matched neither convention and was slightly too wide, that of a sample one case smaller. It is now formed with lavaan’s own multiplier (N under the default likelihood, N - 1 under likelihood = "wishart" or a least squares estimator passed through ...). This was a defect, and no argument restores it.
    • Each interval was also formed from the replication’s RMSEA, which lavaan truncates at 0 when the statistic is at or below its degrees of freedom. From an RMSEA of 0 the statistic can be rebuilt only as equal to its degrees of freedom (see ci_rmsea()), so every such replication was given the interval of that statistic, wider than the interval of its own. Each interval is now formed from the replication’s chi square statistic, as lavaan and sem_fit_measures() form it, and equals the interval lavaan reports for the sample whatever the statistic; its upper limit is 0 when the statistic is at or below the (1 - conf_level) / 2 quantile of the central chi square, the convention the two share. A model that fits well, many of whose replications fall below their degrees of freedom, gets narrower intervals: for the two-factor population of the help page fit by its own two-factor model (8 df), with N = 200, G = 40, conf_level = 0.90, and set.seed(113), 21 of the 40 statistics fell below 8, the mean width, .0920 in DMAR 1.0.x, is .0802, and the proportion of intervals narrower than a width of .05, 0 before, is .10. This was a defect too, and no argument restores it. A replication whose statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom gets the interval it had, so a markedly misspecified model, such as that of the help page’s example, is not affected.
    • The simulated sample is still the planner’s necessary_N, the size a study would collect. The width depends on the sample size only through the multiplier, and ss_aipe_rmsea() plans with N - 1 (Kelley & Lai, 2011), so under lavaan’s default, whose multiplier is N, the realized intervals are a little narrower than the planned width, by an amount of order 1/N.
    • For the help page’s example (a population RMSEA of .204 on 9 df, a width of .05, set.seed(113), G = 20), DMAR 1.0.x evaluated a sample of 695 and reported a mean width of .05002; the default now evaluates 493 for the 90 percent interval, with a mean width of .04990, and conf_level = 0.95 evaluates 695, with a mean width of .04998.

  • ecvi(fit) divides by the multiplier lavaan used to form the statistic. For a fit under likelihood = "wishart" or a least squares estimator (GLS, WLS, ULS, DWLS) that multiplier is N - G, and the earlier divisor N disagreed with lavaan::fitMeasures(); the three-factor Holzinger and Swineford model under the Wishart likelihood gave 0.4220 and now gives lavaan’s 0.4234, and the interval limits move with it. Results for ML under the default normal likelihood, and for summary input, are unchanged. The help page now states the identity N ECVI = AIC + 2 l_s only for the likelihood ratio statistic.

  • ecvi() applies the checks of the SEM fit family and states its boundary cases. A fitted model with an inadmissible solution is now refused, as sem_fit_measures() and sem_information_criteria() refuse it; a 60 case two-factor fit of the Holzinger and Swineford tests with a latent variance of -72.9 had an ECVI of 1.116 [0.799, 1.598]. A well fitting model, whose statistic is below the upper alpha/2 quantile, no longer warns about a prob_greater row that ecvi() does not return. When the statistic lies at or below the lower alpha/2 quantile, the upper limit is still NA, now with a warning in ecvi()’s own terms. The help page says why that limit is not set to the lower one, and that the untruncated estimate lies below the interval when the statistic is below its degrees of freedom. n = 0, which returned Inf and NaN, is refused.

  • An ML fit is read as ML under lavaan 0.7-3. lavaan 0.7-3 lists Browne’s residual based statistic beside the standard one for an ML fit by default, and measurement_invariance(), which asked whether the test option was exactly "standard", labeled an ML ladder as using the scaled difference test and robust fit indices. It now sets aside the standard statistic and every Browne residual statistic (alternative tests, not corrections) when deciding whether a fit carries a robust test. The profile likelihood interval for model implied omega and alpha no longer warns at every refit that lavaan cannot compute Browne’s statistic under its equality constraint. No number changes.

  • measurement_invariance() reports one version of the test and of the fit indices at every rung, and its attributes name the versions. Outside FIML the ladder read the names of its measures from its first rung alone. In the examples, hs_factors is the verbal and deduction model of the help page.

    • With the older mean and variance adjusted statistic (test = "mean.var.adjusted"), for which lavaan computes no robust indices, the cfi and rmsea columns held the standard indices while the fit_indices attribute said "robust". The columns now hold the robust indices, which DMAR computes because they do not depend on which corrected statistic accompanies them (Savalei, 2018); they equal lavaan’s under estimator = "MLM", and a line under the table says so. On the help page’s first ladder (measurement_invariance(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors, group = "school", test = "mean.var.adjusted")) the configural CFI was .9916 and is .9928, the configural RMSEA was .0520 and is .0478, and the metric delta_cfi was -.0127 and is -.0134. A ladder whose configural rung is saturated gets them too: on the three verbal tests (model = "verbal =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning", configural, metric, and scalar) the metric delta_cfi was -.0109 and is -.0100.
    • With a bootstrap test (test = "bollen.stine"), the chi_square column and the difference test were the standard ones, while fit_indices said "robust" and test named a scaled difference test. Those numbers stand, and the attributes now say "standard".
    • Where the robust indices of a maximum likelihood ladder of continuous items cannot be had, the columns hold the standard indices, which estimate the population values the robust ones estimate with the bias corrected as if the data were normal; the scaled ones do not (Savalei, 2018).
    • An ordered ladder under the default delta parameterization reported the robust CFI and RMSEA of its configural rung beside NA at every later rung, and no delta_cfi. lavaan leaves the robust indices NA at the rungs that constrain the thresholds. Every rung now reports the scaled indices, and fit_indices says "scaled". On the help page’s ordered example (the verbal and deduction tests cut at their quartiles, configural and thresholds rungs):
      • the configural CFI was .980 and is .999;
      • the configural RMSEA was .084 and is .029;
      • the thresholds rung’s CFI and RMSEA were NA and are .996 and .040;
      • delta_cfi was NA and is -.0023.
    • A line under the table names any fallback.
    • A saturated rung (no degrees of freedom) no longer decides the version, since lavaan forms its robust CFI there from a ratio of zeros (1 on one data set and NA on another) or does not compute it. Such a rung now reports a CFI of 1, which every version implies (see the entry on a saturated rung).

  • measurement_invariance(missing = "fiml") reports the FIML corrected fit indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023), and a line under the table says so. The corrected indices estimate the values complete data would give, the values a cutoff for a change in fit (Cheung & Rensvold, 2002) is a statement about, where lavaan’s standard cfi and rmsea move with the amount and kind of missing data; fa_confirmatory() reports the corrected indices for the same kind of fit. Under FIML the cfi and rmsea columns, and delta_cfi and delta_rmsea with them, are lavaan’s robust versions, chosen as fa_confirmatory() chooses them: Zhang and Savalei’s version 6, or version 3 with estimator = "MLR".

    • Through 1.0.1 an ML ladder under FIML reported the standard indices with lavaan 0.7-2, the oldest lavaan it accepted. With lavaan 0.7-3 it reported the corrected ones, but only because it read every ML fit as robust (see the entry on lavaan 0.7-3), and with estimator = "MLR" it reported them with either lavaan; those numbers stand.
    • On the verbal and deduction tests with 90 sentence completion scores deleted at random (set.seed(113), then t7_sentence[sample(301, 90)] <- NA), the standard and the corrected indices are:
      • configural CFI .9936 and .9930;
      • configural RMSEA .0426 and .0473;
      • the metric rung’s delta CFI -.0106 and -.0104, and its delta RMSEA .0195 and .0193.
      On the help page’s FIML example the metric RMSEA is .137 and .140.
    • One version holds every rung. When lavaan cannot compute the corrected indices at some rung with degrees of freedom, every rung falls back to the scaled indices of a scaled fit or to the standard ones. A saturated rung does not decide the version: its robust CFI, formed from a ratio of zeros, can be NA, and that rung reports a CFI of 1, which every version implies. On visual perception, cubes, and lozenges by school (model = "visual =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges") with 60 cube scores deleted at random (set.seed(1), then t2_cubes[sample(301, 60)] <- NA), configural, metric, and scalar, lavaan’s robust CFI of the saturated configural rung is NA. Every rung reports the corrected indices (scalar CFI .852 and RMSEA .172, where the standard indices are .861 and .159), and the configural CFI is 1.
    • Whether a ladder used FIML is read from its fits: lavaan fits the complete cases instead, with a warning, when FIML meets a test it cannot combine with it (test = "satorra.bentler" or "mean.var.adjusted"), and such a ladder is reported and labeled as the listwise ladder it is.
    • The fit_indices attribute names the version ("robust", or "scaled" or "standard" in the fallback). A line under the table, kept in the new fit_columns attribute, says which indices the columns hold, at the console and in a knitted report. Complete data and listwise and pairwise deletion are not affected by this entry.

  • A saturated rung of measurement_invariance() has a CFI of 1.

    • A rung with no degrees of freedom and a statistic of zero reproduces the moments exactly. A binding inequality can give a nonzero statistic instead, as the entry on zero degrees of freedom explains. Its statistic is zero in every version, and so is the model term of the CFI, whatever the scaling constant, which is 0/0 there.
    • lavaan’s robust CFI of such a rung is NA or 1 by rounding. The table reported the NA, and the next rung’s delta_cfi with it. On the verbal tests of holzinger_swineford under estimator = "MLR" (items = c("t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning"), group = "school"; configural, metric, and scalar), the configural CFI was NA and is 1, and the metric delta_cfi was NA and is -.0097. The three visual tests with 60 cube scores deleted under FIML (see the entry above) behaved the same way.
    • The RMSEA of a saturated rung is 0/0, which no version defines. It keeps lavaan’s 0, the convention lavaan applies in every version to a model that fits exactly.

  • measurement_invariance() reports no fit index or difference test of a ULS ladder of continuous items that is formed from the ULS statistic and changes with their units. The examples are the help page’s first ladder, the verbal and deduction tests by school.

    • The ULS statistic, (N - G) times the ULS fit function, is in the units of the squared covariances. With estimator = "ULSM" or "ULSMV" and continuous items, the rmsea column held lavaan’s robust RMSEA, which lavaan forms by putting that statistic into a correction derived for the ML fit function. It was 1.57, 4.92, and 4.50 at the configural, metric, and scalar rungs of a ULSM ladder, and 0.0157, 0.0492, and 0.0532 with every score divided by 10. The rmsea and delta_rmsea columns are now NA.
    • At the scalar and strict rungs, which restrict the means, the ULS fit function adds the squared mean residuals to the squared covariance residuals, which are in other units, so the statistic, the loadings, and the CFI change with the units too. The scalar CFI was .9885, against .9840 with the scores divided by 10, and the scalar delta_cfi was -.00005 against -.0046: a judgment against the cutoff of Cheung and Rensvold (2002) that turned on the units. The cfi and delta_cfi of those rungs are now NA. The configural and metric CFI (.9991 and .9886) do not depend on the units and are unchanged. So are the chi_square column and the scaled difference test, whose reference distribution does not depend on the units, though their values do.
    • With estimator = "ULS" and test = "standard", the cfi and rmsea columns held the standard indices formed from the ULS statistic: CFI .9956 and .9818 and RMSEA 3.51 and 6.37 at the configural and metric rungs, and CFI 1 and RMSEA 0 at both with the scores divided by 10. Both columns are now NA.
    • With estimator = "ULS", alone or with test = "standard", lavaan’s difference test refers the difference of the ULS statistics to the chi square distribution. The metric rung’s delta_chi_square was 91712 (p < .0001), against 9.17 (p = .057) with the scores divided by 10, and the test attribute named a scaled difference test (a standard one with test = "standard"). delta_chi_square, p_value, and test are now NA.
    • With estimator = "ULS" alone, Browne’s residual statistic remains a valid test. CFI and RMSEA at configural and metric rungs, which leave the means free, are unchanged. At scalar and strict rungs, restrictions link means and covariances through the latent means, so the ULS estimates change with the units. Browne’s statistic at those estimates and its indices change too: CFI, RMSEA, and their differences are now NA there. On the help page’s first ladder, measurement_invariance(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors, group = "school", estimator = "ULS"), the scalar CFI was .8874 and its RMSEA .0680 in 1.0.1; both are now NA.
    • Lines under the table say which columns are NA and why. estimator = "MLR" is the estimator for nonnormal continuous items.

  • measurement_invariance() under FIML leaves an auxiliary variable’s mean and variance free at every rung. An auxiliary variable passed through ... as lavaan’s aux enters a FIML fit as a saturated correlate (Graham, 2003). lavaan makes its mean and variance parameters of each group, and the ladder’s group.equal reached them. The scalar rung equated the auxiliary’s means across the groups and the strict rung its variances, so each of those rung tests also tested, with one more degree of freedom, whether the auxiliary is distributed alike in the groups. They are now added to group.partial at every rung, beside any group_partial terms. The ladder then has the degrees of freedom of the ladder without the auxiliary, and its differences are those of the same ladder with the auxiliary’s moments free.

    Example: a spatial factor of visual perception, cubes, and lozenges and a verbal factor of paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning by school, with 60 sentence completion scores deleted at random (set.seed(1), then t7_sentence[sample(301, 60)] <- NA) and general information as the auxiliary (means 44.8 and 36.6 in the two schools).

    • The scalar test was 57.59 on 5 df (p < .0001) with a delta CFI of -.081. It is now 23.88 on 4 df (p = .0001) with -.031; without the auxiliary it is 24.03 on 4 df with -.031.
    • The strict test goes from 10.85 on 7 df to 11.04 on 6.

    Under two-stage estimation the auxiliaries enter the first stage only, so its ladders hold no such parameters.

  • measurement_invariance() merges lavaan’s group.partial passed through ... into group_partial, and refuses group.equal there. Each rung passes lavaan one group.partial, so through 1.0.1 a call that gave both group_partial and group.partial stopped with lavaan’s error that a snake_cased name is duplicated. The terms of both are now freed at every rung, beside those of an auxiliary variable under FIML. On the six tests by school above under FIML, without the auxiliary, group_partial = "t2_cubes ~ 1" with group.partial = "t4_lozenges ~ 1" gives a scalar test of 1.56 on 2 df, where 1.0.1 stopped.

    group.equal in ... constrained the configural rung, which was still reported as configural, and a ladder that went past it stopped with the same error. On the six tests by school above under listwise deletion, group.equal = "loadings" with levels = "configural" gave a configural rung of 25.62 on 20 df against the configural model’s 15.27 on 16. It is now an error that names levels and group_partial.

  • htmt() returns the same four columns whatever B. ci_upper existed only when B > 0, so the shape of the table depended on an argument. It is now always present, NA when no bootstrap is run. A bootstrap bound also carries the B_used attribute (the resamples left after any were dropped), which glance() reports. No value changes.

  • htmt() takes the absolute value of every correlation, the monotrait correlations within each block as well as the heterotrait correlations between blocks. Through 1.0.1 only the heterotrait correlations were absolute, a mix that matches neither the signed ratio nor the absolute one semTools::htmt() computes. A reverse keyed item that was not recoded then lowered its block’s average within-construct correlation while the numerator kept its size, so the ratio was inflated. Take one such item in a block of four:

    set.seed(113); n <- 300
f1 <- rnorm(n); f2 <- 0.5 * f1 + sqrt(0.75) * rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(a1 = .8 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                a2 = .7 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                a3 = .8 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                a4 = -.6 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .8),
                b1 = .8 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                b2 = .7 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                b3 = .6 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .8))
blocks <- list(A = c("a1", "a2", "a3", "a4"),
               B = c("b1", "b2", "b3"))
htmt(d, blocks)
fa_confirmatory(d, factors = blocks, output = "measurement")

    The two constructs, which correlate .5 in the population, had an HTMT of 1.346, a discriminant validity failure that is not there, and fa_confirmatory(output = "measurement") reported it beside phi = .473 without a word; a block of three with such an item stopped the call. Every correlation now enters as an absolute value, so the ratio does not depend on how an item is keyed (1.346 becomes .463, the value of the recoded data). When no correlation within a block is negative, as with consistently keyed items, the point estimates are unchanged, the example of ?htmt and three factors of holzinger_swineford included. The bootstrap bound can move, though: a resample that draws a negative correlation within a block now enters it with its size, where 1.0.1 averaged it with its sign or dropped the resample. Take two blocks whose within-block correlations for B are .04, .11, and .20:

    set.seed(4); n <- 80; f <- rnorm(n); g <- rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(a1 = f + rnorm(n, sd = .5),
                a2 = f + rnorm(n, sd = .5),
                b1 = .45 * g + rnorm(n), b2 = .45 * g + rnorm(n),
                b3 = .45 * g + rnorm(n))
htmt(d, list(A = c("a1", "a2"), B = c("b1", "b2", "b3")), B = 200,
     seed = 113)

    The HTMT is .408, as before, and the bound .728 from 200 resamples, where it was .869 from 198. The bound of the ?htmt example is unchanged. On complete data the values agree with semTools::htmt(htmt2 = FALSE, absolute = TRUE). On incomplete data they agree only when semTools is given the same pairwise-complete correlations through sample.cov, since by default it deletes incomplete rows listwise. The help page no longer credits the absolute form to a 2021 paper missing from its references, and a pair whose ratio cannot be computed is reported as the next entry describes.

  • htmt() reports a pair whose ratio cannot be computed as NA, with a warning, and fa_confirmatory(output = "measurement") keeps its table. A correlation that cannot be computed leaves a pair’s ratio undefined. That happens with two items never observed together, as in a planned missing data design whose forms give two blocks to different respondents, or with a constant item. Through 1.0.1 such a pair across two blocks was NA without a word, and a pair undefined within a block stopped the call with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”.

    The pair is now NA, as is its bootstrap bound, with a warning that names the pair and the reason, and the other pairs are reported. The call stops, with a message that says why, only when no pair is defined. A call with only two blocks whose one pair is undefined, which returned NA, therefore stops.

    fa_confirmatory(output = "measurement") keeps every phi, omega, AVE, and H row and reports the undefined htmt row as NA with the warning, as 1.0.1 did without the warning. Take two three-item factors of 300 cases with a1 and b1 on different forms:

    set.seed(113); n <- 300
f1 <- rnorm(n); f2 <- 0.4 * f1 + sqrt(.84) * rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(a1 = .8 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                a2 = .7 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                a3 = .7 * f1 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                b1 = .8 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .6),
                b2 = .7 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .7),
                b3 = .7 * f2 + rnorm(n, 0, .7))
d$a1[c(TRUE, FALSE)] <- NA; d$b1[c(FALSE, TRUE)] <- NA
fa_confirmatory(d, factors = list(A = c("a1", "a2", "a3"),
                        B = c("b1", "b2", "b3")),
      missing = "fiml", output = "measurement")

    This gives phi .380 [.239, .521], omega .793 and .784, AVE .558 and .549, and H .798 and .792.

  • krippendorff_alpha() returns the same seven rows whatever boot. The ci_lower, ci_upper, and B_used rows existed only when boot = TRUE, so the shape of the table, and of its tidy() and glance(), depended on an argument, as htmt()’s did. They are now always present, and NA when no bootstrap is run, which is the default: the nominal ratings of Krippendorff (2011, Table 1) give seven rows where they gave four, with alpha .743 and every other value unchanged. As in htmt() and average_variance_extracted(), the confidence level is recorded, and printed, only beside an interval that was formed. A script that tested for the rows by name ("ci_lower" %in% x$term) should test for a finite value instead. results_sentence() now refuses a table whose limits are NA rather than writing “95% CI [NA, NA]”. average_variance_extracted() has returned its ci_lower and ci_upper columns under every ci_method since 1.0.0, and its tests now pin the columns of its tidy() and glance() as well.

  • krippendorff_alpha() checks B and reports the bootstrap resamples it drops. B must now be a whole number that meets the rule for bootstrap replications when boot = TRUE (400 at the 95 percent level; see One Rule for Bootstrap Replications); through 1.0.1 any value was accepted, and B = 10 gave a percentile interval from ten resamples. A resample on which alpha cannot be computed (too few pairable values, or values all alike) is dropped as before, but now with one warning that gives the count, and the limits are withheld when too few resamples remain. When the data themselves leave alpha undefined (every value alike), no bootstrap is run: the interval rows stay NA and no confidence level is recorded, where the table had said B_used = 0 beside “Confidence level: 95%”. Intervals are unchanged.

  • The bound for close fit in sem_residual_fit() is credited to the paper that proposed it. The help page attributed the bound of .05 times the average R squared to Ximénez, Maydeu-Olivares, Shi, and Revuelta (2022). It is the bound of Shi, Maydeu-Olivares, and DiStefano (2018). Their criterion also requires the largest absolute standardized residual covariance to be at most .10 (with .10 times the average R squared and .15 for acceptable fit), and they apply both as population values through an interval or a test. The page and the SEM fit vignette now say so, and say that the function tests the first part and reports the second as a sample value. Ximénez et al. (2022) are cited for finding that the bound works reasonably well for the unbiased SRMR in finite samples, except when the loadings are small. The sem_fit_measures() page and the vignette now also cite Steiger (1990, p. 178), which states in print the result of Steiger (1989) behind gamma hat: gamma hat and adjusted gamma hat estimate the population values of the GFI and the adjusted GFI.

  • The Steiger and Fouladi (1997) chapter is cited by its title. The help pages of smd(), ci_smd(), ci_smd_c(), ci_sm(), cles(), ci_mahalanobis(), ci_nc_t(), ci_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_smd(), ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sm(), ss_aipe_sm_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), and ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity() gave its title as “Noncentrality interval estimation and the evaluation of statistical methods”; the chapter is “Noncentrality interval estimation and the evaluation of statistical models” (pp. 221–257). The help page of sem_fit_measures() and the SEM fit vignette, both new in 1.1.0, cite it by that title for the intervals of gamma hat.

  • The journal and subtitle of Kelley, Maxwell, and Rausch (2003) are given as published. The help pages of ci_smd(), design_consequences(), ss_aipe_c(), ss_aipe_c_ancova(), ss_aipe_equivalence_r(), ss_aipe_equivalence_smd(), ss_aipe_mean(), ss_aipe_smd(), and ss_power_smd() gave the journal as “Evaluation and the Health Professions” and the subtitle as “Delineating methods of sample size planning”; the journal is Evaluation & the Health Professions and the subtitle is “Delineating methods of sample-size planning”, as the DOI record of the article (10.1177/0163278703255242) has them. The volume, issue, and pages, 26(3), 258–287, already matched the record and are unchanged.

  • The edition of Rencher and Christensen (2012) is given as published. The help page of manova_split_plot() gave Methods of multivariate analysis (Wiley, 2012) as the fourth edition; the 2012 book is the third edition, as the catalog record of its print edition (ISBN 978-0-470-17896-6) and the Crossref record of its review in International Statistical Review, 81(2), 328–329, have it. The entry gains the book’s DOI, 10.1002/9781118391686.

  • The edition of Anderson (2003) is given as published. The help pages of ci_eigenvalue() and ci_mahalanobis() gave An introduction to multivariate statistical analysis (Wiley, 2003) as the fourth edition; the 2003 book is the third edition, as the publisher’s page for it (ISBN 978-0-471-36091-9) and catalog records of the print edition have it, and as the pages of expected_r() and expected_partial_r() already cite it. The entry on the ci_mahalanobis() page also sets the title in sentence case, as the other entries do. Crossref holds no record of the book, so the entries carry no DOI.

  • ss_aipe_reliability() returns the AIPE planner class with an assurance. The closed form plan carried class dmar_ss_aipe and the assurance plan did not, so tidy() and glance() answered differently by path: for an assurance plan tidy() gave five term and estimate rows rather than the planned N beside the width. Both paths now carry the class, so an assurance plan’s tidy() is one row (term = "sample_size", estimate, width) and its glance() adds assurance, assurance_attained, and G as columns. The values of the table are unchanged (its rows are renamed; see Breaking Changes in 1.1.0). Two arguments are now checked before they are used: a vector true_residual_var for the Parallel model stopped with R’s “the condition has length > 1” and now stops with the function’s own message, and a True Score plan from true_factor_loading without n_items stopped with “argument is of length zero” and now says that n_items is needed. A vector true_factor_loading for the Parallel model was recycled across the items, so it planned the congeneric pattern it describes under the Parallel label without saying so (loadings .8, .7, .7, and .8 with true_residual_var = .4 returned N = 96). It is now an error, as it already was for the True Score model, with a message that names the Congeneric model, and both models refuse any true_factor_loading that is not one number.

  • ss_aipe_reliability() plans for the coefficient of the raw items. The tau equivalent model on every route, and the congeneric model given by S, turned the population covariance matrix into a correlation matrix before the closed form and the Monte Carlo draws. That plans for alpha or omega of standardized items rather than for the coefficient reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() estimate, and the same congeneric population entered by loadings or by S got different searches. Every route now uses the covariance matrix itself. With equal loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2, the normal theory plan for a width of .10 goes from 206 to 367 cases (the factor analytic one to 242; see the entry on that interval). At 367 the corrected interval averages .1004 wide and covers .941, while at 206 the 1.0.1 interval was as narrow as planned (.1008) but covered .869 (1,000 samples of each size, drawn as in the entry on that interval and analyzed by reliability_alpha(S = S, N = N, ci_method = "ml")). A correlation matrix still plans for standardized items, and items of equal variance keep the closed form they had.

    Seeded assurance searches with the normal theory interval of the tau equivalent model move a little for any population. Each sample’s interval now takes its standard error from that sample’s covariance matrix, whose variances differ even when the population’s do not, and a population whose equal variances are not one is now drawn from its covariance matrix. With true_item_covariance = .3 and error variances of .2 on five items, a width of .10, an assurance of .85, G_initial = 50, G = 200, and seed 113, the plan goes from 81 cases (empirical assurance .905) to 79 (.885). The True Score example of the 1.0.1 help page (true_item_covariance = .3, true_residual_var = c(.2, .3, .3, .2, .3), width .10) goes from a closed form of 84 to 86 and, with an assurance of .85 (G_initial = 50, G = 200, seed 113), from 115 to 118. The page now plans for items near unit variance (true_item_covariance = .5, true_residual_var = c(.4, .5, .6, .4, .6)): 108 cases, or 140 with that assurance (106 and 138 under 1.0.1). Its plan from a correlation matrix (pop_mat, width .15) with that assurance goes from 120 cases (empirical assurance .85) to 121 (.855), because its Monte Carlo intervals now use the sample covariance matrix. The Parallel examples give the plans they gave (38 cases, and 57 with an assurance of .85).

  • ss_aipe_reliability() plans coefficient omega from omega’s own variance. Without an assurance the congeneric model returned Terry and Kelley’s (2012) Eq. 19, the variance of alpha, which they used only as a starting value for a Monte Carlo search on omega’s mean width (p. 390). The closed form is now the delta method variance of the model implied omega from the expected information of the single-factor model at the population (Raykov, 2002), the variance behind reliability_omega(denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"). When the population is given by S or data, the model is first fit to it by maximum likelihood. Eq. 19 was too large when standardized items have unequal loadings and could be far too small when the item variances differ. At width .15, loadings .9, .8, .3, and .2 of standardized items go from 297 to 177 (the interval averages .114 wide at 297 and .153 at 177); loadings .3, .5, 1, and 2 with error variances .1, .3, 1, and 3 go from 75 to 151 (.211 wide at 75, .148 at 151); and the help page’s example goes from 53 to 52. At width .10, loadings 2, 1, .6, and .4 with unit error variances go from 360 to 229, and six standardized items with loadings from .4 to .8 from 197 to 183. The widths come from 1,000 samples of each size, drawn as in the next entry and analyzed by reliability_omega(S = S, N = N, denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"); three of those at 177 return no interval.

    The first-order approximation can miss the mean width when samples at the planned size approach improper solutions or empirical underidentification. The median can also exceed the target. The loadings, item count, and sample size act together; no lower bound on individual loadings separates these populations. Three-item models are just identified, and a sample covariance near zero can make their estimated loadings run away. Wider targets can create the same problem with more items. The help describes these cases and points to an assurance above one half, whose search counts the realized widths. A congeneric population with two items is refused.

  • ss_aipe_reliability() plans the factor analytic interval of the tau equivalent model for that interval. Without an assurance the True Score model returned the normal theory size whatever type was, so type = "Factor Analytic" planned for the van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000) interval of alpha, which through 1.0.1 was evaluated on the correlation matrix. It did not plan for the interval the user asked for: the delta method interval of the coefficient implied by the single-factor model with equal loadings. That is the interval of reliability_alpha(estimator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml") and the one the assurance search draws. That coefficient is the maximum likelihood estimator under the model, so its variance is no larger than the normal theory variance of alpha. The closed form now takes its delta method variance, with the information and gradient of the one loading summed over the items. A population given by S or data is first fit by the equal loadings model. Take equal loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2 at a width of .10. 1.0.1 returned 206 cases, too few for this interval, which averages .108 wide at 206 cases; about one sample in eight gives an interval no wider than .10. The normal theory plan for these items is 367, and the factor analytic plan is now 242, at which that interval averages .10 wide. These widths come from 1,000 samples of each size drawn after set.seed(1) as the assurance search draws them, each S <- var(MASS::mvrnorm(N, rep(0, 4), Sigma)) from the population matrix Sigma, and analyzed by reliability_alpha(S = S, N = N, estimator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"). With equal error variances the two variances coincide, so the Parallel model keeps its closed form, and no normal theory plan is affected.

  • ss_aipe_reliability() refuses a population it cannot plan for. Through 1.0.1 each of the following was planned without a word:

    • Every error variance in true_residual_var must now be above zero for the Congeneric model and for the True Score model with the factor analytic interval, as it already had to be for the Parallel model. These plans fit the single-factor model, at whose boundary an error variance of zero lies. At a width of .15, loadings .7, .6, .5, and .5 with error variances .51, -.1, .75, and .75 gave 81 cases for the congeneric model, and one loading of .7 on all four items with those error variances gave 46 for the tau equivalent one.
    • With the normal theory interval of the True Score model nothing is fit. The loading and error variances only build the covariance matrix the plan is made from, which must be a covariance matrix, as S must.
