The plan is the one the same matrix gives as S: 74 cases for that tau equivalent population at a width of .15, by either route.
    • A matrix with a negative eigenvalue, which no population has, is refused, whether it is given as S or implied on that normal theory route. Loadings .7, .6, .5, and .5 with error variances .51, -.3, .75, and .75 imply a matrix whose smallest eigenvalue is -.144; given as S at a width of .15, it gave 25 cases for the True Score model and 115 for the Parallel model.
    • A congeneric population given by true_cov_matrix or data whose single-factor fit is improper or has no solution is refused.
    • A population with fewer than three items whose loading is not zero is refused, since the congeneric model is not identified there. true_factor_loading = c(.7, .6, 0) with true_residual_var = c(.51, .64, 1) gave 937 cases at a width of .15.
    • With the factor analytic interval of the Parallel and True Score models, the fitted equal-loading model decides whether the common factor is absent for a population supplied as true_cov_matrix or data. Alpha at or below zero is equivalent only when the item variances are equal: at a zero loading, the likelihood weights each covariance by the inverse of the two item variances, and alpha does not. A population supplied through true_item_covariance or true_factor_loading is refused when its loading is zero. A Parallel plan whose alpha is not positive despite a nonzero fitted loading is refused as far from parallel, with the True Score model named as the alternative. The normal theory interval still plans for alpha of such items.
    • The congeneric closed form is refused where its delta method is degenerate. Omega grows with the square of the sum of the loadings. When that sum is small relative to its standard error, as when loadings of opposite sign nearly cancel, the first-order variance understates the width of the interval, and where they cancel it vanishes. For standardized items at a width of .10, loadings .7, -.7, .5, and -.5 have an omega of zero, for which the delta method gives one case (1.0.1, with alpha’s closed form: 14078). Loadings .7, -.7, .5, and -.4 (omega .0038) give 49 cases, at which the interval averages .20 wide for a target of .10 (12 of the 1,000 samples return none), and about 95 are needed (1.0.1: 12606).
    • The closed form is checked at the N it gives, rounded up, or at one more case than there are items when it gives fewer. Take the sum of the loadings to be normal. The interval the estimation functions report, clamped at zero, then averages less than the target until the standard error of that sum is about 1.5 times the sum at 95 percent confidence (1.36 at 90 percent, 1.66 at 99), and the plan is refused beyond that. In simulation the rule errs a little toward refusing: loadings .7, -.7, .5, and -.35, whose sum has a standard error 1.52 times its size at the 110 cases of the closed form, give intervals averaging .099 wide for a target of .10.
    • The refusal says to reverse score items when the loadings differ in sign, and in any case to give an assurance. An assurance plan is never refused, since its search counts the widths of the intervals themselves. Loadings of one sign with a small omega are planned as in 1.0.1: four loadings of .1 at a width of .10 still take 3787 cases.

    The widths in this entry come from 1,000 samples of each size, drawn as in the previous entry and analyzed by reliability_omega(S = S, N = N, denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml"). With the factor analytic interval, the assurance search now starts at no fewer than one more case than there are items, the fewest a single-factor model can be fit to. A highly reliable population planned for a wide interval can have a closed form below that: loadings .95 on four items need two cases for a width of .2. The search used to stop there.

  • ss_aipe_reliability() warns when the loadings of a congeneric population differ in sign. The warning names the items that load in the direction opposite to the others. Such items lower omega of the unweighted sum, as an item keyed in the opposite direction does when it is not reverse scored, and the plan is for omega of the sum of the items as given. Standardized items with loadings .7, -.7, .5, and .5 at a width of .10 now plan 1419 cases with the warning; 1.0.1, with alpha’s closed form, planned 4884 without one.

  • The assurance of ss_aipe_reliability() counts a simulated study that returns no interval as one whose interval is too wide. The assurance is the probability of an interval no wider than desired (Terry & Kelley, 2012), and a study that ends without an interval has not had one. Through 1.0.1 a Monte Carlo sample whose single-factor fit did not converge was set aside, and the proportion was taken over the rest. A sample whose solution had run away (error variances summing below zero, a model implied coefficient above one) was kept, and its interval, often inverted (an estimate of 104 between 104 and 1), was counted as narrow or wide. reliability_omega() now returns no coefficient for a runaway solution, and the search treats each sample as the estimation functions treat it. A sample that returns no interval, whether its fit did not converge, had no solution, or ran away, counts as wide. Every assurance plan carries their count in no_interval, zero when all samples returned an interval, and glance() carries the count as a column. A nonzero count is printed under the table. Both confidence limits are clamped into [0, 1], as the estimation functions clamp them, which changes no count. The rule changes nothing in a search in which every sample returns an interval, as every normal theory search does. Samples without an interval are rare unless several loadings are .3 or below. Take standardized items with loadings .8, .3, .2, and .2 and a width of .40 (200 samples of each size, drawn and analyzed as in the entry on the populations the planner refuses):

    • At 100 cases, 47 of 200 samples return no interval. The share of studies with an interval no wider than .40 is .410, against .536 among the samples that return one.
    • At 140 cases, 49 return none, and the two shares are .545 and .722.
    • With an assurance of .5 (G_initial = 50, G = 200, seed 1), 1.0.1 returned 110 cases at an empirical assurance of .626, taken over the samples whose fit converged. The plan is now 118, at .545, and 39 of the 200 samples of the final pass return no interval.

  • ss_aipe_reliability()’s assurance search can go below its starting size, says why it stops, and works from data. The search started at the closed form size and only went up. When that size already met the assurance, as with an assurance near one half or below, or with the factor analytic interval of the tau equivalent model, which is narrower than the normal theory interval 1.0.1’s closed form described, the search returned the closed form size whatever the assurance needed. For the tau equivalent population of equal loadings .7 and error variances .1, .2, 1, and 2 with the factor analytic interval, a width of .10, and an assurance of .80, 1.0.1 planned from the correlation matrix and returned its start, 207 cases, at an empirical assurance of .99 for standardized items. That is too few for alpha of the items as they are: at 207 cases .156 of the samples give an interval no wider than .10 (1,000 samples, drawn as in the entry on that interval). The plan is now 263 (G_initial = 100, G = 400, seed = 1), searched up from the factor analytic closed form of 242. The search now moves down to where the widths it drew would meet the target and then up one case at a time; a search whose start falls short, and in which every sample returns an interval, draws what it drew before from the same matrix (a tau equivalent population whose variances are not one is now drawn from its covariance matrix rather than its correlation matrix, and so draws differently). A size at which no Monte Carlo sample returns an interval stops with the first error, where the search stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. How a sample that returns no interval counts is in the entry on the assurance of ss_aipe_reliability(). The congeneric model with type = "Normal Theory", which the help already called an error, is refused at once (the closed form returned an N without reading type). A population given by data now sets the number of items, so an assurance plan from data no longer stops with “invalid ‘times’ argument”.

  • ss_aipe_reliability() names the common covariance of the items for what it is. The argument was cor_est and was called the presumed inter-item correlation, but the function takes its square root as the common loading beside the error variances, so it is the common inter-item covariance, and it is the correlation only when true_residual_var = 1 - true_item_covariance, Terry and Kelley’s standardized design. It is now true_item_covariance, and the help says what it is. The Parallel examples planned from a covariance of .3 with error variances of .2, items that correlate .6; they now give the same populations as standardized items (true_item_covariance = .6, true_residual_var = .4) and say so, and their plans are the same. The True Score example now plans another population (see the entry on the coefficient of the raw items). The page also says that a correlation matrix plans for standardized items, and how the closed forms and the assurance search work.

  • The help says what seed = NULL does. The pages of the reliability family, krippendorff_alpha(), randomization_test(), randomization_test_paired(), mlmr(), mlmr_mv(), R2_mixed_effects(), plot_trajectories(), and plot_trajectories_fitted() said that a NULL seed leaves the random number state intact. In fact the draws come from, and advance, the caller’s stream; it is a supplied seed that leaves the state as it was. The help of reliability_alpha() and reliability_omega() also now names the delta method behind bootstrap_se_logistic (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016, Eq. 32). No number changes.

  • Suggested packages. lavaan’s floor rises from 0.7-2 to 0.7-3, the version every two-stage and factor score result was checked against (factor_scores() refuses ordered fits under 0.7-2 in any case); mice (3.18.0 or newer, which keeps ordered factors ordered when it augments the data) is added for multiple imputation in categorical omega; and mvtnorm is no longer suggested.

  • A confidence level is displayed with the digits it needs, never as 100% when it is below 1, and whatever getOption("digits") is. Through 1.0.1 the labels of plot_ci(), plot_smd(), plot_R2(), and plot_mediation_mbco() and the caption of correlations_test() rounded the level to a whole percent, so a 97.5% interval was labeled 98% and a 99.9% interval 100%, a level only an unbounded interval has: plot_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.975) read “98% CI [0.043, 0.954]” and now reads “97.5% CI [0.043, 0.954]”, plot_R2(R2 = 0.25, N = 100, p = 5, conf_level = 0.999) read “100% CI [0.017, 0.477]” and now reads “99.9% CI [0.017, 0.477]”, and a correlations_test() result at conf_level = 0.975 is captioned “Correlations (Pearson, 97.5% CI)”, where it read “98% CI”.

    • results_sentence() wrote the level with getOption("digits") significant digits: under options(digits = 2), results_sentence(ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.975)) gave “smd = 0.50, 98% CI [0.04, 0.95]”; it gives “smd = 0.50, 97.5% CI [0.04, 0.95]”.
    • The line beneath the table and the sentence wrote a level within 5e-8 of 1 as 100: ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.99999995) printed “Confidence level: 100%” and the sentence “100% CI [-0.61, 1.61]”. Digits are now added until a level below 1 no longer reads 100 (“99.999995%”).
    • The line beneath the table follows getOption("OutDec"), as the table’s numbers and the sentence already did: under options(OutDec = ",") it reads “Confidence level: 97,5%” beneath a table of 0,043 and 0,954, where it read “97.5%”.
    • summary() of an mlmr() fit and confint() of mlmr() and mlmr_mv() wrote the level and the interval columns with getOption("digits"): under options(digits = 2), a fit with conf_level = 0.975 gave its intervals at “level = 0.97” over columns “1.3 %” and “99 %”. It gives them at “level = 0.975” over “1.25 %” and “98.75 %”, the labels stats::confint() writes. At the default settings nothing changes.
    • The texts that are new in 1.1.0 write the level the same way: the Bonferroni line of pairwise_within() and contrast_test() (each of 28 intervals at a family level of .999 is at 99.996%, which four significant digits would have written as 100%), the interval columns of a printed factor_scores() table, and the interval that equivalence_rmsea() names.

    No interval and no stored level changes; only the display does.

  • An interval formed from unequal tail areas says so, and a one-sided interval is written as the confidence bound it is. An interval with tail area alpha_lower below its lower limit and alpha_upper above its upper limit has confidence coefficient 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper whatever the split (Neyman, 1937), and that is the level the table records, but “95% CI [L, U]” is read as the equal-tailed interval. Through 1.0.1 nothing recorded the split: ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, alpha_lower = 0.01, alpha_upper = 0.04) gave the sentence “smd = 0.50, 95% CI [0.03, 0.85]”, read as the equal-tailed 95% interval, which is [0.10, 0.90]. Each constructor that takes alpha_lower and alpha_upper (ci_c(), ci_cv(), ci_eta_squared(), ci_eta_squared_generalized(), ci_mahalanobis(), ci_omega_squared(), ci_pvaf(), ci_r(), ci_R(), ci_R2(), ci_rc(), ci_reg_coef(), ci_rmsea(), ci_sc(), ci_sm(), ci_smd(), ci_smd_c(), ci_snr(), ci_src(), and ci_srsnr()) now records the two areas when they differ, and:

    • the line beneath the table reads “Confidence level: 95% (unequal tail areas: 0.01 below the lower limit, 0.04 above the upper limit)”, and results_sentence() writes “smd = 0.50, 95% CI [0.03, 0.85] (unequal tail areas: 0.01 below, 0.04 above)”;
    • an interval with a tail area of 0 is a one-sided confidence bound, whose other limit (infinite, or the parameter’s own bound, 0 for an RMSEA or 1 for a squared multiple correlation) carries no information, and the sentence writes the bound alone. With alpha_lower = 0 and alpha_upper = 0.05 the sentence of the ci_smd() call above was “smd = 0.50, 95% CI [-Inf, 0.83]” and is “smd = 0.50, one-sided 95% upper confidence bound 0.83”; ci_rmsea(rmsea = 0.06, df = 24, N = 300, alpha_lower = 0.05, alpha_upper = 0) was “rmsea = 0.06, 95% CI [0.04, Inf]” and is “rmsea = 0.06, one-sided 95% lower confidence bound 0.04”; and ci_R2(R2 = 0.2, N = 100, p = 3, alpha_lower = 0.05, alpha_upper = 0) was “R2 = 0.20, 95% CI [0.08, 1.00]” and is “R2 = 0.20, one-sided 95% lower confidence bound 0.08”. The line beneath the table says which limit is the bound (“one-sided: the upper limit is the 95% upper confidence bound, with tail area 0.05 above it and none below the lower limit”). An interval is taken to be one-sided only from a tail area of 0, never from a limit, since an equal-tailed interval can have a lower limit of 0 because the statistic fell below its critical value;
    • tidy() and glance() add alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns after conf_level, holding the two areas on the rows of the interval (NA on the other rows of a long tidy()), so that rows stacked from several results keep their own split and their sentence states it. A stack built with rbind() from an equal-tailed and an unequal-tailed result stops on their different columns rather than state either split for the other’s rows, and one built with dplyr::bind_rows() holds NA, read as equal tails, on the equal-tailed rows;
    • plot_ci() names the split in a subtitle (see the entry on plot_ci()).

    An equal-tailed interval, the usual one, is unchanged: it records no areas, prints and reads as before, and its tidy() and glance() gain no column. No limit changes.

  • ci_c(), ci_sc(), ci_c_ancova(), ci_sc_ancova(), and ci_c_ancova_bp() require the standard deviation of the errors and refuse one that is not a single positive, finite number. The standard error of a contrast is that standard deviation times a function of the weights and the sample sizes (and, in ANCOVA, of the covariate means), and it cannot be recovered from the means. Through 1.0.1 it was checked only on some paths:

    • ci_c(means = c(1, 2, 3), c_weights = c(1, -1, 0), n_per_group = c(10, 10, 10)), with no s_anova, returned a zero-width interval at the estimate, -1, -1, and -1, labeled “Confidence level: 95%”, with the sentence “contrast = -1.00, 95% CI [-1.00, -1.00]”;
    • ci_c_ancova(adj_means = c(7.5, 12, 14), c_weights = c(1, -1, 0), n_per_group = c(10, 10, 10), cov_means = c(5, 6, 7), SSwithin_x = 750), with no s_ancova, returned -4.5, -4.5, and -4.5 labeled 95%, and s_ancova = 0 returned the same;
    • a negative value swapped the limits: s_anova = -1 in the ci_c() call gave a lower limit of -0.08 above an upper limit of -1.92, and s_ancova = -2 in the ci_c_ancova() call gave -2.66 above -6.34;
    • ci_sc() with means and no s_anova, and ci_sc_ancova() with no s_ancova, stopped with “argument is of length zero”; ci_sc_ancova() with s_ancova = 0 stopped with “lower < upper is not fulfilled”;
    • ci_c_ancova_bp() stopped on an NA with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” and returned infinite limits for Inf.

    Each of these is now refused with a message that names the argument and says what it is: s_anova for ci_c() and ci_sc() on every path, s_ancova for ci_c_ancova() (either procedure), ci_sc_ancova(), and ci_c_ancova_bp(), and s_anova for ci_sc_ancova() when it is the standardizer. A call with neither the means nor the contrast, which failed with “arguments imply differing number of rows: 3, 0” in ci_c(), is refused in words. Every interval formed from a valid standard deviation is unchanged.

  • plot_ci() titles a DMAR table with the level the table records. The title came from the conf_level argument, used only for the label, so a table formed at another level was titled with its default: plot_ci(ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50, conf_level = 0.90)) was titled “95% Confidence Interval” above the limits of a 90% interval, and a 97.5% table the same. The level the table records (its conf_level attribute, or a conf_level column holding one value) is now used when conf_level is not given (“90% Confidence Interval”), and a conf_level that differs from it is refused, since the plot draws the limits it is given and cannot change their level; rows that record several levels are refused as well. A frame that records no level, and explicit estimate, lower, and upper values, keep the argument’s level, .95 by default. An interval with unequal tail areas is drawn with a subtitle in the words of results_sentence() (“Unequal tail areas: 0.01 below, 0.04 above”, or “One-sided: the upper limit is the 95% upper confidence bound”). The limits drawn are unchanged.

  • equivalence_c() has one more row and one more verdict. An interval that contains -contrast_lower and whose upper limit is below contrast_upper (delta_lower and delta_upper in 1.0.x) was labeled “Inconclusive” through version 1.0.1 and is now “Not relevantly superior only”, in the verdict attribute and in plot_equivalence()’s colors. The second example of the help page, equivalence_c(contrast = -5.28, se = 2.49, df_error = 399, contrast_upper = 5), with 90% limits -9.39 and -1.17, reads so now. “Inconclusive” is left for an interval that contains both bounds. Code that reads the rows by term is unaffected; code that reads them by position meets an 18th row, nonsuperior, after inferior, and the first 17 keep their places. No estimate, limit, or p-value changes.

  • ss_power_R2() stops when null_R2 is not 0, and the test of an increment in R^2 has its own function. ss_power_R2() plans the omnibus test that the population squared multiple correlation coefficient of all p predictors is zero. A nonzero null_R2, which DMAR 1.0.x accepted, is now an error of class dmar_null_R2_unsupported (a dmar_refusal) whose message says what MBESS calculated with a nonzero null_R2 and writes the call to ss_power_R2_change() with the values given. No value is returned for such a call, in place of the following.

    With fixed predictors, 1.0.x and MBESS formed (true_R2 - null_R2) / (1 - true_R2), which is Cohen’s

    1. f^2 for the increment when predictors are added to a model that already explains null_R2, and referred it to an F distribution with p and N - p - 1 degrees of freedom and noncentrality N f^2. With p read as the number of predictors added, that is Cohen’s calculation for a total sample size of N plus the number of predictors in the restricted model: true_R2 = .30, null_R2 = .25, p = 4, alpha_level = .01, and specified_N = 85 gave a power of .2225 with a noncentrality of 6.071, which is the value Cohen’s formula gives at N = 90 with five predictors in the restricted model, and the search gave 242 where Cohen’s form gives 247. With p read as all of the predictors, as the function defines it, the number is not the power of the test of the increment, whose numerator degrees of freedom are the number of predictors added: for .25 against .20 with p = 5 and specified_N = 200 it was .8047, where the test of one predictor added to four has power .953 and the test of two added to three .911 (fixed predictors; .945 and .901 with random predictors), and the search for power .80 gave 199, where those two tests need 120 and 148 (127 and 154 with random predictors). With random predictors, the default, 1.0.x did not form that effect size: given true_R2 it returned alpha_level when true_R2 was at or below null_R2 and the power of the omnibus test above it (.0500 at true_R2 = .20 and .9999 at .200001 with p = 5, specified_N = 200, and null_R2 = .20; a search for .25 against .20 returned 47, the sample size of the omnibus test of .25), and given true_f2 it took the population value as (true_f2 + null_R2) / (1 + true_f2) and returned the power of the omnibus test at it (.9975 for true_f2 = .1, null_R2 = .2, p = 5, and specified_N = 100, where the same call without null_R2 gave .6378). The argument alone cannot say which calculation is meant, because the test of an increment needs the number of predictors in the restricted model.

    What to call instead. The test of the increment: ss_power_R2_change(true_R2_full = a, true_R2_restricted = b, p_full = , p_restricted = ). The number 1.0.x returned with fixed predictors, and MBESS returned: ss_power_R2(true_f2 = (a - b) / (1 - a), p = p, random_predictors = FALSE), which gives .8047 and 199 for the second design above and .2225 and 242 for the first. A call that gave true_f2 with a nonzero null_R2 is refused in the same way. With fixed predictors 1.0.x took that true_f2 as the effect size of the increment, so the same call without null_R2 returns its number; with random predictors ss_power_R2(true_R2 = (true_f2 + null_R2) / (1 + true_f2), p = p) returns the number 1.0.x gave (.9975 in the case above). When true_R2 is at or below null_R2 there is no increment to test: 1.0.x returned alpha_level (MBESS returns NaN), and the message says so in place of the two calls, which would stop on a negative effect size. Whether the population squared multiple correlation coefficient exceeds a stated value above zero is a third question, for which DMAR has no planner in this release; that test rejects when the one-sided lower confidence limit from ci_R2() exceeds the value. null_R2 stays in the signature so that an existing call is answered with the explanation, and null_R2 = 0 is accepted. An invalid null_R2 (not a single number of at least 0 and below 1) keeps its own message.

    A search with true_R2 = 0 stops with “With ‘true_R2’ of 0 the null hypothesis is true, so power equals ‘alpha_level’ at every sample size and no sample size attains ‘desired_power’.” The sample size search doubles the size and then bisects, so a small effect returns promptly (true_R2 = .00005 with p = 5, desired_power = .80, and fixed predictors gives 256,545); the size it returns is the smallest that attains desired_power, as before, and the search stops with an error at ten million. No power is returned from an evaluation at which R’s noncentral F warned of lost accuracy (“full precision may not have been achieved in ‘pnbeta’”); with a null value of zero no call was found that reaches that warning. Results with null_R2 = 0 are unchanged from DMAR 1.0.0: on 1,500 combinations of true_R2 (from .000001 to .999), p, specified_N, alpha_level, and predictor model, and 500 searches, version 1.0.0 and this version returned the same sample size in every search and powers that differ by at most 6e-11 (the entry below on a very small true_R2 describes a true_R2 near 1e-8).

  • ss_power_R2() checks its arguments. alpha_level must be a single number strictly between 0 and 1 (0 and 1 were accepted and returned NaN, 0, or 1); true_R2 and null_R2 must be single numbers of at least 0 and below 1 (true_R2 = 1 returned NaN with an infinite effect size, and null_R2 = 1 a power of .05 with an effect size of -1); p must be a whole number of at least 1 (p = 5.5 was accepted); true_f2 must be nonnegative; and a call with neither true_R2 nor true_f2 says so, where it stopped with “object ‘f_Squared’ not found”. random_predictors must be TRUE or FALSE; 1, 0, and the character strings “TRUE” and “FALSE” were accepted and are now refused.

  • The random-predictor power of ss_power_R2() no longer returns NaN for a very small nonzero true_R2. The parameters of Lee’s approximation need the square root of a difference that cancels when rho^2 is small, and near rho^2 = 1e-8 the difference came out negative: ss_power_R2(true_R2 = 1e-8, p = 10, specified_N = 12) returned NaN with the warning “NaNs produced” and now returns .05. The root has a closed form with no subtraction, which the function shared by ss_power_R2(), ci_R2(), and ss_aipe_R2() now uses. The limits of ci_R2() and the sample sizes of ss_aipe_R2() did not change on the grids compared (1,500 and 65 calls). The power of ss_power_R2() changes by less than 1e-13 for a true_R2 of .001 or more and by up to 9e-11 at 1e-6, where the earlier square root carried the larger rounding error.

  • ss_aipe_semipartial_r() without true_R2_full returns a larger sample size when true_r_sp squared is above 1/2. DMAR 1.0.x planned with (1 - r_sp2)2, the variance when the variables partialed out explain none of the outcome. That is the largest the variance can be when r_sp^2 is at most 1/2, and there the plan is unchanged. Above 1/2 it is the smallest, and the 1.0.x plan was too small unless the variables partialed out explained none of the outcome: for r_sp = .8, one variable partialed out (p = 2), and a width of .10 it gave 202, where an interval of that width needs 331 when the full-model R2 is .94 (at N = 202 the mean width in 4,000 replications was .127). The plan without true_R2_full now uses the largest variance over every possible full-model R2, r_sp^2 (1 - r_sp^2) when r_sp^2 is above 1/2: necessary_N for that call was 202 and is 357; for r_sp = .9, p = 3, and a width of .10 it was 59 and is 240; and for r_sp = .75, p = 2, a width of .10, and assurance = .90 it was 329 and is 386 (with seed = 113; the plan with assurance is now found by simulation, as the entry on the assurance step describes). true_R2_full = true_r_sp^2 restores the 1.0.x plan made without assurance (with assurance it does not: the same call then returns 363, because the assurance step changed too).

  • ss_aipe_partial_r_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity() simulate p - 1 variables partialed out, the count their planners plan for, where DMAR 1.0.x simulated one fewer for the same model. In 1.0.x the count was the argument J (p = J + 1). It was documented there as the total number of predictors and the simulated data had J + 1 columns, while the planner each function calls, and the standard error of the interval each one formed, took the same J as the number of variables partialed out. With J = 1 the “partial” correlation simulated was the simple correlation of two variables, given the interval of a partial correlation with one variable removed. Both functions now simulate the model the rest of the family describes: Y, X, and p - 1 variables partialed out, so the simulated data have p + 1 columns. The planner call and total_N are unchanged, and the results at a given seed change, by little, since the interval already allowed for the variables partialed out: with set.seed(113), true_cor = .40, specified_N = 30, three variables partialed out (p = 4; J = 3 in 1.0.x), a width of .40, and G = 2000, the standard deviation of the partial correlations was .1666 and is .1717, and with fisher_z = TRUE, the interval 1.0.x formed, the proportion of intervals that missed the true value was .048 and is .057 (Monte Carlo standard error .005). With the default interval of this release, on the raw scale, that proportion is .091, which also reflects the change of interval described in the entry on fisher_z. This was a defect, and no argument restores the earlier results; a model with nothing partialed out is ss_aipe_r_sensitivity().

  • ss_aipe_semipartial_r_sensitivity() forms the interval the planner plans for. Each replication’s interval was formed on Fisher’s Z scale with standard error 1 / sqrt(N - p - 1), by analogy with the partial correlation. No function of a semipartial correlation alone stabilizes its variance, which depends on the full-model R2, and ss_aipe_semipartial_r() plans the width of a Wald interval on the correlation’s own scale. Each interval is now that Wald interval: the estimate plus and minus the normal critical value times the square root of the first-order variance (var_semipartial_r() with under_null = FALSE) at the sample semipartial correlation and the sample full-model R2, with the limits not truncated at -1 and 1. In the population 1.0.x simulated, in which the controls explain none of the outcome, the two intervals nearly coincide: with set.seed(113), true_r_sp = supposed_r_sp = .30, p = 4 (J = 3 in 1.0.x), a width of .20, and G = 2000, the mean width was .1988 and is .1986 at the same total_N of 323. With true_r_sp = .80, p = 2 (J = 1 in 1.0.x), and a width of .10 the planner’s change above moves total_N from 202 to 357 and the mean width from .1007 to .0754. This was a defect, and no argument restores the earlier interval.

  • randomization_test() and randomization_test_paired() count tied reassignments by the rounding of the arithmetic, and the studentized statistic no longer drops the reassignments with no within-group spread. A reassignment whose statistic equals the observed one counts as at least as extreme. Earlier versions compared with a tolerance relative to the largest reference statistic, formed each variance as a sum of squares less n times a squared mean, and set a statistic with a zero standard error to 0. The comparison now allows the rounding bound of the statistic compared, which is proportional to the size of the scores; variances come from residuals about each group’s own mean; and a reassignment in the reference set whose standard error is zero is ordered as an infinite statistic with the sign of its difference (0 when every score is equal). When the observed data themselves have a zero standard error and a nonzero difference, statistic = "t" is refused (see the entry on that refusal below). The p-values that change:

    • Studentized statistic, two-valued or tied scores. randomization_test(group_1 = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 0), group_2 = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1), statistic = "t") gave 0.198413 and gives 52/252 = 0.206349. For g_1 <- c(4.800000002, 4.8, 4.800000003, 4.800000001, 4.800000002) and g_2 <- c(8, 8.000000001, 8.000000003, 8.000000003, 8.000000003) it gave 0.003968, half the smallest value ten scores can produce, and gives 2/252 = 0.007937 (the statistic reported for that call was -339,547,000 and is -3,938,927,000, the value of the Welch formula for those scores). randomization_test_paired(rep(0, 6), c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, -1), statistic = "t") gave 0.1875 and gives 14/64 = 0.21875 (0.09375 and 7/64 = 0.109375 with alternative = "greater").
    • Paired test, constant differences, statistic = "t". randomization_test_paired(1:5, 1:5 + 2, statistic = "t") gave a statistic of 0 and p = 1. The paired t has a zero standard error there and no value, so the call is now refused (class dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined) with a message that says why and gives the p-value of the mean difference, 2/32 = 0.0625, which statistic = "mean" returns.
    • Difference in means, scores with many digits. For x <- c(1000000.002, 1000000.005, 1000000.000, 1000000.002, 1000000.001, 1000000.001) and y <- c(1000000.003, 1000000.007, 1000000.002, 1000000.001, 999999.999, 1000000.001), randomization_test_paired(x, y) gave 0.75 and gives 0.8125, the value for the same scores in thousandths without the offset. The independent test was too small in the same way: randomization_test(group_1 = 1000000 + c(2, 2, 2, 0) / 1000, group_2 = 1000000 + c(3, 3, 0, 7, 4) / 1000) gave 0.214286 and gives 28/126 = 0.222222.
    • Difference in means, one score far larger than the rest. randomization_test(group_1 = c(3e9, 4, 7, 2), group_2 = c(3, 5, 6, 9, 1)) gave 0.444444 and gives 35/126 = 0.277778; randomization_test_paired(c(3e9, 4, 7, 2, 5), c(3, 5, 6, 9, 1)) gave 1 and gives 0.6875.
    • Differences that are distinct by more than rounding are no longer merged. randomization_test_paired(rep(0, 6), c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1 + 1e-12, -1)) gave 0.21875 (and 1 with statistic = "t") and gives 12/64 = 0.1875 with either statistic.

    Scores with no ties and no extreme offsets give the p-values they gave: 3,240 seeded calls on continuous data (exact and Monte Carlo, both statistics, three alternatives, and procrustes_phi()) returned the same p-value before and after the change. The limits of the shift interval move by up to about two millionths of a standard error, because the earlier tolerance counted near ties at the edge of the interval. Checked against rational arithmetic in 1,800 comparisons on unbalanced designs, the studentized p-value is exact for binary, three-valued, Likert, three-decimal (with and without an offset of a million), and constant scores; with one score of 3e9 among single digits, or scores within a millionth of one of two values, statistics closer than the rounding bound are counted as tied and the p-value was above the exact one in 96 of 600 comparisons and below it in none. ?randomization_test says so under “Ties”. The repaired statistic costs time, since each reassignment now keeps the scores of both groups and forms its own residuals: with the default 10,000 reassignments and the shift interval, a call with 150 scores per group and statistic = "t" takes about 2.8 s where it took 0.16 s, and one with 1,500 per group about 26 s where it took 1.7 s (statistic = "mean": 0.30 s against 0.11 s, and 3.0 s against 1.1 s). Most of the time is the inversion for the shift interval: with shift_ci = FALSE the two studentized calls take 0.27 s and 1.3 s.

  • randomization_test() with statistic = "t" reports the whole line as the shift interval where no shift can be rejected. With three scores per group the smallest two-sided p-value is 2/20, so the 95 percent interval is unbounded, as the help says. Under the studentized statistic the earlier arithmetic lost the reassignments with no within-group spread at large shifts and returned limits such as -77,486,400 and 78,526,226 for group_1 = c(80, 84, 79), group_2 = c(72, 75, 68); the limits are now -Inf and Inf, as they were for statistic = "mean". The studentized statistic is now computed on scores divided by a power of 2 near their largest absolute value, so scores near 1e-200 or 1e200, whose squared residuals underflow or overflow, give the statistic and p-value of the same scores in ordinary units (c(3, 5, 9, 4) * 1e-200 against c(1, 2, 2, 6, 3) * 1e-200 stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”). The division is exact, and no other result changes.

  • statistic = "t" is refused in randomization_test() and randomization_test_paired() when the observed standard error is zero and the observed difference is not. The studentized statistic is the mean difference divided by its standard error. When both observed groups are constant at different values, or every paired difference is the same nonzero value, that standard error is 0 and the statistic has no value. DMAR 1.0.0 reported a paired t of 0 with p = 1 for such differences (randomization_test_paired(1:5, 1:5 + 2, statistic = "t")) and, for two constant groups (randomization_test(group_1 = rep(5, 4), group_2 = rep(3, 4), statistic = "t")), stopped with an error raised while the standardized mean difference was computed. Both calls now stop with an error of class dmar_studentized_statistic_undefined (a dmar_refusal), made before any arrangement is enumerated or drawn, so a refused Monte Carlo call leaves the random number stream where it was. The message says that the denominator is zero, that the observed data lie at the boundary of the reference set (of the 32 sign patterns, only the observed one and its mirror image have a zero standard error; of the 70 reassignments of 4 and 4 scores, only the observed one and the one that exchanges the groups), that this concerns the statistic and not the evidence, and what statistic = "mean" gives: the mean difference 2 with the exact p-value 2/32 = 0.0625 for the first call and 2/70 = 0.02857 for the second. The condition carries that value as p_value_mean, with reason ("constant_differences" or "constant_groups"), alternative, and n or n_1 and n_2. The value is the smallest the design allows in the direction of the data: 1/2^n one-sided and 2/2^n two-sided for n pairs; for a first group of n_1 among N scores, 1/choose(N, n_1) one-sided, and two-sided 2/choose(N, n_1) with equal group sizes and 1/choose(N, n_1) otherwise (1/56 for 3 against 5); it is 1 for the alternative that points away from the data. When the call would have been run by Monte Carlo sampling the message adds that such a run estimates the value and cannot report less than 1/(n_resamples + 1): for 30 against 30 constant scores the exact value is 2/choose(60, 30), about 1.7e-17, and statistic = "mean" reports 1/10001 = 0.00009999. statistic = "mean" is unchanged in every case. What is kept: a reassignment inside the reference set whose standard error is zero is still ordered as Inf or -Inf, because such reassignments occur in ordinary two-valued and coarsely measured data and the limit puts them where the difference in means does (group_1 = c(1, 1, 1, 0) against group_2 = c(0, 0, 0, 1) with statistic = "t" returns t = 1.4142 and p = 34/70 = 0.4857, with one -Inf and one Inf among the 70 reference values, the same p as the difference in means; randomization_test_paired( rep(0, 5), c(2, 2, 2, -2, 2), statistic = "t") returns t = 1.5 and p = 12/32 = 0.375); and when every score is equal the statistic is 0 and p is 1 under either statistic, as before. The comparison that decides whether the observed data are constant uses the tolerances already in place, so c(5, 5, 5, 5 + 1e-12) against rep(3, 4) is not refused and returns t = 8.0e12. ?randomization_test and ?randomization_test_paired have a paragraph, “When the studentized statistic is undefined”, and an example of the refusal.

  • The shift interval of randomization_test() rejects a shift whose p-value equals 1 - conf_level. A shift is in the interval when its p-value is above alpha, and alpha was computed as 1 - conf_level, which for 0.90 is 0.09999999999999998 in binary arithmetic, just below the p-value 1/10 that the test at the 0.10 level rejects. Shifts with exactly that p-value were therefore kept, and the interval was too wide whenever alpha times the number of reassignments is a whole number (at 0.90 with 10, 20, 70, or 210 reassignments; at 0.80 likewise). For group_1 = c(-1.5, 3.6, 0) and group_2 = c(4.2, 3.0, -1.7) the 90 percent limits were -Inf and Inf and are -5.7 and 5.3, and the 80 percent limits were -5.7 and 5.3 and are -4.5 and 1.7. The comparison now allows a few units of rounding in alpha. Intervals at 0.95 and 0.99 are unchanged; the defect was in 1.0.0 as well, and an interval was never too narrow.

  • randomization_test() returns its table when the standardized mean difference is undefined. With no within-group variance (group_1 = c(1, 1, 1), group_2 = c(2, 2, 2), or every score equal) the call stopped inside ci_smd() with “lower < upper is not fulfilled” or with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. It now reports the test, the shift interval, and Cliff’s delta, with the rows smd, smd_ci_lower, smd_ci_upper, cles, cles_ci_lower, and cles_ci_upper as NA and a warning of class dmar_smd_undefined. For rep(1.1, 4) against rep(0.2, 4) with statistic = "mean" the statistic is 0.9, p is 2/70, and both shift limits are 0.9; statistic = "t" is refused there, since both groups are constant. A response that is not finite (Inf, -Inf) is refused in both randomization tests (“must be finite”), where it gave a base R error or a p-value of NA.

  • plot_randomization_test() shades the reassignments the p-value counted. The figure used an absolute tolerance of 1e-12 of its own. For the scores of the first help example multiplied by 1e-13 it shaded every reassignment (share 1.000 beside p = 0.0238), and for 1e5 + c(.1, .4, .7, .2) against 1e5 + c(.3, .5, .6, .9) it shaded 0.2571 beside p = 0.3143. randomization_test() now stores the logical vector it counted as the attribute reference_extreme, and the plot shades those. A reassignment with an infinite studentized statistic is not drawn, and the subtitle says how many are not, on a second line. Infinite values occur in the reference distribution only: the observed statistic is always finite, since randomization_test() refuses the one case in which it is not, and its line is always drawn. When every reassignment the p-value counted is infinite, which can happen only in a Monte Carlo sample (under enumeration the observed assignment is among those counted), the subtitle gives p without calling it a shaded area and says that none is shaded.

  • procrustes_phi() counts a permutation tied with the observed arrangement. A permutation that exchanges two items with the same loading reproduces the observed coefficient, but was compared with it exactly and could fall one unit in the last place below. With l1 <- c(0.6, 0.72, 0.65, 0.72, 0.81), l2 <- c(0.61, 0.76, 0.64, 0.68, 0.85), and set.seed(113), procrustes_phi(l1, l2, n_resamples = 60000) gave 0.00772 and gives 0.01637; 2 of the 120 permutations are at least as extreme, 0.01667. The denominator is computed once and the comparison allows 4(n + 2) units of machine precision. A call with no tied loadings gives the p-value it gave.

  • n_resamples must be a whole number. randomization_test_paired(x, y, exact = FALSE, n_resamples = 4.5) drew four sign patterns and divided by 5.5, and procrustes_phi(l1, l2, n_resamples = 2.5) drew two permutations and divided by 3.5; randomization_test() truncated 4.5 to 4, and procrustes_phi(n_resamples = -3) returned the coefficient with no message. Each now stops with an error of class dmar_count_invalid unless the count is a single whole number of at least 1 (the two randomization tests) or at least 0 (procrustes_phi(), where 0 skips the test). A whole count gives what it gave. The count is checked whether or not the call draws: randomization_test_paired(x, y, n_resamples = NULL) with eight pairs, which enumerates, returned its table and now stops, as randomization_test() already did. The check of n_resamples applies under exact enumeration as well, where the count is not used.

  • Help corrections for the randomization tests and procrustes_phi(). ?randomization_test_paired said that the paired t is more robust to pair-to-pair variability than the mean difference. Over the sign patterns the paired t is an increasing function of the mean difference, so the two give the same p-value for every data set and differ only in the statistic reported; the page now says so, and says that exact enumeration is the default through 20 pairs and available through 25. ?randomization_test said that the mean difference and the studentized statistic agree in a balanced design with equal variances “to within the discreteness of the reference distribution”; they give the same p-value in every balanced design, whatever the variances, and differ only when the groups are unequal in size, and the second example’s comment no longer recommends the studentized statistic for two groups of five. ?procrustes_phi called the permutation distribution a sampling distribution and said the function reports the coefficient “with its uncertainty”; the test takes the two sets of loadings as given, and the function reports the coefficient and the permutation p-value, with no standard error or interval.

  • mediate(): the bootstrap limits of the indirect effect change in data where a resample makes the predictor or the mediator a linear combination of the covariates. lm() returned a finite product a b in such a resample, by dropping a covariate column in place of the predictor, and that product entered the interval although the effect is not estimable there. These resamples are now dropped and counted (see “mediate() codes its covariates once” above). With a binary predictor (8 of 40 cases) and a binary covariate that differs from it in two cases, B = 2000, seed = 113: 248 of the 2000 resamples are of this kind; the percentile limits were [-0.0401, 0.7202] over all 2000 and are [-0.0369, 0.6800] over the 1752 in which the effect is defined, with the warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped. The estimate (0.1925) and every other row are the same. The same holds in a small sample with several covariates, where a resample can hold fewer distinct cases than the model has coefficients: with 12 cases, three continuous covariates, and B = 600, 12 resamples are dropped and the limits, which were [-1.397, 2.023] with 127 warnings from lm() about a perfect fit, are [-1.177, 1.881]. A call whose resamples all leave a and b estimable returns the limits it returned before, to rounding error (relative difference below 1e-10; up to 1e-9 for a date-time predictor, where the earlier fit lost digits to the size of the origin). No argument restores the earlier limits.

  • mediate() refuses a logical outcome. A logical y was read as 0 and 1 and the linear model fit to it; the call now stops and says that the column must be numeric. as.numeric() of the column gives the earlier table. (A logical x or m stopped before, with subscript out of bounds.)

  • mediate() returns 18 rows, not 17: B_used follows B. Code that reads rows by term is not affected; code that reads the table by position past row 17 is.

  • mediate(ci_method = "boot_bca") stops where it returned an interval from an incomplete jackknife. With one case carrying all the variation in the predictor (x = c(3, rep(0, 19)), B = 300, seed = 113) it returned [-0.1173, 0.4605]; it now stops with dmar_bca_undefined, naming case 1.

  • mediate() stops when a column is named more than once. A covariate named twice returned the answer for the covariate entered once; y among the covariates returned a table from a model with the outcome among the predictors of the mediator. Both now stop.

  • nnt_from_smd() reports the confidence set for the number needed to treat correctly when the interval for the standardized mean difference includes zero, where DMAR 1.0.0 returned its two ends in reversed order as if they bounded an interval. The reciprocal of an interval for the success rate difference (SRD) that includes zero is two intervals that meet at infinity, the NNT of no effect (Altman, 1998). DMAR 1.0.0 put the two finite ends of that set in the rows nnt_lower and nnt_upper, the lower above the upper and the estimate outside them, with nothing to mark the case: nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.3, smd_lower = -0.10, smd_upper = 0.70), the fourth example of the help page (now nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.3, smd_ci_lower = -0.10, smd_ci_upper = 0.70)), returned nnt 5.953, nnt_lower 2.636, and nnt_upper -17.739, and nnt_from_smd(smd = 0.1, n_1 = 30, n_2 = 30) returned 17.739, 3.015, and -4.417. In that case the NNT limits, now the rows nnt_ci_lower and nnt_ci_upper, are NA, as the NNT limits of responder_analysis() are, the set is in the new nnt_confidence_set attribute (for the first call, the rows (-Inf, -17.739) and (2.636, Inf)), the new nnt_set attribute is "two_intervals", and the table prints the set beneath it: “NNT <= -17.739 (harm) or NNT >= 2.636 (benefit), joined at infinity (Altman, 1998)”. Read as an interval, the two rows of 1.0.0 held the true NNT in none of the samples when the population difference is zero and in 34 percent of them at a population standardized mean difference of 0.5 with 20 per group (95 percent intervals); the set of two intervals holds it at the stated level. When the upper limit of the standardized mean difference is exactly zero, the lower NNT limit is now -Inf, where 1.0.0 gave Inf (nnt_from_smd(smd = -0.3, smd_lower = -0.7, smd_upper = 0) returned nnt_lower Inf and nnt_upper -2.636, and nnt_from_smd(smd = -0.3, smd_ci_lower = -0.7, smd_ci_upper = 0) returns -Inf and -2.636). A result whose interval excludes zero, or has a lower limit of exactly zero, is unchanged in its first seven rows, with one exception at the edge of the arithmetic: the SRD is computed without the subtraction that lost digits for a standardized mean difference near zero, so results for |d| below about 1e-8 differ from 1.0.0 in their later digits (at d = 1e-12 the NNT was 1.772373e12 and is 1.772454e12, which is sqrt(pi) / d), and a d so small that the SRD rounded to zero keeps its sign (nnt_from_smd(-1e-200) gave an NNT of Inf and gives -Inf). Every result has the leading class dmar_nnt, which prints the set, ahead of dmar_tbl and data.frame, and dmar_metadata()$result is "dmar_nnt"; code that tests inherits(x, "dmar_tbl") is unaffected. tidy() and glance() return the rows without the two attributes; the finite ends of a set of two intervals are 1 / srd_ci_lower and 1 / srd_ci_upper.

    • Two rows, srd_ci_lower and srd_ci_upper, are appended after nnt_ci_upper: the confidence interval for the SRD, which is an ordinary interval in every case and is the interval Kraemer and Kupfer (2006) prefer. The seven rows of 1.0.0 keep their positions; four are renamed (see Renamed Output Rows and Columns).
    • The arguments are checked. smd must be a single finite number, conf_level a single number in (0, 1), the limits and the sample sizes each given as a pair or not at all, and smd_ci_lower not above smd_ci_upper; DMAR 1.0.0 returned the point estimate without an interval and without a message when one limit or one sample size was given, accepted reversed limits, and printed “Confidence level: 700%” for conf_level = 7. An estimate outside its supplied limits is accepted with a warning. Supplied limits are still used in place of n_1 and n_2.
    • With supplied limits, a confidence level is recorded and printed only when conf_level is given in the call; DMAR 1.0.0 printed “Confidence level: 95%” for limits whose level it did not know.
    • The help page states what is estimated: the SRD of Kraemer and Kupfer (2006), the probability that a randomly chosen treated person has the better outcome minus the probability of the reverse, and its reciprocal. It no longer describes a median cut, which the conversion does not use. It distinguishes this NNT from the NNT at a response threshold, corrects the title of Furukawa and Leucht (2011) (“Comparison of two methods”) and what they found (the control event rate conversion was closer to the observed NNTs, where the page had said they recommended the conversion computed here), and adds Altman (1998).

  • The responder_analysis() help page no longer cites Altman (1998) for withholding the NNT limits. The page said that an interval on the NNT scale would mislead when the interval for the difference includes zero. Altman (1998) argues for reporting it: the confidence set is then two intervals that meet at infinity, with the reciprocals of the difference limits as its two finite ends. The page now says that, and that one lower and one upper limit cannot hold such a set, which is why the two NNT limits are NA. No result changes.

  • responder_analysis() carries the confidence set for the number needed to treat, as nnt_from_smd() does, and the help pages of both functions are written out in full. When the interval for the difference of the two responder proportions includes zero, the NNT limits are NA, as before, and the set they could not hold is now in the result. With two groups the table has the attributes nnt_set ("interval" or "two_intervals", one value per threshold) and nnt_confidence_set (columns lower and upper, with threshold first under sweep), on the signed scale 1 / difference, and group_labels; for two intervals a line under the table states the set. For the first example of the help page (30 of 60 control and 35 of 60 treated participants at a threshold of 10; difference 0.083, interval -0.093 to 0.252; NNT 12 with NA limits), earlier versions printed the table alone, and the table is now followed by “NNT <= -10.806 (control responds more often) or NNT >= 3.966 (treatment responds more often), joined at infinity (Altman, 1998)”, the reciprocals of the two limits of the difference. Every result has the leading class dmar_responder, which prints that line, ahead of dmar_tbl and data.frame, and dmar_metadata()$result is "dmar_responder" where it was "dmar_tbl"; code that tests inherits(x, "dmar_tbl") is unaffected. No row of any table changes (152 calls compared with the build before this change: largest difference 0). ?responder_analysis now states what is estimated and how it differs from the NNT of nnt_from_smd(); the assumptions, among them that the threshold is fixed before the data are seen and that sweep describes dependence on the threshold and is not a search; the Wilson and Newcombe formulas as computed; the construction of the confidence set; what is returned when the proportions are equal, when no one or everyone responds in one group or in all (in the last case the chi square statistic is 0/0 and is reported as NaN), for a group of one, for outcomes at the threshold, for missing values, and for more than two groups; what each row is; the example read number by number; and what dichotomizing costs, from MacCallum, Zhang, Preacher, and Rucker (2002): a split at the mean multiplies a correlation by 0.798 and its square by 0.637, about the loss of 36 percent of the sample. ?nnt_from_smd now states the estimand in words; which assumptions serve the point conversion and which the interval; the conversion with a table of the SRD and the NNT for standardized mean differences of 0.1 to 1.0, which agrees with Table 1 of Kraemer and Kupfer (2006); case by case why the reciprocal of an interval that includes zero is two intervals and why one pair of limits cannot hold it; the edge cases; the threshold NNT beside this one in numbers (at a standardized mean difference of 0.5: 3.62 here, and at least 5.07 at any threshold under the same normal model); and two worked examples. No result of nnt_from_smd() changes (154 calls compared: largest difference 0).

  • vargha_delaney_A() stops on input it used to order by a rule the user did not choose. It converted whatever it was given with as.numeric(). An unordered factor was read through its integer codes, which follow the alphabetical order of its labels: vargha_delaney_A(factor(c("10", "9", "8")), c(10, 9, 8)) returned A = 0 with limits [0, 0], and a five-category agreement item supplied as an unordered factor through outcome ~ group returned the value of its alphabetical codes. Two time differences in different units were compared as bare numbers: vargha_delaney_A(as.difftime(c(1, 2, 3), units = "hours"), as.difftime(c(30, 90, 150), units = "mins")) returned A = 0 with limits [0, 0], where the value is 0.667. A Date beside a POSIXct was compared as days against seconds. A matrix outcome in a formula, cbind(s, t) ~ g, was strung out column after column under a recycled row index, so that 3 rows per group were reported as 6 observations per group. Each of these calls now stops with an error of class dmar_scores_not_ordered that says what to supply. Two time differences in the same units, and a time difference outcome in the formula interface, are on one scale and are ordered as before. Convert time differences in different units with as.numeric(x, units = "hours"), and supply an ordinal response as an ordered factor or as numeric scores.

  • probability_of_superiority_paired() reports both limits at the estimate, with a warning, when every pair favors the same member. It returned NaN for both limits and no warning: probability_of_superiority_paired(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(4, 5, 6, 7)) gave an estimate of 1 with limits NaN, NaN, and now gives 1 with limits 1, 1 and the warning of class dmar_interval_degenerate, which says that the limits are not a confidence interval with the stated coverage. With a missing value it returned a table of NA; it now removes the pair.

  • vargha_delaney_A() and cliff_delta() agree with their earlier values to rounding, not to the last bit. The rank-based computation gives the same A bit for bit. On 3,000 samples with and without ties (2 to 60 observations per group), the largest differences from the earlier results were 8e-17 in the standard error of A, 8e-16 in its limits, 8e-15 in Cliff’s delta, 2e-16 in its variance, and 2e-14 in its limits; the proportions of pairs won, lost, and tied were identical. These are the largest differences on the samples compared, not bounds. Cliff’s delta is now the difference of two exact proportions where it was the mean of the signs of all pairs (on one sample of 3,000 per group it was 0.170807999999525 and is 0.170808, the exact ratio). The z statistic of vargha_delaney_A() moved by at most 1e-13 and its p-value by at most 4e-16.

  • meta_es(), meta_smd(), meta_r(), and plot_forest() warn when the effect sizes are identical under the Hartung-Knapp adjustment, and the warning states what the conventional analysis gives. When every effect size is the same, exactly or up to rounding error, the weighted residuals are zero and so is the adjusted standard error: meta_es(rep(.5, 4), rep(.04, 4)) returns a standard error of 0, a t of Inf, and confidence and prediction limits of 0.5 and 0.5. Those numbers are unchanged (they are what test = "knha" in metafor returns). Earlier versions returned them with no message. The functions now give one warning of class dmar_meta_hk_zero_se. It says that the adjustment multiplies the conventional standard error by the square root of q, the weighted mean square of the effect sizes about the pooled estimate, and that q is 0 when the effect sizes do not differ; it shows the limits (0.5, 0.5); it says that this is not evidence that the effect is known exactly, since each effect size has a sampling variance that agreement among four estimates does not remove; and it states the conventional standard error and the normal interval at the level of the call, 0.1 and 0.304 to 0.696 for that call, which hartung_knapp = FALSE reports. The condition carries n_studies, estimate, se_conventional, lower_conventional, and upper_conventional (4, 0.5, 0.1, 0.3040036, 0.6959964). When the common effect size is 0 the message says that the t statistic is undefined (0 divided by 0), and when the standard error is only numerically zero (meta_es(c(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3, 0.3), rep(.04, 3)), standard error 2e-17) it says that the statistic is the estimate divided by a rounding error. For meta_r() the limits and the normal interval in the message and in the condition are correlations, as the reported rows are, and the conventional standard error is on the Fisher Z scale and is labeled so (meta_r(r = c(.3, .3, .3), n = c(40, 60, 90)): 0.07433 on the Fisher Z scale, normal interval 0.1624 to 0.4262). Effect sizes that differ, however little (0.5, 0.5, and 0.5 + 1e-9), do not raise the warning, and no warning is given for a q between 0 and 1, which is the method working as defined.

  • Meta-analysis results record q and the conventional standard error. Whenever the Hartung-Knapp adjustment is applied, the tables of meta_es(), meta_smd(), and meta_r() carry two new attributes: hartung_knapp_q, the weighted residual mean square on k - 1 degrees of freedom, and se_conventional, the standard error without the adjustment (both on the Fisher Z scale for meta_r()). The adjusted standard error is the square root of the first times the second. For effect sizes of .30, .32, .29, .31, and .33 with variances of .04, .05, .03, .06, and .04 they are 0.006860532 and 0.0912870929, and the reported standard error is 0.007561158. The tables keep their 20 rows, and no reported number changes (1,104 fits compared with the build before this change: largest difference 0). ?meta_es has two new paragraphs. “When q is small” says that the adjusted interval is narrower than the normal interval exactly when q is below the squared ratio of the normal quantile to the t quantile on k - 1 degrees of freedom (0.02, 0.21, 0.50, and 0.75 at k = 2, 3, 5, and 10 for a 95 percent interval), that a small q belongs to the reference distribution of the method, and that both intervals should be reported when the adjusted one is much the narrower. “Identical effect sizes” describes the case the warning is for.

  • The help of meta_es() no longer says that the Hartung-Knapp adjustment keeps the confidence interval near its nominal coverage. It now gives the adjusted standard error, the conventional one times the square root of the weighted residual mean square q (Röver, Knapp, & Friede, 2015), and says that the function applies the unmodified method: q is not replaced by max(1, q), so when q < 1 the interval is narrower than the normal interval. For effect sizes of .30, .32, .29, .31, and .33 with variances of .04, .05, .03, .06, and .04, q is 0.0069 and the interval is 0.287 to 0.329, against 0.129 to 0.487 with hartung_knapp = FALSE. The help says where the coverage of the adjusted interval is at or near the nominal level (homogeneous or equally precise studies) and where it falls below it (studies that differ greatly in precision, with heterogeneous effects, where the normal interval covers less still), and that the prediction interval uses the same standard error. No result changes.

  • The REML estimate of the between-study variance is now carried to the maximum of the restricted likelihood, in whatever units the effect sizes are. meta_es(), meta_smd(), meta_r(), and plot_forest() with method = "reml" (the default) searched over tau2 itself with the default tolerance of optimize(), the fourth root of the machine epsilon. That search stops within about 0.00003 of the maximum in the units of tau2, whatever the size of the effects. The search is now made on tau2 divided by the scale of the data (the largest sampling variance plus the variance of the effect sizes), stopping at a distance relative to the estimate, so the estimate for effect sizes multiplied by a constant c is c squared times the estimate for the original ones. The change is small for effect sizes of the order of 1. On 600 random sets of 2 to 15 studies with sampling variances between .005 and 3, the largest distance of tau2 from the solution of metafor run to convergence (control = list(threshold = 1e-12)) fell from 0.00003 to 0.0000004 (598 sets drawn afresh; the remaining distance is the flatness of the restricted likelihood at its maximum), and no estimate moved between zero and positive; on those sets tau2 changed by at most 0.000028, the pooled estimate by at most 0.00006, and its standard error by at most 0.00003 (0.04% of its size). These are the largest changes on the sets compared, not bounds. For the 12 simulated studies of the package’s tests, tau2 was 0.0279437 and is 0.0279387, the pooled estimate was 0.416452 and is 0.416453, and its Hartung-Knapp standard error was 0.080996 and is 0.080995. The change is large for effect sizes in small units, where 0.00003 is of the size of tau2: the earlier estimate could be zero where the maximum is positive, or several times too large. For ten simulated risk differences near .02 with 4,000 to 40,000 per group (sampling variances near 1e-5; set.seed(2718) in the test file), tau2 was 0 and is 0.0000090755, which is metafor’s converged value; the pooled estimate was 0.021151 and is 0.021255, I2 was 0 and is 52.2 percent, and the prediction interval was 0.0181 to 0.0242 and is 0.0137 to 0.0289. On 300 random sets with sampling variances between 1e-6 and 1e-4, the earlier estimate disagreed with metafor on zero against positive in 76 and was off by more than 1 percent in 184; the estimate now disagrees in none and is within 0.002 percent in all. An analysis of risk differences, proportions, or other effect sizes with sampling variances below about .001 should be rerun. The estimate is now accurate relative to itself, including when one study’s sampling variance is far above the others’ (1.0.0 stopped within about 0.00003 of the maximum in the units of tau2, about 0.5 percent of a tau2 near .01): for the twelve studies of the package’s tests with one sampling variance of 1e6 (.outlier_yivi() in the test file), tau2 was 0.012048 and is 0.012058, the root of the score equation; the pooled estimate, -0.0510, and its Hartung-Knapp standard error, 0.0328, are unchanged to the digits shown. The results of the other estimators are unchanged by this entry (the Paule-Mandel estimate and the Q-profile interval for tau2 are the subject of an entry under Bug Fixes). metafor at its default threshold of 0.00001 gives 0.0279436 for the 12 studies above, so a comparison with its default output can differ in the fifth significant digit of tau2 where it agreed before.

  • meta_es(), meta_smd(), and plot_forest() refuse an infinite effect size or sampling variance with a message that says so, and meta_r() and meta_smd() an infinite sample size. Under method = "reml", meta_es(c(.1, Inf, .3), rep(.1, 3)) stopped with “invalid ‘xmin’ value” from the search and an infinite variance with “invalid ‘xmax’ value”; under "pm" and "dl" both stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. They now stop with “Supply finite effect sizes” and “Supply a finite sampling variance for each effect size”. Under method = "fe" these calls returned a result and now stop as well: meta_es(c(.1, .2, .3), c(.1, Inf, .1), method = "fe") gave an estimate of 0.2 (the study with an infinite variance had a weight of zero), and an infinite effect size gave an infinite estimate. To pool without a study, leave it out. An infinite n in meta_r() stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed” or, under method = "fe", returned an estimate of NaN with a standard error of 0 and no message; an infinite n_1 or n_2 in meta_smd() stopped with a message about the effect sizes. Each now stops with its “must give an integer sample size” message.

  • moments_nc_t() is right at large degrees of freedom and at a large noncentrality parameter, where DMAR 1.0.0 lost digits, changed the sign of the excess kurtosis, or returned a negative variance. DMAR 1.0.0 formed the variance, skewness, and excess kurtosis as differences of the raw moments, which grow with the noncentrality parameter while the differences do not, so the digits left fell as either argument grew: the excess kurtosis was off by 1e-7 of its value at 1000 degrees of freedom and a noncentrality parameter of 5 and by 4e-4 at 2000 and 30, and moments_nc_t(df = 1e4, ncp = 100) returned -0.0022675 where the value is 0.0013340. moments_nc_t(df = 1e16, ncp = 2.5) returned a mean of 1.97e14 and a variance of -3.9e28 (now 2.5 and 1), moments_nc_t(df = 20, ncp = 1e80) an excess kurtosis of NaN, and moments_nc_t(df = Inf, ncp = 2) NaN for the mean, variance, skewness, and excess kurtosis and NA for the standard deviation. The mean now comes from the logarithm of the chi mean factor that sd_unbiased() uses, and the other three from the central moments of the square root of the degrees of freedom over a chi square variate, so that no raw moments are subtracted; from 100 degrees of freedom on, the third central moment and fourth cumulant of that square root are their expansions in the reciprocal of the degrees of freedom. Against values computed to several hundred digits, for degrees of freedom from just above each boundary (1, 2, 3, and 4) to 1e300 and a noncentrality parameter up to 1e6 in magnitude, the largest relative errors found are 3e-16 for the mean, 9e-16 for the variance, 4e-14 for the skewness, and 1.3e-12 for the excess kurtosis; the same limits hold at a noncentrality parameter of 1e10, 1e100, and 1e300. df = Inf now returns the normal distribution with mean ncp and variance 1, and an infinite ncp is refused. For degrees of freedom up to 300 and a noncentrality parameter up to 5 in magnitude the values differ from those of 1.0.0 by at most 1.5e-8 of their size (df = 20, ncp = 2.5 agrees to ten digits).

  • cv(), ci_cv(), sd_unbiased(), ci_proportion(), and power_equivalence_c() refuse inputs for which DMAR 1.0.0 returned a number that meant nothing or an error from inside base R. Each refusal names the argument. In cv(): a negative sd (cv(mean = 2, sd = -1) returned -0.5), a mean of 0 (cv(mean = 0, sd = 1) returned Inf), cv given with one of mean and sd (cv(cv = .2, mean = 999) returned 0.2 and ignored the mean), a cv that is not one finite number (cv(cv = "a") returned a table holding “a”), an N of 1 or less, or an infinite N, with unbiased = TRUE (cv(cv = .2, N = 0, unbiased = TRUE) returned Inf, and N = Inf returned the uncorrected 0.2), and an unbiased that is not TRUE or FALSE (unbiased = "yes" returned the uncorrected value). cv() documented single values and now requires them: a vector cv, mean, sd, or N, and unbiased = 1, were accepted and are refused (cv(cv = .2, N = c(10, 20), unbiased = TRUE) returned two rows). A negative mean still gives a negative coefficient. In ci_cv(): a coefficient of variation that is not positive, whether given as cv, through sd, or by the data (ci_cv(cv = -.2, N = 20) and ci_cv(mean = 10, sd = -2, N = 20) returned the limits -0.298 and Inf, and ci_cv(data = c(-1, -2, -3, -4)) returned -6.859 and Inf), data with a missing or infinite score or fewer than two scores, data that are not numeric (a logical vector was read as 0 and 1), and an N that is not one finite number above 1; ci_cv(cv = 0, N = 20), ci_cv(cv = .2, N = Inf), and ci_cv(data = c(1, 2, NA, 4)) stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”. A fractional N above 1 is still accepted. In sd_unbiased(): a negative or infinite s (sd_unbiased(s = -1, N = 20) returned -1.013, and s = Inf returned Inf), s without N (which stopped with “arguments imply differing number of rows”), a single score as X (sd_unbiased(X = 5) returned NA), scores X that are not numeric (a logical vector was read as 0 and 1), an N of 1 or less, a single s or N that is missing, and vectors s and N of different lengths other than 1. One inadmissible element refuses the whole call: sd_unbiased(s = 2, N = c(10, 1)) returned 2.056 and NaN and now stops. A missing element of a vector still gives a missing row (sd_unbiased(s = c(1, NA), N = 10) returns 1.028 and NA). A fractional N and vectors of equal length give what they gave in 1.0.0; an infinite N gives s (1.0.0 returned NaN). In ci_proportion(): an infinite count (ci_proportion(1, Inf) returned the limits 0 and 0). In power_equivalence_c(): a missing or infinite true_contrast, n_per_group, true_sd, bound, or df_error, and a missing alpha_level (true_psi = NA_real_, an infinite per-group size, and delta_upper = Inf, in the 1.0.x names, each returned a power of 0, where n_per_group = 1e12 and contrast_upper = 1e6 return 1; a missing per-group size, true_sd, df_error, or alpha_level given as NA_real_ stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”). A fractional n_per_group or df_error gives what it gave.

  • ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() leaves a replication whose sample mean is not positive out of its width and coverage summaries, where DMAR 1.0.0 entered it with the limits ci_cv() gave for a negative coefficient, an infinite upper limit among them. Such a sample has no confidence interval for the coefficient of variation, which ci_cv() now refuses. The replication is left out of every statistic row, mean_cv, median_cv, and sd_cv included (see the next entry): all ten are taken over the replications that have an interval; one warning of class dmar_replications_without_interval states how many were left out, and the count is attr(x, "simulation")$failed. The case needs a large coefficient of variation and a small sample: with true_cv = 1 and specified_N = 10 the sample mean is not positive in about 8 of 10000 replications. With set.seed(7) and G = 3000 there, 3 replications are left out: pct_ci_miss_low was 0.0287 and is 0.0277, total_type_I_error was 0.0553 and is 0.0544, and median_ci_width was 3.743 and is 3.735. mean_ci_width was Inf there in 1.0.0, since ci_cv() has no finite upper limit for some samples with a positive mean, and is now taken over the finite widths (see the next entry). A study in which every sample mean is positive, which is every study at the coefficients of variation the help page and the vignette use, differs from DMAR 1.0.0 only where the limits of ci_cv() changed with the exact noncentral t (see Exact Noncentral t and Studentized Range Distributions).

  • ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() summarizes the same replications in every row. A replication whose sample mean is not positive has no interval, and its sample coefficient is negative. All ten statistic rows, mean_cv, median_cv, and sd_cv among them, describe the replications with a positive mean (DMAR 1.0.0 entered such a replication in every row; see the entry above). An interval with an infinite upper limit made mean_ci_width infinite and sd_ci_width undefined; the two are now over the finite widths, median_ci_width stays over every width, an infinite width counts as not meeting the target (as it did), and the number of infinite widths is attr(, "simulation")$n_infinite_width. DMAR 1.0.0 repeated the warning ci_cv() gave for such an interval in every replication that had one. ci_cv() no longer gives that warning (see the entry on ci_cv() and an infinite upper limit), and the sensitivity function gives one warning of its own, of class dmar_replications_with_infinite_limit, that states how many replications had an infinite upper limit and how they enter the rows (the count is also the field n_replications of the condition). With set.seed(88), true_cv = 3, specified_N = 5, width = .5, and G = 500 (114 replications without an interval, 346 infinite widths): mean_cv -3.499 in DMAR 1.0.0 and 4.870 now, median_cv 1.400 and 1.884, sd_cv 118.98 and 22.16, mean_ci_width Inf and 14.85, sd_ci_width NaN and 37.25. With true_cv = 1, specified_N = 10 (no replication without an interval, 96 infinite widths): mean_ci_width Inf in DMAR 1.0.0 and 15.55 now, sd_ci_width NaN and 188.3. A simulation in which every mean is positive and every width finite differs from DMAR 1.0.0 only through the exact noncentral t limits of ci_cv(). The table also carries the simulation attribute (replications attempted, with and without an interval, and exact binomial limits for the share that met the width) and prints the counts beneath it. In the first example the coverage rows differ from those of DMAR 1.0.0 as well, for the reason of the entry above.

  • The number of replications G must be a whole number, in every function that has the argument. The 31 sensitivity functions with a G argument, ss_aipe_indirect_effect(), ss_aipe_composite_sem(), and ss_power_composite_sem() check it with the one check of a count (an error of class dmar_count_invalid), before anything is simulated. The smallest G is what it was: 10 for the three planners, 2 for ss_seq_c_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_crossed_sensitivity(), and 1 elsewhere. In DMAR 1.0.0 most of them did not check G: ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(G = 0) returned a full table from one replication and G = 2.7 ran two, ss_aipe_r_sensitivity(G = 0) returned a table of NA, ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(G = 0) stopped with “subscript out of bounds”, and G = -3, Inf, NA, or a vector stopped with “invalid ‘times’ argument”; ss_seq_c_sensitivity() accepted G = 2.5. The messages of the functions that did check G now read “‘G’ must be a single whole number of at least 1.” (or 2, or 10), in place of “‘G’ must be a positive integer.”, “‘G’ must be a single positive whole number.”, “‘G’ must be a single number of at least 2.”, and “‘G’ must be a positive whole number of attempted studies.”.

  • The six ss_aipe_crd_es_*() planners check G (nrep in 1.0.x) the same way at entry: a fractional number, 0, a negative number, NA, a character string, an infinite value, or more than one value is an error of class dmar_count_invalid, before any simulation starts (earlier such a value reached the simulation unchecked). G = NULL remains the default of the two planners that fix a size and a budget, where it skips the simulation. Results for a valid G are unchanged.

  • The Hofmann (1977) entry of simple_structure() gives the issue and pages of the article. The help page gave The Journal of General Psychology, 96, 58–66; the DOI record of the article (10.1080/00221309.1977.9920803) has 96(1), 103–110. The entry now gives that issue and those pages with the DOI, and the Hofmann (1978) entry on the same page gains its DOI, 10.1207/s15327906mbr1302_9, which fa_exploratory() already cites. The title, the journal, and the 1978 volume, issue, and pages, 13(2), 247–250, already matched the records and are unchanged.

  • The Owen (1968) entry of moments_nc_t() gives the DOI of the article. The entry carried the DOI of a letter to the editor in the preceding issue (10.1080/00401706.1968.10490590); it is now 10.1080/00401706.1968.10490594.

  • The Phillips (1990) entry gives the first page of the article. The help pages of power_equivalence_c(), power_equivalence_md(), power_density_equivalence_md(), and power_equivalence_md_plot() gave the pages as 139–144; they are 137–144.

  • The correction factor of Hedges (1981) is right at a very large sample size, in smd(), smd_c(), meta_smd(), expected_smd(), and var_smd(). The factor J(df) = Gamma(df/2) / {sqrt(df/2) Gamma((df - 1)/2)} was computed as a difference of two lgamma() values that nearly cancel at a large df, the form that design_consequences(), sd_unbiased(), and var_ete() gave up earlier in this release (the entry on E(S)/sigma). It is now formed from the logarithm of E(S)/sigma on df - 1 degrees of freedom, log J(df) = L(df - 1) + log1p(-1/df)/2, two negative terms with nothing to cancel, through one internal helper that the five functions share. Against a 60-digit evaluation J is right to a relative 3.4e-16 from 2 df to 1e14; the earlier form was off by a relative 5e-11 at 1e5 df and 8e-9 at 1e7, and at 1e8 it returned a J above 1.
