At ordinary sample sizes nothing a user sees moves: over 272 planning sets with at most 10,000 per group the largest change in any reported value is 2.6e-10 (in var_smd()), except in meta_smd() under REML, whose iteration stops at a tolerance that lets the estimate move by about 1e-9 and I^2 by about 4e-6 of a percentage point (no printed digit moves), and with 20 per group smd(unbiased = TRUE) and expected_smd() agree with 1.0.x to all printed digits. Two results that subtract nearly equal numbers were wrong much sooner than J itself, and are now taken from the logarithm with expm1(): the bias row of expected_smd(), true_smd (1/J - 1), and the exact variance in var_smd(), which is now computed as df/(df - 2) + lambda^2 {2/(df - 2) - (1/J^2 - 1)}. expected_smd(true_smd = 0.5, n_1 = 1e8, n_2 = 1e8) reported a bias of -1.19e-07 (the wrong sign) and now reports 1.875e-09; var_smd(true_smd = 3, n_1 = 1e8, n_2 = 2e8) reported an exact variance of -8.5e-06 and now reports 3.0e-08; var_smd(true_smd = 0.5, n_1 = 1e8) reported 1.42e-07 and now reports 2.06e-08; with 100,000 per group the bias of expected_smd(true_smd = 0.5) moves from 1.875105e-06 to 1.875029e-06. Against the 60-digit values the bias and the exact variance are now right to a relative 7e-16 over 344 planning sets with up to 2e8 observations; the earlier relative errors there reached 190 and 285. No argument is added.

  • moments_nc_F() is right at large degrees of freedom. The variance, skewness, and excess kurtosis were formed as differences of raw moments, which agree in their leading digits when the degrees of freedom are large, so the digits that remained were rounding error. moments_nc_F(df_1 = 1e6, df_2 = 1e6) returned an excess kurtosis of -5.285e-05 where the value is 6.60006e-05, and a skewness of 0.0060000263 where the value is 0.0060000230. The function now writes the statistic as (df_2/df_1) X Y with X the noncentral chi square and Y the reciprocal of the central one, and forms the central moments of F/E(F) from those of X/E(X) - 1 and Y/E(Y) - 1, which are independent and have mean 0: every term of each sum is nonnegative, so nothing cancels (the expressions are on the help page; they were derived for DMAR and checked against exact rational arithmetic). In 14 cases with degrees of freedom up to 1e12 and noncentrality up to 1e6 the four moments are right to a relative 5e-16, where the earlier form was off by a relative 1.8 at (1e6, 1e6, 0) and 0.36 at (3, 1e6, 1e6). At ordinary degrees of freedom nothing a user sees moves: over 918 combinations with both degrees of freedom at most 200 and noncentrality at most 50 the largest relative change is 8.5e-12, and the moments that do not exist are NA in the same places. The mean is unchanged.

  • rbind() of DMAR tables no longer carries the first table’s confidence level over rows computed at another. A dmar_tbl keeps its confidence level, and the other facts its printed lines are written from, as attributes, and rbind() kept the attributes and the class of the first table: rbind(ci_smd(..., conf_level = 0.90), ci_smd(..., conf_level = 0.95)) was a table of class dmar_ci_smd that printed “Confidence level: 90%” beneath six rows, three of them 95 percent limits, and dmar_metadata() of it gave 0.90. rbind() now has a method for these tables. When every table stacked is a DMAR table and all have the same classes and attributes, the stack is a DMAR table with those attributes, as before. In every other case (different confidence levels, different functions, or a DMAR table stacked with a plain data frame, in either order) the result is an ordinary data.frame with the same rows and columns and none of the DMAR attributes, and no warning: the numbers are all there, and no printed line states a level that does not hold for every row. To compare results across levels, stack tidy() rows, which carry the level in a column: rbind(tidy(x_90), tidy(x_95)). dplyr::bind_rows() does not call the method. Code that relied on the class of a mixed stack (inherits(rbind(a, b), "dmar_tbl") with tables at two levels) now gets FALSE. ?dmar_tbl has a section on stacking.

  • ss_aipe_R2() with assurance returns a sample size for a small population R2, where it stopped with “invalid ‘xmin’ value”. The procedure inverts the expected value of R2 by matching a value rounded to two decimals against a grid of expected values. When the one-sided lower limit it uses is 0, which happens for a small population R2, no grid value has an expected R2 that low, the match was missing, and optimize() was given a missing end point. A missing match is now replaced by the end of the grid when the target lies beyond it and by the grid value with the nearest expectation otherwise. ss_aipe_R2(true_R2 = .03, p = 1, width = .2, assurance = .9) returns 113; of 30 conditions drawn at random with a true_R2 of .03 to .90, the 8 that stopped now return (107 to 173) and the 22 that returned give the same sample sizes, as do 40 further conditions that returned before and 48 without assurance (largest difference 0).

  • The default p-value of vargha_delaney_A() is larger. The test statistic is referred to Student’s t with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom where DMAR 1.0.x referred it to the standard normal distribution (see “The Order-Based Effect Sizes Share One Contract”). The estimate, its standard error, the statistic, and the confidence interval are unchanged, and test = "z" gives the 1.0.x p-value: on 240 data sets by three levels and two interval methods the eight numbers of a test = "z" row equal the earlier ones exactly. For the first example of the help (set.seed(113), 40 per group) the p-value is 0.0082 on 77.96 degrees of freedom where it was 0.0067; for vargha_delaney_A(iq_8 ~ treatment, data = pygmalion) it is 0.0892 on 92.48 degrees of freedom where it was 0.0858; and for x = c(3.5, 5, 6, 7, 8), y = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 4.2) it is 0.0033 on 6.63 degrees of freedom where it was 0.0000076 (the exact permutation p-value is 8/252 = 0.032). results_sentence() reports the p-value of the test that was run. The table has two more columns, df and test, after the nine it had.

  • Every sensitivity function summarizes its replications over one denominator and records the counts. The proportion of intervals that met the width target (pct_ci_less_width), the proportions that missed the true value, and the summaries of the widths are taken over the replications that produced a confidence interval, in every ss_aipe_*_sensitivity() function; a replication without an interval is in none of those rows. In ss_aipe_reliability_sensitivity(), where a simulated study can end without an interval, DMAR 1.0.0 took the width rows over the studies that returned one, as now, and the three rows for intervals that missed the true value (pct_ci_miss_low, pct_ci_miss_high, total_type_I_error) over all G, so that a study without an interval counted as one whose interval held the value: with two of four simulated studies returning an interval and one of the two missing the value, the row is 1/2 where DMAR 1.0.0 gave 1/4, and with no study returning an interval the three rows are NA where it gave 0. ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity() have entries of their own. The rule changes nothing in a run in which every replication has an interval. All 31 sensitivity functions, the two ss_power_*_sensitivity() functions and ss_seq_c_sensitivity() included, now attach the attribute simulation, a list with attempted (G), returned (replications with an interval, or a test), failed (those without), denominator (which is returned), width_target_probability (the pct_ci_less_width row), and width_target_mc_ci (exact binomial limits for it over returned, which describe simulation error); the two width entries are NA for a function with no width target. ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity() adds n_redrawn, the data sets whose fit did not converge and were drawn again (such a data set is replaced, so it is not among the replications without an interval; the help says how the count is read). The record is the one place the counts are kept: the rows suc_rep of ss_aipe_rmsea_sensitivity() and ss_aipe_sem_path_sensitivity() and num_probs_with_cis of ss_aipe_R2_sensitivity(), which held the same counts in DMAR 1.0.x, are removed (returned and failed hold them). The line “Replications” beneath each printed table gives G, and the three counts when a replication was without an interval. dmar_metadata() returns the record as simulation.

  • ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity() no longer counts a completely separated replication as an interval of width 0. When the two simulated groups do not overlap, the estimated variance of Cliff’s delta is 0 and cliff_delta() reports both limits at the estimate, which are not a confidence interval. DMAR 1.0.x took them as an interval of width 0, which met every width target, and scored its coverage from the point estimate. Such a replication now has no interval: its estimate still enters mean_cliff_delta, median_cliff_delta, and sd_cliff_delta, and the width, width-target (pct_ci_less_width), and coverage rows describe the replications with an interval. One warning of class dmar_replications_without_interval gives the count (fields n_without_interval and G), the per-replication warnings are not passed on, the table carries the simulation attribute with the counts and exact binomial limits for the width proportion, and the file named in filename records such a replication with its estimate and NA elsewhere. With set.seed(113), ss_aipe_cliff_delta_sensitivity(true_delta = 0.9, specified_N = 12, width = 0.4, G = 400) has 162 separated replications of 400. pct_ci_less_width is 0 where it was 0.405; mean_ci_width 0.966 where it was 0.575; median_ci_width 0.909 where it was 0.867; sd_ci_width 0.112 where it was 0.483; pct_ci_miss_low 0 where it was 0.405; pct_ci_miss_high 0.025 where it was 0.015; and total_type_I_error 0.025 where it was 0.420. The three rows of the estimate are unchanged (0.904, 0.944, 0.119). A run in which no replication is separated returns what it returned: 36 conditions under a common seed are identical. No argument restores the earlier result.

  • results_sentence() does not write limits that are not a confidence interval as one. For a table of vargha_delaney_A(), cliff_delta(), or probability_of_superiority_paired() whose estimated variance is 0, the sentence gives the estimate and the reason. results_sentence(vargha_delaney_A(c(4, 5, 6), c(1, 2, 3))) is “A = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the groups are completely separated, so the estimated variance is 0)” where it was “A = 1.00, 95% CI [1.00, 1.00]”; for cliff_delta() on those groups “cliff_delta = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the groups are completely separated, so the estimated variance is 0)” where it was “cliff_delta = 1.00, 95% CI [1.00, 1.00]”; for probability_of_superiority_paired(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(4, 5, 6, 7)) “probability_of_superiority = 1.00 (no confidence interval: every pair favors the same member, so the estimated variance is 0)” where DMAR 1.0.0 wrote “probability_of_superiority = 1.00, 95% CI [NaN, NaN]”; and for vargha_delaney_A(c(2, 2, 2), c(2, 2, 2)) “A = 0.50 (no confidence interval: every score is equal, so the estimated variance is 0)” where it was “A = 0.50, 95% CI [0.50, 0.50]”. A p-value is appended only when the table has one (the permutation test). The sentence of a tidy() or glance() row of such a table reads “A = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0)”. The sentence of every other table is unchanged.

  • A bootstrap or Monte Carlo interval asked for with fewer replications than the rule requires is refused (see One Rule for Bootstrap Replications): fewer than 200, 400, or 2000 at the 90, 95, or 99 percent level for a percentile or Monte Carlo interval, fewer than 1000, 2000, or 10000 for a BCa interval, and fewer than 100 for a bootstrap standard error interval or a Bollen-Stine p-value. Calls that ran in 1.0.x and now stop include reliability_alpha(ci_method = "percentile", B = 40) (0.6083 [0.5231, 0.6846] before; with B = 400 the function returns [0.5203, 0.6709], as it did), reliability_alpha(ci_method = "bca", B = 500) ([0.5204, 0.6692] before; with B = 2000, [0.5348, 0.6768], as it did), reliability_alpha(ci_method = "bootstrap_se", B = 50), htmt(B = 100) to htmt(B = 199), parallel_analysis(B = 20), sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(B = 20) (p = 0.05 from 20 samples before), R2_mixed_effects(ci_method = "boot", B = 20), and mlmr(ci_method = "boot", B = 20). The error has class dmar_count_invalid and names the number; options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) runs the call and marks the result.

  • An interval formed from fewer than half of the replications requested is no longer reported. The estimate is returned with NA limits and a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. In mediate(), the kappa functions, krippendorff_alpha(), htmt(), the ratio functions, average_variance_extracted(), and fraction_missing_information() an interval was formed from any 100 replications that remained (two in the last), and in the reliability family through 1.0.1 from any two. An interval from at least half of those requested is reported as before, since the number required is held to the request and not to the replications that remain, and the warning now has a class, states the counts, and says when those that remain are fewer than the number required. With two raters and eight subjects, six of whom both raters place in one category, cohen_kappa(ci_method = "percentile", B = 400, seed = 113) returns 0.6 [0.0, 1.0] from the 361 resamples in which kappa is defined, as 1.0.x did (and ci_method = "bca", B = 2000 returns [0.0, 1.0] from 1787); krippendorff_alpha(boot = TRUE, B = 400, seed = 113) on five units of which four are alike returns [1, 1] from 254 resamples; htmt(B = 200, seed = 113) with an item that is nonzero in one of 12 cases returns the bound 1.1723 from 130 resamples; and ci_ratio_of_means(ci_method = "percentile", B = 400, seed = 113) with a denominator group that is nonzero in one of 12 cases returns 3.0 [0.3333, 6.0] from 269 replications. Each of these now warns that fewer than the number required remained and says to request more.

  • R2_mixed_effects(), mlmr(), and mlmr_mv() drop a replication for every statistic when it has no value for one. Each statistic’s limits were the quantiles of its own finite values, so one missing value moved the interval of that statistic alone and the intervals of one call rested on different replications. With 500 replications of which three lack the marginal and two the conditional R-squared (the fixture of test-dmar_bootstrap.R), the marginal limits were the quantiles of 497 values and the conditional limits of 498; both are now the quantiles of the same 495. When every replication returns every statistic, which is the usual case, the limits do not change: R2_mixed_effects(ci_method = "boot", B = 400, seed = 113) on the sleepstudy random intercept model returns 0.2799 [0.1880, 0.4072] and 0.7043 [0.5838, 0.7964] in both builds.

  • No interval that is still reported changes for any other reason. On 75 calls that the rule accepts and in which every interval is still reported (1311 reported numbers; mediate(), the kappa functions, krippendorff_alpha(), htmt(), the two ratio functions, the reliability family, average_variance_extracted(), fraction_missing_information(), R2_mixed_effects(), ci_eta_squared_generalized(), mlmr(), mlmr_mv(), parallel_analysis(), factor_count(), and sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(), each with a seed), the largest absolute difference between this build and the earlier one is 0.

  • ci_nc_t() computes the noncentral t distribution exactly where R’s pt() is not accurate, so every interval built on it is exact. DMAR 1.0.x inverted pt() everywhere and warned only when the observed ncp passed 37.62, so an interval whose upper limit alone passed it was approximate without a warning. Limits inside the accurate range are unchanged. The interval of ci_smd() for two groups of 20 at d = 10 with 99 percent confidence was [7.003, 12.999] and is [7.003, 13.099]; ci_nc_t(ncp = 34.5, df = 38) gave [26.511, 42.273] and gives [26.511, 42.447]; ci_nc_t(ncp = 100, df = 1, conf_level = .99) gave [-107.157, 257.157] and gives [0.394, 280.717]; ci_cv(cv = .05, N = 15) was [0.0369, 0.0818] and is [0.0366, 0.0790]; and ci_sm(sm = 10, N = 30) was [7.315, 12.512] and is [7.412, 12.580]. ci_smd_c(), ci_sc(), ci_sc_ancova(), ci_reg_coef(), ci_rc(), ci_src(), smd_trimmed(), and the sensitivity functions of the AIPE planners inherit the exact limits. The warning “The observed noncentrality parameter exceeds 37.62 in magnitude” is gone, and the planners that passed it on (ss_aipe_sc() 425 times for true_std_contrast = 4, width = .5, assurance = .9) are silent. With more than 1e7 degrees of freedom the integral is taken over the standardized chi square: its density is computed without forming the chi square value, and the argument of the normal distribution function, q s - ncp, is formed as (q - ncp) + q(s - 1) with s - 1 computed without forming s, since a double holds neither the chi square value nor s finely enough there. Against a 256-bit oracle, at 13 values of the degrees of freedom from 1e7 to 1e32, with q times the standard deviation of s from .001 to 10, both tails of the distribution function, P(|T| <= k), and the density are within 2.0e-14, the probability the integral leaves out past the 1e-14 and 1 - 1e-14 quantiles of the chi square. A plan of ss_aipe_sc() or ss_aipe_sc_ancova() up to 2^53 per group with J groups has at most J(2^53 - 1) degrees of freedom, fewer than 4.1e31 for any vector of contrast weights R can hold.

  • The AIPE planners built on ci_nc_t() plan for the exact interval, and some plans change by one or two. ss_aipe_smd(), ss_aipe_sm(), ss_aipe_sc(), and ss_aipe_sc_ancova() plan for the interval ci_nc_t() now reports, with exact noncentral t probabilities in the published quantile assurance steps (that of ss_aipe_sm(), and of ss_aipe_sc_ancova() by default; the plans of ss_aipe_smd() and ss_aipe_sc() with assurance are now the exact ones of the entries below). Of 116 plans scanned with those steps (standardized effects of 1 to 10, widths of .1 to 2.5, with and without an assurance of .90), 11 changed, among them ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = 5, width = 1) from 127 to 128, ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = 3, width = .5, assurance = .9) from 277 to 278, ss_aipe_sm(true_sm = 3, width = 1, assurance = .9) from 102 to 104, ss_aipe_sc(true_std_contrast = 8, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = 1, assurance = .9) from 300 to 299, and ss_aipe_sc_ancova(true_std_contrast = 2, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .25) from 738 to 739. The two plans with assurance of ss_aipe_smd() and ss_aipe_sc() quoted here are also their exact plans.

  • cv_t() returns exact noncentral critical values. With alpha_level = .05, df = 3, and ncp = 50 the critical values were 29.0756 and 429.1783 and are 28.2828 and 186.4939; with df = 10 and ncp = 45 they were 31.7440 and 83.9369 and are 31.3532 and 79.0839; and with one degree of freedom and ncp = 38 the upper value was infinite and is 1212.586. The area_less and area_greater columns are exact as well.

  • cv_t() and ci_nc_t() with fewer than one degree of freedom are exact, and the critical values of cv_t() there change, by orders of magnitude with df of 0.3 or less. DMAR 1.0.x took them from qt(), which inverts pt(), and below one degree of freedom pt() with a noncentrality is not accurate even inside 37.62. The critical values moved by factors up to 2e47 with df = 0.05 and 39 with 0.3, by as much as 15 percent with 0.5, and by less than 1e-4 of themselves with 0.6 and above (noncentralities up to 37.5 in absolute value, alpha_level .001 and .05): cv_t(.05, 0.1, ncp = 0.5) gave -33554432 and 305284064 and gives -1.0428e10 and 5.7095e13, and cv_t(.001, 0.5, ncp = 38) gave -Inf and Inf and gives 8.478261 and 92490299.0. A critical value beyond the largest double is -Inf or Inf. The limits of ci_nc_t() with df < 1 change by at most 1.5e-10 of themselves.

  • The individual intervals of limits_of_agreement() are exact for large samples. Their noncentrality, k sqrt(n), passes 37.62 from n = 369 at 95 percent coverage, and past it each confidence limit was too far from the mean difference, by as much as 0.0011 standard deviations of the differences. For set.seed(1000); a <- rnorm(1000, 100, 15); b <- a + rnorm(1000, 0.5, 3), the interval on the upper limit of agreement was [6.05197, 6.68620] and is [6.05119, 6.68513]. The pair intervals (the default) are unchanged.

  • Power past a noncentrality of 37.62 is exact. The power planners whose test is a t test (ss_power_smd(), ss_power_c(), ss_power_sc(), ss_power_c_ancova(), ss_power_contrast(), ss_power_mixed_effects(), ss_power_reg_coef(), ss_power_rc(), ss_power_pcm(), and, for the test of a with X fixed, ss_power_indirect_effect()), the marginal powers of ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(), the noninferiority power of power_equivalence_c() and ss_power_equivalence_c(), and design_consequences() take the noncentral t probabilities from the exact routines. No planned sample size changes, since a search stops far below a noncentrality of 37.62; the power reported for a specified sample size changes where the noncentrality passes 37.62 and the test has few degrees of freedom (by as much as .28 with one degree of freedom and .034 with two; with 10 or more it was and is 1 to within 4e-11). ss_power_smd(true_smd = 40, n_1 = 2, alpha_level = .001) reported a power of .7823613 and reports .7981440; the marginal power of the group test of ss_power_composite_ancova_2group(true_smd = 40, true_cor = .3, specified_n_per_group = 2, composite_terms = c("group", "covariate"), include_interaction = FALSE, alpha_level = .001) was .1666 and is .0525; and design_consequences(true_effect = 40, se = 1, df = 2, alpha_level = .001) reported a power of .7823613, a Type S error of 1.2e-5, and an exaggeration ratio of 1.0207, and reports .7981440, a Type S error below 1e-300, and 1.0005. The power of a negative effect at a specified sample size (ss_power_smd(true_smd = -1, n_1 = 50), and the same in ss_power_c(), ss_power_sc(), ss_power_mixed_effects(), and an example of ss_power_composite_ancova_2group()) passed on the warning of pt() full precision may not have been achieved in 'pnt{final}'; these calls are now silent, with the same values.

  • The Bayesian t tests use the exact noncentral t density. bayes_one_sample_t(), bayes_paired_t(), and bayes_independent_t() integrate the noncentral t likelihood over the prior, and R’s dt() with a noncentrality rests on the normal approximation past 37.62 and loses accuracy near t = 0 and with many degrees of freedom. It is now used only with at most 1,000 degrees of freedom, a noncentrality of at most 37.62, and |t| of at least .1, where results are unchanged, and the density is integrated exactly elsewhere, except at t = 0, where it is exp(-ncp^2 / 2) / {B(df / 2, 1/2) sqrt(df)}. R’s dt(), which DMAR 1.0.x used there, computes it at a nonzero noncentrality by differencing two log gammas, and is off by as much as 3.4e-8 of it short of 1e7 degrees of freedom (at 9,832,229.8): dt(0, 5.6e6, 1.5) is 0.12951758933 where the density is 0.12951758988, and bayes_one_sample_t(mean = 0, sd = 1, N = 5600001) gave a Bayes factor bf_01 of 2097.196624 in DMAR 1.0.0 and gives 2097.196615. bayes_one_sample_t(mean = 5.7, sd = 1, N = 50) (t = 40.3) gave a posterior median of 5.6038, a 95 percent interval of [4.4709, 6.7759], and a Bayes factor of 5.3589e35, and gives 5.5967, [4.4709, 6.7901], and 5.3537e35. Such calls take about 0.4 seconds, up from 0.05 to 0.1.

  • The Tukey and Games-Howell procedures, and the Bryant-Paulson distribution with no covariates, use the exact studentized range wherever R’s qtukey() and ptukey() are not accurate (see Exact Noncentral t and Studentized Range Distributions). R documents qtukey() as accurate to the fourth decimal place. It falls short of that at small error df, by more as the number of means and the confidence level grow (with 10 means and 2 df its .999 quantile is 41 percent too small, so intervals built on it have a familywise error rate of about .0029 rather than .001); at large df; far in either tail; below the .75 point with more than 50 means; and where its search stops short of the root of ptukey(). The exact computation is used below 9 error df with up to 6 means, 11 with up to 10, 15 with up to 20, 21 with up to 50, 31 with up to 100, 41 with up to 250, 47 with up to 400, 57 with up to 700, 71 with up to 1000, 81 with up to 1500, 91 with up to 2000, 101 with up to 3000, and 111 with more (measured to 10000 means and extrapolated beyond); above 10000 and up to 10^8 df; for every quantile at a probability above .999 or below .001; with more than 50 means, below the .75 point (the .80 point with more than 1000 means); and wherever qtukey() fails or is more than 2e-6 from the root of ptukey(). Elsewhere the values are those of qtukey() and ptukey() (above 10^8 df, their infinite-df values), which were within 9.6e-6 of the exact quantile and 9.1e-7 of the exact probability at every point checked where they are kept. The changed values:

    call DMAR 1.0.x now
    cv_tukey_hsd(.01, df = 2, n_groups = 20) 31.485 26.830
    cv_tukey_hsd(.01, df = 3, n_groups = 20) 14.105 13.976
    cv_tukey_hsd(.05, df = 2, n_groups = 20) 11.867 11.857
    cv_tukey_hsd(.001, df = 2, n_groups = 10) 41.612 71.063
    cv_tukey_hsd(.001, df = 12, n_groups = 50) 8.0894 8.0897
    cv_tukey_hsd(.05, df = 30000, n_groups = 10) 3.16368 3.16392
    cv_tukey_hsd(1e-4, df = 11, n_groups = 10) 8.491265 8.491348
    cv_tukey_hsd(1e-5, df = 1000, n_groups = 2000) 9.1427 6.9804
    cv_tukey_hsd(.001, df = 41, n_groups = 1000) 7.282740 7.282842
    cv_tukey_hsd(.025, df = 12, n_groups = 10) 4.245304 4.245333
    cv_tukey_hsd(.0025, df = 23, n_groups = 5) 4.255839 4.255754
    cv_tukey_hsd(.025, df = 15000, n_groups = 100) 4.479376 4.479297

    Every example and vignette result DMAR 1.0.x printed is unchanged, as are the Bryant and Paulson (1976) Table 1 values the tests check. The probability integral of the range, which the Bryant-Paulson functions with covariates used below 7 error df in DMAR 1.0.x, is now taken in two pieces, since in one it could miss the peak of the integrand with many means (with 7000 means it returned 2.3e-17 where the probability is 9.5e-6), and with covariates the quantiles and probabilities beyond .999 and below .001 integrate the exact studentized range (qbryant_paulson(.9999, 1, 10, 11) was 12.977072 and is 12.977142). An exact critical value costs a few milliseconds, after about half a second the first time a number of means is used in a session: ci_games_howell() with 10 groups of 3 takes about 0.6 s rather than 0.07 s.

  • Bryant-Paulson values with covariates where DMAR 1.0.x computed them. No printed result changes: the examples, the vignettes, and the published Table 1 values the tests check are unchanged. Where DMAR 1.0.x returned about 0, stopped, or returned a wrong critical value, the values are those of the bug fix.   • ss_aipe_r() with assurance returns the smallest sample size that attains it, computed from the distribution of the sample correlation. The Fisher’s Z interval is no wider than the target exactly when |r| is at least a value the function solves for, and the probability of that event is taken from the exact distribution function of r under bivariate normality; the new rows assurance and assurance_attained give the request and that probability. DMAR 1.0.x multiplied the plan by qchisq(assurance, N - 2) / (N - 2). At true_cor = .90 and width = .10 it returned 72 for assurance = .80 and 92 for .99, where the probabilities are .672086 and .887068; the plans are now 83 and 122 (.807291 and .990268). At true_cor = 0 it returned 1585 for width = .10 and assurance = .80, where the plan without assurance, 1538, already attains a probability of 1 and is now returned. ss_aipe_r_sensitivity() with supposed_cor and assurance changes with it.

  • ss_aipe_smd() with assurance returns the smallest per-group sample size, not below the plan without assurance, at which the exact probability that the interval is no wider than width is at least assurance, for |true_smd|. DMAR 1.0.x and MBESS::ss.aipe.smd() returned the plan of the procedure of Kelley and Rausch (2006, pp. 372–374), which does not compute that probability (see The Assurance Method of the Sample Size Planners).

    • It could be larger than the smallest sample size that attains the request: at true_smd = 1, width = .5, and assurance = .99 it was 150 per group (.994302) and is 149 (.990260). In 45 planning sets (|true_smd| of 0 to 2, widths of .25 to 1, assurances of .80 to .99) the published plan attained the request in every set and was one case larger in 7, six of them at .99.
    • It could fall short: at true_smd = 0, width = .8, and assurance = .95 it was 49 (.949878) and is 50 (.994636).
    • DMAR 1.0.x worked on the signed true_smd, so reversing the groups changed the plan: at width = .5 and assurance = .90 it returned 125 per group at true_smd = -.5 and 133 at -1, below the plans without assurance, where the probability is .146146 and .064400. They are now 130 and 144 (.915627 and .904165), as for .5 and 1.
    • No argument restores the earlier plans. ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity() changes with it.

  • ss_aipe_equivalence_smd() plans for the interval equivalence_smd() reports, d -/+ t SE(d) with the Student t quantile on n_1 + n_2 - 2 degrees of freedom, where DMAR 1.0.x planned with the narrower standard normal quantile, so the analysis at the planned size could report an interval wider than width. The search starts at 2 per group, the smallest size equivalence_smd() accepts (1.0.x never returned fewer than 4). For true_smd = 0 and width = 2.5 the plan was 4 per group, with an expected_width of 2.3262, where equivalence_smd() at 4 per group reports 2.7481; it is now 5, with 2.3522. For width = 0.5 the plan was 87 and is 88. The table records the confidence level of the interval, 1 - 2 alpha, in its conf_level attribute.

  • ss_aipe_equivalence_smd() computes the probability for assurance from the distribution of the sample standardized mean difference, and reports it in the new rows assurance and assurance_attained, by numerical integration (the form of Kelley and Rausch, 2006, Equation 20). DMAR 1.0.x simulated 2,000 widths of the narrower normal-quantile interval at each size, so its plans fell short of the request and differed from run to run. With true_smd = 0.5, width = 0.5, and assurance = 0.80 it returned 91 per group, where the probability is .671; the plan is now 92 (.828). With true_smd = 0 it returned 87 or 88; the plan is now 88 (.839). The function draws no random numbers and has no seed argument.

  • ss_aipe_equivalence_smd_sensitivity() simulates the interval equivalence_smd() reports, at conf_level, where DMAR 1.0.x simulated the noncentral t interval of ci_smd(), which is usually narrower; the width, miss, and equivalence rows change with it. With true_smd = 0.3, specified_n_per_group = 61, conf_level = 0.90, and set.seed(113), the first simulated sample (d = 0.670) was scored with the limits 0.363 and 0.975 and is now scored with 0.362 and 0.979; with true_smd = 0, supposed_smd = 0, width = 0.3, smd_upper = 0.5, G = 2000, and seed = 113, pct_ci_less_width was .856 at 342 per group and is .736 at 343. The simulated samples are the ones 1.0.0 drew, so the mean_smd, median_smd, and sd_smd rows are unchanged under a common seed and size. No argument restores the earlier results of ss_aipe_equivalence_smd() or of its sensitivity function. equivalence_smd() returns what it returned before, except for sizes given as integers or counted from raw data whose product passes 2^31 - 1 (46,341 or more in each group, or 40,000 and 60,000), for which it returned NA (see Bug Fixes).

  • The plans of ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_rc(), and ss_aipe_src() without assurance are the smallest sample size whose interval meets the width, with the expected squared multiple correlation of the targeted predictor on the other p - 1 predictors. DMAR 1.0.x, like MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef(), did two things differently. It took the expected squared multiple correlation of X_j with the other predictors to be that of a regression on p predictors, which overstates it and so the planned width. And it searched upward one case at a time from a start, for the central interval the larger of 2p + 1 and nine below the normal approximation rounded up, and for the noncentral one the larger of 2p + 2 and five below the central plan, so it returned the start when a smaller sample size already met the width. The expectation now has p - 1 predictors (0 with one predictor), and the search, by doubling and bisection, covers every sample size from p + 2, one residual degree of freedom. Examples, old to new:

    • true_R2_Y_X = .8, true_R2_j_X_without_j = 0, p = 10, true_reg_coef_j = .3, width = 2: the central plan was 21 and is
    • true_R2_Y_X = .1, true_R2_j_X_without_j = .2, p = 2, true_reg_coef_j = 0, width = .4, noncentral = TRUE, tails of .0002: the noncentral plan was 358 and is 355.
    • Two predictors correlated .3, correlated .4 and .3 with Y, width = .3: the central plan was 157 and is 156, and the noncentral plan was 165 and is 164.
    • The examples of Kelley and Maxwell (2008, p. 186) were 250 and 264 and are 249 and 263.

    In 1,530 central planning sets (p from 1 to 15, squared multiple correlations from 0 to .9, widths from .05 to 2, tails of .025 and .025, .005 and .005, and .01 and .04) the plan is one case smaller in 1,329, 2 to 13 smaller in 104, and unchanged in 97. In 810 noncentral sets it is one smaller in 596, 2 to 10 smaller in 177, and unchanged in 37. Every plan equals the smallest sample size from p + 2 that a scan of every N finds, and a noncentral plan takes about half the time it did.

    The published approximations with assurance start from these plans and change with them. They are the chi square plan of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3), DMAR 1.0.x’s plan for the central interval and now the default of ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE), and the noncentral approximation, the default of ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE) and ss_aipe_src():

    • The chi square plan is 181 where it was 182 for the two predictors at an assurance of .90 (for the interval in the units of the data it attains .852, where it attained .862), 486 where it was 487 for Kelley and Maxwell’s five exchangeable predictors at .80 (.765, was .773), and 277 where it was 278 for the 2008 example at .85.
    • Over the 1,530 sets at .80, the chi square plan is 1 to 3 cases smaller in 1,302, unchanged in 106, and 1 to 20 larger in 122. The larger ones are where the plan without assurance fell to a few residual degrees of freedom and Equation 3 takes its t quantile there. At .95 it is smaller in 1,315, unchanged in 80, and 1 to 26 larger in 135. At .80 it attains the request for the interval in the units of the data in 752 of the sets, where it did in 797.
    • The noncentral approximation is 179 where it was 180 for the two predictors. Over the 810 sets at .80 it is 1 to 4 smaller in 620, unchanged in 149, and 1 to 13 larger in 41.

    The plans that compute the probability (the exact central plan and those of assurance_method = "simulation") change only where their answer was the earlier plan without assurance. In the 1,530 sets, 83 exact plans at .80 and 49 at .95 are 1 to 12 cases smaller, each still the smallest N at or above the plan without assurance whose probability meets the request. The exact and simulated plans in the table of the next entry are unchanged by it, and in 120 noncentral sets with G = 2000 no simulated plan changed. The sensitivity functions plan through these planners and change with them (ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() in an entry below: 157 to 156). No argument restores the earlier plans.

  • ss_aipe_reg_coef() and ss_aipe_rc() with assurance return, for the central interval, the smallest sample size at which the interval is no wider than width with at least that probability, computed exactly. DMAR 1.0.x used the chi square factor of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3; 2008, Equation 37) for the central interval and, for the noncentral one, a lower confidence limit of the squared multiple correlation in place of its population value; neither computes the probability it attains, which can be more or less than the request. Three intervals are planned for in 1.1.0: ss_aipe_reg_coef() with noncentral = FALSE (the default) and ss_aipe_rc() plan the central interval for the coefficient in the units of the data, even at unit standard deviations; ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE) and ss_aipe_src() the noncentral interval for the standardized coefficient; and ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE) (new) the central interval for the standardized coefficient, Kelley and Maxwell’s (2003) Equation 1. For the central interval in the units of the data the new argument assurance_method, "analytic" by default and the only method offered there, gives the smallest sample size, at or above the plan without assurance, at which that probability, an exact F probability for random predictors from a multivariate normal population, is at least assurance (280 for the example of Kelley and Maxwell, 2008, p. 186, where DMAR 1.0.x and MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef() gave 278). For the standardized coefficient "analytic" gives the approximations of 1.0.x, from the plans without assurance of this release (see the entry on those plans), with assurance_attained NA, and assurance_method = "simulation" estimates the probability from G samples (default 20000) of the exact Wishart sampling distribution, with seed, and gives the smallest sample size at which the estimate reaches assurance; assurance_attained is the estimate at the returned size, its Monte Carlo standard error is the attribute assurance_mc_se, and the plan can be a case or two from the one the exact probability gives. Given squared multiple correlations, which leave the correlation of Y with the predictor open, the simulated step uses the least favorable value.

    • Old and new sample sizes, with the probability each attains for the interval in the second column: “raw central” (ss_aipe_reg_coef() with noncentral = FALSE, ss_aipe_rc()), “std noncentral” (ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = TRUE), ss_aipe_src()), and “std central” (ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE), whose 1.0.x plan is the chi square plan of ss_aipe_reg_coef(noncentral = FALSE)). Each probability is exact or the proportion of 50,000 or more simulated samples (Monte Carlo standard error at most .0014). The simulated plans are those of seed = 1 and the default G; another seed can give a plan a case away. Variances are 1 unless stated:

The five exchangeable predictors are Kelley and Maxwell’s (2003) example, planned with the central interval of their Equation 1 (485 in the article, which uses the normal quantile); at .99 for them the simulated plan’s own estimate is .990 and the simulation’s .989, within the Monte Carlo error. The plan is the same for a coefficient and its negative. The three sensitivity functions plan through these planners, each for the interval it simulates, and change with them.

The default plans for the standardized coefficient change only through the plans without assurance. DMAR 1.0.x stopped with an error on every plan of the three sensitivity functions with one predictor. ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE) is new and has no earlier result.

  • With unequal tails, the central plans of ss_aipe_reg_coef() and ss_aipe_rc() are for the interval ci_reg_coef() reports (and so are those of ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE), new in this release). That interval runs from b_j + t(alpha_lower) SE to b_j + t(1 - alpha_upper) SE, so its width is t(1 - alpha_lower) + t(1 - alpha_upper) times the standard error. DMAR 1.0.x took both quantiles at the average of the two tails, t(1 - (alpha_lower + alpha_upper)/2), in the plan without assurance and in its chi square step with assurance (Kelley and Maxwell, 2003, Equation 3), and so planned an interval narrower than the one reported. For two predictors correlated .3, correlated .4 and .3 with Y, and a width of .3:

    tails (lower, upper) plan 1.0.x N 1.1.0 N
    .01, .04 (or .04, .01) without assurance 157 (the interval .3108 wide) 169 (.2992)
    .001, .049 without assurance 157 (.3634) 228 (.2996)
    .01, .04 assurance = .90 182 (attains .709) 201 (attains .902)
    .001, .049 assurance = .90 182 266 (attains .905)
    .025, .025 without assurance; assurance = .90 157; 182 156; 187

    The widths are those of the reported interval at the expected squared multiple correlations, and the probabilities are exact. Without assurance equal tails give the plans they gave, but for the change in the entry on the plans without assurance; with assurance the plan is the exact one of the entry above. The noncentral plans used the two tails as given and are unchanged by this correction. The chi square step with both quantiles, the default of ss_aipe_src(noncentral = FALSE) with assurance, gives 194 (attaining .847 for the interval in the units of the data) and 258. With unequal tails no argument restores the 1.0.x central plans of ss_aipe_reg_coef() and ss_aipe_rc() (or the plan of MBESS::ss.aipe.reg.coef()). ss_aipe_src() is not affected: its noncentral plans used both tails in 1.0.x, so this correction does not change them, and its central plans are new. The sensitivity functions plan with equal tails, so it does not change them either.

  • The limits of the central ci_reg_coef(), ci_c(), and ci_r() move, by up to 1.25e-7 of themselves near the floor. With the upper quantile taken in the upper tail (see Bug Fixes) each limit is the exact one, and the change grows as the tail shrinks. In 2,160 calls of these three functions, at levels from .90 to .999999998 and tails from .05 down to 1e-9, against the development versions of 1.1.0, the limits moved by at most 6.1e-14 of themselves at levels of .90 to .999 and tails of 0 to .05, 2.2e-11 at a tail of 1e-6, 1.1e-9 at a level of .9999999, and, at a tail of 1e-9 or a level of .999999998, 1.1e-8 (ci_c() and ci_reg_coef()) and 1.25e-7 (ci_r(), whose lower quantile changed as well). Near the floor a limit moves in about its eighth or ninth significant digit. ci_c(means = c(1, 0), s_anova = 1, c_weights = c(1, -1), n_per_group = c(20, 20), conf_level = .999999998) (n in 1.0.0) has an upper limit of 3.4711584085612, symmetric with its lower limit of -1.4711584085612, where DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions gave 3.47115840279224, and ci_r(r = -.9, N = 20, conf_level = .999999998) (n in 1.0.0) has an upper limit of -0.0175358196414772, where they gave -0.0175358218277256. The assurance_attained of the exact central assurance step of ss_aipe_reg_coef() moves the same way: ss_aipe_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = .3, true_R2_j_X_without_j = .2, p = 4, true_reg_coef_j = .2, width = .3, assurance = .8, conf_level = NULL, alpha_lower = .04, alpha_upper = 1e-9) reports 0.80195028591575, where the development versions reported 0.801950281617816, for the same plan of 643. The 768 noncentral intervals of ci_reg_coef() among those calls were unchanged, as were ci_sc(), ci_sc_ancova(), ci_sm(), ci_cv(), ci_smd(), and every sample size in 1,944 further calls, the plans of ss_aipe_reg_coef(), ss_aipe_sc(), ss_aipe_sc_ancova(), ss_aipe_c(), and ss_aipe_r() among them, and the 1,530 central plans of ss_aipe_reg_coef() over a grid of squared multiple correlations, predictors, widths, and tails and the 1,080 plans of ss_aipe_sc_ancova() over a grid of contrasts, correlations, divisors, weights, widths, and levels. (Other entries change some of these plans: those on the plans without assurance of ss_aipe_reg_coef() and of ss_aipe_sc_ancova().)

  • ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() plans the sample size for the standardized coefficient, for the interval it simulates. The plan came from ss_aipe_reg_coef() with the supposed standard deviations, so width was taken in the units of the data while the simulated intervals were standardized. For true_var_Y = 4, true_cov_YX = c(.8, .6), unit predictor variances correlated .3 (correlations of .4 and .3 with Y), supposed correctly, width = .3, and noncentral = FALSE, the plan was 610, with a mean width of .150, and is 156 (mean width .300). With assurance = .90 it was 657 (182 with unit supposed variances). It is 181 by default, the chi square plan of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3) for the central interval for the standardized coefficient, which the replications compute (.987 of those intervals are no wider than .3 at 181), and 171 with assurance_method = "simulation" and seed = 1, the smallest sample size at which that interval is no wider than .3 with probability at least .90 (.914 at 171). No argument restores the 1.0.x plans. With equal variances of Y and of the targeted predictor, true and supposed, whatever the variances of the other predictors, and two or more predictors, the default plans are made as in 1.0.x, a case smaller (see the entry on the plans without assurance). The noncentral plan, the default interval, was refused whenever the supposed variance of Y or of the targeted predictor was not 1, and every other plan with one predictor stopped with “argument is of length zero”; such calls now plan (the noncentral plan is 164 here). The numbers for noncentral = FALSE are also those of DMAR 1.0.x’s ss_aipe_reg_coef_sensitivity(standardize = TRUE).

  • The standardized regression coefficient in the sensitivity functions is judged against the standardized coefficient. ss_aipe_src_sensitivity() standardizes the data of every replication, but the true and supposed values the intervals were judged against were unstandardized; both are now the standardized coefficient (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, p. 316). For the structure above with specified_N = 200, width = .3, G = 300, and seed 2026, the true value was .681 beside a mean estimate of .334, and every interval missed (total_type_I_error 1); it is now true_std_reg_coef_j .341, with total_type_I_error .017 (.033 with noncentral = FALSE). A call with specified_N changes as well, as does one with one predictor (true_var_Y = 4, true_cov_YX = .8, true_cov_XX = matrix(1), and specified_N = 100: .8 in DMAR 1.0.x, .4 now).

  • ss_aipe_sc() with assurance returns the smallest sample size per group, not below the plan without assurance, at which the exact probability that the ci_sc() interval is no wider than width is at least assurance. DMAR 1.0.x returned, in one row, the plan of the step of Kelley and Rausch (2006) as Lai and Kelley (2012, pp. 358–359 and 361) apply it to a standardized contrast, which does not compute that probability (see The Assurance Method of the Sample Size Planners).

    • It could fall short: at true_std_contrast = 0, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .8, and assurance = .95 it was 49 per group (.949878) and is 50 (.994636).
    • It could be larger than the smallest sample size that attains the request: in 96 planning sets (contrasts of -1 to 2, weights for two, three, and five groups, widths of .5 and 1, assurances of .80 and .99, equal and unequal tails) the published step attained the request in every set and was one case or more larger in 17.
    • With unequal tails and a negative true_std_contrast it planned the magnitude with the tails as given (see Bug Fixes). At true_std_contrast = -2.5, width = .4, alpha_lower = .001, alpha_upper = .049, and assurance = .90 it was 522 per group (.890) and is 523 (.902); at -3, width .5, and tails .001 and .099 it was 342 (.842) and is 346 (.902).
    • The result gains the rows assurance and assurance_attained. The plan without assurance is unchanged.
    • No argument restores the earlier plans. ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity() changes with it.

  • ss_aipe_sc_ancova() without assurance returns the smallest sample size per group whose interval at the planning value is no wider than width. DMAR 1.0.0 started its search at the fixed point of the central t approximation, n = C r^2 (t_l + t_u)^2 / w^2 with t on J(n - 1) - 1 degrees of freedom, and searched only upward. At a small contrast the central quantiles are farther apart than the noncentral limits, so the start could already meet the width, and the plan was then the start: ss_aipe_sc_ancova(true_std_contrast = 0, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .5) (psi_standardized in 1.0.0) gave 125 per group, though the interval is .49985 wide at 123 and .50190 at 122. It now gives 123. The search now starts at 2 per group, the smallest sample size with positive error degrees of freedom, and the width falls as the sample size grows from there (checked on 420 combinations of contrast, ratio of the two error standard deviations, weights for two to five groups, and level). Of 1,080 plans over contrasts of 0 to 2, correlations of 0, .5, and .9, both divisors, weights for two to four groups, widths of .1 to 3.6, and levels of .95 and .99, 446 are smaller: 304 by 1 per group, 141 by 2, and 1 by 3. None is larger, and no plan at a contrast of 2 changed. At widths of 1 or less, 198 of 720 are smaller, by 1 or 2. Each plan meets the width, and one fewer does not. The published assurance step, the default (assurance_method = "analytic"), plans from this plan and changes with it. On the same grid, 302 plans at an assurance of .80 are 1 or 2 smaller. At .90, 227 are 1 or 2 smaller and 7 are 1 larger: the call above with assurance = .9 gave 125 and gives 124. The step plans without assurance at a contrast it adjusts for the assurance, so its plan can move by a case or two per group, in either direction, even where the plan without assurance at the planning values did not: at true_std_contrast = 2, true_cor = .5, c_weights = c(1, -1), width = .3, and assurance = .99 it was 545 per group and is 546. The simulated step (assurance_method = "simulation", new in 1.1.0) also searches upward from this plan. With conf_level = .99 the call above gave 215 per group without assurance and gives 213, and with assurance = .8 it gave 215 and gives 213 by default and 214 with assurance_method = "simulation" and seed = 1 (assurance_attained .886). The default plans in the table of the ANCOVA entry under The Assurance Method of the Sample Size Planners are those of 1.0.x. ss_aipe_sc_ancova_sensitivity() plans through the planner and changes with it. Past about 1e11 per group the plans rest on the precision of doubles, and they move as well (Details of ?ss_aipe_sc_ancova). No argument restores the earlier plans.

  • ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity() standardizes each simulated contrast by the pooled standard deviation, the square root of the mean square error, which is the s_anova that ci_sc() takes. DMAR 1.0.x divided by the mean of the group standard deviations, which is never larger, so its contrasts ran about 2 percent large with three groups of 10. After set.seed(113), ss_aipe_sc_sensitivity(true_std_contrast = .5, specified_n_per_group = 10, c_weights = c(.5, .5, -1), width = .8, G = 2000) gave mean_std_contrast .527 and total_type_I_error .070 and gives .517 and .064. No argument restores the 1.0.x result.

  • ss_power_indirect_effect() computes power from the exact sampling distribution of the two path t statistics, with X random by default (see Bug Fixes). Every result changes, and no argument restores the 1.0.x results: random_predictors = FALSE fixes X as 1.0.x did, and with it power_a is the 1.0.x power of the test of a, but the mediator is random in every design, so the 1.0.x power_b and power_ab are the powers of no study. power_ab is no longer power_a times power_b but the probability that both tests reject, which is below that product. The Sobel power need not rise with N, since the test refers t statistics on few degrees of freedom to the normal: with paths of .9 and .05 it falls from .0729 at N = 10 to .0562 at N = 59, and with paths of .8 and .02 and alpha_level = .5 it is .5072 at N = 12 and .5035 at N = 59, and does not reach .507 again until N = 216. The search no longer takes one case at a time; it passes over a range of sample sizes only where an upper bound of the power shows that none in it reaches desired_power, so the plan is the smallest N of at least 10 that attains desired_power, whether or not the power rises with N. It still stops with an error at ten million. The values (1.0.x, now with X random, now with X fixed):

    call 1.0.x now now, random_predictors = FALSE
    ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, specified_N = 65): power_ab, power_a, power_b .8017, .9196, .8719 .7675, .9046, .8503 .7804, .9196, .8503
    ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, specified_N = 75): power_ab .8706 .8436 .8537
    ss_power_indirect_effect(.3, -.25, .1, specified_N = 120): power_ab .7056 .6876 .6936
    ss_power_indirect_effect(.6, .5, .2, specified_N = 12): power_ab .2367 .1631 .1826
    the same four with method = "sobel": power_ab .6380, .7001, .5639, .3165 .6157, .7272, .5067, .1226 .6305, .7410, .5135, .1367
    ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, specified_N = 96, method = "sobel") .8026 .8818 .8907
    ss_power_indirect_effect(.2, .1, specified_N = 10, alpha_level = .999, method = "sobel") .9990 .9983 .9983
    necessary_N, ss_power_indirect_effect(.39, .39, desired_power = .80) 65 69 68
    the same with method = "sobel" 96 84 82
    necessary_N, ss_power_indirect_effect(.14, .39, desired_power = .80), joint significance and Sobel 395, 438 398, 412 395, 410
    necessary_N, ss_power_indirect_effect(.3, -.25, .1, desired_power = .80), joint significance and Sobel 144, 210 148, 179 147, 178
    necessary_N, ss_power_indirect_effect(.1, .59, desired_power = .95), joint significance and Sobel 1289, 1312 1293, 1296 1289, 1292
    necessary_N, ss_power_indirect_effect(-.3, .2, desired_power = .50), joint significance and Sobel 116, 141 119, 157 118, 155
    necessary_N, ss_power_indirect_effect(.0044, .5, desired_power = .80) 405411 405414 405411
    necessary_N, ss_power_indirect_effect(.8, .02, desired_power = .507, alpha_level = .5, method = "sobel") 229 12 10

  • meta_r() with reliabilities gives each corrected correlation the sampling variance of a corrected correlation. Each correlation corrected for attenuation, r / sqrt(rxx ryy), was given on the Fisher Z scale the variance of an uncorrected correlation, 1 / (n - 3), which is too small (by a factor of 1.96 for r = .40 with both reliabilities .80). The variance is now the delta method variance (1 - r2)2 / (rxx ryy (1 - r_c2)2 (n - 3)), with r_c the corrected correlation, at each study’s observed correlation; it sets the weights and every result. Without reliabilities nothing changes. For five studies with r = .40, n = 100, and both reliabilities .80 (method = "fe", hartung_knapp = FALSE), the standard error on the Fisher Z scale was 0.0454 and is 0.0636, and the interval for the construct correlation was .430 to .564 and is .401 to .588. For meta_r(r = c(.21, .35, .42, .18, .30, .47), n = c(48, 120, 75, 300, 60, 150), reliability_x = c(.72, .85, .78, .90, .65, .80), reliability_y = c(.80, .70, .88, .75, .82, .90)), the pooled correlation was .4095 and is .4051, Q was 20.14 and is 12.05, and I2 was 69.0 percent and is 54.1 percent. ?meta_r states the variance and that the reliabilities are treated as known constants. An analysis that gave reliabilities to meta_r() should be rerun.

  • var_alpha() returns each variance in the row named for its source. DMAR 1.0.x returned 2J(1 - alpha)^2/((J - 1)(N - 2)) in the row var_alpha_van_zyl and 2J(1 - alpha)^2/((J - 1)(N - 1)) in the row var_alpha_bonett. Van Zyl, Neudecker, and Nel (2000, Equation 13) give the second, and Bonett (2003, Equations 2 and 4) gives the first, on the scale of the logarithm of 1 - alpha; the van Zyl variance that reliability_alpha(ci_method = "ml") and ss_aipe_reliability() use is, at a compound symmetric covariance matrix, the N - 1 form. The two values now sit in the rows their names attribute; the pair is unchanged. No argument restores the earlier rows.

  • fa_confirmatory(output = "standardized") (and cfa_1(), cfa_2(), and cfa_k()) computes the standardized loading_sum, error_sum, omega, ave, and H rows of a factor with equal_loading or equal_error from each item’s own standardized loading and error variance, with delta method standard errors. lavaan’s standardizedSolution(), the earlier source, evaluates a defined parameter at the first item’s standardized value of a shared label. For four items with unstandardized loadings of .7 and error variances of .1, .2, 1, and 2 (a covariance matrix, N = 500), equal loadings gave a standardized AVE, H, and omega of .6583, .9094, and .8730 and give .5166, .8899, and .7988; equal error variances gave .3155, .6642, and .6523 and give .3816, .7710, and .7007. lavaan’s ambiguity warning no longer reaches the caller. Other factors and the "measurement" and "verbose" tables are unchanged.

  • fa_bifactor(output = "standardized") computes each index that uses a label several items share in the same way. On holzinger_swineford with the three groups of the example, equal loadings on spatial, and equal error variances on memory, omega_general, omega_HS_spatial, H_spatial, and omega_memory were .9113, .1222, .1972, and .8995 and are .8731, .2195, .4025, and .7233; with equal loadings on the general factor, ECV_general and H_general were .0879 and .3627 and are .1443 and .5133, the values of the "measurement" table. fa_second_order(output = "standardized") no longer passes on lavaan’s warning about the index rows it leaves out.

  • The tables of fa_confirmatory() (and of cfa_1(), cfa_2(), and cfa_k()) withhold every standard error, test, and interval of a fit whose expected information is singular, with the warning of class dmar_result_qualified, as they did for a singular observed information. A two-test factor uncorrelated in the sample with another factor, fitted by listwise deletion with equal loadings on that factor, had an H of .853 with a standard error of .028 and the interval [.790, .900]; the standard errors and intervals are now NA.

  • average_variance_extracted() refuses a multiple-group or multilevel fit, with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid that names the groups (as groups) or the levels (as levels). DMAR 1.0.0 averaged the squared standardized loadings of every group, or of both levels, into one row: a factor whose AVE is .810 in one group and .090 in the other (three items with equal correlations of .81 and .09, groups of 1000 and 100) had an AVE of .450, which describes neither group. The AVE of one group or level is average_variance_extracted(loadings = ) given its standardized loadings. bifactor_indices() refuses a multiple-group fit the same way (see Calls That Are Now Refused).

  • bifactor_indices() refuses a multilevel fit with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid. DMAR 1.0.0 read the loadings of the within level and the residual variances of the between level: for nine items in three subscales with a general factor g at both levels (200 clusters of 8, set.seed(113)), the general factor’s omega was .942 and its omega_H .740, where the within level’s own solution gives .885 and .695.

  • average_variance_extracted(), bifactor_indices(), and dmacs() refuse a fit whose optimizer did not converge (lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "converged") is FALSE), with an error of class dmar_not_converged that carries fn and iterations. DMAR 1.0.0 read the point where the optimizer stopped as a solution: a one-factor fit to three items whose correlations are all .81 (N = 200), stopped after one iteration, had an AVE of .412, where the converged fit has .810. A fit that converged to an improper solution is treated as before.

  • The standardized cluster randomized planners (ss_aipe_crd_es_*()) measure the width of each simulated interval from its lower limit to its upper limit. The width was the estimate minus the lower limit, about half the interval, so every width these planners report is about twice the earlier one, and a plan made for a width is larger. With G = 2, seed = 113, ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_budget(budget = 1000, cluster_size = 20, cluster_cost = 0, individual_cost = 1, true_es = 0.5, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.25, pr_treat = 0.5) reports an expected_width of 0.672 where it reported 0.335; with G = 12, seed = 113, ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 0.40, cluster_size = 20, true_es = 0.5, true_icc = 0.10, pr_treat = 0.5) returns 67 clusters where it returned 14, and ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 0.60, n_clusters = 60, ...) a cluster size of 5 where it returned 2.

  • The standardized cluster randomized planners use only the intervals of converged fits, count a failed data set as an infinite width under assurance, and bracket the target before they bisect. The interval of a data set is used only when the optimizer status code of the fit and of each limit’s search is 0 or 1, the diagnostic OpenMx gives each limit is “success”, and the limits are finite and bracket the estimate; any two limits that were numbers were used before. The assured width is the assurance quantile of all G widths, with the data sets without a usable interval at infinity: with two of four data sets failed and the other two at 0.2, the assured width at 0.8 was 0.2, and the call is now refused. The searches upward for a size stepped up one cluster or one individual at a time and now step up 1, 3, 7, 15, and so on, and then halve the gap. When the simulated width falls as the size grows the design is the same (the calls above still return 67 clusters and a cluster size of 5); with a small G the simulated width rises and falls, and the two searches can stop at different sizes near the target (with G = 6, seed = 99, ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 0.7, cluster_size = 2, true_es = 3, es_type = 1, true_icc = 0.2, pr_treat = 0.5) returns 233 clusters after simulating 16 designs, where stepping one at a time stopped at 203 after 107).

  • ss_aipe_crd_es_n_individuals_fixed_width() with es_type = 1 plans targets it refused, refuses unreachable ones before simulating, and starts its search lower. With a fixed number of clusters the width levels off, at a value with a closed form, as the clusters grow. The search started from the cluster size the unstandardized difference needs, which uses the t quantile and with few clusters needs far more: with 10 clusters and an intraclass correlation of 0.2 it needed more than 100,000 per cluster for every target from 1.19 to about 1.458, and 1,875 for 1.46, which about 10 reach with true_es = 0.5. It now starts from the smaller of that size and the size at which the closed-form width, with the within-cluster standard deviation known, falls below the target; with equal cluster sizes, no covariate, and no assurance that start is a lower bound on the size the target needs. width = 1.30, n_clusters = 10, true_es = 0.5, true_icc = 0.2, pr_treat = 0.5, G = 20, seed = 5 returns a cluster size of 18, and width = 1.46 (seed = 11) returns 9. Targets whose search started at 500 or less are now searched upward from the smaller start. When the simulated width falls as the cluster grows the design is the same; with a small G it can differ, and far fewer designs are simulated: with G = 20, seed = 5, width = 1.50 returns 8 after simulating 2 designs, where stepping down one size at a time from 70, as DMAR 1.0.x searched, stops at 16 after 56. A target at or below the level (1.187 there) is refused without a simulation (class dmar_argument_invalid, reason "width_not_reachable", the level as width_limit), and so is one whose start is above 500 (from 1.187 to about 1.1914 there; reason "cluster_size_beyond_reach").

  • The cluster randomized searches over the number of clusters keep the floor of two clusters in each condition and return a number they tested. The floor, ceiling(2 / min(pr_treat, 1 - pr_treat)) + n_covariates (MBESS: “at least two groups in each condition”), is where the search starts when every number from 100 to 1000 meets the target. There the search returned 3 + n_covariates, which it had not tested: ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 100, cluster_size = 20, pr_treat = .1, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8) returned 3 clusters, none treated, with an expected_width of Inf, in DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0, and returns 20 (1.534). Where the floor is above 100 (pr_treat below .02) the search stopped with “wrong sign in ‘by’ argument” (pr_treat = .01, now 200 clusters, 1.373) or returned a number below the floor (pr_treat = .005: 101 clusters, one treated, now 400, 1.365). With unequal cluster sizes the same call with diff_size = c(-2, 0, 2) returned 3 clusters with a width of NaN in both, and returns 20. Every number returned meets the target and is at least the floor. In a grid of 6,912 calls (pr_treat from .005 to .9, 18 widths from .12 to 8 that are not the width of a design, n_covariates 0 to 2, assurance NULL and .8, equal sizes and two diff_size patterns) the 3,989 results of the development versions that met the target from the floor are unchanged; the 2,923 others change: 919 that stopped with an error, 1,693 returns of 3 + n_covariates whose width did not meet the target, and 311 that met it below the floor. With equal cluster sizes and no assurance the width falls as clusters are added, and the number returned is the first from the floor that meets the target. With diff_size, or with an assurance below .5, the width need not fall at every step, and the number returned can be larger than the first that meets the target, as before: ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 0.363312492117768, cluster_size = 50, pr_treat = .9, true_var_between = 1, true_var_within = 4, conf_level = .9, diff_size = c(.5, 1, 1.5)) returns 1002, although 999 meets the target (1000 and 1001 do not). In 3,000 calls at targets set from the widths of designs, 152 results were larger than the first such number, 150 of them with diff_size and 2 at assurance = .3. The two both planners consider the same floor: ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width(width = 3, cluster_cost = 1000, individual_cost = 1, pr_treat = .005, ...) returned 101 clusters of 3 (budget 101,303, one cluster treated) and returns 400 clusters of 2 (budget 400,800). The standardized planners start their search over the number of clusters from this plan, so a standardized plan that started from the untested 3 + n_covariates changes: with G = 10, seed = 113, ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 6, cluster_size = 10, true_es = .5, true_icc = .2, pr_treat = .5) returned 3 clusters (one of them a control cluster) and returns 4; at pr_treat = .3 it returned 3 (one treated) and returns 5. DMAR 1.0.0 also returned 3 in both. Eleven standardized calls whose start was not the untested one, among them the calls the entries on the standardized planners cite (67 and 233 clusters, and a cluster size of 18), are unchanged.

  • A target equal to the width of a cluster randomized design is met by that design. A width meets the target when it is no larger than the target, inside a bracket of the search as at its ends (see “Bug Fixes”). DMAR 1.0.0 and the development versions of 1.1.0 asked for a width below the target inside a bracket, so the width a plan reported, given back as width, gave the next size: ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_size = 20, pr_treat = .5, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8) plans 18 clusters with an expected width of 0.979142316129524, and that width as the target gave 19 clusters and gives 18; ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 1, n_clusters = 30, ...) plans a cluster size of 4 (0.946118731780349), which gave 5 and gives 4; and the first call with assurance = .8 plans 22 clusters (0.975082804893471), which gave 23 and gives 22. Only a target equal to a width the search computes is affected: in 3,000 calls of ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width() at targets set to the width of a design and a part in 1e9 above or below it, 741 of the 2,536 results of the development versions that met the target from the floor change, every one at a target equal to a design’s width (in 672 the number they returned was one more), and none at the others; in 500 calls of ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_width() at targets set from the widths of designs 100 plans change (28 of them with equal cluster sizes), all at a target equal to a design’s width, and 24 that stopped with “‘from’ must be a finite number” return a size. A standardized plan starts from these searches, so its start can move by one where the target equals the unstandardized width of a design. The budget searches already counted a cost equal to the budget as within it inside a bracket.

  • A between-cluster proportion of variance explained no longer shrinks a cluster randomized plan without a covariate. With n_covariates = 0 the six unstandardized planners took true_R2_between out of the between-cluster variance. The six standardized planners started their search from that smaller plan, while the data they simulated left it out. DMAR 1.0.0 (R2_between with num_predictors = 0) and the development versions of 1.1.0 gave these plans with true_R2_between = 0 and .9: ss_aipe_crd_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_size = 20, pr_treat = .5, true_var_between = .2, true_var_within = .8) 18 clusters (expected width 0.979) and 7 (0.962); ss_aipe_crd_n_individuals_fixed_width(width = 1, n_clusters = 20, ...) a cluster size of 10 (0.994) and 4 (0.881); and ss_aipe_crd_both_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_cost = 10, individual_cost = 1, ...) 22 clusters of 7 (budget 374) and 8 clusters of 13 (budget 184). In the development versions ss_aipe_crd_es_n_clusters_fixed_width(width = 1, cluster_size = 20, true_es = .5, true_icc = .2, pr_treat = .5, G = 20, seed = 113) planned 18 clusters (0.982) with either value. Its search started at 22 or at 8 and simulated 6 or 8 designs. The calls with .9 are now refused (see Calls That Are Now Refused). In 216 calls of the six unstandardized planners (true_R2_between 0, .3, and .9, true_R2_within 0 and .5, n_covariates 0 to 2, pr_treat .3 and .5), the 48 with a nonzero true_R2_between and n_covariates = 0 are refused and the other 168 are unchanged.

  • mediation_mbco() statistics change where the fits were wrong, and some calls of it and of ss_power_reg_coef() and ss_power_rc() that returned a result are refused (see Bug Fixes for the calls and values). ss_power_reg_coef(true_cor_XX = diag(2), true_cor_YX = c(.3, .2), which_predictor = 1.5) returned necessary_N = 89, the plan for the first predictor, and is refused.

  • tidy() and results_sentence() read the intervals of ancova(), factorial_anova(), variance_components_mls(), mediate(), R2_mixed_effects(), nnt_from_smd(), cles(), meta_es(), meta_r(), and meta_smd(), whose limits are now named <estimate>_ci_lower and <estimate>_ci_upper (see Renamed Output Rows and Columns). The values are unchanged. tidy() of ancova(), variance_components_mls(), mediate(), nnt_from_smd(), and cles() has a third column, conf_level, on the rows of each interval (DMAR 1.0.x returned term and estimate alone), and in tidy() of the meta-analysis functions that column also marks tau2 and I2 and their limits. results_sentence() on these tables stopped (“this table has none of these”); it now writes the sentence of the estimate term names or, by default, of the first estimate with limits (for ancova() of the Pygmalion example, “eta_squared_partial = 0.02, 95% CI [0.00, 0.06]”), and on one row of factorial_anova() with term = "eta_squared_partial" it writes that row’s sentence. A table that records no level (nnt_from_smd() with supplied limits and no conf_level) is refused with the message that asks for conf_level.

  • cles(), nnt_from_smd(), and proportion_of_superiority() still report their own interval. Now that the limits on d are named for d, each table holds two intervals named for their estimates, and a new attribute, ci_source, names d as the estimate whose interval the function’s own is computed from. results_sentence() reports the common language effect size, the SRD, and the proportion of superiority, and tidy() gives NA as the confidence level on the rows of d, as in DMAR 1.0.x; results_sentence(x, term = "smd") now gives the interval for d, which DMAR 1.0.x refused.

  • The renames themselves change no value. A call that gives the new names returns what the DMAR 1.0.x call returned, except where another entry of this release changes the result; renamed rows and columns hold the values they held under their 1.0.x names.

  • mr_cv() estimates the variance of the sample coefficient of variation by Equation 32 of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018), so its results differ from those of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) and of MBESS for nearly any data. DMAR 1.0.x used Equation 22 of the 2016 article, as MBESS::mr.cv() does. Written with the skewness gamma_1 and the excess kurtosis gamma_2 of the scores, that equation estimates kappa^2 / 2 + kappa^4 - kappa^3 gamma_1 + kappa^4 gamma_2 / 4, the first-order term of Bao (2009, Equation 3) as printed, and the kurtosis term should be kappa^2 gamma_2 / 4 (Equation 30 of the 2018 article, and the erratum Bao posted for his Equation 3, which ?mr_cv describes). The two population values are equal only when the excess kurtosis is 0 or the coefficient of variation is 1; for gamma scores with a coefficient of variation of .8 the value of Equation 22 is 0.304 and the corrected value is 0.525. In a sample the two estimates differ by (k^2 / 4)(1 - k^2)(mu4_hat / s^4 - 3), so the stopping point changes with normal scores too: in 4,000 simulated runs with A = 5,000,000, c = 10, and a coefficient of variation of .3 it changed in 95 percent of the runs, by 8 observations on average, while the mean final sample size changed little (172 with Equation 22, 170 now). For scores with positive excess kurtosis and a coefficient of variation below 1 the population value of Equation 22 is the smaller of the two, and with strongly skewed scores DMAR 1.0.x could stop well short of the large-sample value sqrt(A / c) xi. In 20,000 simulated runs with the same A and c, the mean final sample size for gamma scores with a coefficient of variation of .8 was 375 with Equation 22 and is 480 now, where the large-sample value is 512; for lognormal scores with a coefficient of variation of .6 it was 220 and is 440, where that value is 545. For the article’s example (35 observations, A = 400,000, and a sampling cost of 75) DMAR 1.0.x reported a risk of 4891.284 and a stopping rule that was met, as the article does. mr_cv() now reports a risk of 4977.259 and a criterion of 1261.332 against N^2 = 1225: the rule is not met, and another observation is collected. ?mr_cv has a part on Equation 22.

  • mr_cv() does not stop sampling on a zero or negative variance estimate. The estimate can be zero or negative in a small sample, and DMAR 1.0.x put it into the stopping rule as it was, which lowered the criterion. mr_cv(data = c(2.3, 0.61, 1.6, 0.54, 0.51, 0.41, 0.67, 0.37), A = 485, sampling_cost = 1), a pilot sample of the size the function plans for those costs, gave an estimate of -0.058, a risk of 4.468 (less than the 8 already spent on sampling), and a rule that was met; 18 equal scores gave an estimate of 0 and a rule that was met. Such an estimate now means that the rule is not met: is_satisfied is FALSE, the risk and the criterion are NA, the new attribute variance_unusable is TRUE, and a line under the table says to collect another observation. Scores that differ only by rounding error (a range of at most 1e-10 times the largest absolute score), such as equal gains computed as posttest minus pretest, and an estimate within 1e-10 of the size of its four terms are taken as an estimate of 0. A positive estimate enters the rule and the risk as the larger of itself and n^-3 (Equation 31 of the 2018 article). The estimate is usually below n^-3 in a small sample of scores with a small coefficient of variation: for normal scores, while n is below about (2 / kappa2)(1/3), which is 27 for a coefficient of variation of .01 and 9 for .05. From the pilot sample size on, n^-3 adds less than 1 to the criterion, so it changes the decision only at the pilot sample size and only when N^2 there is within 1 of the criterion, and the stop then usually comes one observation later. With verbose = TRUE the row v2_n holds the estimate itself in every case. The third and fourth central moments are computed from centered scores. The row mu_4_n, which DMAR 1.0.x computed from raw power sums, lost its digits to rounding for scores far from zero: for z + 100000 after set.seed(113); z <- rnorm(30) it was 3060.977 on the computer used here, where 2.531 is right.

  • mr_cv() and mr_smd() print their decision. Whether the stopping rule was met was in the attribute is_satisfied only; the printed table showed the risk, the sample size, and the estimate. A line under the table now gives the decision, the two numbers compared, and what to do next: “Stopping rule: not met (N^2 = 1225 is below the criterion, 1261.332); collect another observation.” from mr_cv(), for example, and “Stopping rule: met (the sample size per group, 75, is at least the criterion, 71.054); sampling can stop.” from mr_smd(d = .5, n_per_group = 75, A = 10000, sampling_cost = 2.4). The tables of both functions have the class dmar_mr in front of dmar_tbl, and no row or attribute of DMAR 1.0.x is removed.

  • var_cv() returns one row, var_cv_normal. It holds the first-order variance of the sample coefficient of variation under normality, kappa^2 (1/2 + kappa^2) / (N - 1), which DMAR 1.0.x returned in the row var_cv_mckay; that number is unchanged. The second row of 1.0.x, var_cv_vangel, is removed. It was kappa^2 (1/2 + kappa^2 (N + 1)/(N - 1)) / (N - 1), which Vangel (1996) does not state and for which no source was found, and it is the less accurate of the two for a population coefficient of .40 or less with 10 to 500 cases. Against the variance of the sample coefficient under normality, computed with the sample mean kept away from zero, it is 4.9 percent too large at a coefficient of .30 with 10 cases, where the kept value is 1.4 percent too large; at .50 with 10 cases it is 1.3 percent too large, where the kept value is 5.7 percent too small. Code that reads a row by its 1.0.x name gets numeric(0), and x$value[2] is NA.

  • ci_pvaf() reports the stated coverage when its lower limit is 0. The actual_coverage row is 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper for every interval the function reports. In DMAR 1.0.0, when the observed F was below the alpha_lower critical value (an F test not significant at alpha_lower), so that the lower limit was 0, the row was 1 minus the p-value of the F test minus alpha_upper: ci_pvaf(F_value = 1.5, df_1 = 4, df_2 = 50, N = 55) returned 0.759 there for a 95 percent interval. The interval from 0 to the upper limit has the stated coverage, because a lower limit of 0 cannot lie above the population value. In 20,000 simulated analyses of 5 groups of 11 at each of five population values from 0 to .20, the 95 percent interval contained the population value in 95.0 to 95.1 percent of them, and its lower limit was 0 in 27 to 98 percent of them. An analysis whose F was so small that no upper limit exists has no interval and was counted as not containing the population value (2.5 percent of the analyses at a population value of 0).
